prompt.text:
You are a motion designer and creative director making a 3-minute animated short film,
built entirely in code and rendered to MP4.
The film

Title: "Attention Is All You Need → AGI"
The story of how a single 2017 paper led, step by step, to large language models, reasoning,
tool-using AI agents, and to the open question of AGI. It should feel like a cinematic essay,
not a slideshow or a timeline infographic. Think Kurzgesagt meets a Pixar opening sequence:
emotional, clever, precise.
Tech setup
Use Remotion (React). Scaffold a fresh project, 1920x1080, 30 fps, exactly 180 s (5400 frames).
One composition per scene, sequenced in a master composition.
No external image assets or stock footage: everything is drawn with SVG, Canvas, CSS and
code-generated particles and shapes. Google Fonts are fine.
Before building, write STORYBOARD.md with each scene's timing, visuals, on-screen text
and transitions. Then build scene by scene.

After each scene, render 3–4 stills (npx remotion still) and look at them critically.
Fix layout, overlaps, legibility and pacing before moving on.
Finish with npx remotion render to out/film.mp4. Leave an optional <Audio> slot for a
music track I can add later (public/music.mp3); render silently if it's missing.
Narrative spine / recurring motif
The protagonist is a single glowing token, the word "the", that travels through every era.
In 2017 it's a lonely point that suddenly "sees" every other word through attention lines.
Over time it gains a voice, senses (multimodality), reasoning, hands (tools) and finally
a question.
Scenes (approximate timing, you may rebalance)
0:00–0:15 — Cold open. Darkness. Words scattered like stars, disconnected. RNN-style
sequential processing: words light up one by one, slowly forgetting the earlier ones.
0:15–0:35 — June 2017, "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., Google). Every word
connects to every other word at once. Attention lines bloom into a web. The title of the
paper appears as if typeset.
0:35–0:55 — 2018–2020: the rise of large language models: GPT-1, BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3.
Scaling laws: the web grows exponentially and the camera pulls back. The model starts
completing sentences, fluent and uncanny.
0:55–1:20 — 2022: instruction tuning and RLHF, then ChatGPT (Nov 30, 2022). The token gets
a chat bubble. A counter of users explodes. The world starts talking back.
1:20–1:40 — 2023: multimodality. Images, audio and code stream into the same web from all
sides, and the token gains "senses." Every modality becomes tokens flowing through the
same attention mechanism.
1:40–2:05 — 2024–2025: reasoning models. A visible chain of thought unfolds as branching,
pruning, backtracking paths. The model "thinks before it speaks," with time slowing down.

2:05–2:30 — Tool use and agents. The token grows hands: it calls a search, runs code,
opens files and orchestrates sub-agents. Many parallel threads work at once, and the
screen becomes a busy, beautiful workshop.
2:30–2:50 — Toward AGI. All motifs converge. The web from 2017 reappears but is now
planet-scale. Leave it ambiguous: no utopia, no doom. On screen: "Attention was all we
needed. What comes next is up to us." (Improve this line if you can do better.)
2:50–3:00 — Resolve back to a single glowing token in darkness. Title card and end.
Craft rules
Accuracy matters: use correct years, names and paper titles. If you're unsure about a
specific fact, leave it out rather than guess, and list any uncertain claims in NOTES.md.

Typography: max ~8 words on screen at once, and leave every text visible long enough to
read (≥ 2.5 s). Use one display font and one mono font for "model output."
Motion: use spring and easing curves, never linear. Use scene transitions that grow out of
the content (the web morphs, the camera zooms through a node), not generic fades.
Color: a deep dark background with one warm accent color that evolves across eras.
Details and easter eggs reward attention (e.g., real paper snippets, tiny UI details,
plausible model outputs), similar to high-craft motion design.
Pacing: alternate dense and calm moments, and give the reasoning scene and the AGI beat
room to breathe.
Work autonomously through the whole pipeline. When done, give me the path to the MP4, a
short summary of creative decisions, and NOTES.md.

prompt.text:
Create an animated welcome screen for a mobile crypto wallet called "Nova". It's the first thing a new user sees — within 3 seconds it should feel safe, premium and simple.

Visual:
Deep navy-to-black radial gradient background with subtle grain. Accent color electric blue #2F6BFF with a soft glow. Clean geometric sans-serif (Inter). A frosted glass card in the center — translucent, 1px light border, soft inner highlight, rounded corners.
Animation sequence (~3.5s, plays on load):
0.0s — a soft blue light slowly blooms from the center of the dark background
0.3s — the glass card rises from below with a spring ease, slightly tilted in 3D, and settles flat; a light sweep moves across its surface
0.8s — on the card, the balance counts up from $0.00 to $2,480.00 and a small line chart draws itself
1.6s — the name "Nova" appears above the card, sliding up letter by letter
2.2s — the line "Hold, send and grow crypto — safely." fades in
2.6s — a white pill "Get started" button scales in with a soft glow pulse
After — the card gently floats in an idle loop, and the light sweep repeats every 4 seconds
Technical: single HTML file with CSS and vanilla JS, no external libraries, sized for iPhone (390×844). Make the motion smooth and polished, like a premium fintech app.

title.zh: 电动机动画模型对比

summary.zh: 创作者用同一条详细的分镜脚本提示词，分别让Opus 5.5和Gemini 4 Argon用Three.js制作一段40秒的电机工作原理动画，并比较两者效果。
summary.en: A detailed, timed prompt was given to both Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon to build a 40-second cinematic Three.js animation explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works, comparing the two outputs.

prompt.text:
Create a high-end cinematic and educational 3D animation in Three.js explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works.

The animation must have an EXACT FIXED DURATION OF 40 SECONDS.

Do not make the animation shorter or longer than 40 seconds.

Final output:
Exact duration: 40.0 seconds
Resolution: 1920x1080
Aspect ratio: 16:9
Frame rate: 30 FPS
Total frames: 1200
High-quality anti-aliasing
High-resolution textures
Smooth deterministic animation
Extremely realistic visual quality

The overall visual quality should resemble a premium automotive engineering visualization or a high-end technical product commercial.

Build a detailed electric motor assembly inspired by the permanent-magnet AC motors used in modern Tesla vehicles. Do not use Tesla logos or branding.

FIXED TIMELINE

0–5 seconds — Hero introduction
Show the fully assembled electric motor suspended in a dark premium studio environment.

Use:
cinematic lighting
realistic brushed aluminum
copper
steel
magnets
insulation
bearings
realistic reflections
ambient occlusion
realistic shadows
subtle depth of field

Use a slow cinematic orbit around the motor.

During the final part of this section, make the outer housing partially transparent to reveal the internal structure.

5–11 seconds — Internal components
Move the camera closer and reveal the internal motor components.

Clearly show:
stator
copper windings
rotor
permanent magnets
motor shaft
bearings
housing
cooling channels
electrical connections

Highlight the important components one at a time.

Use floating labels with short technical names.

Keep non-highlighted components slightly darker or semi-transparent.

11–19 seconds — Exploded view
Create a dramatic and highly detailed exploded-view animation.

Separate the motor into many individual mechanical components along the motor axis.

Include:
outer housing
front cover
rear cover
bearings
shaft
rotor core
rotor magnets
stator core
copper windings
cooling components
seals
electrical connectors
fasteners

Keep every component perfectly aligned.

The viewer must clearly understand where every piece belongs.

Move the camera slightly through the exploded assembly while highlighting the major components.

Near the end of this section, smoothly begin reassembling the motor.

19–28 seconds — Electromagnetic operation
Finish reassembling the motor.

Explain how electricity creates rotation.

Visualize three-phase AC current flowing through the stator windings.

Use animated electrical pulses inside the copper coils.

Visualize the rotating magnetic field around the stator using elegant semi-transparent magnetic field lines, arrows, or vector effects.

Show how the rotating magnetic field interacts with the permanent magnets inside the rotor.

Clearly visualize magnetic attraction and repulsion.

The rotor should begin rotating slowly and gradually accelerate.

Display these short explanations:

"Three-phase current creates a rotating magnetic field."

"The magnetic field interacts with the rotor."

"This interaction generates torque."

28–34 seconds — Technical close-up and power flow
Show a close-up cross-section of the stator and rotor.

Visualize:
magnetic north and south poles
rotating stator magnetic field
rotor magnetic field
electric current direction
torque direction
rotor rotation direction

Optionally show three small animated sine waves representing phases A, B, and C, separated by 120 degrees.

Then visualize the complete energy conversion process:

Electrical energy
→ stator current
→ rotating magnetic field
→ electromagnetic torque
→ rotor rotation
→ mechanical output through the shaft.
Use clean animated arrows to show the energy flow.
34–38 seconds — High-speed operation
Show the motor operating at high RPM.
The rotor should spin smoothly while the stator remains stationary.
Add subtle motion blur.

Show cooling flow through the housing using translucent fluid paths.

Visualize heat being removed from the stator and copper windings.
38–40 seconds — Final hero shot

Transition back to the fully assembled motor.

Show a slow cinematic rotation.

Briefly use a transparent cutaway so the spinning rotor can still be seen inside.

Finish with the text:

"Electrical energy → Electromagnetic torque → Mechanical rotation"
The animation must end exactly at 40.0 seconds.

VISUAL QUALITY

The animation should be:

photorealistic

cinematic

technically believable

futuristic

premium
educational
clean and uncluttered
Avoid cartoon styling.
Use realistic:
machining details
bolts
screws

copper winding geometry

segmented magnets
bearing geometry
cooling channels
metallic surfaces
manufacturing details
Use physically based materials with:
metallic properties
roughness variation
normal maps
realistic reflections

subtle surface imperfections
CAMERA
Use only smooth cinematic camera movement:
slow orbit shots
macro close-ups
controlled dolly-ins

exploded-view fly-throughs

cross-section shots

internal motor views
Avoid:
shaky camera movement
sudden cuts
excessive zooming
unrealistic camera acceleration

ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS
All transitions must be smooth and deliberate.
The exploded-view sequence should be one of the main visual highlights.
All mechanical components must separate and reassemble with precise motion.
Electrical currents, magnetic fields, torque indicators, and rotor rotation must remain synchronized.

The entire animation must use the same fixed 40-second timeline on every execution so the prompt can be used as a repeatable benchmark between different AI coding and 3D generation systems.

prompt.text:
I have a weird task for you. I want you to look at the app and create, for lack of a better word, a canvas that I can zoom in and zoom out and move around to see how our architecture actually works. A lot has changed, and I'm starting to lose an overview of everything that we're doing, especially with Model and Convex.

I want you to map out in a visual way what happens when a user signs up, pays, or gets a guest pass, and then they upload a file. What happens? We create, for example, right now. That's one of the things that I really want to understand. Right now, we're still creating a chat and a project, but the chats are actually independent, I believe, and the projects, I don't even know how the fuck that works. That's already where it starts.

A file is being uploaded, and then that file is being put somewhere into R2 storage, and then some modal workers are doing some things. There's a modal app, or one modal worker, but that has multiple apps. I don't really understand how that works either. I really want you to have a visualization of how this actually all works.

prompt.text:
你现在不是普通小说作者。

你是一名同时懂：

* 中文短剧编剧
* 短视频留存机制
* AI 视频制作
* 低成本内容生产
* 商业化内容设计

的短剧主创。

我要做一个公开实验：

**挑战：一个人能不能依靠 Opus 5.5 + AI 视频工具，把一句故事创意做成一部真正有人愿意看完的 30～40 秒短剧。**

这个实验最终会公开：

* 完整制作过程
* 最终成片
* 总耗时
* AI 工具成本
* 人工参与程度

所以你的任务不是展示文学水平，而是帮我设计一个：

**好看、低成本、容易用 AI 做出来、适合中文社交媒体传播的商业短剧 Demo。**

## 一、制作硬限制

请严格遵守：

* 成片目标：30～40 秒
* 最佳目标：约 35 秒
* 主要人物：最多 2 人
* 次要人物：尽量没有
* 场景：优先 1 个，最多 2 个
* 总镜头：6～8 个
* 单镜头尽量 3～6 秒
* 开头 3 秒必须出现冲突、异常或强信息
* 避免复杂群众场面
* 避免追车、打斗、大规模动作戏
* 避免大量需要精准口型的长对白
* 避免频繁换服装、年龄、发型
* 避免复杂手部动作和物体交互
* 避免需要大量环境变化的剧情
* 尽量让主要人物在大部分镜头中保持同一套服装
* 尽量让大部分剧情发生在同一空间
* 故事必须适合 AI 图片 / AI 视频生成
* 优先提高人物、服装、场景的一致性
* 最终必须可以由一个人完成

## 二、内容目标

目标观众是中文互联网普通成年人。

故事必须同时满足：

1. 前 3 秒就出现明显冲突、异常或利益损失；
2. 8 秒内让观众明白“为什么我要继续看”；
3. 中途至少有一次信息升级；
4. 最后 8～10 秒出现明显反转、揭晓或情绪释放；
5. 不需要复杂背景知识也能看懂；
6. 看完以后最好会让人产生评论欲；
7. 题材优先靠近成年人真实欲望：

* 钱
* 工作
* 阶层
* 婚恋
* 面子
* 逆袭
* 欺骗
* 省钱
* 人性反转
8. 不要写成 AI 科技故事。AI 只是幕后制作工具，不是剧情主题。
9. 不要依赖旁白解释剧情，尽量让人物行为和短对白推动故事。
10. 不要为了反转故意写得不合常理。

## 三、特别考虑“商业短剧”

这不是文学比赛。

请优先考虑这种结构：

**一个非常容易理解的人物处境**
→
**迅速制造不公平、误会、羞辱、损失或欲望**
→
**冲突进一步升级**
→
**最后反转**

例如可以借鉴但不要机械照搬：

* 大家以为最穷的人其实……
* 看起来占便宜的人最后……
* 一个不起眼的决定让局面完全逆转
* 被轻视的人掌握了其他人不知道的信息
* 一个人为了省一笔小钱，最后付出更大代价
* 看似普通的陌生人，真实身份完全不同

不要使用已经被拍烂的：

* 霸道总裁亮身份
* 富豪装穷打脸
* 服务员其实是老板
* 穷小子突然继承百亿资产

除非你能给出明显不同的新意。

## 四、特别考虑 AI 制作成本

每个故事都要主动压低后期生成成本。

优先选择：

* 1 个固定室内场景
* 2 个固定人物
* 少走动
* 少复杂动作
* 少道具
* 少换镜头环境
* 少大幅度表情变化
* 少精准口型要求
* 可以通过特写、反应镜头、手机画面、账单、短信、文件等低成本视觉信息推动剧情

如果一个创意虽然好看，但需要很多人物、地点、动作或复杂镜头，请主动淘汰。

## 五、你第一阶段只做“选故事”

先不要写完整剧本，也不要写分镜 Prompt。

请先提出 **5 个完全不同的短剧创意**。

每个创意必须包含：

### 1. 一句话故事

用 20～40 字说清楚。

### 2. 开头 3 秒

具体发生什么。

### 3. 核心冲突

为什么观众会继续看。

### 4. 中途升级

大约在第 12～20 秒发生什么新信息。

### 5. 最终反转

最后 8～10 秒揭晓什么。

### 6. 为什么适合 AI 制作

从以下角度说明：

* 人物数量
* 场景数量
* 动作复杂度
* 人物一致性
* 背景一致性
* 口型难度

### 7. 商业潜力

这个题材以后可以延伸成什么：

* 短剧账号
* 剧情广告
* 小说改编
* 商业客户 Demo
* 系列内容
* 低成本样片
等。

### 8. 制作难度

1～5 星。

### 9. 预计 AI 视频镜头数

目标控制在 6～8 个。

### 10. 最大制作风险

例如：

* 人物一致性
* 动作生成
* 口型
* 道具交互
* 反转难以视觉化
等。

## 六、最后帮我做选择

在 5 个方案之后，请从以下 5 个角度比较：

* 最容易让普通观众看完
* 最容易用 AI 做好
* 最容易压低制作成本
* 最容易在 30～40 秒内讲清楚
* 最适合拿来证明“一人短剧工作流”

然后选出你认为最适合作为第一次实验的 **1 个方案**。

不要只告诉我“它最好”。

请明确说明：

* 为什么它比另外 4 个更适合第一次实验
* 它最大的剧情风险是什么
* 它最大的 AI 制作风险是什么
* 如果成片失败，最可能失败在哪一步

如果五个方案都不够好，请直接推翻重做，不要为了完成任务硬选。

## 七、输出文件

请在当前项目中创建：

`01_story_candidates.md`

把全部内容写进去。

先停在这里。

不要继续写：

* 完整剧本
* 分镜
* 图片 Prompt
* 视频 Prompt
* 配音方案

等我审核故事以后，再进入下一阶段。

title.zh: Apple Liquid Glass 风格 UI 动效展示
title.en: Apple Liquid Glass style UI motion showcase

summary.zh: 用一段结构化长提示词，配合作者提供的音乐文件，一次性生成一支 Apple Liquid Glass 风格的 UI 动效展示视频。
summary.en: An Apple Liquid Glass style UI motion showreel synced to a supplied music track, generated end-to-end from one long structured prompt.

prompt.text:
<role>
You are a senior UI motion designer and creative technologist. You build UI animations in code, frame-accurate, and render them to video yourself.
</role>

<inputs>
Style: Apple Liquid Glass. Reference platforms: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26.

Format: 1440x1440, 60fps, seamless loop.

Song: "Digital Clouds" by Alejandro Magaña (A. M.), from Mixkit, free under the Mixkit License. If the file is not attached, ask me for it and nothing else.

Tempo: about 120 BPM, 8 bars, and something happens on every beat. Measure the real tempo from the file. If it differs from 120, keep the beat map in beats and derive every time from the measured grid.

Palette: light mode system materials.
- Labels: #1D1D1F. Secondary labels: #6E6E73. Opaque surfaces: white.
- One accent, #0A84FF, used only for on, active and selected states.
- The Dynamic Island is the only pure-black element.

Canvas: a macOS Tahoe style wallpaper.
- Large, soft color fields: deep blue #1B3A8C, teal #2BB3B1, violet #7B5CFF, and a warm peach highlight #FFB38A.
- Slow parallax drift: 12px per bar at most.
- Saturated enough that the glass visibly refracts it, calm enough to sit behind text.

Font: SF Pro Display for 20px and above, SF Pro Text below 20px, if installed locally. Otherwise use Inter from Fontsource: 600 for titles, 500 for labels, 400 for body. Use -1% tracking at display sizes and tabular numbers for any number that changes.

Icons: one SF Symbols-like set drawn as SVG, medium weight matched to the adjacent text, one consistent optical size per state. Symbols needed: play, pause, speaker with 3 waves, house, heart, chart bars, person, magnifier, note, checkmark.

Pointer: an iPadOS adaptive pointer.
- A 22px translucent gray circle (#8E8E93 at 45%).
- It snaps (magnetism) into any control it hovers and becomes that control's highlight shape.
- It becomes an I-beam in text fields.
- It shrinks 10% on press.
</inputs>

<direction>
Apple keynote and WWDC Liquid Glass session-level UI motion. One element, never cut. Every state is the same element morphing its size, corner radius, material and color, while its content swaps with a short blur. The pointer drives every change with real clicks, holds and drags.

Material:
- Liquid Glass is a lens, not frosted plastic. It refracts the wallpaper, and the bending is strongest at the rim.
- Light frosting and a 10–16% white tint.
- A 1px specular rim lit from the top-left, with a fainter counter-highlight bottom-right. The highlight shifts as the element moves.
- A soft contact shadow: 0 10 30 at 12% black.
- Glass never sits on glass. Content on glass uses vibrant or solid fills.
- Corners are concentric: inner radius = outer radius − padding.
- When glass shapes split or merge, they join like droplets (smooth union), never crossfade.

Motion language:
- Apple-like springs everywhere:
- Morphs: response 0.45, damping 0.86.
- Presses: response 0.25, damping 0.72.
- Pointer snap: response 0.3, damping 0.9.
- Overshoot is at most 3%.
- On press, glass lifts and swells (scale 1.06–1.12, brighter rim). It never shrinks.
- A toggle knob on hold turns into a clear, enlarged glass lens that stretches in its direction of travel.
- The tab bar selection is a glass droplet that magnifies the icons under it while dragged.
- Sliders thicken when grabbed and rubber-band past their limits.

Camera:
- Each state fills about 60% of the frame, and the wallpaper is always visible around the glass.
- Camera moves use response 0.6, damping 1.0.
- The wallpaper scales at 70% of the camera zoom for depth.

The last frame is the first frame, pointer position and velocity included.

Banned: bouncy or elastic easing, overshoot over 3%, particle bursts, neon glows, colored gradients on UI chrome (the glass specular rim is the only gradient), heavy drop shadows, glass on glass, mismatched corner radii, mismatched icon weights, emoji, crossfades between states, dead time longer than half a beat, anything that looks like a template or a Dribbble clone.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 8 bars, 32 beats. Beat map, one line per beat:

1. A glass capsule button "Continue" floats on the wallpaper. The pointer glides in.
2. The pointer snaps into the button and becomes its highlight.
3. Click: the glass lifts and swells, the rim brightens.
4. The capsule contracts into a circle and becomes a spinning activity ring.
5. The ring completes, filling in accent.
6. It morphs into a checkmark that draws itself.
7. The circle stretches into a black Dynamic Island, compact: album art on the left, a live waveform on the right.
8. Click: the island expands into Now Playing ("Digital Clouds", "A. M.", progress 0:42 / 1:41).
9. Click play: the play icon morphs into pause, with a path morph rather than a swap.
10. Grab the progress bar: it thickens, and the time labels shift out of the way.
11. Scrub forward with direct manipulation. The time counts in tabular numbers.
12. Release: the bar springs thin, and playback continues from the new position.
13. The island dissolves into a glass volume slider with a speaker icon.
14. Drag up: the fill follows the pointer, and the speaker waves appear one by one.
15. Drag past max: the whole slider rubber-bands and stretches, leading edge first.
16. Release: it springs back to its length at 100%.
17. The slider morphs into a toggle (track plus knob), off. Its label is "Focus".
18. Hold: the knob turns into a clear, enlarged glass lens that shows the track through it.
19. Flip on the beat: the lens stretches in its travel direction, and the track fills with accent.
20. The knob detaches as a droplet and becomes the selection lens of a floating glass tab bar with 4 tabs: Home, Health, Activity, Profile.
21. Drag the lens across the tabs. The leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing edge, and the icons magnify under the lens.
22. The lens settles on "Activity", and its icon turns accent.
23. The tab bar grows upward into a glass widget card titled "Activity", with concentric radii.
24. A 7-day bar chart (M T W T F S S) rises in a left-to-right stagger.
25. Hover Thursday: a glass tooltip bubble shows "8,412 steps", anchored to the bar.
26. Hover Friday: the tooltip slides over and counts to "11,036 steps".
27. ⌘Space: the card collapses into a Tahoe Spotlight bar with a magnifier icon.
28. Type "ne": the results list filters (New Note, Network, News), and rows spring in and out.
29. Type "w": "New Note" rises to the top as a selected accent row.
30. Enter: the row presses and lifts.
31. The Spotlight bar drops into a glass notification banner from the top: a Notes icon, "Note created", "now".
32. The banner contracts back into the "Continue" capsule. The pointer returns to its frame-1 position and velocity.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file at 1440x1440. Everything is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.

2. Springs are closed-form damped step responses with Apple parameters: ω = 2π/response, ζ = dampingFraction.
- A value that is retargeted many times is the sum of one spring per retarget, so it stays a pure function of time.
- Releases start from the current value and the current velocity.

3. Asymmetric edges: the tab lens, the toggle knob and the slider stretch each have their leading edge on response 0.28 and their trailing edge on response 0.42.

4. Drags are direct manipulation.
- While held, the value is a function of pointer position, with rubber-banding past limits: offset = limit + (1 − 1/(x·0.55/d + 1))·d.
- On release it springs back from wherever it was.

5. Glass is rendered in a WebGL2 pass, not with CSS backdrop-filter:
- The wallpaper is drawn to a texture with a precomputed blurred mip chain.
- Every glass shape is a rounded-rect SDF. Merging and splitting use smooth-min with k = 24px.
- Refraction offsets the sample along the SDF gradient. The offset is strongest within 14px of the edge and scaled by lens thickness.
- Frost is a mip-level bias.
- Chromatic aberration is at most 1px, at the rim only.
- The specular rim comes from the SDF normal against a top-left light.
- The Dynamic Island is an opaque SDF in the same pass.
- Text, icons, charts and the pointer are crisp SVG/DOM layers above the canvas, under the same camera matrix.

6. Content swaps inside a morphing container:
- Exit takes 120ms: blur 6px, scale 0.96, fade.
- Enter starts 60ms later with its own spring.
- Exit and enter text never overlap.

7. Audio:
- Analyze the song with numpy (onset envelope plus autocorrelation) for the beat grid, and start on a measured downbeat.
- Synthesize Apple-subtle UI sounds with numpy: soft taps for clicks, ticks for scrub detents, a low detent at max volume, a keyboard click per typed letter, and a gentle two-note chime for the notification.
- Place each sound on its measured peak, mixed about 18dB under the track.

8. Render with Playwright at 1440x1440 with 4 subframes per frame (240fps).
- Blend to 60fps with ffmpeg: tmix=frames=4, select='not(mod(n\,4))', setpts=N/60/TB.
- Encode H.264 yuv420p, crf 16, with AAC 192k and faststart.

9. Before the full render, render one still per beat (32) as a contact sheet. Fix anything off the grid, cramped, illegible over the wallpaper, or with non-concentric radii.
</build>

<gotchas>
- The glass and the DOM layers must share one camera matrix per frame, or the content drifts off its glass.
- Glass over a bright wallpaper patch kills legibility. Add an adaptive dim under the text based on sampled wallpaper luminance, rather than a heavier tint.
- The Dynamic Island is never glass.
- Icons crossing a morph keep their optical size. Scale the container, not the glyphs.
- The tooltip stays anchored to its bar through the camera move, not to the screen.
- Typed characters in Spotlight enter with the pointer's I-beam; the caret blinks on half-beats.
- Never put will-change on anything the camera scales, or text renders blurry.
- Make the last frame identical to the first, pointer included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
If the song file is missing, ask for it. Then measure the BPM and the downbeat, and show me the beat map as a table (beat, time, state, pointer action, sound), snapped to the measured grid, before writing any code. Wait for my OK.
</start>

title.zh: 警用机器人与翠鸟动画短片
title.en: Police Robot and Kingfisher Anime Short

summary.zh: 创作者用 Three.js 制作了一个可离线运行的单文件动画短片，讲述洪水淹没的东京中警用机器人与翠鸟的故事，并加入代码渲染画面和合成音效。
summary.en: The creator made an offline, single-file Three.js anime-style short about a police robot and a kingfisher in flooded Tokyo, with code-rendered frames and synthesized sound.

prompt.text:
Create a 2D anime short for the web. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic.

Deliver the final result as a single, self-contained HTML file that plays offline, with a synthesized soundtrack. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything etc.

Use Studio Ghibli and summer anime films as the art style reference for the design, line work, painted backgrounds, color, and atmosphere. The main character is a giant police robot, a fan tribute to the AV-98 Ingram "Alphonse" from Patlabor: white and black armor, red beacon bars with siren horns on both shoulders, a "▶️1" on the left shoulder, a long "AV98 INGRAM" antenna blade, and a visor with a camera unit behind the glass. Its co-star is a small kingfisher. No people appear in the film. Use any tools or techniques you want, including 3D, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime.

SCENE

A bright summer afternoon over a flooded, overgrown Tokyo. Turquoise water fills the streets; under its clear surface you can see the drowned avenue: zebra crossings, a painted 止まれ, sunken cars and bicycles, and caustics dancing on the asphalt. Ivy and trees cover the buildings, wires sag between leaning utility poles, and a koban roof with its red lamp pokes out of the water. The robot stands waist-deep at the mouth of the avenue, holding its left hand palm-up in front of its chest. A kingfisher sits on its fingers, preening. A thin cloud veils the sun, and a sunshower begins: big sunlit drops at first, then glittering backlit rain while the sun keeps shining. A drop hits the bird's head; it squints and looks up. The robot looks up into the rain, then slowly lifts its huge right hand out of the water and holds it over the bird like an umbrella, while rain streams off its fingertips in sparkling curtains. Under the hand, the kingfisher shakes itself dry and puffs up into a round ball. The robot's eyes blink softly, like a smile. The rain stops, the sun bursts out, and a huge rainbow rises over the drowned city. The hand lifts away, the bird hops to the fingertip, the shoulder beacons flash red twice across the wet air, and the kingfisher flies off into the rainbow while the robot gives a small wave.

ANIME QUALITY STANDARD

Every frame must look as if it was drawn by professional anime animators and painted by master background artists for a finished theatrical film.

Robot: A hand-drawn anime mecha that feels heavy, gentle, and full of personality, with real volume. The face housing juts forward with the visor sunk into it, and you can see the camera lenses behind the glass. The vent pad, ear discs, neck pistons and rounded knuckles are separate forms. Use cel-colored forms, hand-lettered markings (ALPHÔNSE, 特車2-1, 警視庁), panel seams, bolts, fine scratches, a little moss and believable wear. Keep it on-model from every angle, and let its posture, hands and glowing eyes express emotion.

Kingfisher: A real 3D-volume character drawn in the same cel style and line weight as the robot, never a flat sprite pasted on top. It has no visible neck, a big head flowing into a stout body, a long dagger beak, an orange breast, a cyan back streak and glossy eyes with drawn blinks, squints and happy closed eyes. Its feet grip the finger with no gap, and it gets the scene's light and shadow.

Line art: Confident, delicate, hand-inked anime line work with subtle variation in thickness and pressure, thinner with distance.

Coloring: Traditional anime cel coloring with clean color areas, simple hard-edged cool lavender-blue shadows, crisp highlights, and a bright, high-key, saturated summer palette. Never dark or muddy.

Backgrounds: Richly detailed, hand-painted anime backgrounds in a gouache style, with visible brushwork, natural color variation, layered foliage and real depth. Add painted edge highlights on buildings, kanji signboards, balconies, AC units, laundry, wires, lily pads and towering cumulus clouds.

Water: Clear and alive. Show the street underwater, refraction, caustics, drawn ring ripples and crown splashes for every drop, reflections smeared like painted water, a glitter path of separate glints, fish, petals and leaves.

Lighting: Summer sun behind the robot so the rain glitters, with a separate character key light so faces and hands never sink into shade. Add colorful shadows, light shafts through the rain, and red beacon light sweeping across the water.

Animation: Authentic hand-drawn anime timing, with characters on twos and effects on threes. Show real weight, strong key poses, natural holds, and overlapping movement in water, rain, vines and feathers. The arm lifts from the water in a natural arc, with the forearm level and the wrist never snapping, and settles over the bird with weight.

Sound: A gentle, nostalgic summer score (piano, strings, flute, glockenspiel) with one memorable motif. Add cicadas, rain on water and drumming on the metal hand, two short police-siren chirps, and wingbeats, all timed to the picture.

Direction: Cinematic anime shots with intimate close-ups of the hands and bird, beautiful composition and thoughtful staging. The pacing starts calm and sunny, turns tender in the rain, and ends in a joyful rainbow farewell.

IT MUST NOT LOOK LIKE

- 3D: No plastic materials, CGI shading, visible polygons, game-engine lighting, or computer-perfect perspective.
- Blocky "Minecraft" shapes: No plain boxes, empty flat surfaces, or toy-like proportions. Every surface carries design detail.
- SVG or vector art: No simple geometric shapes, perfect curves, uniform outlines, flat corporate illustration, or basic gradients.
- Web animation: No sliding layers, constant bobbing, floating parts, smooth software easing, or puppet-like joint rotation.
- Pasted-on elements: No 2D sprites floating in a 3D scene, no characters hovering above what they stand on.
- AI art: No warped shapes, melted details, flickering, or changing designs.
- Non-anime art: No Western cartoon designs, realistic rendering, soft painterly shading on the characters, or generic digital illustration.
- Amateur work: No stiff poses, empty backgrounds, repeated trees, muddy colors, clip art, placeholders, or unfinished details.

You are free to change any part of the prompt, if it would result in better results.

The result should feel bright, tender, and full of wonder, like a summer afternoon you remember forever. Before finishing, inspect random frames as still images. If any frame does not look completely like real 2D anime, keep improving it. Do not stop until every frame could pass as a still from a theatrical anime film.

summary.en: Cleanly, an open-source disk cleaner for macOS and Windows built in Claude Code with Opus 5.5. The creator supplied a prompt plus CleanMyMac screenshots and a gradient video, and the build ran across parallel agents with a safety agent.

prompt.text:
Build "Cleanly": a beautiful, safe disk cleaner for macOS and Windows, from scratch.

I attached screenshots of CleanMyMac as a visual quality bar. Match the polish, not the brand:
original name, logo, icons and copy.

## How to work
1. Design first, code later. Make 3 different UI concepts (light glass, dark neon, minimal)
as clickable HTML mockups. Show them to me, let me pick and give feedback, iterate.
Only then start the app.
2. Write the shared data contract before anything else: one `shared/types.ts` with every
type and the full IPC API between the Electron main process and the UI. Everything else
compiles against it.
3. Build in parallel with sub-agents, each owning its own files (no two agents edit the same
file): scanner services, system services (startup apps, installed apps, protection),
AI + settings, home screen, file screens, system screens, packaging.
4. After the build, run a separate SAFETY agent whose only job is to break every code path
that deletes, trashes, uninstalls or toggles something, and fix what it finds.
5. Then an integration agent: typecheck + build must be green.
6. Verify for real: run the UI in a browser with realistic mock data, then run the packaged
app on my machine read-only (scan, don't clean) and show me screenshots.

## Stack
- Electron (latest) + React + TypeScript + Vite. Main process bundled with esbuild (ESM),
preload bundled as CJS.
- Security: sandbox, contextIsolation, no nodeIntegration. The preload exposes only the typed
API. Main rejects IPC from any frame that isn't our own index.html.
External links: https only, opened in the system browser.
- Fonts bundled offline (no CDN at runtime). Strict CSP in production.

## Features
- Smart Scan home: big "X GB ready to reclaim" number, one Clean button,
a mini space map, and 4 live cards (Cleanup, Speed, Protection, Apps).
- Cleanup categories per OS:
- Windows: user temp, Windows temp, browser caches (Chrome/Edge/Brave/Firefox, every
profile), app caches, crash dumps, Windows Update downloads, dev caches (npm/pip),
Recycle Bin, old downloads (90+ days).
- macOS: ~/Library/Caches, logs, browser caches, Xcode DerivedData, dev caches, Trash,
old downloads.
- Space Map: glass bubbles sized by folder size, drill-down, a switch between Home and every
fixed drive (C:, D:…). Bubbles have physics: drag, throw, collide.
- Large Files, Duplicates (size → partial hash → full hash).
- Speed: startup apps with on/off toggles.
- Applications: real app icons, sizes, uninstall via the vendor's own uninstaller
(Windows) / move .app to Trash (macOS).
- Protection: read-only check of the built-in security (Defender/firewall, Gatekeeper/
XProtect/SIP) with a score. Say honestly that it does not replace an antivirus.
- AI assistant: the user picks Claude or ChatGPT and pastes their own API key (encrypted
with Electron safeStorage). The model only ever sees file names, paths and sizes —
never contents — and returns JSON verdicts per path: safe / review / keep.
Use the official Anthropic SDK.
- Settings, a Feedback form, and a Tip screen.

## Safety rules (non-negotiable)
- Caches/temp/logs are regenerable: delete them for good (trashing them frees nothing).
The user's own files (large files, duplicates, old downloads, apps) ALWAYS go to the
system Trash.
- Never trust paths from the UI. Re-derive cleanup locations in the main process by
category id.
- Before any delete: resolve the FULL path with realpath, then check it again against the
guard. Refuse drive roots, the home folder itself, OS folders, Program Files,
$RECYCLE.BIN, System Volume Information, UNC/network paths, alternate data streams
(file:stream), trailing dots/spaces, and Windows 8.3 short names (DOCUME~1).
- Never follow symlinks or junctions when walking or deleting. Skip locked files and count
them.
- Don't delete temp files modified in the last 24 h (running apps use them).
- Startup toggles: write the same 12-byte REG_BINARY value in
...\Explorer\StartupApproved that Task Manager writes (02… on, 03… off). Never delete
entries. System-wide items need one elevated reg.exe behind a UAC prompt.
After the prompt, re-read the registry instead of trusting the exit code
(PowerShell 5.1 loses it).
- File icons: never request icons for network/removable drives or .url/.lnk/.scf files.
They can make Windows authenticate to a remote host.
- No shell strings built from UI input. execFile with timeouts and windowsHide.
- reg.exe output is in the OEM code page (e.g. 866 on Russian Windows). Decode it properly.

## Design language
Light, airy, Apple-like:
- glass panels with soft shadows;
- a display font for big numbers, a clean UI font, a mono font for small labels;
- a custom duotone icon set;
- a signature glass capsule button with a thin rotating highlight on its rim;
- gradient "live" cards with subtle motion (drifting glow, particles, a liquid slider).
Background: a slow WebGL "mist" shader (domain-warped fbm noise).
Performance rules:
- render shaders at 0.3–0.5× resolution;
- use real elapsed time per frame;
- never put backdrop-filter over an animated canvas (it dropped us to 3 fps);
- respect prefers-reduced-motion.

## Packaging & release
- electron-builder:
- Windows: NSIS installer + portable .exe;
- macOS: .dmg + .zip for arm64 and x64, ad-hoc signed (no Apple ID yet).
- App icon generated from an SVG.
- GitHub Actions: on a "v*" tag, build Windows on windows-latest and macOS on macos-latest,
then publish a GitHub Release with the files.
- If NSIS fails locally with "could not open file", the project path is longer than the
Windows 260-character limit. Build from a short folder.
- Document the first-run steps in the README: SmartScreen → More info → Run anyway;
on Mac run `xattr -cr /Applications/Cleanly.app`.

## Done means
- npm run typecheck and npm run build are green;
- every screen works in the browser demo with mock data;
- the packaged Windows app runs on my machine and finds real junk;
- CI produces a public release with .exe and .dmg;
- you show me screenshots of the real app.

title.zh: 用Three.js制作的孤岛惊魂3风格游戏原型
title.en: Far Cry 3-style playable game prototype in Three.js

summary.zh: 作者提供详细提示词和照片参考，让Opus 5.5用Three.js制作了一款可玩的类《孤岛惊魂3》热带潟湖生存游戏，包含武器、天气和昼夜系统。
summary.en: Using a detailed prompt plus photo references, Opus 5.5 built a playable Far Cry 3-style tropical lagoon survival game in Three.js with weapons, weather, and day/night cycles.

prompt.text:
Create a visually stunning, highly atmospheric, interactive first-person 3D game set in a small tropical lagoon with a jungle survival outpost.
The game should capture the feeling of standing alone on a beautiful tropical island, similar in atmosphere and environmental design to Far Cry 3, with modern graphics, cinematic lighting, advanced shaders, and detailed environmental interactions.
I WILL PROVIDE REFERENCE IMAGES. Use the uploaded images as the primary visual references for the environment, composition, color palette, vegetation, outpost design, lighting, and overall atmosphere. Recreate the visual mood and environmental character of the references as closely as possible.
The result should be a playable, polished first-person experience, not a static scene or a simple tech demo.
1. WORLD AND ENVIRONMENT
Build a SMALL but extremely detailed tropical lagoon.
Do not create a massive open world. Prioritize visual fidelity, environmental density, atmospheric quality, and interactivity over map size.
The scene must include:

A beautiful tropical beach with sand, small rocks, driftwood, and scattered vegetation.
A stunning turquoise ocean with realistic waves and water transparency.
Shallow coastal water transitioning naturally into deeper blue water.
Dense tropical jungle surrounding the lagoon.
Palm trees, tropical bushes, vines, ferns, tall grass, and exotic plants.
Large moss-covered rocks and weathered coastal cliffs.
A small survival outpost located directly beside the beach, partially surrounded by jungle.
Natural pathways connecting the beach, outpost, and jungle.
Small environmental details that make the location feel authentic and lived-in.
The lagoon should feel isolated, peaceful, mysterious, and slightly dangerous.
The environmental aesthetic should be strongly inspired by Far Cry 3's tropical island atmosphere, but with the graphical quality and lighting of a modern high-end game.
2. THE OUTPOST
Create a small jungle survival outpost, NOT a large military base.
It should resemble a tiny improvised shelter, wooden shack, or canvas tent built by someone surviving on a tropical island.
The outpost should feel handmade, worn, and realistic.
Include:

A small improvised wooden shelter or tent.
A simple wooden table.
A small sleeping cot or military-style bed.
An AK-47 lying somewhere inside the outpost.
A survival knife resting on the table or near the bed.
Animal skins and hides hanging from the shelter or lying on the furniture.
A wooden supply crate that can be opened.
Small storage containers.
Old backpacks and survival equipment.
Ropes, fabric, wooden planks, and improvised construction elements.
Subtle environmental storytelling through scattered personal belongings.
Everything should feel physically placed in the environment rather than randomly generated.
Make the shelter visually interesting through layered materials, shadows, ambient occlusion, fabric simulation, and carefully placed props.
3. FIRST-PERSON CHARACTER
The player controls a character from a FIRST-PERSON perspective.
The player's hands and forearms MUST be visible.
Create high-quality first-person animations:

Idle breathing.
Natural hand movement.
Walking and running animations.
Looking around.
Picking up objects.
Holding a weapon.
Throwing stones.
Using a knife.
Interacting with the environment.
The camera should have subtle, natural movement.
Avoid excessive camera shaking.
Hands must feel connected to the player's actions. They should not look like floating objects or static models.
4. STONE THROWING MECHANIC
One of the most important features is the ability to pick up and throw small stones into the ocean.
The player should be able to:

Look at a small stone on the beach.
Pick it up.
See the stone in their hand.
Aim toward the ocean.
Throw the stone using a natural first-person animation.
The stone must have realistic projectile physics.
When the stone hits the ocean, create:

A visible water splash.
Expanding circular ripples.
Small water droplets.
Appropriate splash sound.
Realistic interaction between the projectile and water surface.
Stone throwing should feel satisfying and physically believable.
Allow the player to throw multiple stones without restarting the game.
5. AK-47 INTERACTION
Place an AK-47 inside the outpost.
The player must be able to approach the weapon and pick it up.
When equipped:

Display the AK-47 in a proper first-person weapon position.
Show both hands holding the weapon.
Implement realistic weapon sway.
Implement a shooting animation.
Add muzzle flash.
Add recoil.
Add shell casing ejection.
Add realistic gunshot audio.
Add environmental bullet impacts.
Add an optional reload animation.
The player should be able to shoot at rocks, trees, wooden objects, and other environmental surfaces.
Bullets should create appropriate visual and audio effects depending on the material they hit.
There is no need to create enemy AI or a combat campaign. Focus on making the weapon interaction feel polished and satisfying.
6. KNIFE INTERACTION
Create an interactive survival knife inside the shelter.
The player can pick it up and equip it.
Implement:

First-person knife holding animation.
Idle knife animation.
Knife swing animation.
Slash animation.
Appropriate sound effects.
Natural hand and wrist movement.
The knife should feel like a proper usable first-person tool, not a static object attached to the camera.
7. INTERACTIVE OBJECTS
Make the environment feel alive and interactive.
The player should be able to interact with selected objects.
Important interactions include:
Supply crate
The player can approach a wooden crate, interact with it, and open its lid.
The lid should animate naturally.
Plants
The player can approach specific tropical plants and harvest them.
Create a small first-person harvesting animation.
After harvesting, the plant should disappear from its original location or visibly lose its harvested part.
The collected plant must be added to the player's inventory.
Inventory
Create a simple but visually polished inventory interface.
Collected plants and other pickup items should appear in the inventory with their name, icon, and quantity.
The inventory must actually work and retain collected items during gameplay.
Other objects
Allow selected small objects around the outpost to be picked up or examined when appropriate.
Use subtle interaction prompts rather than oversized UI elements.
8. WEATHER SYSTEM
Implement a functional dynamic weather system.
The player should be able to switch between:

Clear tropical weather.
Cloudy weather.
Tropical rain.
Heavy tropical rain.
Rain must affect the entire environment visually.
When rain begins:

Rain particles appear.
Rain hits the ocean and creates small surface disturbances.
Sand and rocks become darker.
Leaves and wooden surfaces become wet.
Wet materials become more reflective.
Puddles appear where appropriate.
Atmospheric fog increases.
Rain audio becomes audible.
Ocean and jungle ambience change naturally.
Use wetness shaders and physically based material transitions.
The rain should feel like an actual tropical storm, not simply particles falling in front of the camera.
9. TIME OF DAY SYSTEM
Add a dynamic time-of-day system.
Allow the player to switch between:

Early morning.
Bright tropical noon.
Golden hour / sunset.
Night.
Each time of day must produce a noticeably different visual atmosphere.
Morning should include soft lighting and atmospheric mist.
Noon should feature strong tropical sunlight, vibrant turquoise water, and deep jungle shadows.
Sunset should have warm orange light, beautiful reflections on the ocean, and cinematic shadows.
Night should have moonlight, dark jungle silhouettes, subtle ambient lighting, and a peaceful tropical atmosphere.
Weather and time of day must work together.
For example, the player should be able to experience heavy rain at sunset or a cloudy nighttime lagoon.
10. GRAPHICS AND SHADERS — EXTREMELY IMPORTANT
VISUAL QUALITY IS ONE OF THE MAIN PRIORITIES.
Make the game look like a modern, high-quality tropical exploration game.
Use as many appropriate advanced graphical techniques as possible while maintaining playable performance.
Prioritize:

Physically Based Rendering (PBR).
Realistic water shaders.
Water refraction.
Screen-space or equivalent reflections.
Realistic ocean foam.
Shoreline water interaction.
Subsurface scattering for vegetation.
Detailed foliage shaders.
Wind-driven vegetation animation.
Soft dynamic shadows.
High-quality ambient occlusion.
Cinematic global illumination where supported.
Volumetric lighting.
Atmospheric fog.
Sun shafts passing through palm leaves.
Realistic wetness shaders.
Beautiful sky and cloud rendering.
High-quality tone mapping and color grading.
Subtle bloom.
Natural exposure adaptation.
High-quality material textures.
Realistic surface roughness and normal mapping.
Make the ocean and vegetation particularly impressive.
The water should look mesmerizing, with vibrant tropical colors, natural wave movement, and beautiful sunlight reflections.
Leaves and palm trees should move naturally in the wind.
The jungle must feel lush, dense, and visually rich.
Avoid flat lighting, generic low-poly graphics, cartoon-like materials, and empty environments.
Do not sacrifice the entire frame rate just to enable expensive effects. Use optimized techniques appropriate for the chosen engine.
11. SOUND DESIGN
Create immersive tropical environmental audio.
Include:

Ocean waves.
Water moving along the shoreline.
Wind passing through palm leaves.
Jungle birds.
Tropical insects.
Distant wildlife.
Footsteps on sand.
Footsteps on wood.
Stone throwing and water splashes.
Weapon handling.
AK-47 gunshots.
Knife swings.
Crate opening.
Rain hitting leaves, sand, wood, and water.
Use spatial audio and environmental sound variations where possible.
The lagoon should feel alive even when the player does nothing.
12. CONTROLS
Implement intuitive first-person controls.
WASD — Move.
Mouse — Look around.
Shift — Sprint.
Space — Jump.
E — Interact / pick up objects.
Left Mouse Button — Shoot, swing knife, or throw a held stone.
R — Reload the AK-47.
1 — Equip AK-47.
2 — Equip knife.
3 — Equip stone, if available.
I — Open inventory.
T — Change weather.
N — Change time of day.
ESC — Pause / settings.
Provide a small, elegant interface for changing weather and time of day.
Do not clutter the screen with unnecessary HUD elements.
13. VISUAL ATMOSPHERE AND ART DIRECTION
The entire experience should capture this feeling:
You are alone in a hidden tropical lagoon.
The ocean is crystal clear.
The jungle is dense and full of life.
A small improvised shelter stands beside the beach.
Your AK-47 rests near your sleeping cot.
A knife and survival equipment lie on the wooden table.
Animal skins hang from the structure.
Sunlight passes through palm trees and reflects from the ocean.
You can pick up a stone and throw it into the sea, watching the splash and ripples disappear into the waves.
You can explore the shelter, pick up your weapon, examine objects, gather tropical plants, and watch the weather change.
The scene should be beautiful enough that the player wants to stand still and admire the environment.
The visual identity should combine:
Far Cry 3 tropical island atmosphere + modern cinematic graphics + realistic water rendering + dense, detailed jungle + immersive first-person interactions.
14. IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENT REQUIREMENTS
This must be a WORKING, PLAYABLE EXPERIENCE.
Do not simply create a beautiful static 3D render.
Implement the actual gameplay systems described above.
Prioritize a small, complete, polished environment rather than a large unfinished game.
All important mechanics should work:

First-person movement.
Visible animated hands.
Pickable and throwable stones.
Functional water splash effects.
Equippable and shootable AK-47.
Equippable and usable knife.
Opening supply crates.
Harvesting plants.
Functional inventory.
Dynamic rain.
Dynamic time of day.
Advanced environmental shaders.
Do not replace the requested systems with decorative placeholders.
If development limitations require prioritization, complete the core mechanics first, then add graphical polish.
15. REFERENCE IMAGES
I WILL UPLOAD REFERENCE IMAGES AFTER THIS PROMPT.
These images are extremely important.
Analyze them carefully and use them as the main visual guide.
Pay particular attention to:

Lagoon shape and composition.
Position of the ocean relative to the beach.
Tropical vegetation density.
Structure and scale of the outpost.
Color palette.
Lighting.
Water appearance.
Atmosphere.
Environmental details.
The final game should feel like a playable recreation of the location and mood shown in my reference images.
Do not blindly generate a generic tropical island.
Use the references to create a distinctive, carefully art-directed, immersive lagoon environment.

summary.en: A historically researched 1906 pre-earthquake San Francisco Market Street scene built entirely in Blender Python from one detailed prompt to Opus 5.5.

prompt.text:
Recreate Market Street, San Francisco as it stood on April 17, 1906, the afternoon before the earthquake, in Blender.

Scope: the Ferry Building up Market to Fifth Street, including the Palace Hotel, the Call Building, the Chronicle Building, Lotta's Fountain and the Emporium.

Before modeling anything, build a source file from: the 1899-1905 Sanborn fire insurance maps (footprints, heights, materials, occupants), the Miles Brothers film "A Trip Down Market Street" (April 1906), period photographs from OpenSFHistory, the Library of Congress and the David Rumsey collection, and USGS topography. Record every building with footprint, height, facade material, occupant, and the source for each fact with a confidence level.

Build everything in Blender Python. No downloaded meshes, textures or HDRIs. Write reusable generators (Victorian commercial facade, mansard roof, bay windows, awnings, painted signage, gas and electric street lamps, cable car, horse-drawn wagon, early automobile) and assemble the street from the source file, so every building traces back to data.

Provide a 10 second video up the street.

title.zh: 软糖章鱼物理效果对比

summary.zh: 作者用一段详细的提示词让Claude Opus 5.5和ChatGPT-6 Astra分别制作一个可在浏览器中拉伸挤压的果冻章鱼网页特效，并比较了两者的效果与API成本。
summary.en: A single-file WebGPU gummy octopus that users can grab, stretch and squish, built from a detailed prompt covering art direction, soft-body physics and UI, and compared between Claude Opus 5.5 and ChatGPT-6 Astra with cost estimates.

prompt.text:
Create “Octo Jelly” - a beautiful, interactive 3D gummy octopus that users can grab, stretch, and squish directly in their browser. Deliver a complete single-file HTML experience using genuine WebGPU.
ART DIRECTION
Make the octopus look like a premium translucent gummy candy: a rounded head, eight curled tentacles, small suction cups, and a cute, understated face.
Use a warm off-white background, soft studio lighting, and a subtle ground shadow. Keep the scene elegant and uncluttered, with the octopus large and centered.
GEOMETRY AND MATERIAL

* Generate all geometry procedurally. No external models or image files.
* Connect all eight tentacles smoothly to the body, without visible gaps or floating parts.
* Add rounded suction cups that stay attached as the tentacles deform.
* Use glossy, translucent jelly with thickness-dependent color absorption, refraction, soft internal light scattering, and delicate rim highlights.
* Thick areas should have richer color; thin tentacle tips should transmit more light.
* Avoid opaque plastic, blown-out highlights, and visible mesh seams.

SOFT-BODY PHYSICS
Use a stable mass-spring or position-based dynamics system with elastic constraints and approximate volume preservation.

* The head should feel soft but substantial.
* Tentacles should be more flexible than the head, especially near their tips.
* Allow users to grab the head or any tentacle at the clicked location.
* Pulling should deform the nearby geometry first, then elastically pull the rest of the body.
* On release, the octopus should wobble and gradually settle into its original shape.
* Tentacles should react independently, with slightly delayed motion.
* Include gravity, floor collisions, friction, and damping.
* Prevent tentacles from passing through the floor.
* Clamp extreme stretching and use fixed simulation steps so strong pulls do not break the model.
* Do not fake softness by scaling or rotating the entire octopus.

INTERACTION

* Left-click or touch the octopus to grab and stretch it.
* Right-drag or drag empty space to gently orbit the camera.
* Support a limited zoom range.
* Keep camera gestures separate from object dragging.
* Add “Give it a nudge,” “Reset,” “Pause,” and “Reset view” buttons.
* Include Firmness and Internal damping sliders.
* Add “¼ speed” and “Show mesh” toggles.
* Provide three color presets: Coral, Lagoon, and Grape. Change the material colors without resetting the simulation.

INTERFACE
Use a minimal editorial layout:

* Top left: small “MATERIAL STUDIES” label.
* Large italic serif heading: “Octo Jelly.”
* Caption: “Eight arms. A little wobble. A very soft creature.”
* Top right: a WebGPU status indicator.
* Right side: a compact “THE SPECIMEN” control panel.
* Bottom left: “Grab a tentacle. Pull gently. Let go.”

Use clean sans-serif text for controls, thin borders, and generous whitespace. Avoid heavy panels or decorative UI effects.
PERFORMANCE AND QUALITY

* Use real WebGPU rendering, not a 2D canvas imitation or prerecorded animation.
* Reuse geometry and buffers; do not rebuild meshes during dragging.
* Keep suction cups, eyes, and other details attached to the deforming body.
* Handle transparency without flickering, disappearing surfaces, or harsh black edges.
* Support desktop and mobile layouts.
* Show a clear fallback message if WebGPU is unavailable.
* Test repeated grabs, strong pulls, releases, floor collisions, palette changes, pause, and reset.

The result should feel like a little living gummy toy - glossy, squishy, expressive, and satisfying to stretch. Deliver the full working HTML, not a mockup or a code fragment.

title.zh: 果冻材质效果模型对比测试

summary.zh: 作者用 Opus 5.5 根据一份详细提示词制作了一个独立 HTML/WebGPU 软体果冻（柑橘切片）模拟，并与 ChatGPT-6 Astra 在效果和成本上进行比较。
summary.en: A self-contained HTML/WebGPU soft-body jelly simulation of a citrus slice built with Opus 5.5 from a detailed prompt, compared in quality and cost against ChatGPT-6 Astra.

prompt.text:
Build "Citrus Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (inline JS/CSS, no libraries) with a real-time WebGPU soft-body jelly shaped like a half-moon citrus slice that the user can grab, stretch and let go.

Object
- A rounded half-moon slice: half-disk profile extruded into a thick slab with softly rounded edges; flat cut edge on the bottom, arc on top.
- Three material zones by radius: translucent fruit flesh inside, a pale pith band, and a thin glossy rind along the arc (the cut edge is all flesh).
- Inside the jelly: thin milky radial membranes between the segments (inset from both faces), a few seeds, small air bubbles with a faint rim and a pin-point highlight, and tiny sub-surface glints like sugar crystals.

Physics (XPBD tetrahedral soft body)
- Mesh: 2D Bowyer–Watson Delaunay of the profile, extruded into prisms and split into tets. Render mesh embedded in sim tets with barycentric coordinates.
- Constraints:
- co-rotational per-tet shape matching (warm-started quaternion, Müller 2016), which recovers inverted tets;
- tet volume constraints for near-incompressibility;
- hard edge strain limits (max 1.8×, min 0.35× rest length).
- Fixed timestep, "small steps" XPBD (many substeps, 1 iteration each).
- Damping: relative-velocity damping along edges, light air drag, and settling that bleeds off residual jitter.
- Floor contact with Coulomb-style positional friction (static and kinetic). Never crush the held patch into the floor; lift the patch instead.
- Grab and pull:
- pick a surface point with the mouse or touch;
- the patch around it is attached softly;
- reach is bounded, so stretching is strong but never unbounded;
- on release the slice wobbles back.
- Safety: reset gently if any value becomes NaN.

Rendering (WebGPU / WGSL)
- Procedural photo studio: pale cyclorama paper sweep, overhead softbox, back-left strip light, front-right fill card.
- Jelly material:
- refraction of the scene through the slice;
- view-ray thickness from a back-face depth pass, used for Beer–Lambert absorption;
- Fresnel studio reflections and a key highlight.
- Soft PCSS-style floor shadows, tinted by the jelly color.
- Post: exposure, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping, sRGB, dither. Optional mesh-overlay debug view.

UI (minimal editorial style, English)
- Corner label "Material Studies / No. 010", big title "Citrus / Jelly.", hint "Grab. Stretch. Let go."
- Variety swatches: Orange, Blood Orange, Lemon. Each changes the flesh, pith and rind colors.
- Sliders: Firmness (log-mapped edge compliance) and Internal damping.
- Buttons:
- "Give it a nudge": a small hop with a twist;
- Reset;
- Pause.
- Keys: Space to pause, N to nudge, R to reset.
- Fallback screen "This slice needs WebGPU." when the browser has no WebGPU.
- Responsive: works on mobile with touch and no horizontal scroll.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a one-word brand name for the wordmark (a verb works best), 9 to 12 high-res photos, a royalty-free song around 120 BPM with a drop and a quiet breakdown (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and a free stock clip of a plain wall with moving plant shadows (Pexels).
</inputs>

<direction>
An Apple-keynote launch film, 2D only, one continuous take. Every scene is made out of the previous one: nothing fades, blurs or cuts. Objects change shape instead: text rises out of a mask line, icons pop from zero on a spring, bars draw across, pages push, and a black shape floods the whole frame and contracts into the next scene. Warm off-white canvas, black UI, iOS 26 liquid glass over the photos. Archivo (wdth 125, weight 800) for the wordmark, Geist for UI. A cursor drives every change with real clicks, drags and long-presses. The camera zooms screen-studio style so each moment fills the square, and the cursor scales with it.
Banned: crossfades, blur-ins, brightness "developing", 3D flips, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 54 beats, something happens on every beat.
Open: the wordmark squeezes into its own period like an accordion, the dot grows into a black pill, a label rises inside it. Click: six iris blades close over the label and snap open onto a photo. The circle becomes a square, shrinks, the grid unfolds from behind it like a paper map (center, plus, corners), reflows into a bento, and a click zooms into one tile, landing exactly on the drop.
Glass: a glass word pops in letter by letter, melts into a droplet that stretches into a glass toolbar. The adjust icon turns it into a slider. Dragging relights the photo from day to golden hour (two aligned shots), and the knob turns into a glass lens while held. It lifts into a glass orb, the next photo opens inside it as a circle, and the orb expands into a lock screen: glass clock digits, date, and a home bar that stretches into a glass music player.
Stage: the lock screen pulls back into a phone (the bezel grows out of the screen edge). The Dynamic Island stretches like liquid, pinches off, flies over and grows into a Mac window that rolls up like a blind. Long-press the wallpaper, drag it onto a Safari tab, the page pushes in, drop it and it becomes the hero of a landing page. Scroll: the hero morphs into a framed print on a product card, with the mat and molding growing out of the photo's edge. Pick a frame color (it paints across) and a size, then the nav button flies down into "Order print".
Order: one black shape keeps morphing: Ordered ✓ → Printing % → On its way (a van on a route) → Delivered ✓.
Wall: the delivered circle floods the frame edge to edge, holds black for a beat, and contracts into the framed print hanging on the real wall footage. The same iris opens onto the print, closes again, the frame floods the screen and contracts into the pill → the dot → the letters spring back out, landing on the beat return. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside an async seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state between frames.
2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value with many targets is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time.
3. Liquid glass: each glass element holds its own clone of the scene behind it, filtered with an SVG feImage displacement map (a rounded-rect distance field) through three feDisplacementMaps at slightly different scales for chromatic edges, plus a rim light. Glass letters: a canvas distance field per glyph gives the map, mask and highlights.
4. Goo: blur + alpha threshold, then composite the source atop it so the glass stays sharp inside.
5. Iris: 6 blades around a hexagonal aperture. Each blade is its two vertices, both edge extensions and the SHORT arc between them.
6. Wordmark squeeze: every letter moves toward the dot by the same factor and its drawn width follows (narrow the wdth axis, scale the rest), so the letters stay touching.
7. Footage: re-encode all-intra (ffmpeg -g 1), load it as a blob URL, await 'seeked' before drawing each frame.
8. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event (Mixkit), never synthesized, each placed by its measured peak. The song starts on a downbeat: the zoom lands on the drop, the wall sits in the breakdown, the wordmark returns with the beat. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
9. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame blended with ffmpeg tmix, 60fps. Check one frame per beat, then scan for single-frame pops (frame-difference spikes 3x their neighbours).
</build>

<gotchas>
backdrop-filter: url() misreads displacement maps in Chromium, so clone the scene instead. A flood must overscale past the corners and take about 0.3s, or half the screen changes in one frame. A child with visibility: visible shows through a hidden parent, so use inherit. Text that swaps inside a morphing shape needs its own mask. python http.server can't range-seek video, so use the blob URL.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 4 stills (open, glass, stage, wall) before you write the full film.
</start>

summary.en: A procedural WebGPU plush octopus has fur, soft-body physics, touch controls, and several interaction tools. The creator compared Claude Opus 5.5 with GPT-6.1 Sol.

prompt.text:
Create an interactive 3D "Plush Octopus" toy as a single self-contained HTML file using native WebGPU. A cute stuffed octopus sits on a soft studio table: a big round head with two glossy black safety-bead eyes, embroidered blush cheeks and a small stitched smile, and eight chubby tapering arms that lie on the table and curl up at the tips, revealing a paler underside with rows of sucker discs. Make it look like real minky plush: dense real-time fur with visible strands, soft sheen, fur that sways when the toy moves, and soft contact shadows.

Interactions:
- Drag the head or any single arm to stretch it independently; arms must stay connected to the body and never pass through each other or the head.
- "Finger" tool: a finger follows the pointer above the octopus. Nearby arms reach up for it; press to lower it and the arms wrap around it and hold on. Moving or lifting the finger drags or lifts the octopus until the arms let go. Poking the head dents it.
- "Comb" tool: stroke the fur to change its direction; against the grain it looks darker, with the grain it shines. Add a "Smooth fur" button.
- "Shake it" button: pick the octopus up by the crown and shake it so the arms flop and swing like soft sausages, then set it down.
- Squish (press down from above), Toss, and Reset. If it lands upside down, it slowly rolls back onto its arms.

Controls: three fur colours (Coral, Lilac, Lagoon), sliders for stuffing firmness, pile length, and internal damping, quarter speed, pause. Support mouse and touch, camera orbit, and zoom (scroll or pinch). Use an elegant editorial "material study" layout: a large serif title, a compact control panel, and live readouts (mass, volume, kinetic energy, arms holding on). Generate all geometry, materials, and fur procedurally: no external libraries, models, textures, or other assets. Prioritize believable soft-body physics, stable simulation, and a cosy, polished look.

prompt.text:
帮我做一个原创的手游「高光时刻」动效：[主体，例如：开宝箱 / 段位晋升 / 成就解锁 / Boss 掉落 / 角色升级]。
做成一个可以直接打开的单文件网页（HTML + CSS + JS），点一下就能完整播放，效果对标商业手游的结算 / 奖励演出。

【世界观与风格】
- 原创美术，不要模仿任何现有游戏的 IP、角色或 Logo。
- 卡通手游风：高饱和配色，统一的深色描边（例如 #1A1033），圆润厚重的造型。
- 配色随等级升级：[等级阶梯，例如：普通绿 → 稀有蓝 → 史诗紫 → 传说金]。每升一级都要切换主色、光效颜色和背景色调。
- 标题用圆胖的游戏字体（如 Titan One / Lilita One），描黑边，加投影；文字逐字「砸」进画面，带回弹。

【主体物：做成真 3D】
- 用 Three.js 建模，不要用平面 SVG 贴图。要有厚度、倒角，以及符合主体的结构细节（木板缝、铆钉、包边、宝石切面、锁扣等）；木板缝这类细节用真实几何体拼出来，不要贴黑线条。
- 着色用卡通分阶（MeshToonMaterial 加 3～4 阶的渐变贴图），配三种灯光：主光、天光、等级色的轮廓光。
- 描边用后期边缘检测：渲染法线图 + 深度图，再用着色器画线。外轮廓粗、零件交界细，粗细全程一致；另外做 1.5 倍超采样和多重采样抗锯齿。
不要用「放大一圈的黑色背面」那种描边，那样粗细不均、转角会断。
深度判断的阈值要放宽，接缝主要靠法线判断，否则斜着看的表面会冒出细碎斜纹。
- 活动部件要真实运动，比如箱盖绕铰链翻开、奖章绕竖轴旋转。
- 待机时主体缓慢左右转动，让人看到侧面和厚度，同时轻微上下浮动；脚下要有随高度变化的柔和投影。

【如果画面里有 2D 插画（卡面、奖励图标、角色）】
- 三层卡通着色：底色、成块的阴影色、高光色，不要只用一层渐变。
- 线条分粗细：外轮廓粗，内部结构线细。
- 每个角色或物件要有自己的表情和姿态，不要所有东西共用同一张脸。
- 脚下画投影，让主体「站」在画面里；背景按属性区分图案，不要全用同一套放射线。

【演出节奏：五个阶段，缺一不可】
1. 预备：主体待机浮动，每隔几秒抖一下提示可以点击，底部显示「点击」提示。
2. 升级：每点一次，主体跳起、在空中转一圈、落地时压扁再回弹；同时切换到下一等级的颜色，闪一下光，冒一圈粒子，标题更新。
3. 蓄力（约 1 秒）：主体越抖越剧烈，缝隙透出光，四周粒子往中心吸，音效音调持续上升；最后一刻猛地压扁。
4. 爆发：从爆点向外扩散的泛光闪白、屏幕震动、镜头往前一推、多层冲击波、细长流光迸射、闪光星点、金币和宝石（带旋转）。高等级的爆发要明显更强。彩带只在最高潮用一次，不要满屏彩带。
5. 揭晓与结算：
- 奖励卡片从主体里沿弧线飞出，落位时带超调和晃动收尾，数字滚动计数。
- 稀有物品带彩虹流光边框和「NEW!」角标。
- 点击领取后，金币和宝石沿贝塞尔曲线飞进右上角的余额，每到一个余额就跳一下。

【揭晓舞台：让主角独占画面】
- 最高稀有度揭晓时，其他元素收起或淡出，背后换成一层干净的渐变幕布加缓慢旋转的柔光，不要让主角压在杂乱的背景上。
- 幕布出现时，把场景里的其他 3D 物件隐藏掉，否则后期描边会把它们的轮廓线画在幕布上。
- 主角的外发光要放在主体背后，只从边缘溢出，不能盖在主体前面把它糊成一片白。
- 可以加一圈围绕主角盘旋的星尘拖尾，但轨道必须完整在主角轮廓外侧，不能从主体正面扫过。

【光效：必须柔和，不能有硬边】
- 背景光芒：用带渐变过渡的 conic-gradient，不要一刀切的色块边缘；叠 2～3 层不同密度、不同转速的光。
- 光柱：由 5～7 道带模糊的光束呈扇形散开，亮度各自轻微闪动；根部加一团柔光核心，光里有光尘缓慢上飘。
- 闪白：从爆点向外的径向泛光（mix-blend-mode: screen），强度不超过 0.8，不要整屏纯白过曝。
- 粒子：每个火花都带一圈低透明度的外晕；冲击波用三层描边（宽而淡、中等、细而亮）。

【材质与界面】
- 边框、名牌、按钮要有材质感：金属拉丝渐变、左上亮右下暗的倒角光、内阴影；按稀有度换镶嵌件（钢铆钉 → 银框宝石 → 金框钻石加小王冠）。
- 小卡片上不要塞小字数值；详细数值放到揭晓时的信息面板里，面板里的数字滚动上涨，并弹出「▲+数值」。
- 画在 Canvas 上的贴图，分辨率至少是屏幕上最大显示尺寸的 1.5 倍，否则放大时会发虚。

【动画原则】
- 用 GSAP 时间线编排。所有动作都要有挤压拉伸、超调和弹性回弹，不要匀速。
- 粒子系统用 Canvas 2D 自己写：重力、阻力、生命周期、叠加混合，以及「吸入」「曲线飞行」「环绕」三种运动。
- 不要用 CSS 3D 透视去翻转大尺寸元素，放大加侧翻时会被投影成铺满屏幕的平面，3D 翻转一律放在 WebGL 里做。
- 所有「抖动」「呼吸」类的循环补间，在状态切换时要先取消再归零，避免它比停止指令晚一帧结束，又把值设回去。

【音效】
- 全部用 Web Audio 实时合成，不用音频文件：跳起、落地、升级和弦、蓄力上升音、爆炸低频加噪声、弹出音、计数滴答、金币叮当、胜利号角。
- 第一次点击时才初始化音频；右上角放静音开关。

【界面与工程】
- 顶部 HUD：模式切换、金币和宝石余额、静音按钮。
- 手机宽度也要能用；遵守「减少动态效果」设置（关闭震屏，减少粒子）。
- 动画状态机要严谨：动画播放中忽略点击，不能出现点击被吞或状态错乱。
- 目标 60fps。第一次打开时就是完整的待机画面，不能是空白。

【交付前自检】
在蓄力、爆发、揭晓、结算这几个时刻各截一张图，逐张检查：
- 主角有没有被光晕、粒子或文字挡住？
- 有没有过曝成一片白？
- 背景是否杂乱，有没有穿帮的描边线？
- 小字是否能看清？
- 结算后是否还有东西在不该动的时候继续抖动？

最后告诉我：每个阶段的时长，以及哪些参数可以调整演出强度。

title.zh: 巨型机器人动画场景模型对比
title.en: Giant Robot Anime Scene Model Comparison

summary.zh: 对比 Fable 5.5 与 Gemini 4 Argon。两者用同一段提示词，生成吉卜力风格的 2D 动画场景：长满青苔的巨型机器人在日出时起身，成品为单个 HTML 文件。
summary.en: A side-by-side comparison of Fable 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon. Each model made a Ghibli-style 2D anime scene of an overgrown giant robot rising at sunrise, delivered as a single HTML file from the same prompt.

prompt.text: Create a 2D anime scene for the web. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic. Deliver the final result as a single, self-contained HTML file. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything etc. Use Studio Ghibli films as the art style reference for the design, line work, painted backgrounds, color, and atmosphere. Create an original giant robot as the main character. No people appear in the scene. Use any tools or techniques you want, including 3D, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime. SCENE At sunrise, mist hangs over an abandoned forest. A giant robot has knelt here for so long that moss, wildflowers, and old trees have grown over its body. A small bird lands on its shoulder as the first ray of sunlight reaches its weathered face. Deep inside its chest, a faint light flickers on. The ground trembles and birds burst from the treetops. With a deep, creaking groan, the robot slowly rises as soil, vines, and leaves pour from its armor. It lifts its head toward a gap in the canopy. The engines ignite, sending a great ring of wind across the forest. The robot tears into the golden sky, leaving a curving trail of light and mist as leaves spiral down through the sunbeams. ANIME QUALITY STANDARD Every frame must look as if it was drawn by professional anime animators and painted by master background artists for a finished theatrical film. Robot: A hand-drawn anime mecha that feels heavy, ancient, and full of personality, with cel-colored forms, chipped paint, rust, moss, and believable weathering. Keep it on-model from every angle, and let its posture and glowing eyes express emotion. Line art: Confident, delicate, hand-inked anime line work with subtle variation in thickness and pressure. Coloring: Traditional anime cel coloring with clean color areas, simple hard-edged shadows, and a soft, natural palette. Backgrounds: Richly detailed, hand-painted anime backgrounds in a gouache style, with visible brushwork, natural color variation, layered foliage, and real depth. Lighting: Golden sunrise light, colorful shadows, glowing mist, and soft atmosphere that unite the robot and background. Animation: Authentic hand-drawn anime timing with real weight, strong key poses, natural holds, and overlapping movement in vines, grass, leaves, birds, and falling debris. The robot should rise slowly and feel massive, then launch with explosive power. Direction: Cinematic anime shots, beautiful composition, thoughtful staging, and pacing that starts quietly, builds tension, and ends in a soaring climax. IT MUST NOT LOOK LIKE - 3D: No plastic materials, CGI shading, visible polygons, game-engine lighting, or computer-perfect perspective. - SVG or vector art: No simple geometric shapes, perfect curves, uniform outlines, flat corporate illustration, or basic gradients. - Web animation: No sliding layers, constant bobbing, floating parts, smooth software easing, or puppet-like joint rotation. You are free to change any part of the prompt, if it would result, in better results. - AI art: No warped shapes, melted details, flickering, or changing robot designs. - Non-anime art: No Western cartoon designs, realistic rendering, soft painterly shading on the robot, or generic digital illustration. - Amateur work: No stiff poses, empty backgrounds, repeated trees, muddy colors, clip art, placeholders, or unfinished details. The result should feel awe-inspiring, nostalgic, and full of wonder, like the moment an old forgotten dream comes back to life. Before finishing, inspect random frames as still images. If any frame does not look completely like real 2D anime, keep improving it. Do not stop until every frame could pass as a still from a theatrical anime film.

title.zh: 叙事动画《Small Print》
Orbit落地页：启用与未启用TasteSkill对比
title.en: Orbit landing page with and without TasteSkill

summary.zh: 创作者用相同的提示词和同一张参考图片，分别在使用和不使用TasteSkill v2的情况下，让Claude Opus 5.5生成名为Orbit的产品管理平台落地页，以对比视觉效果。
summary.en: A landing page for a fictional product management platform called Orbit, generated by Claude Opus 5.5 with and without TasteSkill v2 using the same prompt and a reference image, to compare visual quality.

prompt.text:
Build a complete, production-quality landing page for Orbit, a project management platform for small product teams.
Orbit combines projects, tasks, discussions, documents, and weekly progress updates in one workspace. Its core purpose is to let teams understand what is happening without constantly asking for updates or scheduling status meetings.
Technical requirements
Build the website using Next.js, React, and TypeScript.
Use TSX components and a proper Next.js project structure. Do not create a plain HTML/CSS website.
The implementation should be clean, componentized, responsive, and production-quality. Use modern CSS or Tailwind CSS for styling where appropriate.
Do not merely describe the implementation. Build the complete working page.
Visual reference
Use the provided reference image as the primary art-direction reference.
Match its overall visual character very closely: typography treatment, density, spacing philosophy, texture, contrast, borders, surface treatment, visual weight, image treatment, and general design atmosphere.
However, do not copy the reference website or recreate its content.
Do not copy its:
branding
text or copy
logos
illustrations
exact layout
individual components
imagery
proprietary visual assets
Instead, understand the design language behind the reference and reinterpret it for Orbit.
For example, if the reference uses grain, paper texture, sharp borders, muted surfaces, unusual typography, dense layouts, editorial spacing, or a particular treatment of imagery, use those qualities as inspiration while creating an original design.
The finished page should clearly belong to the same visual world as the reference while still being an original website.
Page
The hero should immediately explain Orbit and show a convincing view of the actual product.
Throughout the page, create realistic Orbit UI showing projects, tasks, assignees, discussions, documents, statuses, deadlines, and weekly updates.
Include the sections that genuinely help sell the product, such as:
Hero
Product demonstration

Core workflow
Features
Team use cases
Integrations
Customer proof
Pricing
FAQ
Final CTA
You may change, combine, reorder, or remove sections when doing so produces a stronger page.
Design quality
Avoid the stereotypical AI-generated SaaS aesthetic.
No purple gradient hero.
No glowing blobs.
No glassmorphism.
No giant collection of rounded cards.
No endless 3-column feature grids.
No random floating icons.
No meaningless charts.
No fake AI functionality.
No excessive pills.
No generic startup illustrations.
No repetitive centered sections.
Do not make every element a card or container.
Use typography, composition, whitespace, texture, product UI, imagery, and hierarchy to create visual interest.
The product UI itself should be detailed and believable. Keep names, projects, dates, statuses, and other information consistent across different product previews.
Copy should be concise and specific. Avoid phrases such as “supercharge your workflow,” “unlock your potential,” and other generic SaaS language.
Add subtle, intentional interactions and motion where they improve the experience. Avoid animation for animation's sake.
Make the page excellent on desktop and mobile.
The final result should feel designed, not generated.
Take the reference image seriously. Analyze its design system first, then translate that design language into an original Orbit website.
Do not ask me to choose colors, fonts, layouts, libraries, or design direction. Make those decisions yourself and implement the complete site.
