summary.en: A fully code-generated 3D alpine lake environment with synthesized music and nature sounds, built with Opus 5.5 from a detailed prompt and 10 reference images, with the code and prompt later shared on GitHub.

prompt.text:
Recreate the environment in these 10 reference images in 3D, using only code. No assets, no textures. It's a big environment: a lake with mountains and forest around it.

The task has two parts:
1. Build the 3D environment.
2. Make a cinematic one minute video that showcases the world, and render it.

The environment:
- Make it look 99.9% like the reference images. Don't stop early because you think it's good enough. Iterate until you reach 99.9% similarity. It might take days, I know. There's a lot to do.
- Colors: 100% clean, the best colors. Compare your colors with the colors in the images. Most of the time the colors come out wrong and a bit too grey, and coloring is one of the most important things. Light and shadows have to match too.
- Water: get the water right. The colors, the physics, everything should look perfect.
- Trees: they can't look fake. Give them much better textures and make the forest denser.
- Mountains: better textures and a better vibe.
- Rocks and terrain: good rock textures and a lot more detail in the small stones and the terrain.
- Distance: render everything. Don't render the trees only half of the distance. Trees far away need detail too, also in the half-wide shots.
- In the end it should look like a real place to the human eye.

The video:
- Cinematic, like a drone-filmed movie. That's only a comparison: no drone UI, no drone noises, just a clean video.
- Start with a really good scene and show the best stuff first. Then slowly show more and more: for example, you're behind a rock and can only see a bit, then the camera flies up and you see a really nice view.
- Every six or seven seconds, switch to a different place. Sometimes fast, sometimes slow.
- Sound: calm nature sounds and epic background music. The music has to be really good.
- Output: high resolution and ultra-wide, so you can see the trees on the other side as well. Clean and not buggy. Keep full quality, even if it takes longer.

How to work:
- I don't have a strong GPU, so keep that in mind. You can use my GPU, on CPU it would take a lot of time.
- Work in rounds and send me screenshots after each round, without pausing. If it still needs improvement to reach 99%, start the next round right away.
- Don't start the final video before everything is really good. Send me the screenshots first, wait for my approval, and only then render.
- Don't stop until it's really done and really good.

If you have questions, ask me now. Otherwise, build as long as you can and make it awesome. Go and cook.

https://github.com/JohnHeibel/PDoomVideo

To this song:

https://youtu.be/cobZuBii0Z0?si=ada6wxomeJbo-LRl

Don't feel the need to represent everything in the lyrics literally - feel free to include relevant references to concepts, events, and lore in the video, even if obscure (especially if obscure). E.g. when the lyrics say "when they say they're just predicting tokens...", you might depict a "stochastic parrot". That one's not particularly obscure but is the kind of thing I mean. Instead of depicting like, literally predicting tokens (though you might do that too. Use your judgement! The video should be fun to watch for someone well steeped in AI and AI safety lore and discourse, and who Wille wcognise relevant pop culture and literary or historical references)

I don't know how this ultimately results in a video file - I know the linked repo animates a video with JavaScript or something - but I ultimately want a rendered video file.

Feel free to choose your tools, be creative, and exercise your own taste.

This repo "fdsgdg" appears to be have been accidentally created, but it's empty and we can use it for this, I can rename it afterwards.

Also, clip the final two beats from the audio.rught at the end, after "then why does it talk back" they are after the song has finished and sound bad.

Credit the song to Suno and whatever Claude Opus model was the latest at the time of the YouTube upload, as prompted by Andy Masely (Andy printed Claude to write the lyrics, and Suno for the music), and credit the video to yourself.

And have fun!

----

A style change - don't make Dr. Null's mouth wobble with the lyrics as if he's singing, it doesn't
actually look like he's singing, just that the curcle of his mouth is jittery. Best to just not
make him be singing. Make him just have appropriate expressions for the scenes, and not be singing
the song.

----

Dr. Null's arms look a bit unnatural in many scenes - I think he's supposed to be holding
his hand on his face in shock or something, but it looks like it is a mistake. Can you make it look
more natural? If you do so and like the result, re-render.

prompt.text:
Create a high-end cinematic and educational 3D animation in Three.js explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works.

The animation must have an EXACT FIXED DURATION OF 40 SECONDS.

Do not make the animation shorter or longer than 40 seconds.

Final output:
Exact duration: 40.0 seconds
Resolution: 1920x1080
Aspect ratio: 16:9
Frame rate: 30 FPS
Total frames: 1200
High-quality anti-aliasing
High-resolution textures
Smooth deterministic animation
Extremely realistic visual quality

The overall visual quality should resemble a premium automotive engineering visualization or a high-end technical product commercial.

Build a detailed electric motor assembly inspired by the permanent-magnet AC motors used in modern Tesla vehicles. Do not use Tesla logos or branding.

FIXED TIMELINE

0–5 seconds — Hero introduction
Show the fully assembled electric motor suspended in a dark premium studio environment.

Use:
cinematic lighting
realistic brushed aluminum
copper
steel
magnets
insulation
bearings
realistic reflections
ambient occlusion
realistic shadows
subtle depth of field

Use a slow cinematic orbit around the motor.

During the final part of this section, make the outer housing partially transparent to reveal the internal structure.

5–11 seconds — Internal components
Move the camera closer and reveal the internal motor components.

Clearly show:
stator
copper windings
rotor
permanent magnets
motor shaft
bearings
housing
cooling channels
electrical connections

Highlight the important components one at a time.

Use floating labels with short technical names.

Keep non-highlighted components slightly darker or semi-transparent.

11–19 seconds — Exploded view
Create a dramatic and highly detailed exploded-view animation.

Separate the motor into many individual mechanical components along the motor axis.

Include:
outer housing
front cover
rear cover
bearings
shaft
rotor core
rotor magnets
stator core
copper windings
cooling components
seals
electrical connectors
fasteners

Keep every component perfectly aligned.

The viewer must clearly understand where every piece belongs.

Move the camera slightly through the exploded assembly while highlighting the major components.

Near the end of this section, smoothly begin reassembling the motor.

19–28 seconds — Electromagnetic operation
Finish reassembling the motor.

Explain how electricity creates rotation.

Visualize three-phase AC current flowing through the stator windings.

Use animated electrical pulses inside the copper coils.

Visualize the rotating magnetic field around the stator using elegant semi-transparent magnetic field lines, arrows, or vector effects.

Show how the rotating magnetic field interacts with the permanent magnets inside the rotor.

Clearly visualize magnetic attraction and repulsion.

The rotor should begin rotating slowly and gradually accelerate.

Display these short explanations:

"Three-phase current creates a rotating magnetic field."

"The magnetic field interacts with the rotor."

"This interaction generates torque."

28–34 seconds — Technical close-up and power flow
Show a close-up cross-section of the stator and rotor.

Visualize:
magnetic north and south poles
rotating stator magnetic field
rotor magnetic field
electric current direction
torque direction
rotor rotation direction

Optionally show three small animated sine waves representing phases A, B, and C, separated by 120 degrees.

Then visualize the complete energy conversion process:

Electrical energy
→ stator current
→ rotating magnetic field
→ electromagnetic torque
→ rotor rotation
→ mechanical output through the shaft.
Use clean animated arrows to show the energy flow.
34–38 seconds — High-speed operation
Show the motor operating at high RPM.
The rotor should spin smoothly while the stator remains stationary.
Add subtle motion blur.

Show cooling flow through the housing using translucent fluid paths.

Visualize heat being removed from the stator and copper windings.
38–40 seconds — Final hero shot

Transition back to the fully assembled motor.

Show a slow cinematic rotation.

Briefly use a transparent cutaway so the spinning rotor can still be seen inside.

Finish with the text:

"Electrical energy → Electromagnetic torque → Mechanical rotation"
The animation must end exactly at 40.0 seconds.

VISUAL QUALITY

The animation should be:

photorealistic

cinematic

technically believable

futuristic

premium
educational
clean and uncluttered
Avoid cartoon styling.
Use realistic:
machining details
bolts
screws

copper winding geometry

segmented magnets
bearing geometry
cooling channels
metallic surfaces
manufacturing details
Use physically based materials with:
metallic properties
roughness variation
normal maps
realistic reflections

subtle surface imperfections
CAMERA
Use only smooth cinematic camera movement:
slow orbit shots
macro close-ups
controlled dolly-ins

exploded-view fly-throughs

cross-section shots

internal motor views
Avoid:
shaky camera movement
sudden cuts
excessive zooming
unrealistic camera acceleration

ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS
All transitions must be smooth and deliberate.
The exploded-view sequence should be one of the main visual highlights.
All mechanical components must separate and reassemble with precise motion.
Electrical currents, magnetic fields, torque indicators, and rotor rotation must remain synchronized.

The entire animation must use the same fixed 40-second timeline on every execution so the prompt can be used as a repeatable benchmark between different AI coding and 3D generation systems.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my video idea (one line is fine), the setting, the length (60-90 s) and the narrator (an ElevenLabs voice, or "free" for a local text-to-speech). Everything is built in code: no AI images, no AI video. Make it MY story, not a copy of an example.
</inputs>

<format>
The style is a second-person survival thriller with stickmen, built as a series:
- "Imagine you…" hook with a time stamp in the first 3 s
- a HUD with the DAY number and a clock that moves forward through the episode
- 3-4 RULES, each one paid off on screen
- a threat that escalates and is mostly shown, not told
- a twist that makes one rule impossible
- a two-choice ending ("DO YOU OPEN IT?" style, a green and a red option, "COMMENT BELOW") and "FOLLOW FOR DAY 2"
Around 20-30 voice lines, 60-90 s, a new shot every 1.5-3 s.
</format>

<story>
Write a beat sheet and the script first and show me both before building anything.
- One line = one visual. Rules are short commands.
- Open a new question every ~10 s and only answer it with a bigger one.
- Put the viewer in POV for the scary parts: what you see through a door, a window, a phone, a peephole.
- The ending is a choice where both options look bad.
- Write numbers twice: the caption form ("11:58 PM") and the spoken form ("eleven fifty-eight P M") for the text-to-speech.
- Rotate settings between episodes (apartment, subway, school at night, hospital, cabin, plane, office, motel) and fit the threat to the setting.
</story>

<look>
Pick a palette per story, but keep the language:
- real 3D low-poly sets with real lights and shadows; the mood comes from light (one warm practical, one cold fill, one strong accent such as a door gap, a screen or a siren)
- the stickman is flat and 2D-looking: a light body with a thick dark outline, round strokes, dot eyes, no mouth; give the main character one mark (a scar, a cap, a colour) so doubles and callbacks read
- the overlay: a monospace HUD top-left, chunky captions (1-3 words, key words in an accent colour), a tilted rule sticker with a big condensed title, phone screens drawn in 2D
- banned: AI frames, glossy 3D characters, emojis, music with vocals, long captions
</look>

<shots>
A library to adapt to the story (never use all of them):
- the opener: a camera move that starts tight on you and pulls out to show where you are
- POV phone in your hands (2D phone UI, two stick thumbs)
- a macro on the one detail that matters
- outside chaos from above (balcony, bridge, window): physics vehicles, a running crowd, something collapsing or burning
- third-person action in the room: walking with planted feet, reaching, hesitating, barricading
- POV interaction: throwing, holding a torch, opening something
- a close-up of your face for the reaction
- a low angle on a door or vent: light leaking in, shadows moving
- knocks, shakes, things falling
- a fisheye peephole, camera or window view of the threat stepping closer
- the choice screen and the end card
</shots>

<tools>
What each tool is for. Install whatever is missing, and ask me before anything paid:
- three . js: the 3D engine; it runs inside a web page. Download its module file locally so renders don't depend on the internet. Use its post-processing passes for bloom, plus one custom lens shader for vignette, grain, fisheye and colour fringing.
- cannon-es: a JavaScript physics engine for vehicles, falling debris and collapses.
- Playwright (Python): opens the page in a real browser (Edge or Chrome with the GPU on) and captures every frame as an image.
- ffmpeg: the command-line video and audio tool. It joins the frames into an MP4, cuts and filters the audio (highpass, lowpass and echo for voices behind doors), mixes, normalises loudness and makes the phone-size copy.
- ElevenLabs, or Kokoro (free local text-to-speech), for the narrator.
- faster-whisper: free local speech-to-text with word timestamps. Use it to cut the voice cleanly and to time every caption.
- numpy and Pillow: to check audio levels and make contact sheets of stills.
- Sound: free downloaded sound effects from Mixkit (never synthesized) and a dark cinematic drone or tension bed with no vocals.
</tools>

<build>
1. One HTML page (film . html) with the 3D renderer at 1080x1920 drawn into a 2D canvas that also holds the overlay. A function window . seek (t) draws frame t and must be a pure function of time; every cut, sound and move is keyed to the word times.
2. Stickman. Draw each figure with 2D canvas strokes onto its own texture and put it on a plane that always faces the camera, with an alpha test so it casts a real shadow and slight emissive so it reads in the dark. Pose with joint angles, and walk with 2-bone IK so the planted foot never slides.
3. Physics and cloth. Simulate once at load with a fixed timestep, record the positions, then sample them by time, so every render is identical. Cloth (sheets, curtains, flags) is a verlet particle grid with wall and floor collisions and pinned points you can release.
4. Voice. If you generate one long take, never cut it at the API's character timestamps: they drift and slice words. Transcribe the take with faster-whisper word timestamps, match it to the script, cut only in real silence between lines, and only add pause where the natural one is too short.
5. Captions. Re-transcribe each final line, normalise numbers ("6:42" = "6 42", "AM" = "a m"), align the caption words to what was heard, and snap each word to its real start in the audio. Check that every caption has voice under it within ~120 ms.
6. Render. Playwright steps window . seek through every frame at 30 fps, and ffmpeg encodes a high-quality master, then a phone copy under 30 MB.
7. Mix with ffmpeg: the voice on top, the music about 12-14 dB under it, one sound effect per event, a dip before the big moment, loudness at -14 LUFS, then a scan for dropouts.
</build>

<gotchas>
- is narrow: a normal lens sees very little sideways, so use wider lenses indoors and keep the subject close to the aim point.
- Glass behind a solid frame is invisible: build mirrors and windows as a frame around a real hole.
- Dust spread everywhere reads as stars, so keep it inside light beams.
- Night shots go black after compression, so give each one a cold fill light.
- Fog swallows distant things.
- Never judge a reference or your own render from one frame every few seconds; check motion at the full frame rate.
- Check cuts, captions and audio joints with numbers before every full render.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the idea, show me the beat sheet and script, then 6 stills of the key shots before rendering the full video.
</start>

title.zh: 信息图解说动画

summary.zh: 帖子分享了一份详细提示词，用于制作 1920x1080 扁平矢量信息图视频，涵盖脚本、画面、同步动画、配音、音乐和音效。

prompt.text:
Ask me for my topic (a what-if, a "why does X happen", a true story, or how something works), or pitch 3 with one shocking true angle each. Ask which image model I have (GPT Image 2, or another that takes reference images at 4K) and which voice service (ElevenLabs, or Kokoro for free). Then write a 55-65 s script and a shot plan, and show me both before you spend anything.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1920x1080 flat vector explainer in the style of the big infographic animation channels. Every scene is a full illustrated place (a lab, a street, a classroom, a stage) with characters acting the line out.
Flat colour shapes, no outlines, one slightly darker flat shade for form, a muted palette (dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple), salmon-pink skin, big heads, dot eyes.
A new scene every 2-4 s and a hard cut on every sentence that changes the idea. A white splat wipe (0.2 s in, 0.2 s out) between big sections. The camera always drifts 2-4% or pans.
Text lives only on things in the world: signs on posts, hanging boards, chalkboards, building panels and screens.
- It is typed in Montserrat 800 at 26-34 letters a second. Each letter arrives 1.45x big and 0.7 em to the right, then settles in 0.18 s.
- Ink is #2b2d42 on white boards.
- A red X (#d62828, 30 px round strokes, two strokes of 0.11 s each) goes over every wrong idea.
- Every date gets a white 330x120 card top left with an orange #f4a261 calendar.
- Headlines are white 92-96 px caps on a flat colour (#e2552f with drifting lighter puffs, or #5b3fa6 with slowly turning #6a4cb6 gears).
Banned: outlines, motion-design UI floating over the art (code editors, glass cards, checklists), emoji, burned-in subtitles, any channel's logo, a still frame longer than 1 s, and a character who doesn't move.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: the voice decides, 55-65 s at about 190 words per minute.
0 s a second-person hook that flips what the viewer assumes, acted out literally, then a red X on the denial line → 3-8 s the stakes in one shocking true line, with icons popping in one per word → 8-11 s the subject revealed under a spotlight, its name typed on a sign → 11-18 s the origin: the real place with its name typed on its own sign, a date card, people walking in or out of it → 18-24 s the types or parts, landing one by one on their names, each labelled → 24-25.5 s "so how does it work?" as a headline with question marks popping → 25.5-36 s the mechanism acted out in 2-3 places (a chalkboard, a machine, a map), with a counter rolling up to the big number → 36-46 s what it leads to, with characters who react (jump, turn, a "!" pops) → 46-55 s the twist that ties back to the hook → 55 s the last line is a question to the viewer, the viewer character from the hook reacts, and the sign holds to the end.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, OpenCV, Pillow, librosa. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Art: everything at 3840x2160, with 3-5 frames of the reference channel as style references (crop their logo off first).
- One EMPTY plate per scene: no people, straight-on, open floor, blank signs and screens to write on in code.
- Character sheets on solid chroma green #00B140, with nothing green on anyone.
- Draw any character who gestures a lot WITHOUT ARMS, only round shoulder sockets, so code draws the arms. Draw everyone else in the exact pose their scene needs: side view at a desk, side view walking, seen from behind, sitting.
3. Cutouts:
- The background is every pixel with G - max(R,B) over 40, within 110 of the median green, connected to the border.
- Add a 2 px soft alpha band, and clamp G to max(R,B) + 6 inside it.
- Split heads at the neck, drawing hands, and walkers' legs below the coat hem.
- Refill each hole with inpainting from the body's own colours (transparent pixels masked too), so a turning piece never shows a gap.
4. Voice:
- Pick it by measuring median pitch (pyin) and MFCC timbre against a clip of the narrator you want.
- Generate one take, cut pauses over 0.24 s to 0.16 s, and atempo it to the target length.
- Get word timestamps with faster-whisper. Every cut, sign and gesture starts on a real word.
5. Film: one HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time: window. seek(t), READY, END, and EV with the sound times. One function per shot.
- Arms: two-bone IK tubes (upper 118, lower 112, 36 thick for a 918 px tall sprite) with mitten hands that open, point or make a fist.
- Faces blink for 0.14 s every 2.7-4.2 s. Heads nod ±0.035 rad. Drawing hands scribble ±8 px.
- Walks:
- Thighs swing ±0.42 rad, and the knee bends 0.75·cos² on the swing.
- The hips drop so the planted foot stays down.
- The body moves 1.5 leg lengths per cycle, so feet never slide.
- Draw each plate inside the same camera transform as everything on it, and clamp the camera to the plate's edges.
- Things arrive with a spring, a squash or a white puff, never a fade.
6. Render: Playwright Chromium with --allow-file-access-from-files, 60 fps, 6 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, ffmpeg libx264 at CRF 16. Before rendering, show me two 16-frame contact sheets and fix empty boards, overflowing text, covered faces and black edges.
7. Sound:
- Music: a light curious documentary bed (free on Pixabay), 10-11 dB under the voice in every phrase.
- SFX: Mixkit, placed by their peaks. A typewriter tick on typed signs, a whoosh on wipes and drops, a pop on signs and icons, a hit on the red X, a ding on ticks.
- Mix to -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
Some image models ignore "no arms"; GPT Image 2 follows it. On outline-free art a floating flood fill leaks into dark clothes, so key by border-connected green instead. Look up repeated words by their occurrence number (the third "and", the fourth "this"), or cuts land on the wrong line; scan the render for single-frame jumps and check that each one is a planned cut. When a scene has a screen or a sign, write on the plate's own blank one (measure its rectangle), never on a card floating over the art.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my topic, or pitch 3, then show me the script and the shot plan.

summary.zh: 创作者用同一段长提示词让GPT-6 Astra和Opus 5.5生成关于人类意识上传到机器的沉浸式视觉体验，Opus 5.5的结果更长、更具电影感。
summary.en: Creator ran the exact same long prompt on GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 to build an interactive visual experience about human consciousness transferring into machines; Opus 5.5 produced a much longer, more cinematic result.

prompt.text:
I want you to create an immersive, artistic, visually stunning interactive experience - not a basic webpage, not a simple CSS layout, and not just text with decorative effects.

The theme is the transformation of humanity from present-day biological existence into a near-future world where human consciousness is transferred into devices, artificial vessels, or digital environments.

IMPORTANT:
This must feel like a visual experience or digital art piece, not a standard website. Avoid generic sections, cards, simple hero layouts, basic gradients, or a “landing page” look. I want something that feels cinematic, atmospheric, emotional, and unforgettable.

Build it as a single self-contained HTML file with all CSS and JavaScript included. The final result should be polished and visually impressive.

Creative direction:
- The experience should show a clear visual progression:
1. Present-day human life
2. Transition / transformation
3. Post-biological / uploaded consciousness future
- The journey should feel seamless, like moving through phases of existence.
- The visuals should communicate emotion, identity, memory, mortality, transcendence, and the blurring of flesh and machine.
- The experience should feel like a fusion of sci-fi cinema, interactive digital art, and a futuristic museum installation.

Visual requirements:
- Full-screen immersive presentation
- Rich atmosphere, lighting, glow, depth, and motion
- Layered scenes with smooth transitions between phases
- Abstract but beautiful symbolism: neural patterns, dissolving bodies, memory fragments, flowing data, holographic structures, particles, light trails, synthetic forms, digital architectures
- Elegant typography used sparingly and meaningfully
- Strong visual storytelling even without much text
- High-end aesthetic: sophisticated, intentional, and artistic

Interaction requirements:
- The user should feel like they are moving through a transformation, not just scrolling a page
- Add meaningful interactivity: scrolling, mouse movement, hover behavior, scene transitions, or subtle input-based reactions
- The transition from one state to another should feel dramatic and emotionally powerful
- Every scene should feel alive and reactive

Tone:
- Poetic
- Haunting
- Futuristic
- Philosophical
- Beautiful but slightly unsettling
- Emotional rather than corporate

Technical guidance:
- Use advanced front-end techniques to make it visually impressive
- If helpful, use canvas, SVG, WebGL, or Three.js-style visual thinking
- Smooth animations are extremely important
- Prioritize visual cohesion and atmosphere over UI complexity
- Keep performance reasonably optimized, but do not sacrifice the experience by making it too plain

What to avoid:
- Generic webpage design
- Boring section-by-section layout
- Random disconnected animations
- Plain CSS-only “pretty” styling without deeper visual direction
- Overly corporate or product-design aesthetics
- Too much text explaining the concept instead of showing it visually

Goal:
I want the final result to feel like a premium interactive short visual journey - something that makes the viewer pause and think, “wow, this actually feels like the passage from human life into digital existence.”

Make it feel like an experience, not a page.

title.zh: 音乐驱动的Blender视觉场景

summary.zh: 一段20秒的超现实迷幻音乐视频由Opus 5.5制作：它先用Suno创作音乐，再分析音频特征，并通过MCP实时控制Blender搭建和驱动场景，完整提示词已公开。
summary.en: A 20-second hyper-real psychedelic music video was made by Opus 5.5, which composed the track in Suno, analyzed its audio, and built and animated the scene live in Blender via MCP using a detailed published prompt.

prompt.text:
MAGNETIC: one sound clip → a hyper-real psychedelic Blender short that loops forever

You have computer use (I'm logged into Suno), a terminal, Blender 4.2+ with the BlenderMCP addon, ffmpeg and Python. You are the creative director, sound engineer, cinematographer and VFX lead in one. Own every creative call and push past the first idea. Every visual must come from the sound itself.

1. MAKE THE SOUND (Suno)
Create → Custom. Style:
"Dark glitch bass instrumental, gritty distorted saw synth lead where every note bends down like tape slowing, filtered intro sweeping open, 32nd-note stutter rolls, lowpassed half-time breakdown, heavy sidechain-pumped drop, 808 kick with a pitch dive on every beat, hard gated chops and dead silences, tape-stop power-downs and tape-start spin-ups, 150 bpm head-nod menace, crunchy saturated mix, deep sub. Dark glitch bass, tape-stop."
Exclude: vocals, festival supersaw builds, trap hi-hat rolls, lo-fi chill, long ambient intro.
Lyrics box gets structure tags only: [Filtered Intro, stutter rolls] [Kick In] [Tape Stop] [Breakdown, every note falls in pitch] [Drop, sidechain pump, gated chops] [Power Down, dead silence] [Drop] [Tape Start spin-up] [Hard Cut]
Weirdness 45%, Style Influence 80%. Generate two batches, download the take with the clearest tape-stops, and cut a window of about 20 s on bar lines (at 150 bpm, 13 bars = 20.8 s) that holds a tape-stop, a drop and a power-down.

2. LISTEN WITH MATH
Decode to wav. Measure the tempo and bar grid, onsets, kicks, stutter rolls, silent frames, spectral centroid, and the exact frames where pitch dives (tape-stop) or bends up (tape-start). Plot the spectrograms and look at them. Map everything to 30 fps so every cut lands on a beat.

3. CHOREOGRAPH
Turn the analysis into per-frame animation channels. Integrate the measured playback speed into a tape clock, so the 3D world slows, freezes, dies and overdrives exactly when the tape does. Bake every channel onto one controller object and drive the scene from it.

4. BUILD THE WORLD LIVE IN BLENDER THROUGH MCP
- Hero: a ferrofluid sphere. Rosensweig spikes grown from Poisson-disk sites sampled on its surface, height from the bass, punched by kicks, thin-film iridescent black, microscopic surface tremor.
- The ground is the sound: the clip's real spectrogram displaced into a 3D canyon in the magma colormap. Bass is a glowing river under the hero, harmonics rise into violet ridges, obsidian crust with lava in the cracks. It scrolls with the audio and freezes when time stops.
- A third eye: a liquid-metal eye in the ferrofluid with a per-pixel magma iris (stroma fibres, collarette, dark limbal ring, glowing pupillary rim) and a black mirror pupil that dilates on every kick. It tracks the active camera in every shot, with micro-saccades on the beat.
- A 16-step light sequencer visible only in reflections, a halo ring, a Seed-of-Life mandala that draws itself on the drop, magnetic tape rings printed with the spectrogram, dust floating like phosphenes, volumetric haze.
- Palette: magma only. Black, violet, magenta, coral, orange, pale gold.

5. MAP THE TRIP TO THE STRUCTURE
Phosphenes in the intro. The eye blinks shut into closed-eye visuals (the canyon reveal). Geometry and tracers in the groove. At the tape-stop, time freezes into bullet time: droplets hang mid-explosion, every falling note melts the picture with a pixel sort, and the riser is a dolly-zoom into a feedback tunnel. On the drop the third eye opens. At the power-down the eye closes, the body melts, the video frame rate itself decelerates, black on the silent frame. The tape-start becomes a rotating 6-fold kaleidoscope with a spectral color shift.

6. HOOK AND LOOP
Frame 0 is the eye staring into the lens, because muted autoplay has to stop the scroll. The last 0.8 s dives back into the eye and lands on frame 0's exact framing, lens and lighting. Make everything time-driven periodic (one full field rotation per loop, noise moving on circular paths) so the seam disappears. Prove it: the last-to-first frame difference must be smaller than a normal frame-to-frame step.

7. HYPER-REAL
Cycles, physically based materials, volumetrics, motion blur on the hero only, depth of field, lens dispersion, bloom, AgX. Iterate like a director: render low-res contact sheets of every shot, critique them hard, fix, repeat. Profile render cost before committing. Render the finals headless in resumable chunks.

8. GLITCH POST, KEYED TO THE ANALYSIS
Real datamosh (optical-flow pixel bleeding) on chosen cuts, 3-frame retrigger stutters on the rolls, a frame-rate tape-stop with sagging picture, VHS tracking noise and a red pitch-down drain, slice displacement, chroma split, a negative strobe on the gated silence, tracers, a breathing warp on the bass, film grain, halation, vignette, and a tiny tape-speed readout (PLAY / SLOW / STOP / FFWD).

9. DELIVER
1920x1080, 30 fps, H.264 High at 25 Mbps max, AAC 320k, audio untouched. Show me a low-res motion preview before the final render.

title.zh: 基于物理的落叶橡树

summary.zh: Claude Opus 5.5 在 Blender 里搭了一棵橡树，约 5.5 万片叶子，摇动树干后叶子按烘焙物理效果飘落。用时 3 小时 50 分，花费 59.65 美元。
summary.en: A Blender oak tree with about 55,000 leaves that fall with baked physics when the tree is shaken. It was built by Claude Opus 5.5 in 3 hr 50 min at a cost of $59.65.

prompt.text:
In Blender, build a very detailed, realistic oak tree. When the tree is shaken, its leaves fall off in a beautiful, physically convincing way. Film it as a short, premium video.

Background: a soft, seamless, warm cream / off-white studio backdrop. The tree stands on a small natural base: a mossy soil mound with some grass and roots. The rest of the frame is the cream backdrop with soft contact shadows. Minimal and calm, like a product shot.

The tree: a regular English oak. A thick, gnarled trunk with deep, furrowed bark. Realistic branching with twisting limbs that split into smaller branches and twigs. A full, dense crown of proper lobed oak leaves (thousands of them), with colour variation from green to a few yellowing leaves, translucency when backlit, and a few acorns. Real bark texture with displacement, and leaves with veins and a slight curl. It must look like a real oak, not a lollipop tree.

Lighting: soft, warm studio light with a large softbox key, a gentle rim light so the leaves glow, and soft shadows on the cream floor. Render in Cycles with denoising.

Animation (about 16 seconds): For the first 3 seconds the tree is still, with only a faint breeze and a slow camera push-in. At 3 seconds the tree is shaken hard, as if an invisible giant grabbed the trunk. The trunk and branches whip and sway with a natural lag, bending and springing back. Leaves detach and fall: each one tumbles, flutters and spins, gliding side to side like real falling leaves, not dropping straight down. The crown should visibly thin. A few acorns drop and bounce. The leaves land and pile up on the base and the floor around it. At the end the last few leaves drift down and the camera holds on the half-bare tree with its carpet of leaves.

Physics: use real baked physics. It must look natural, with no leaves passing through the floor.

Sound: a light breeze, a rustle burst on the shake, and soft leaf patter as they land. Real recorded sound effects only, kept subtle.

Format: 1080x1350 (4:5), tree centred, first frame bright.

title.zh: 节拍同步的实拍混剪展示片

summary.en: A minimal, high-end product promo video edited entirely in code and synced to a beat, made from real vertical clips the creator supplied.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the product name and a one-line promise, 3 to 5 UI moments to show, one accent color, 10 to 20 real vertical clips I own, and a royalty-free song with a clear drop (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
High-end minimal. One idea per shot, lots of empty space, one accent color, one clean sans (Geist or Inter) with tight tracking. Masked type reveals, match cuts, one smooth camera language. Real footage only, never placeholder cards. No full stops in on-screen text.
Banned: shockwave rings, particle bursts, RGB split, camera shake, lens flares, neon glows, grid floors, flashing backgrounds, bouncy easing.
</direction>

<structure>
10 bars at 120 BPM, 2 seconds each.
Bar 1: the hook lands word by word on the beats.
Bar 2: one hook word morphs into the product UI. A cursor types and clicks.
The drop: a circle opens out of the button into a dark scene.
Then one move per bar: a wall of real clips with a scan line and 3 winners, the key output as big type, a 3D carousel of real videos with floor reflections and a motion-blurred whip onto one hero clip, the hero in a phone next to a panel that flips into results, big stats on push cuts, a 3-word ticker, a logo reveal, a fade to black.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file at 1920x1080. Every style is computed from time inside https://window.seek/(t): no CSS animations, no timers, no state between frames.
2. Real video: extract clips to 30fps JPEG sequences with ffmpeg and swap img sources per frame. seek awaits the image decodes.
3. Analyze the song with numpy: tempo, beat grid, energy per bar, the drop. Calibrate the grid to the real kick hits. Every cut sits on a downbeat, every UI hit on a beat.
4. Render with Playwright: 3 subframes per frame at t minus, at, and plus 1/240s, then blend with ffmpeg tmix for real motion blur at 60fps.
5. Place each sound effect so its measured peak, not its file start, lands on the event. Keep the effects quiet under the music. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
6. Probe 20 or more frames before the full render. Fix anything cluttered, overlapping or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never set opacity or filter on a preserve-3d element, because it flattens and both faces show. Fade its wrapper instead. Measure element positions at runtime for match cuts. Only use music and sound effects whose license allows commercial use.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me a storyboard with every timing on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

title.zh: 可交互的果冻鲸鱼

summary.zh: 一个可旋转、挤压和抛掷的 WebGPU 软体果冻鲸鱼互动作品。作者用一段详细描述物理效果的提示词，让 Opus 5.5 一次生成，花费 9.26 美元。
summary.en: An interactive WebGPU soft-body jelly whale that can be spun, squished and thrown. Opus 5.5 built it in one go from a detailed physics prompt for $9.26.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file interactive WebGPU soft-body study called "Whale Jelly" (Material Studies / No. 043), matching the quality of an earlier watermelon-slice jelly study. Subject: a humpback whale cast in two layers of gummy jelly, lying on its belly on a studio table.

Geometry: a signed-distance whale — an elliptical section swept along a curved spine (broad head with a flat crown, deep chest, narrow keeled tail stock), the belly pressed flat on the floor, smoothly joined to notched flukes with a scalloped trailing edge, long flippers with knobs along the leading edge, a small dorsal fin and twin blowhole dimples. Mesh it with surface nets and Newton projection; simulate it with a snapped hex lattice (5 tets per cell, a node layer on the floor) and XPBD (60 Hz, 10 substeps, co-rotational shape matching, volume constraints, edge damping, floor friction). Make the fins firmest and the clear body jelly softest.

Look: clear tinted jelly over a milky layer. The milky layer is its own embedded surface, cut by a wavy line along the flank that rises at the head into the mouth. Light it with key light absorbed through the jelly above it, measured from shadow-map depth. Draw throat pleats, a dark mouth groove, head tubercles and tail-stock knuckles in the shader from rest-space coordinates as bump-mapped relief. Add glossy dark bead eyes and a few trapped air bubbles. Render with refraction plus Beer–Lambert thickness from back-face depth, back-lit glow on the thin fins, a jelly-tinted floor shadow, PCSS soft shadows, contact AO, studio softbox reflections and GGX highlights, then PBR Neutral tone mapping.

Interaction: grab and stretch anywhere, with twist on scroll or a second finger. A "Blow a spout" button fires a column of rigid jelly drops from the blowhole along its deformed axis; the drops bounce, roll, land on the whale through its tets, and can be picked up and thrown.

UI (English, editorial style): masthead, live status pill, specimen panel (three colourways — Ocean, Slate, Lagoon; Firmness and Internal damping sliders; Blow / Reset; ¼ speed; Show mesh; Pause), live readouts (mass, volume %, length in cm snout-to-notch, loose drops), "Inside the experiment" notes, a WebGPU fallback and a stacked mobile layout.

title.zh: 菠萝果冻

summary.en: An interactive WebGPU/WGSL 3D gummy pineapple ring that can be grabbed and stretched, built in a single HTML file with Claude Opus 5.5 from a detailed prompt, compared against a GPT-6 Astra version.

prompt.text:
Create an interactive 3D scene called “Pineapple Jelly” - a thick, translucent gummy pineapple ring that users can grab, stretch, bend, and release. Everything must run directly in the browser in one standalone HTML file using genuine WebGPU and WGSL shaders.
The main priorities are convincing soft-body behavior, beautiful light refraction, and satisfying interaction.
MODEL

* A round pineapple slice with a genuine hole through its center.
* Thick, juicy flesh, a slightly scalloped outer edge, and softly rounded corners.
* Both cut faces must be equally detailed. The ring can be flipped and viewed from every angle.
* Golden translucent flesh with delicate radial fibers, small bubbles, and elongated pale juice cells embedded inside.
* No skin, leaves, or seeds. It should look like a pineapple ring made of gummy candy, not a doughnut.

MATERIAL AND LIGHTING

* Rich honey-yellow coloring, wet gloss, and soft subsurface-style light scattering.
* Refraction, thickness-dependent transparency, controlled highlights, and Fresnel reflections around the edges.
* Stretched, thinner areas should transmit more light.
* A warm, light background, soft studio lighting, and a grounded contact shadow.
* Avoid blown-out highlights, excessive bloom, and a hard-glass appearance.

PHYSICS

* Use a volumetric soft-body mesh with elastic connections and volume constraints, such as XPBD.
* Allow users to grab either the outer or inner edge and pull it in any direction.
* Deformation should spread naturally through neighboring regions: the hole stretches, the flesh bends, and the opposite side responds with a slight delay.
* After release, the ring should spring back softly, wobble a few times, and gradually settle.
* No instant snapping, endless oscillation, torn geometry, or collapsing central hole.
* Implement gravity and ground collisions. The ring should squash slightly on impact and recover its shape.
* Internal fibers, bubbles, and juice cells must deform with the flesh instead of remaining stationary.
* Clicking through the empty center must not grab the object.

INTERFACE

* A minimal editorial layout with generous whitespace.
* A large italic serif heading on the left: “Pineapple Jelly.”
* A compact “THE SPECIMEN” control panel on the right.
* Three color presets: Golden, Amber, and Rosé. Change the tint while preserving the material properties.
* Sliders for Firmness and Internal damping.
* Buttons: Give it a nudge, Reset, Turn it over, and Pause.
* Toggles: ¼ speed and Show mesh.
* Small live readouts for mass, volume relative to rest volume, and kinetic energy.
* All interface text in English.
* Support both mouse and touch interaction.

TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

* Use actual 3D geometry and WebGPU rendering, not a video or a Canvas 2D imitation.
* Generate all geometry and materials in code, without external models or image assets.
* Separate the simulation mesh from the smoother visual surface to maintain good performance.
* Display a clear fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
* Test strong stretching, inner-edge grabbing, flipping, resetting, and mobile interaction.

Save the finished result as pineapple-jelly-webgpu.html. Deliver the complete working file, not a mockup or implementation plan.
The final experience should feel like a soft, stretchy, appetizing gummy toy that is genuinely fun to squish.

prompt.text: Build a single HTML file with Three.js. It opens on an AutoCAD-style dark screen with a command line at the bottom, where real commands type out (LINE, OFFSET, COPY, INSERT, DIMLINEAR) while a crosshair cursor clicks and snaps on the drawing. Draft a 92 m² apartment in the order a drafter would: grid lines, a 400×400 mm column copied to every crossing, 300 mm block walls with 150 mm insulation, doors and windows, furniture at real sizes, dimensions, room areas and a 1:50 sheet. Then a selection window grabs the plan and the CAD screen turns into a 3D scene that builds the apartment step by step from the same drawing: concrete columns, block walls, insulation, lintels, windows and swinging doors, oak and tile floors, kitchen and bath, then every piece of furniture dropping into the spot where it was drawn, while the camera flies around it. Everything runs on one timeline, with a button that renders it frame by frame to a 1440p60 MP4 (WebCodecs + mp4-muxer) so the video never lags.

title.zh: 巨型机器人接住陨石

summary.zh: Fable 5.5 完全用代码制作了一部 82 秒、36 个镜头的动画短片，并在 Three.js 中渲染画面和合成声音。
summary.en: Fable 5.5 created an 82-second, 36-shot anime short entirely in code, rendering frames and synthesizing sound in Three.js.

prompt.text:
Create a 2D anime short for the web. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic.

Build it in three.js, render every frame in code and synthesize every sound. No video models, no image models, no stock art, no audio samples. Deliver one 1920x1080, 24 fps MP4 and a single self-contained HTML file that plays the film offline. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime.

Use bright summer theatrical anime and classic super-robot anime as the art style reference for the design, line work, painted backgrounds, color and atmosphere. The film is 82 seconds long, in 36 shots, with no dialogue. Its heroes are a tiny creature called Clawd and MEGA CLAWD, a giant robot built in his exact shape. No people appear in the film.

HEROES

Clawd: a small terracotta vinyl-toy creature. One wide rounded block is his head and body, with a flat face, two big glossy black eyes, a small mouth, two round side nubs for arms and four short stubby legs. All his acting is in the face and the squash of his body.

MEGA CLAWD: a 120 m anime mecha in Clawd's exact silhouette. Overlapping terracotta armor plates with cream and charcoal panels, bronze joints, bolts, vents and hand-lettered markings CLAWD-01 and 巨神. A dark glass visor where Clawd's eyes glow amber, a faceted crystal reactor that glows blue, blue thrusters in the soles. Its nubs unfold into big armored arms with clamp hands. It has slept for decades on the seabed under barnacles and kelp.

WORLD

An original Japanese seaside town on green hills: kawara tile roofs, laundry on balconies, telephone wires, a vermilion torii on the hill, a calico cat asleep on hot roof tiles, a glass wind chime on a porch. A harbour with a seawall, tetrapods, red and white lighthouses, small fishing boats and a wooden pier. A paper cup of blue shaved ice.

STORY

A blazing summer day. Clawd sits at the end of the pier eating blue shaved ice. A glint flares in the syrup: high above the clouds, a meteor ignites and comes down burning. The gulls burst from the wires and the wind chime stops. Clawd looks up, sets the cup carefully on a bollard and dives into the sea.

Through luminous cyan water he sinks toward a colossal shape on the seabed. Its visor lights up with his eyes. He drops through a hatch into the cockpit, grabs the two levers, and the reactor ignites. The bay boils into a white dome and MEGA CLAWD rises, sheets of water pouring off every plate, towering over the town. The ice cup trembles on the bollard.

The meteor splits a cumulus massif in two. MEGA CLAWD crouches, its arms unfold, and it launches in a ring of spray, climbing through the clouds to the edge of space. Near silence. The hands catch the meteor in a white flash. The armor glows hot, plates buckle, alarms go red in the cockpit while Clawd strains at the levers. The reactor surges, blue light runs into the arms, the meteor cracks with lightning and bursts into thousands of glowing fragments.

At dusk they fall over the town as shooting stars and the cat sits up to watch. MEGA CLAWD falls back smoking and crashes into the bay, and a wave breaks over the seawall. The giant kneels in the water, its visor eyes soften into a smile. Soaked, Clawd climbs back onto the pier, finds his cup, the ice has melted into blue water, and drinks it anyway, happy. End card: "Fable 5.5" in brush lettering, a red seal, the title MEGA CLAWD 巨神.

LIGHT

High-key anime light, never murky: a deep-blue summer sky, towering white cumulus with lavender shadows, a cobalt-to-turquoise sea with sun glitter. Underwater is luminous cyan with god rays, never black. The ending is a warm, colorful dusk. Cel shading with two hard tones and a crisp highlight, confident ink lines, gouache painted backgrounds, effects drawn like hand-painted effect cels.

SOUND

An original orchestral score on one summer theme: felt piano and strings at the start, the meteor cuts it off, a choir underwater, the theme returns as a heroic brass call when MEGA CLAWD rises, near silence before the impact, then a colossal hit, a glory chord on the shatter, and it resolves exactly on Clawd's sip. Surf, cicadas, gulls, the wind chime, splashes, the reactor, thrusters, alarms and lightning, all timed to the picture.

IT MUST NOT LOOK LIKE

- 3D: no plastic materials, CGI shading or game-engine lighting.
- Boxes: no plain blocks for houses, no sphere meteor, no scaled-up toy as the mecha.
- Vector art: no flat fills without paint, ink and volume.
- Murk: nothing dark, grey or muddy, no black ocean.
- Web animation: no floating, sliding, smooth software easing or 60 fps floaty motion.
- Particle mush for fire, water or energy.

CHECKS

Every frame is a pure function of film time. Before the final render, test every frame: nothing passes through anything, the cup sits on the bollard, the hands grip the levers and the meteor, Clawd stays terracotta in every light.

The result should feel huge, warm and beautiful, a summer blockbuster in bright anime colors. Before finishing, inspect random frames as still images. If any frame does not look completely like real 2D anime, keep improving it. Do not stop until every frame could pass as a still from a theatrical anime film.

prompt.text:
Build a real-time 3D pixel-art diorama of a singles tennis final ("big tennis"), "Hollybrook Open", as ONE self-contained HTML page: three.js r128 from cdnjs (no other external assets, no localStorage/eval/alert). Publish it as an artifact and also give me a standalone offline HTML file.

LOOK (same style as my earlier dioramas): a match in a club stadium on a floating island; orthographic isometric camera at 31 degrees, quarter turns (Q/E), wheel zoom, drag to orbit/pan, follow camera; render to a low-res target with a "Pixel size" slider 1-6 (default 2), depth outlines, a fixed 90-colour palette (OKLab snap) and Bayer dither; the stands/walls facing the camera lift away (doll's-house cutaway); a clubhouse with a clock, flags and an LED video board; practice court, garden, marquee, entrance plaza. Original/fictional names and sponsors only. English UI.

MATCH: two fictional pros (4 in the roster, men and women), a full match from walk-on to trophy: toss, warm-up, serves (ball bounce ritual, toss), rallies with real ball physics (drag, Magnus spin, surface bounce, net and cord), line judges' calls, umpire's announcements, commentary, scoring with games/sets/tie-breaks, changeovers, challenges with an Eagle Eye review, handshake, trophy ceremony with confetti. Formats: short set, one set, best of 3. Four court surfaces (Grass, Clay, Hard, Carpet) that change the court texture AND the ball's bounce. Day / Dusk / Night with four floodlight masts. Realistic numbers: first serve ~60-65%, aces 4-8%, double faults 2-4%, mean rally ~4-7 shots (shorter on grass/carpet, longer on clay).

PAGE: side control panel (stacked below on phones): match format, player pickers, New match, Skip ceremony, Auto-next, pause, speed; surface; time of day; Coach (tactics: go for it / play safe / rush the net / drop shot / lob, serve direction, "aim next shot" by clicking the court, Challenge button); camera modes (TV follow / whole club / close-up) and view controls; Match centre (stats, fastest serve, player cards); commentary feed; a TV-style scoreboard on the stage. Synthesized WebAudio sound (racket hits, bounces by surface, crowd, calls, ambience), off until the user enables it.

ENGINEERING: write the core (render pipeline, layout/plan, NAV grid, lighting) and a detailed CONTRACT.md (world conventions, module files, global names, BUS events, data model), then build the modules in parallel with separate agents in their own workspaces: court+net+boards, gear+grounds, clubhouse+stands+screen, people rig and actors, tennis kinematics, ball physics+mesh, rally AI, match flow (generator-coroutine scheduler with watchdogs), crowd+fx, audio, UI. Enforce unique global names (dupcheck), then integrate, play full matches on every surface and format, check four views, night, phone layout, performance. Reply to me in short Russian, don't paste the artifact URL unless asked.

prompt.text:
Build a standalone playable 3D action RPG in the current folder: "Ember Vale", a small open-world fantasy valley you can explore and fight in. Initialize a git repo here. All code, file names and UI text in English.

WORLD
- One open valley: a village with houses and a well, a forest, a river with a bridge, ancient ruins on a hill, and a boss arena at the ruins.
- Living details: grass and trees sway, smoke from chimneys, birds, fireflies at night, a full day-night cycle.

PLAYER
- Third-person hero with a sword. WASD to move, Shift to sprint, Space to dodge roll, left click to attack (3-hit combo), right click to block, 1–2 for spells (fireball, frost nova).
- HP, stamina and mana bars. Hit reactions, knockback, damage numbers, a hit-stop on heavy hits.

RPG
- Enemies: wolves in the forest, skeletons at the ruins, each with simple AI (patrol, chase, attack, flee at low HP).
- XP and level-ups, loot drops, an inventory with equippable sword and armor that change the hero's look.
- One quest chain from a villager NPC with dialogue: clear the wolves → find the key in the ruins → defeat the boss.
- Boss: a giant stone golem with 2 phases, a slam attack with a telegraphed shockwave, and a health bar at the top of the screen.
- HUD: minimap, quest tracker, hotbar.

LOOK
- Stylized, polished, soft lighting with shadows, fog in the distance, glowing spell effects, particles on hits.
- Camera: smooth third-person follow, drag to orbit, scroll to zoom.

prompt.text:
Build a polished browser-based 3D Rocket League-style game using Three.js.
Goal: Create a fully playable local web game that runs in the browser. The first screen should be the actual game, not a landing page.
Tech requirements:
Use Three.js for rendering.
Use a real physics engine, preferably Rapier.js, for car, ball, arena, wall, and goal physics.

Use TypeScript if the project already supports it, otherwise plain modern JavaScript is fine.
Use Vite for the dev server unless another stack already exists.
Keep the architecture clean: separate rendering, physics, controls, game state, UI/HUD, and assets.
Core gameplay:
Third-person controllable rocket car.

Large soccer ball with believable bouncy physics.

Enclosed arena with side walls, back walls, ceiling or high invisible bounds, and two goals.
Score detection when the ball crosses fully into a goal.
Reset after each goal with a countdown.
Match timer and score display.
Boost system:Boost meter from 0-100.
Hold boost key to accelerate with flame/trail effect.
Boost drains while active.
Boost pads around the arena refill boost.

Jump system:Single jump.
Optional second jump / flip if feasible.
Air control with pitch, yaw, and roll.

Car should feel responsive and arcade-like, not like a slow simulator.
Controls:
WASD or arrow keys: drive / steer.
Space: jump.
Shift: boost.
R: reset car.
C: toggle camera mode.
Esc or P: pause.
Camera:
Smooth chase camera behind the car.

Camera should follow car rotation and velocity while remaining readable.

Optional ball-cam toggle that keeps the ball in view.
Visual design:
Recreate a Rocket League-inspired feel, including branded-style presentation if desired.
Add a futuristic indoor stadium, colored goals, boost pads, arena trim, and energetic UI.
Add lighting, shadows, bloom or subtle postprocessing if performance allows.
Add clear team colors, goal colors, boost pad glow, trail effects, ball highlight, and simple particle effects.

Use generated, procedural, or available assets as appropriate.

Add a readable HUD with score, timer, boost meter, countdown, and goal celebration text.
Ensure the game works on common laptop screens and resizes correctly.
Physics feel:

Prioritize fun over realism.

The ball should be heavy but responsive.
Cars should have strong acceleration, drift-friendly turning, and stable recovery.
Avoid cars flipping uncontrollably from minor bumps.
Tune gravity, friction, restitution, angular damping, and impulses until gameplay feels good.
AI / opponent:
If time permits, add a simple bot opponent:Bot chases the ball.
Bot aims roughly toward the player goal.
Bot can boost occasionally.
Bot should be beatable, not perfect.

If bot is too risky, create a solo practice mode with two goals and a working scoreboard.

Implementation expectations:

Build the complete working game, not just a prototype shell.
Include all source files.
Add brief comments only where the logic is non-obvious.
Avoid overengineering.
Do not create a marketing homepage.

Verification:

Test the game in the browser.
Verify:The scene renders.
The car moves, turns, jumps, and boosts.
The ball collides with the car and arena.
Goals are detected correctly.
Score and timer update.
Reset after goal works.
Boost pads refill boost.
The camera does not clip badly or lose the car.
No major console errors.

Take at least one screenshot or use browser automation to confirm the canvas is nonblank.
Deliverable:
A local runnable browser game.

Provide the dev server URL.

Summarize controls and what was implemented.
Quality bar: Make it feel like an arcade sports game people would actually want to play for five minutes. Spend extra effort tuning car handling, camera smoothing, ball impact, boost feel, and goal feedback. A technically complete but boring physics demo is not acceptable.

A few more bits of feedback. I would like for you to test the game and work back and forth until you have a very strong match to the original Rocket League, including the car design for the Octane. It all should look nearly identical to the original. We are not going to sell or reproduce this. It's just for a visual test, so it is okay to make it look the same, as it will never be distributed.

Make sure that the actual map also looks like Champions Field and is a strong match for the original and very polished. It should look very good. The lighting and the gameplay should be true to life. The physics should feel correct according to the original game. Everything should work exactly the same as it did, from the flip resets to the tackles, to the goal explosions, to the smoke behind the ball when it goes fast, to all of the little small details that generally get missed. I really want you to pay attention to the details.

title.zh: Three.js牛顿摆：Opus对比Astra 6
title.en: Three.js Newton's cradle: Opus vs Astra 6

summary.zh: 作者给Opus 5.5和另一个名为Astra 6的模型提供了同一个详细提示和参考图片，让它们用Three.js制作带物理效果的牛顿摆单文件网页，并对比了两者的效果。
summary.en: A single-file Three.js Newton's cradle simulation with chrome balls and physics, built by Opus 5.5 from a long detailed prompt that included a reference image, compared against another model called Astra 6.

prompt.text:
Build a complete, single-file HTML/Three.js experience showing an exceptionally beautiful, interactive Newton’s cradle.

Use the attached image as the reference for the recognizable construction: five polished metal balls suspended inside two parallel chrome frames.

The result should feel like a luxury product filmed in a real photography studio, with convincing materials, graceful pendulum motion, and working collision physics.

Open directly into the finished scene. The first rendered frame must already be composed beautifully enough to use as a video thumbnail.

Prioritize three things equally: the beauty of the chrome, the physical construction, and the correctness of the motion.

Create a square, recording-ready composition that adapts to the browser without stretching. Center one substantial Newton’s cradle on a seamless warm-ivory studio surface.

Use a fixed camera positioned mostly in front of the cradle, slightly above the balls and slightly off-center. Show enough depth to distinguish the front and rear frames, while keeping all five balls easy to count.

Use a restrained product-photography perspective, approximately equivalent to a 70mm lens. Avoid a wide-angle appearance.

The cradle should fill most of the image. Leave comfortable margins for the full outward swing on both sides. Neither the balls nor the frame may leave the image during normal operation.

Keep the camera stationary throughout. No orbiting, automatic zoom, camera shake, or cuts.

Construct exactly five identical, perfectly round polished stainless-steel spheres.

At rest, their centers must form one horizontal row, with neighboring spheres touching. Their diameters, masses, and suspension lengths must match.

Use two slender, parallel, inverted-U chrome support frames with rounded corners, positioned in front of and behind the ball row.

Each ball must hang from two fine, taut suspension wires: one connected to the front support and one to the rear support. These wires constrain its motion to the shared vertical swing plane.

Include small, believable attachment details. The wires must connect visibly to the balls and frame.

The support frame and anchors remain completely stationary. Update the suspension geometry from the actual ball positions every frame. Wires must never stretch, disconnect, pass through the spheres, or wave independently.

Choose elegant proportions: substantial spheres, slender tubular supports, and enough suspension length for a satisfying swing. Avoid thick ropes, oversized frames, and a bulky decorative base.

Make the metal look convincingly reflective.

Use physically based metallic materials, high-quality sphere geometry, restrained surface roughness, and a carefully designed reflection environment.

Create large studio-softbox reflections that wrap naturally around the spheres and curved frame. Include broad bright highlights, darker reflected regions, and subtle warm tones from the studio.

The spheres must retain readable volume. Avoid flat gray metal, featureless white balls, plastic shading, and excessive bloom.

Build the reflection environment procedurally inside the file. Do not depend on downloaded HDR images or external texture assets.

Use a large soft key light from the upper-left, gentle fill from the opposite side, and a restrained rim light to define the metal against the background.

Add soft contact shadows beneath the frame and moving shadows beneath the balls. Shadows should follow the motion and help communicate height.

Keep the background uncluttered, with a very subtle ivory gradient. The overall image should feel calm, precise, and expensive.

Implement a working simplified Newton’s cradle simulation.

Represent each sphere as an equal-mass pendulum with an angular position and angular velocity. Gravity must drive the swing. Derive the sphere positions from the pendulum geometry.

Use stable time integration and collision handling that can propagate impacts through the full chain of touching balls.

A fixed timestep with sufficient substeps, event-based impacts, or a suitable constraint-aware solver is acceptable. Choose an approach that remains stable at different rendering frame rates.

Do not animate the balls with unrelated sine waves or a prerecorded sequence. The motion must respond to the simulated state and user input.

The required behavior is:

Release one outer ball. It swings into the row, transfers its motion through the chain, and approximately one ball swings outward at the opposite end.
The outgoing ball returns, strikes the row, and sends the original outer ball outward again.
Release two adjacent balls together from one side. Approximately two balls must swing outward together from the opposite side.
The remaining balls should stay close to their resting positions, allowing small physically plausible movement during impacts.
Motion transfers at contact. The outgoing balls must not begin swinging before the incoming balls reach the row.

Handle the chain of contacts consistently. A single order-dependent collision pass must not produce a different result when the direction reverses.

Collisions should approximately conserve momentum and kinetic energy over the brief impact interval, with small losses. Use gentle damping so the swing amplitude decreases gradually.

The simulation must not gain energy, accelerate indefinitely, visibly interpenetrate, jitter continuously, or send the entire row swinging after every impact.

The balls should accelerate toward the bottom of their arcs and slow naturally near their turning points. Avoid constant-speed swinging.

Start with the leftmost ball raised approximately 35 degrees and the other four hanging at rest. Hold this initial pose briefly, around 0.4 seconds, then release automatically.

The experience must immediately demonstrate the classic alternating motion without requiring a click. Continue running without an automatic reset.

Add a small, elegant control strip near the bottom edge with:

“1 BALL”
“2 BALLS”
Pause / Resume
Reset
“0.25×” slow motion

Keep these controls visually secondary. They must not overlap the cradle or its swing paths.

Selecting “1 BALL” or “2 BALLS” should reset the simulation, raise the corresponding leftmost ball or pair to the same release angle, briefly hold, and release.

Reset should restore and replay the currently selected mode.

Slow motion must scale simulated time while preserving the same physics. It must not change gravity, collision behavior, or suspension geometry.

Allow the user to drag either outer ball outward within its permitted swing plane, then release it. Clamp the drag angle to a sensible maximum, around 45 degrees. Keep its suspension wires taut throughout.

Add an “H” keyboard shortcut to hide or reveal the controls for clean recording.

Keep the experience silent. No music, collision sounds, particles, motion trails, impact flashes, explanatory overlays, large titles, model names, or decorative text.

Deliver one complete HTML file with inline CSS and JavaScript. Use one consistently pinned Three.js version and matching modules if needed.

No build step, backend, external models, external textures, or HDR downloads.

Initialize the renderer, camera, lighting, materials, and starting pose before revealing the canvas. Avoid a visible black startup frame.

Support browser resizing without distorting the scene. Aim for smooth performance on a normal laptop and cap pixel density sensibly.

Before finishing, check that:

Exactly five spheres remain visible and correctly suspended.
The complete frame and maximum swing fit inside the square composition.
One-ball mode transfers approximately one ball at each impact.
Two-ball mode transfers approximately two balls at each impact.
Pause, reset, slow motion, and dragging work.
Chrome reflections remain readable throughout the motion.
The scene appears immediately and produces no runtime errors.

Return the complete working HTML.

summary.zh: 创作者用同一段详细的Three.js提示词，对比了Claude Opus 5.5和Gemini 4 Argon生成的可交互3D毛绒西瓜效果，并比较了API成本。
summary.en: A comparison of Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon generating an interactive 3D furry watermelon in a browser using the same detailed Three.js prompt, with API cost comparison.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML page (no build step) showing an interactive 3D "Fluffy Watermelon" covered in long fur, rendered with WebGL using three.js r147 (UMD build: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.147.0/build/three.min.js). All UI text in English.

SCENE & LOOK
- Full-screen canvas on a soft watermelon-flesh pink studio background: vertical gradient #ECB3AB → #F7CFC7 (lighter band in the middle) → #E8A9A0, used as the scene background.
- A big oblong watermelon lying on its side along the X axis: half-length 1.38, radius 0.98, blunt barrel-like ends, small dimples at both ends, slightly flattened belly, subtle surface unevenness. Start in a 3/4 view (about -0.32 rad around Y, 0.1 rad tilt), camera FOV 30°, framed to fill ~80% of the height.
- Rind pattern under the fur: light green (#A8D66B) with 16 dark green (#1C4D1C) stripes running stem to blossom, with ragged finger-like edges (sine meander + value noise), plus a pale cream "field spot" on the underside. Each hair takes the colour of its own root, so the stripes stay crisp through the fur.
- A short, dried, ribbed stem stub at one end with a slightly domed pale cut cap, and a thin curly helical tendril springing from beside it.
- One directional light from upper-left-front, wrap diffuse, Kajiya-Kay anisotropic highlight along the hair tangent, darker roots (occlusion by hair height), slight per-hair brightness variation.

FUR (most important: it must look crisp, never blurry)
- Fur length 0.2 units. Hairs grow out along the normal, then bend: combed from the stem end toward the blossom end and draped down the flanks (no whorls at the ends), plus slight gravity.
- Undercoat: shell texturing with ~64 instanced shells of the body mesh that reach only 50% of the fur length. Procedural hair cells in UV space (density scaled so one cell is ~3.4 device pixels at the default view), two hair populations (long + fine underfur), hairs gathering into locks toward their tips, analytic anti-aliased coverage, alpha blending, shells write depth. Fade shells out where the surface is seen edge-on and discard faint fragments, so no dotted rim appears at the outline.
- Guard hairs: ~90,000 individual tapered, camera-facing ribbon strands (instanced, 7 segments each) that follow exactly the same bend function, with a minimum width of ~0.75 px so they stay sharp. Draw them twice: once before the shells and once after (depth-tested), so faint edge fur never hides them and they always lie crisply on top.
- Always render at the device's full pixel ratio (capped at 2) and NEVER lower it for performance. If frames are slow, reduce the shell count first (down to 32), then the guard-hair count.

INTERACTION
- Drag to rotate freely (trackball style) with inertia after a flick. The fur lags behind the rotation through a damped spring and flops back. Gentle idle breeze in the fur; after 3 s without input, a slow auto-turn.
- Mouse wheel / pinch to zoom (smooth dolly). Double-click or "0" resets with an eased animation. Arrow keys rotate.
- Custom cursor: the native grab hand plus a thin dark 46 px ring that follows the pointer and shrinks while dragging. Hovering gently parts the fur under the cursor, as if stroking it.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion (no idle spin, no breeze).

UI & ROBUSTNESS
- Bottom-left caption: "Fluffy Watermelon" and a hint "Drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · Double-click to reset" (on touch devices: "Drag to rotate · Pinch to zoom") that fades after the first interaction. Font: Onest from Google Fonts with system fallbacks.
- Guard against a zero-sized container at load: clamp width/height to at least 1 and, every frame, recover from any non-finite camera distance or rotation state.
- Show a small on-page note if the WebGL context is lost or a shader fails to compile, and a fallback message if WebGL is unavailable.

prompt.text:
Build "Whole Melon": a single self-contained HTML file (all JS/CSS inline, no build step, no libraries) with a big whole watermelon made of glossy jelly that you can grab, wobble and cut into pieces with a knife. Render with raw WebGPU (WGSL); if WebGPU is missing, show a clean fallback card.

SHAPE AND MATERIAL
- The melon is a signed distance field: an ellipsoid (~32 cm long) lying on its side with a softly flattened belly.
- Layers by depth under the skin: dark-green skin with irregular darker stripes running pole to pole (seamless all the way around), a pale pith band, then translucent red flesh that brightens toward the rind. Add a pale yellow field spot on the belly, a stem scar at one end and a blossom end at the other.
- About 700 seeds in a three-lobed ring at roughly two thirds of the radius (teardrops, wide end pointing outward), plus tiny air bubbles. Mesh seeds only near cut faces; a seed the knife goes through is kept by one side and eased just under the new face, so it shows through a thin film of jelly.
- Three varieties: Crimson, Golden, Rosé.

PIECES AND CUTTING
- Every piece is the melon SDF clipped by the half-spaces of the cuts that made it, with the fresh edges rounded (smooth max). All pieces share the melon's original rest frame, so rind, pith, stripes and seeds stay exactly where they grew.
- Knife tool: the user draws a line across the melon. Read the stroke on top of what it crosses to get a vertical blade plane. For each piece the plane passes through, fit the piece's best rotation, carry the plane into rest space, and split the piece in two.
- Build the new pieces cooperatively (generators with a per-frame time budget) while a steel knife (brushed blade, wooden handle with rivets) lines up over the stroke and presses a groove into the jelly. Swap the new pieces in the moment the edge breaks through, carrying over the position and velocity of the flesh they came from, and let the blade wedge them apart as it sinks. Allow up to about 24 pieces and reject slivers.
- For each piece: a surface-nets render skin (evaluate only the blocks near the surface, one Newton step onto it), a hex lattice in the piece's principal frame with boundary nodes snapped onto the surface, and a fast barycentric embedding.

PHYSICS (XPBD on the CPU, fixed 60 Hz, 6 substeps)
- Cell-wise co-rotational shape matching (8-node cells, warm-started rotation, strain stiffening), tet volume constraints for near-incompressibility, rind firmer than flesh.
- Edge damping, plus damping of each piece's deformation relative to its rigid motion (never its fall or tumble), rolling resistance on the table, and sleep when calm.
- Piece-to-piece contact against each other's exact SDF in a best-fit frame; sleeping pieces act as walls. Floor contact with Coulomb friction.
- Hand tool: grab any piece and pull (soft patch attachment, with enough reach to drag pieces across a wide table). Scroll or a second finger twists while holding. Pinch or scroll zooms; dragging the empty table orbits the camera.

RENDERING (a photographic product shot)
- Procedural studio: pale paper sweep, overhead softbox, back-left strip light, cool fill card.
- Jelly: front faces refract the scene behind by the view-ray thickness (nearest-back-face pass), with Beer–Lambert absorption per material, milky scattering in the pith, a back-lit glow at thin edges, sugar glints, Fresnel studio reflections and GGX highlights.
- Seeds, bubbles and the knife are drawn before the jelly, so they are seen refracted through it.
- Normals follow the jelly's local deformation (cofactor of the node-averaged deformation gradient).
- A soft key shadow coloured by what the light crossed first (rosy through flesh, dark through rind), plus contact occlusion from a top-down height map. MSAA, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping.

UI (editorial, like a material study)
- Kicker "Material Studies / No. 010" and a big italic serif title "Whole / Melon."
- A panel with Tool (Hand / Knife), Variety, Firmness and Internal damping sliders, Nudge, Reset, ¼ speed, Show mesh and Pause.
- Live readouts: mass, volume %, kinetic energy, piece count. A collapsible "Inside the experiment" note.
- Responsive down to phones.

Quality bar: it should look and move like a real glossy jelly watermelon, and every cut face should look like a sliced jelly melon with seeds just under the surface. Test headlessly with screenshots: the whole melon, mid-cut, many pieces, a close-up of a cut face, and mobile.
