title.zh: 《The First Spark》程序化手绘动画短片

summary.zh: 作者用一份很长的结构化提示词（并附带一张参考风格图）让 Opus 5.5 用 JavaScript/Canvas 2D 纯代码程序化生成了一部手绘风格动画短片《The First Spark》，成本比用 Astra 模型低约三成。
summary.en: A procedural, hand-drawn-style animated short ('The First Spark') rendered with JavaScript/Canvas 2D by Opus 5.5 from a long structured prompt with a reference style image, ~30% cheaper than Astra's.

prompt.text:
PROJECT: THE FIRST SPARK — Procedural Animated Short Film

You are a senior creative coder, generative artist, animation director, and JavaScript graphics engineer.

Your task is to create a visually stunning, fully animated short film using procedural JavaScript drawing.

I have attached a reference image showing a minimalist black-ink animation on an off-white background.

Use the reference to understand the visual language, but create an original animation with its own story, composition, and movement.

Do not create a slideshow, static illustration, or simple particle demo. Build a genuine animated short film with evolving scenes, expressive character animation, cinematic transitions, and continuous visual storytelling.

1. Technical requirements

Build the project using:

JavaScript
HTML5 Canvas 2D
requestAnimationFrame for real-time playback
Procedural geometry and vector-based drawing
Bezier curves, paths, particles, and custom brush strokes
Deterministic animation based on a master timeline

All visual elements must be generated through JavaScript code.

Do not use:

AI image-generation APIs
AI video-generation APIs
External images or pre-rendered video
Stock footage
CSS-only animation
Static illustrations disguised as animation

The animation must be genuinely generated by code.

You may use lightweight JavaScript libraries if they meaningfully improve the animation, but prioritize Canvas 2D.

2. Visual direction

Create a hand-drawn, minimalist, experimental animation.

Visual characteristics:

Warm off-white paper background
Deep black ink illustrations
Slightly imperfect hand-drawn outlines
Organic brush strokes
Variable line thickness
Ink splashes and subtle paper grain
Expressive silhouette-based character design
Fluid, organic movement
Occasional dramatic camera movements
Cinematic composition

The visual result should feel like a professional independent animated short film.

Avoid generic geometric motion graphics, repetitive particle effects, and simple bouncing shapes.

Every scene should have a clear visual purpose.

3. Story: THE FIRST SPARK

Create an original 60-second animated short film.

The story follows a tiny character that emerges from a drop of black ink and gradually discovers how to create a world.

SCENE 1 — THE BEGINNING (0–8 seconds)

An empty off-white canvas.

A tiny black ink droplet appears in the center.

The droplet begins trembling.

Small irregular brush strokes emerge from it.

The ink slowly transforms into a tiny living character.

The character opens its eyes and looks around.

The camera gradually moves closer.

SCENE 2 — DISCOVERY (8–18 seconds)

The character begins walking across the empty world.

Its movement must feel alive, with animated limbs, body deformation, and subtle secondary motion.

Every step leaves behind small ink marks.

The character notices one of these marks and touches it.

The mark begins growing into an organic structure.

SCENE 3 — CREATION (18–32 seconds)

The character discovers that its movements can create new objects.

It draws a line through the air.

The line becomes a tree.

More brush strokes emerge and transform into hills, plants, and abstract structures.

The camera follows the character as the world expands.

Objects must visibly grow and transform through procedural drawing rather than suddenly appearing.

SCENE 4 — CHAOS (32–44 seconds)

The character loses control of its creation.

Black ink spreads rapidly.

The landscape becomes distorted.

Trees twist into abstract shapes.

Ink splashes fill the screen.

The camera shakes subtly as the character runs.

The animation becomes faster and more intense.

Use fluid transitions between all visual elements.

SCENE 5 — THE FIRST SPARK (44–55 seconds)

The character stops running.

Everything becomes still.

A small glowing point appears in its hand.

This is the only moment where a subtle warm accent color may be used.

The character releases the light.

The light expands into a circular wave.

The chaotic ink reorganizes into a beautiful, balanced landscape.

The camera pulls back to reveal the completed world.

SCENE 6 — ENDING (55–60 seconds)

The character stands on a small hill and looks toward the horizon.

The camera slowly moves backward.

The entire landscape gradually transforms into a single small ink drawing on the original empty canvas.

Fade to off-white.

End.

4. Animation quality requirements

This is the most important part of the project.

Every scene must contain actual animation.

The character must have:

Procedurally animated walking and running
Expressive body language
Head and body rotation
Squash and stretch
Anticipation and follow-through
Smooth transitions between poses

Environmental elements must have:

Organic growth animations
Continuous subtle movement
Non-repetitive procedural variation
Smooth transformations between shapes

Implement a virtual camera with:

Position
Zoom
Rotation
Smooth tracking
Cinematic easing

Use layered depth and camera movement to create visual richness.

Do not rely on random movement alone.

The animation should be deliberately choreographed around the story.

5. Timeline and rendering architecture

Create a centralized animation timeline.

Every visual state must be determined by the current timeline position.

Implement a function similar to:

renderFrame(time)

The function must render the correct animation frame for any requested timestamp.

Use seeded randomness so that rendering the same timestamp always produces the same image.

Do not make the animation dependent on the number of previous frames rendered.

This is essential for deterministic video export.

Target specifications:

Resolution: 1920 × 1080

Aspect ratio: 16:9

Frame rate: 30 FPS

Duration: 60 seconds

Provide an option to switch to 1080 × 1920 vertical format for social media.

6. Preview and controls

Create a local web interface that allows me to:

Play and pause the animation
Restart the animation
Scrub through the timeline
Jump between scenes
Adjust playback speed
Switch between horizontal and vertical formats
Preview the animation in real time

Display the current timestamp and scene name.

7. Video export

Implement a reliable video export workflow.

The final animation must be exportable as a high-quality MP4 file.

Use deterministic frame-by-frame rendering to avoid dropped frames or inconsistent timing.

You may use a suitable browser rendering pipeline, a frame-sequence exporter, or FFmpeg.

Do not assume that recording the browser window in real time is sufficient for production-quality export.

Provide a simple export command or interface.

8. Development process

Do not attempt to create the entire film as one enormous, untested code block.

Work in stages.

First:

Create the project architecture.
Implement the Canvas rendering engine.
Implement the deterministic timeline.
Create the character animation system.
Build Scene 1 as a fully functional visual prototype.
Run the project and inspect the visual result.

After the first scene works, continue implementing the remaining scenes.

Test the animation at multiple timestamps.

Check for rendering errors, broken transitions, inconsistent character proportions, and performance problems.

If a scene looks too simplistic, improve its procedural drawing and choreography.

9. Deliverables

Provide:

Complete JavaScript source code
Working local animation preview
Editable scene definitions
Reusable character animation system
Reusable procedural drawing functions
Video export functionality
Instructions for running the project

The final result must be a functioning animation, not just a technical demonstration.

Start by implementing the first scene and the core animation engine. Once the prototype is functional, continue with the remaining scenes.

prompt.text:
Create a single, self-contained HTML file using vanilla JavaScript and HTML5 Canvas 2D to procedurally animate a running wild red fox in crisp 1080p (Full HD). No external assets or libraries.

Specifications:

Canvas & Resolution:Native resolution: 1920 × 1080 pixels.
Style: Smooth 2D vector-style rendering (anti-aliased Bezier paths, linear/radial gradients, dynamic shading).

Fox Rigging & Locomotion:Spine Dynamics: Smooth multi-joint spline showing agile spinal flexion and extension, with a slightly arched back at the gathered phase of the gallop.
Leg Kinematics: 4 slender, articulated limbs driven by Inverse Kinematics (IK) for a full rotary gallop, with light, springy foot placement.
Secondary Motion: A long, bushy tail streaming behind with inertial, wave-like counterbalancing (spring-damped segments), shoulder-blade sliding, subtle ear flicks, and a stabilized, forward-locked head gaze.
Styling: Rich russet-orange coat with layered fur-tuft edges and soft gradient shading. Cream-white chest, muzzle, and belly. Black "stocking" lower legs, black-backed ears, and a white-tipped tail. Amber eyes with a narrow pupil, a pointed snout, and fine whisker strokes.

High-Res Parallax Environment:
Multi-layer 1080p wild woodland-meadow backdrop:Gradient dawn sky and a distant misty horizon with soft atmospheric haze.
Mid-ground with procedural pine and birch tree silhouettes and rolling hills, each layer scrolling at a different speed.
Foreground terrain of tall grass, ferns, and fallen leaves, with a high-speed particle system generating kicked-up leaves, dirt, and dust plumes behind the paws.

Performance:Optimized for stable 60 FPS execution via requestAnimationFrame.

title.zh: 天空鲸鱼动画短片

summary.zh: 一部约100秒的2D动画风格短片，讲述一头天空鲸的故事。每一帧都用JS和Python代码绘制，多组智能体连续工作19小时完成，没有使用任何视频或图像模型。
summary.en: A 100-second 2D anime-style short film about a sky whale, rendered entirely in code with JS and Python. Teams of agents worked for 19 hours, with no video or image models.

prompt.text:
Create a complete, 100-second, 2D anime short film, drawn and animated entirely in code for the web. It must look exactly like real Japanese theatrical anime, as if every frame were lifted from a finished Studio Ghibli feature with a 500-million-dollar budget. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime: not 3D animation, not a moving illustration, not a stylised web graphic, not AI art.

Deliver it as self-contained HTML/JavaScript scenes that render every frame deterministically to a canvas, plus a render pipeline that exports each frame to PNG and encodes the final film at 1920x1080, 48 frames per second. Use any tools, libraries, references, simulations or techniques you want, including 3D maths, fluid simulation and depth buffers, as long as the final image looks 100% like hand-drawn and hand-painted 2D anime. Draw everything in code. No AI-generated images, no stock footage, no traced photographs.

Use Studio Ghibli films (Laputa, Nausicaa, Porco Rosso, Howl's Moving Castle, Spirited Away, The Wind Rises) as the reference for design, line work, painted backgrounds, colour, light and atmosphere, and Studio Trigger for the confidence of the key poses and the punch of the big moments. Study real humpback and blue whale motion for every movement of the main character. No people appear in the film.

THE MAIN CHARACTER: THE OLD WHALE
An ancient sky-whale that is also an airship: a creature and a vessel at once, so old that the two have grown together. About 120 metres long.
- Hull: overlapping riveted plates in weathered teal and sea-green, chipped and patched, with rust blooms in burnt orange and red, every seam and rivet crisp. A cream, ribbed keel runs along the belly like the planking of an old boat.
- Back: a hanging garden. Moss beds, sod clumps, wildflowers, one wind-bent pine tree and small shrubs ride on its back, with a weathered mast, rigging lines and long faded pennants that stream in the wind.
- Fins: great fan-shaped pectoral fins built like junk sails, with wooden spars and cream sailcloth painted with red stripes, opening and closing like breath.
- Eye: a round brass porthole with a warm amber glow; its light is the whale's emotion.
- Breath: a blowhole vent that exhales a plume of warm vapour, like steam from an old engine.
- Tail: a broad fluke whose stroke drives the whole body.
It must stay perfectly on-model from every angle and distance, from a 900-pixel close-up to a 40-pixel speck in an extreme wide.

THE POD (night only)
Five more sky-whales of the same kind, each with its own silhouette and personality, each with a glowing amber eye: Drover (large, heavy, tall sails), Pip (small and young), Elder (very old, carrying a big pine and a dense garden), Mend (patched and gentle) and Swift (lean and fast, the one who leaps).

THE FILM: FIVE MOVEMENTS, ONE JOURNEY (one day, dawn to night)

I. DAWN: THE BREAKOUT (21.0 s, one continuous take, no cuts)
Open on a vast, scenic sky at first light: a sea of cloud below, pale gold on the horizon, silence. Hold long enough to breathe. Then the cloud sea begins to swell and bulge. Something enormous is rising underneath. The Old Whale breaks out slowly and majestically: the cloud domes, tears and parts along its snout first, then its brow, then its garden. Real cloud physics: vapour pushed aside by a moving solid, rolling collars, torn edges, sheets of cloud sliding off the hull and fraying into strands, a wake closing behind. The fins open, the pine tree sways, the pennants unfurl, the eye catches the sun, and the whale breaches into the golden sky. The camera is a single unbroken crane move: it starts low near the cloud surface, rises with the whale and pulls back to reveal its full scale against the sunrise. Slow, heavy, inevitable, then soaring.

II. MORNING: THE CROSSING (19.0 s, three shots)
The whale crosses a vast valley in clean morning light. A wide from high above: a patchwork world of fields, forests, a winding river and hills a kilometre below, painted like a Ghibli background, with the whale small and swimming above it. Then a close shot of a great fin stroking through the air, every spar and stripe crisp. Then the whale enters a towering cream cloud bank: the cloud must swallow the hull AND everything on its back together. Nothing on the whale may ever show through a cloud that is in front of it.

III. STORM: THE SQUALL (18.0 s)
The whale flies into a storm. The light dies to slate blue and grey. Rain streaks across the frame. Inside the storm cloud the whale labours through the gloom, and lightning cracks: each strike must light the whale itself, a hard rim of white light along the hull and fins and a lit silhouette, with the cloud interiors flashing from within. Not a flat brightness flicker. Then the whale bursts out of the top of the storm: the cloud is ripped open, torn edges, shadowed interiors with structure and light pouring through the tear, and the whale lifts clear into the sunlight under a rainbow, cream and lilac cloud falling away below it. Relief.

IV. DUSK: THE CALLING (17.6 s, two shots joined by a hard cut)
A calm sea at dusk. Sky from apricot (#f2b27a) to rose (#c78aa0), the low sun laying a road of light on the water, violet shadows (#6f5f86). The whale floats low over the smooth sea, its reflection beneath it. It draws a breath and blows: a soft, translucent plume of vapour, never a solid cut-out. Then it calls, head lifting, eye brightening. Then the "ma": a true held stillness, only the gentlest breath of life, while the call hangs in the air. And then a HARD CUT ON THE SILENCE, Ghibli-style, to an extreme lonely wide: the same sky, the same sun at the same height, the same world, but the whale is now tiny on an endless sea. It swims, not slides, slowly across the sun's path on the water, each fluke stroke surging it forward, its reflection trailing beneath. No answer comes.

V. NIGHT: THE ANSWER (24.5 s)
Moonlight on a sea of cloud in indigo and lilac, stars, a full moon. The camera is locked off at first, and the Old Whale crosses the frame alone. A close shot as it sings its song under the moon. Far away, warm points of light appear along the distant cloud band: eyes. Then, one by one, the pod rises out of the cloud sea: the cloud heaves ahead of each snout, parts from snout to tail, a collar of cloud forms behind and rolls out, cel-painted sheets of cloud slide off each hull and fray away, and the opening heals slowly behind. Drover, then Pip and Elder, then Mend, then Swift leaping clear. The Old Whale swims into the pod. The camera pulls back, slowly and not too far, so that the whole family stays big and readable in the frame, on top of the cloud sea and never buried in it, and together they swim toward the moon. Hold on the final image until it settles.

THE ANIME QUALITY STANDARD
Every frame must look as if it was drawn by professional anime animators and painted by master background artists for a finished theatrical film.
- Line art: confident, hand-inked line work with real variation in weight and pressure, heavier on the silhouette, delicate inside. The ink must be stable from frame to frame and must never re-roll, boil or switch between single and double lines.
- Colour: traditional cel colouring with clean colour areas and simple hard-edged shadows (kage) tinted toward the sky's fill light, never grey.
- Light: a cel rim of light inside the ink on every sun-facing or moon-facing edge, light wrap from the real background around the silhouette, a scene key that multiplies through the character, and atmospheric haze with real depth.
- Backgrounds: richly detailed, hand-painted gouache backgrounds with visible brushwork, natural colour variation, layered depth and no repeated elements. The whale is the subject; backgrounds support it and never compete with it.
- Clouds: the heart of this film. Painted like Ghibli clouds (soft, massive, sculpted forms with warm tops and cool bellies), but moving like real vapour: a 3D fluid with the whale as a moving solid inside it, parting, rolling, tearing and healing. Never a rigid lump, never glassy ovals, never a flat cream blanket, never cloud pieces that pop on or swap order in a single frame.
- Finish: the final finishing layer of a theatrical release: crisp ink, clear cel light, rich but controlled colour, density instead of brightening contrast, light-side diffusion and a fine film grain that changes on a 24 Hz cycle.
- Motion: real weight and whale-like movement. The whale moves on every single frame at 48 fps with smooth, heavy, eased motion; every fin, pennant, pine branch and sail has overlapping action and follow-through. Hand-drawn texture and grain update on twos (24 Hz) so the image keeps its drawn feel.
- Direction: cinematic anime staging and composition, deliberate camera grammar (a crane, locked-off wides, a pull-back, a hard cut used only where it means something), and pacing that starts quietly, builds, breaks open in the storm, falls to silence at dusk and resolves at night.

THE SOUND
- Score: an original orchestral score in the register of Joe Hisaishi, played on real sampled instruments only (strings, woodwinds, horn, piano, percussion; VSCO 2 Community Edition and the Salamander Grand Piano, rendered through sfizz). A short motif (D, A, B in D major pentatonic) is the whale's character and carries through all five movements: a swelling bloom as the whale breaches at dawn, open and lyrical across the valley, tense and restrained in the storm, withdrawn to nothing at dusk, and returned warmly as the pod answers at night. Three or four voices at a time, sparse, intentional, always leaving room for the whale.
- Whale voices: built from real humpback recordings blended with mechanical tones (brass valves, steam, creaking timber), so they sound like a living creature that is also a ship: waking songs, the dusk call, breaths from brass vents and steaming lungs, contented hums, effort groans, and a distinct voice for each pod whale. Use them intentionally, never everywhere.
- Air: wind and whooshes only as extremely subtle accents on fins, the storm burst and far cloud-breaks. No wind beds, no room tone.
- Depth: place every sound at its on-screen distance. Near sounds are full and wide, far sounds are quieter, darker, more reverberant and narrower, sounds inside cloud are muffled, and the sound perspective changes at each cut. The music holds one steady, near distance.
- Silence: true digital silence where the film is silent, especially across the hard cut at dusk.
- Loudness: very quiet and intimate, about -32 LUFS integrated, true peak no higher than -3 dBTP.

IT MUST NOT LOOK LIKE
- 3D: no plastic materials, CGI shading, visible polygons, game-engine lighting or computer-perfect perspective.
- SVG or vector art: no simple geometric shapes, perfect curves, uniform outlines, flat corporate illustration or basic gradients.
- Web animation: no sliding layers, constant bobbing, floating parts, a whale that slides instead of swims, a whale pinned to the same spot on screen, or puppet-like joint rotation.
- AI art: no warped shapes, melted details, flickering, boiling textures or a changing whale design.
- Glitches: no decor that flickers or pops in and out, nothing on the whale's back showing through cloud in front of it, no cloud shards popping on and off, no sky or sea that stutters while the whale moves, no hard rectangular shadow edges, no ghosting dissolves, no stray white lines that don't belong to the world.
- Non-anime art: no Western cartoon designs, realistic rendering, soft painterly shading on the whale or generic digital illustration.
- Amateur work: no stiff poses, empty backgrounds, repeated elements, muddy colours, placeholders or unfinished details.
- Bad sound: no synth pads, no procedural tones, no AI-generated audio, no harp, nothing loud.

PROCESS
Design first: lock a model sheet for the Old Whale and the five pod whales before any animation. Then style frames per movement, then motion tests, then full movements. Before finishing, inspect random frames as still images and every frame at full rate for flicker and pops. Have fresh eyes review every render. If any frame does not look completely like a still from a theatrical anime film, keep improving it. Do not stop until every frame could pass as one.

The result should feel awe-inspiring, nostalgic and full of wonder: a lonely old giant of the sky calling out across the world at the end of the day, and finally being answered.

title.zh: 小熊猫科达与巨型桃子
title.en: Red panda Koda and the giant peach

summary.zh: 作者先用Opus 5.5生成了一只名为Koda的小熊猫的角色设定图，再用Seedance 2.5根据详细的文字提示词将其制作成30秒的3D动画短片，整个过程通过Vidfield.ai完成。
summary.en: A 30-second cinematic 3D animated short about a red panda named Koda chasing a giant peach, made by first generating a character reference sheet with Opus 5.5 and then animating it into video with Seedance 2.5 using a detailed written prompt, created via Vidfield.ai.

prompt.text:
Create an exactly 30-second vertical 9:16 premium 3D animated adventure-comedy short. Use the attached @ Koda character sheet as the exact visual reference for Koda. Maintain his identical face, amber-brown eyes, cream facial markings, rust-red fur, dark legs, rounded ears, compact proportions and enormous ringed fluffy tail throughout every frame. The reference defines Koda's appearance only.
The entire story takes place on one continuous sunny green mountain hillside surrounded by distant forested mountains. One old peach tree grows from the slope. It has a thick stable trunk, several strong main branches and one thinner flexible outer branch. One enormous ripe golden-orange peach hangs near the end of that thinner branch. A large dense leafy bush grows directly below that side of the tree. A long fallen bamboo pole lies several meters away on the same hillside. Farther downhill, a narrow wooden footbridge crosses a shallow mountain stream. Keep this geography fixed throughout the entire video.
Koda desperately wants the enormous peach. His first idea is simply to climb the tree. He reaches the fruit but moves too far onto the thin outer branch, causing the branch to bend gradually under his weight. He almost touches the peach, loses traction and slides off into the huge soft bush below. Koda refuses to give up. He returns with the long fallen bamboo pole, places it diagonally against a strong fork in the tree and climbs it like a simple ladder. This time he reaches the peach and pulls it free. The peach is far heavier than expected, drops onto the clearly sloping hillside and begins rolling downhill because of gravity. Koda chases it, jumps onto the rolling fruit and accidentally begins riding it. He becomes thrilled and celebrates until he notices a narrow wooden footbridge directly ahead. The peach is much wider than the bridge entrance. It wedges between the entrance posts, stops instantly and Koda's forward momentum sends him harmlessly into a giant pile of dry leaves beside the bridge.
Open at 0:00 with a low wide tracking shot of Koda already sprinting uphill through tall green grass toward the peach tree. His short legs move rapidly and his huge fluffy tail streams naturally behind him. As he reaches the tree, he suddenly looks upward and sees the enormous peach glowing among the leaves. He skids to a stop, stares at it, looks at the trunk and immediately becomes determined.
From 0:02 to 0:05, follow Koda as he rapidly climbs the thick trunk using all four paws. His claws visibly grip the bark while his hind feet push upward. His tail stays naturally attached behind him and reacts only to his body movement. He pulls himself onto a strong main branch and begins moving toward the peach.
From 0:05 to 0:08, show a clear wide side view of Koda carefully stepping from the thick branch onto the thinner outer branch. The peach is just beyond his reach. As Koda moves farther away from the trunk, his weight causes the thin branch to bend downward gradually. The branch does not bend before Koda steps onto it and does not move for any unexplained reason.
From 0:08 to 0:11, Koda slowly stretches one front paw toward the peach. His paw almost reaches it. He leans slightly farther forward and briefly touches the peach's fuzzy surface. He smiles. His rear paws then lose traction on the increasingly sloped branch. Koda freezes, his eyes widen and he begins sliding backward along the branch.
From 0:11 to 0:13, Koda slides completely off the branch and falls directly downward into the large dense bush below. He disappears into the foliage with a huge soft leafy FWUMP. The bush shakes. After a short comedic pause, Koda's head slowly rises from between the leaves. Small leaves cling to his fur. He looks upward toward the peach again and his dazed expression changes into stubborn determination.
From 0:13 to 0:16, Koda jumps from the bush, runs several meters across the same hillside and grabs the end of the long fallen bamboo pole using both front paws. He drags it across the grass toward the peach tree. The bamboo scrapes naturally over the ground. Koda struggles because the pole is much longer than his body, but he never uses or removes his tail as a tool.
From 0:16 to 0:18.5, show the complete setup clearly in one wide shot. Koda positions one end of the bamboo on the grassy ground near the tree. He lifts the other end with both front paws while the grounded end remains in contact with the earth. As Koda walks forward underneath the rising pole, the bamboo rotates upward around its grounded end until the raised end settles securely against a strong fork in the thick tree. The bamboo now forms a stable diagonal climbing pole. Koda steps back, studies it and smiles proudly.
From 0:18.5 to 0:21, Koda climbs the angled bamboo with all four paws. His front paws pull while his hind feet push against the bamboo surface. The bamboo remains stable against the tree. His fluffy tail remains physically connected to his body and trails naturally behind him. He reaches the upper end beside the enormous peach.
From 0:21 to 0:23.5, Koda braces his hind feet against the bamboo and grabs the peach with both front paws. He pulls once and nothing happens. He adjusts his grip and pulls much harder. The short fruit stem stretches under the force. With one final effort the stem breaks with a clear POP. Koda is suddenly holding the enormous peach and gives a huge triumphant smile.
From 0:23.5 to 0:25.5, the peach's weight immediately pulls downward. Koda cannot support it. The peach slips from his paws and drops onto the steep grassy slope below with a heavy THUMP. Because the ground visibly slopes downhill, the peach naturally begins rolling. It starts slowly and then accelerates. Koda quickly descends from the bamboo and runs after it.
From 0:25.5 to 0:27.5, use a dynamic downhill tracking shot. The enormous peach rolls rapidly through the grass. Koda catches up and jumps onto its upper surface. At first he lies belly-first and panics, but after a moment he gets his paws underneath himself and manages to balance on top. His expression changes from fear to pure excitement. He stretches his front paws outward while his huge attached tail streams behind him. Koda begins enjoying the ridiculous ride.
From 0:27.5 to 0:29, track backward in front of the rolling peach. Koda rides proudly with a huge smile while his fur moves in the rushing air. He suddenly looks ahead. His smile disappears. Pull the camera backward enough to reveal the narrow wooden footbridge directly downhill. The entrance is obviously narrower than the giant peach. Koda's eyes widen. He has no time to stop.
From 0:29 to 0:30, show the bridge entrance in a clear wide side view. The rolling peach reaches the two wooden entrance posts and wedges firmly between them with one heavy THUD. The peach stops instantly. Koda's momentum carries him forward off the fruit and into a large soft pile of dry leaves beside the bridge. Leaves burst upward around him. His head immediately rises from the pile, completely unharmed and dazed. One small green peach leaf drifts down and lands gently on top of his head. Koda slowly looks upward with only his eyes. Cut to black.
Use a premium photorealistic 3D CGI animated-feature aesthetic with detailed soft fur, realistic bark, leaves, grass and peach fuzz, cinematic daylight, rich natural colors and expressive physical comedy. Keep the daylight warm and consistent. Use believable gravity, momentum, friction, collisions and character weight beneath the exaggerated comedy.
Koda has exactly one fluffy tail, permanently attached to the base of his spine throughout all 30 seconds. Never detach it, duplicate it, turn it into a prop or place it in Koda's paws. Koda manipulates objects only with his paws and body weight.
The peach remains attached to the same branch until Koda physically pulls it free. The thin branch bends only because Koda moves his weight farther outward. The bamboo moves only because Koda physically drags and raises it. The peach rolls only after falling onto the visibly downhill slope. The peach continuously travels downhill toward the existing bridge. Do not teleport objects, change geography, create duplicate props or introduce unexplained movement.
No humans, no additional animals, no dialogue, no text, no subtitles, no logos and no HUD.
Use playful adventurous orchestral music throughout. Include rapid soft paw footsteps, mountain wind, grass and leaf movement, claw-on-bark sounds, subtle branch creaking, the soft leafy FWUMP of Koda landing in the bush, bamboo scraping over grass, bamboo contact sounds, the fruit-stem POP, heavy peach THUMP, increasing rolling rumble, stronger wind during the downhill ride, an abrupt musical stop when Koda sees the bridge, a heavy THUD when the peach wedges between the posts, a soft POOF when Koda lands in the leaves, brief silence, gentle leaf flutter and one tiny comedic orchestral note when the peach leaf lands on Koda's head.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file HTML interactive that makes [INDUSTRY] software feel like a strategy game.

Style: light isometric 3D scene (Three.js), soft lavender ground, white buildings with
blue roofs, yellow machines, floating white glass panels. Clean, playful, premium.

Scene: a full [SITE TYPE] with [KEY ASSETS — e.g. open pit, haul trucks, crusher,
conveyors, stockpile, rail load-out]. Everything moves: [WHAT FLOWS — e.g. ore on belts,
trucks cycling, trains loading].

UI:
- Top bar: [BRAND] logo, site name, live clock
- Top left: alert panel (live camera feed, detection box, countdown, 2–3 response buttons)
- Top right: status of whatever I click
- Bottom left: live flow strip showing each stage and its throughput
- No panel overlaps another

Game loop: every few seconds the system detects a hazard ([HAZARD TYPES]).
Pick the right response before the timer runs out. Right call = cost saved,
wrong call or too slow = downtime. Shift ends with a score.

Then make a 30s demo video of it (16:9 and 9:16), with a scripted camera tour,
big short captions, a cursor clicking through alerts, background music,

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: a simple 3D "Jelly Pumpkin" demo using three.js from a CDN. Keep the code short and basic.

SCENE
- One orange pumpkin in the centre made from a low-poly sphere (about 24x16 segments) with 8 shallow ribs, flat shading.
- MeshPhongMaterial, slightly transparent (opacity 0.9), bright orange with a little emissive colour. No transmission, no environment map, no post-processing.
- Jack-o'-lantern face made of flat black 2D shapes (two triangle eyes, triangle nose, zigzag mouth) placed just in front of the pumpkin surface. No glow from inside.
- Simple green cylinder stem on top.
- Three small low-poly pumpkins (purple, green, orange) and four small flattened spheres as candy around it.
- White background, ambient light plus one directional light, basic hard shadows on the floor.

INTERACTION
- Click the pumpkin: it squashes slightly (scale Y down, X/Z up) and springs back quickly with no extra wobble.
- Drag the stem: draw a straight thin green cylinder from the stem to the cursor. Dragging upward lifts the whole pumpkin rigidly; release and it falls, with one small bounce.
- "Carve Face" button: instantly swap to a second face (two black circle eyes, round mouth).
- "Glow" slider: changes the emissive intensity of the pumpkin a little.
- "Add Candy" button: drops 16 small spheres from above; they fall, bounce once on the floor and stop. No collision with the pumpkin.

UI
- Plain HTML: title "Jelly Pumpkin" in bold Arial top left, subtitle "Click the pumpkin to make it wobble!".
- Top right white box with border: colour buttons (Orange, Purple, Green), Glow range input, "Carve Face" and "Add Candy" buttons with default browser styling.
- Bottom left small grey text with stats: "Wobble: 0.6 | Face: 1 | Candy: 0".

prompt.text:
Build an interactive 3D “Jelly Koi Pond” in a single self-contained HTML file.

Create a small oval pond made entirely of soft, translucent jelly, floating just above a warm pastel background. Inside the jelly, add colorful koi fish and smooth little pebbles. Place lily pads, pink water lilies, and one adorable green frog with big eyes on the surface.

The pond should look like a beautiful miniature Japanese garden trapped inside a glossy gummy candy. Give it visible thickness, rounded edges, soft reflections, convincing transparency, and a soft shadow underneath.

Make the jelly physically interactive:
- Click and drag any part of the pond to stretch and lift it.
- Deform the pond locally rather than moving it as a rigid object.
- On release, let it bounce and wobble before gradually settling.
- Keep the fish, pebbles, lily pads, flowers, and frog attached to their positions within or on the deforming pond.
- Let the koi swim slowly when the pond is undisturbed.
- Clicking the surface should create a small ripple.

Add a compact, elegant control bar with Drag and Wobble modes, a jelly softness slider, three color options (mint, blue, and pink), and a reset button.

Use a minimal editorial layout with a large serif “Jelly Koi Pond.” title in the upper-left corner, small interaction hints, generous whitespace, and a soft sage background. Keep the pond as the main focus.

Use procedural geometry and materials, with no external image or model assets. Include lighting, shadows, mouse and touch support, and responsive resizing. Keep the simulation stable during strong dragging and repeated interactions.

Deliver a complete working experience, not a static mockup.

prompt.text:
I want a cinematic motion video built entirely from code. No AI video generators and no stock footage. Every frame should be drawn with code (HTML canvas is fine) and rendered to an MP4.

INPUTS (attached):
- Script / voiceover: [attach audio file] -- line timings: [paste each line with its start time, or tell Claude to work them out from the audio]
- Photos of the real people/places/objects: [attached]
- Style references: [attached -- these show the look I want, match their feel]
- Format: [e.g. 21:9, 3840x1646, 30fps] -- length must match the voiceover exactly.

THE STYLE:
- The whole video is ONE continuous camera move over one big world: a map, a desk, a board, whatever fits the story. Nothing cuts and no slides change. The camera glides, pushes in on details, pulls back to travel, and dives in again.
- Motion must feel smooth and filmed. Every start and stop eases in and out. The camera never stops dead: during holds it keeps drifting slowly in the direction it's about to go. Add subtle handheld movement, motion blur on fast moves, film grain, a soft glow and a vignette.
- Real photos and documents drop onto the world as physical objects (prints, papers, clippings), placed where the story happens.

STORYTELLING AND READABILITY RULES (most important):
1. One idea per line of narration. Each line gets ONE hero on screen (a photo, a word or a document) and everything else dims back.
2. Every phrase appears on screen once, never repeated. If the narrator says it, either show it on a real document or type it on screen, never both.
3. No filler text. Body copy on documents should be soft grey lines that read as paper, not words people try to read.
4. Big, readable type: hero words very large, labels never tiny. If someone can't read it on a phone in one second, it's too small or there's too much.
5. Less is more. Leave out decorative clutter (random tape, stamps, memos, extra labels) that isn't part of the story.
6. Visual moments land exactly on the spoken word: a circle drawn as the word is said, a stamp slamming on the beat.

PROCESS:
- Before you build, write a beat table: time → narration → the one hero on screen → any on-screen text. Show it to me and ask me anything that's unclear.
- Take your time. Quality matters more than speed. Prioritise design, smooth movement and clarity over adding more stuff.
- Before the final render, check your own work: look at stills from every beat and frame sequences of the camera moves. Fix anything that's cluttered, hard to read, overlapping, or that jerks or stops abruptly.
- Deliver the final MP4 with my voiceover synced, in the exact format above.

prompt.text:
Create “Squid Jelly” — a beautiful, interactive 3D gummy squid that users can grab, stretch, and squish directly in their browser. Deliver a complete standalone HTML file using genuine WebGPU.

ART DIRECTION

Make the squid look like a premium translucent gummy candy:
- An elongated, tapered mantle with a rounded tip.
- Two broad, thin, diamond-shaped side fins.
- Eight shorter curled arms and two longer feeding tentacles with rounded club-shaped tips.
- Small suction cups and a cute, understated face.

Use a warm off-white background, soft studio lighting, and a subtle ground shadow. Keep the squid large and centered, with an elegant, uncluttered composition.

GEOMETRY

Generate all geometry procedurally. No external models or image files.

Connect the arms, tentacles, and fins smoothly to the body. Their roots must remain embedded and attached during strong pulls, with no visible gaps or floating parts.

Suction cups and eyes must follow the deforming surface. Give the fins a thin, flexible profile and the longer tentacles slender shafts with thicker tips.

JELLY MATERIAL

Create convincing glossy, translucent jelly:
- Thickness-dependent color absorption.
- Refraction and soft internal light scattering.
- Smooth studio reflections and delicate rim highlights.
- A few tiny bubbles embedded inside the material.
- Richer color in thick areas and greater translucency along thin fins and tentacle tips.

Avoid opaque plastic, washed-out colors, blown-out highlights, visible mesh seams, and flickering transparency.

SOFT-BODY PHYSICS

Use a stable mass-spring or position-based dynamics simulation with approximate volume preservation.

The mantle should feel soft but substantial. Arms should bend independently, while long tentacles and fins should be more flexible.

Let users grab the body, fins, or tentacles at the clicked location. Pulling must deform the nearby geometry first, with the rest following elastically. Do not fake softness by scaling or rotating the entire model.

On release, the squid should wobble, recover its shape, and gradually settle. Include gravity, floor collisions, friction, and damping. Prevent appendages from passing through the floor.

Use fixed simulation steps, bounded stretching, and robust attachment constraints so repeated strong pulls cannot tear the model apart or destabilize the simulation.

INTERACTION

- Left-click or touch the squid to grab and stretch it.
- Right-drag or drag empty space to gently orbit the camera.
- Support limited zoom and mobile touch controls.
- Keep camera gestures separate from object dragging.

Add:
- Give it a nudge
- Reset
- Reset view
- Pause
- Firmness slider
- Internal damping slider
- ¼ speed toggle
- Show mesh toggle

Provide three material palettes: Coral, Lagoon, and Grape. Switching colors must not reset the simulation.

INTERFACE

Use a minimal editorial layout:
- Top left: small “MATERIAL STUDIES” label.
- Large italic serif heading: “Squid Jelly.”
- Caption: “A little ink. A little wiggle. A very sweet sea creature.”
- Top right: WebGPU status indicator.
- Right side: compact “THE SPECIMEN” control panel.
- Bottom left: a short interaction hint.

Use clean sans-serif controls, thin borders, and generous whitespace. Adapt the layout for mobile without covering the squid.

QUALITY AND PERFORMANCE

Use real 3D geometry and native WebGPU rendering with WGSL shaders, not a 2D imitation or prerecorded animation.

Reuse meshes and buffers. Do not reconstruct geometry during dragging. Prioritize stable interactions and smooth performance.

Test strong pulls, repeated releases, appendage attachments, floor collisions, palette changes, pause, reset, and camera controls.

Provide a clear fallback message if WebGPU is unavailable.

Deliver the full working HTML, not a mockup or code fragment. The result should feel like a little living gummy toy: glossy, weighty, flexible, and irresistibly satisfying to stretch.

title.zh: 电影感产品发布影片

summary.zh: 创作者用一份极其详细的导演式提示词，让Claude Sonnet 5.5制作了一段关于自己的电影感产品发布视频，涵盖叙事、视觉、性能数据和音效设计。

prompt.text:
You are an elite creative director, motion designer, product filmmaker, frontend engineer, and cinematic storyteller.

Your task is to CREATE A COMPLETE, POLISHED, PRODUCTION-READY GTM LAUNCH VIDEO FOR:

# CLAUDE SONNET 5.5

This should NOT feel like a generic AI explainer, SaaS promo, Canva presentation, or slideshow.

It should feel like a **premium cinematic technology launch film** produced by a world-class studio.

Think:

* Apple product launch film
* high-end AI research visualization
* cinematic title sequence
* sophisticated motion graphics
* premium brand campaign
* futuristic but restrained
* extremely polished
* visually mesmerizing
* editorial typography
* dramatic pacing
* exceptional sound-design thinking

The viewer should finish the video thinking:

**“This is not just a faster model. This is a fundamentally more capable everyday AI system.”**

---

# 1. CORE MESSAGE

The central narrative:

**Claude Sonnet 5.5 takes the intelligence of the Claude 5.5 generation and makes it faster, more efficient, and more practical for everyday work.**

The story should revolve around three ideas:

**INTELLIGENCE**
**SPEED**
**EFFICIENCY**

Then demonstrate what those mean in the real world:

**Code.**
**Reasoning.**
**Computer use.**
**Visual understanding.**
**Knowledge work.**
**Design.**
**Collaboration.**

Do NOT dump features onto the screen.

Instead, make the viewer EXPERIENCE the capabilities.

---

# 2. LENGTH

Create a cinematic film approximately:

**75–100 seconds**

The pacing should feel intentional.

First 10 seconds:
HOOK.

10–25 seconds:
INTRODUCE SONNET 5.5.

25–65 seconds:
CAPABILITY JOURNEY.

65–80 seconds:
SPEED + COST.

80–95 seconds:
POSITIONING + ENDING.

Do not make every section the same length.

Use pauses and negative space.

Let important statements breathe.

---

# 3. OPENING — THE HOOK

Do NOT begin with:

“Introducing Claude Sonnet 5.5”

That is boring.

Begin with a visual metaphor.

Black screen.

Almost total silence.

A tiny point of light appears.

It begins processing.

The point becomes thousands of rapidly moving particles.

The particles form fragments of:

code,
documents,
charts,
UI,
terminal commands,
images,
graphs,
text.

Everything moves extremely fast.

Then—

**silence.**

Everything freezes.

A single sentence appears:

> “What happens when intelligence gets faster?”

Pause.

Then:

# CLAUDE SONNET 5.5

Minimal.

Beautiful.

Large typography.

Subtle motion.

No cheesy effects.

---

# 4. PRODUCT POSITIONING

Introduce Sonnet 5.5 as:

**A faster, lower-cost complement to Claude Opus 5.5.**

Visually establish the Claude 5.5 family:

OPUS 5.5
SONNET 5.5
HAIKU 5.5

But Sonnet should become the visual focus.

Communicate that:

Opus 5.5 → complex work requiring sustained judgment

Sonnet 5.5 → well-scoped everyday tasks, fixing bugs, creating polished documents, slides and spreadsheets

Haiku 5.5 → high-volume, cost-sensitive applications

Do not spend too much time explaining this.

Use elegant visual hierarchy instead.

Source: Anthropic describes Sonnet 5.5 as the second model in the Claude 5.5 family and positions it as a faster, lower-cost complement to Opus 5.5.

---

# 5. THE BIG PERFORMANCE REVEAL

Create a dramatic data visualization sequence.

Start with:

SONNET 5

Then introduce:

SONNET 5.5

Show Terminal-Bench 4.0:

**10.3% → 70.6%**

Do not simply display a bar chart.

Make the number physically transform.

10.3%

The number fractures.

Explodes into particles.

Reassembles as:

70.6%

Then cut directly into visual representations of an agent working inside a terminal.

Terminal commands appearing.

Files changing.

Tests running.

Code being inspected.

Errors appearing.

Claude fixing them.

The system keeps moving.

Voiceover / typography:

**“From 10.3% to 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0.”**

Then:

**“Agentic coding performance, dramatically upgraded.”**

Important:
Do not claim Sonnet 5.5 is universally superior to every model.

The source explicitly notes that benchmark scores capture only one facet of capability and that Opus 5.5 remains stronger for complex, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment.

---

# 6. CODING SEQUENCE

This should be one of the hero sequences.

Visual language:

A developer's environment.

Dark terminal.

Code.

Git diff.

Architecture diagrams.

Test results.

Logs.

Multiple windows.

Instead of showing static screenshots, create the feeling of an AI actually working.

Show:

READ

UNDERSTAND

PLAN

EDIT

RUN

TEST

FIX

SHIP

These words appear briefly as kinetic typography.

Then accelerate everything.

The interface begins moving faster.

The camera pushes through the screen.

We transition from terminal → code → architecture → finished application.

On-screen statement:

**“Understand the codebase.
Make the change.
Check the work.”**

Mention that early testers reported Sonnet 5.5 understood codebases quickly and often batched tool calls into fewer steps, reducing cost.

---

# 7. KNOWLEDGE WORK

Transition away from code.

A large pile of information appears:

PDFs

spreadsheets

earnings reports

transcripts

charts

documents

slides

The information overwhelms the screen.

Then Sonnet cuts through the noise.

Everything gets organized.

Information flows into:

ANALYZE

SYNTHESIZE

STRUCTURE

CREATE

The output becomes a beautifully designed presentation.

Show a polished operating-review deck being assembled.

Use the Anthropic example:

A public company's quarterly earnings materials + call transcripts + slide template

→

10-slide operating review.

The source says two experts judged one internal test's first draft ready to send as-is. Present this as an example, not a universal guarantee.

---

# 8. VISUAL UNDERSTANDING

Create an elegant sequence involving charts and images.

Start with a complicated chart.

Camera moves toward it.

The chart breaks apart into visual components.

Sonnet identifies relationships.

Numbers transform into explanations.

The visualization becomes understandable.

Use:

**“See the information.”**

Then:

**“Understand the information.”**

Then:

**“Act on it.”**

Reference the published Chartography score:

**61.6%**

versus

**15.6%**

for Sonnet 5.

Also show:

**80.1% OSWorld**

and the broader computer-use story.

Keep benchmark visuals tasteful.

No giant dashboard.

No spreadsheet aesthetic.

---

# 9. LONG-HORIZON / UNEXPECTED CAPABILITY MOMENT

This should be one of the film's most memorable moments.

Introduce:

**Pokémon Red**

But do it cinematically.

Old-school pixel aesthetic appears.

The camera flies into the game world.

A screenshot becomes the environment.

Sonnet interprets what it sees.

Moves.

Adapts.

Continues.

Then pull back from the pixel world into modern AI visuals.

Typography:

**“The first Sonnet model to beat Pokémon Red using only screenshots.”**

This is directly supported by Anthropic's launch page.

---

# 10. SPEED

Now change the energy of the entire film.

Everything becomes faster.

Cursor.

Terminal.

Documents.

Animations.

Responses.

Tool calls.

Words.

Then everything stops.

Huge typography:

# 30%+

A second line:

**FASTER OUTPUTS**

Then:

**Sonnet 5.5 generates outputs more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5.**

This is Anthropic's published positioning.

Use visual motion to communicate speed instead of relying on narration.

---

# 11. COST / EFFICIENCY

This should feel like the “surprise” section.

Show two parallel paths.

SONNET 5

Longer path
More tokens
More steps
Higher task cost

SONNET 5.5

Shorter path
Fewer tokens
Fewer steps
Lower task cost

Then merge the two paths into a single number:

**UP TO 30% LESS PER TASK**

The pricing should appear separately:

INPUT

**$2 / 1M tokens**

OUTPUT

**$10 / 1M tokens**

CACHE READS

**$0.20 / 1M tokens**

CACHE WRITES

**$2.50 / 1M tokens**

Do not imply the list price itself was reduced versus Sonnet 5.

The key point is task efficiency.

## Anthropic states the token prices are the same as Sonnet 5, while Sonnet 5.5 typically requires fewer tokens per task and costs up to 30% less per task in testing.

# 12. EFFORT LEVEL

Create a beautiful visual metaphor for effort.

A single Claude interface.

A slider moves:

LOW → MEDIUM → HIGH

At LOW:

FAST

At HIGH:

DEEPER REASONING

Communicate:

**Choose how much effort Claude spends.**

Show the tradeoff:

Speed ↔ Cost ↔ Quality

Anthropic notes that lower effort produces faster, lower-token responses, while higher effort allows longer reasoning and more checking.

Keep this section under 6 seconds.

---

# 13. COLLABORATION

Show a person working with Claude.

Not “human versus AI.”

Instead:

human → AI → human → AI

Rapid iteration.

A rough idea becomes:

code

document

spreadsheet

presentation

design

finished product

Use the message:

**“Better collaboration.
Faster iteration.”**

Anthropic says early testers described Sonnet 5.5 as a better collaboration partner than Sonnet 5, with speed supporting rapid iteration on less complex tasks.

---

# 14. SAFETY

Do NOT turn this into a scary cybersecurity montage.

Keep it elegant.

Show the system approaching a boundary.

A glowing perimeter appears.

Certain high-risk paths are blocked.

Routine work continues uninterrupted.

Typography:

**CAPABLE**

then:

**CONTROLLED**

Then:

**BUILT WITH SAFEGUARDS FOR HIGH-RISK USE**

Communicate that Sonnet 5.5 launches with cyber safeguards and fallbacks similar to those developed for more capable models.

Do not overstate this.

## Routine software development and most life-sciences work are described by Anthropic as unaffected by these safeguards.

# 15. FINAL SEQUENCE

Return to the original point of light.

But now it is enormous.

It contains everything we saw:

code

documents

charts

images

interfaces

terminal

research

design

All orbiting around one point.

The system contracts into a single elegant symbol.

Silence.

Then:

# CLAUDE SONNET 5.5

Underneath:

**Faster.
More capable.
More efficient.**

Then one final line:

**Built for the work between the big breakthroughs.**

Hold.

Fade to black.

Anthropic logo / Claude wordmark treatment.

End.

---

# 16. VISUAL DIRECTION

The visual quality is critical.

Use:

* cinematic depth
* volumetric light
* subtle particles
* glass interfaces
* realistic screen reflections
* macro details
* sophisticated typography
* smooth camera movement
* 3D space
* depth of field
* subtle grain
* elegant transitions
* premium UI animation
* kinetic typography
* data visualizations
* procedural motion
* intentional negative space

Avoid:

* cheesy AI imagery
* robots
* glowing brains
* generic humanoid AI
* stock footage
* cliché “future city” visuals
* excessive neon
* overused holograms
* template-style transitions
* random particles everywhere
* corporate PowerPoint aesthetics
* excessive text

The visual language should feel **intelligent, restrained, premium and modern.**

---

# 17. COLOR / BRAND

Use a restrained Anthropic-inspired palette.

Primarily:

deep blacks
warm whites
soft neutrals
subtle Claude orange accents

Orange should be used strategically.

Do not turn the entire video orange.

Typography should be editorial and premium.

Use extremely large type for important statements.

Use small precise typography for benchmark data.

---

# 18. SOUND DESIGN

Treat sound as a major part of the experience.

Create a conceptual soundscape that evolves with the intelligence of the system.

Beginning:

near silence

low-frequency ambience

tiny digital clicks

Middle:

keyboard sounds

terminal activity

subtle system pulses

data movement

rising tension

Speed section:

rapid rhythmic elements

compressed transients

increasing tempo

Final reveal:

everything drops away

single tonal hit

silence

then the final title.

The audio should feel like a film, not background music.

---

# 19. EDITING LANGUAGE

Use:

hard cuts where impact is needed

slow cinematic transitions where context matters

match cuts

particle transformations

camera push-ins

screen-to-world transitions

typographic wipes

data morphing

light-based transitions

motion blur

depth transitions

Do NOT over-transition.

Every transition should communicate a conceptual connection.

---

# 20. BENCHMARKS TO FEATURE

Prioritize the benchmarks visually instead of showing every benchmark.

Use:

Terminal-Bench 4.0
70.6%

Sonnet 5:
10.3%

FrontierCode:
46.2% Max

CursorBench:
55.5%

GDPval-AA:
1844

AA-Briefcase:
1811

Humanity's Last Exam:
64.5% with tools

OSWorld:
80.1% partial

Chartography:
61.6% no tools

These figures come from Anthropic's published benchmark table.

Do not misleadingly imply that one benchmark proves overall intelligence.

---

# 21. ACCURACY RULE

This is extremely important.

Do NOT invent:

benchmarks

customers

quotes

performance numbers

capabilities

pricing

features

comparisons

scientific claims

Do not make unsupported claims like:

“best model in the world”

“beats every model”

“AGI”

“human-level”

“revolutionary”

“the smartest AI ever”

unless explicitly supported by the provided source.

Use the supplied Anthropic source as the factual source of truth.

---

# 22. PRODUCTION QUALITY

Do NOT simply produce a storyboard.

Actually build the complete experience.

If this is being implemented as code:

1. Inspect the existing project.
2. Determine the best technology for cinematic motion.
3. Build reusable animation primitives.
4. Build the timeline as modular scenes.
5. Keep typography perfectly synchronized.
6. Make every animation deterministic.
7. Optimize rendering performance.
8. Avoid unnecessarily heavy assets.
9. Ensure the result runs smoothly.
10. Make the entire film feel authored rather than procedurally random.

The final result should feel like an actual professional launch film.

---

# 23. RESPONSIVENESS / EXPORT

Design the composition primarily for:

**1920 × 1080**

16:9 cinematic master.

But structure the scene system so it can later be adapted to:

9:16

1:1

without rewriting the entire animation.

---

# 24. IMPORTANT CREATIVE PRINCIPLE

Do not explain AI.

**SHOW AI WORKING.**

Instead of saying:

“Sonnet 5.5 is good at coding.”

Show:

problem → codebase → reasoning → changes → tests → working result.

Instead of:

“Sonnet 5.5 is good at knowledge work.”

Show:

chaotic information → understanding → synthesis → polished deliverable.

Instead of:

“Sonnet is faster.”

Show the entire world accelerating.

Make the audience FEEL the improvement.

---

# 25. NARRATION

Use extremely sparse narration.

The film should work even with the sound off.

Narration should feel like a premium technology documentary.

Short sentences.

Confident.

No marketing fluff.

Example style:

“What happens when intelligence gets faster?”

“Code.”

“Reasoning.”

“Understanding.”

“Creation.”

“Then everything moves faster.”

“Same model family.”

“Less waiting.”

“Fewer tokens.”

“More work done.”

“Claude Sonnet 5.5.”

Do NOT narrate every fact.

Let visuals carry the story.

---

# 26. FINAL EXPERIENCE

The finished result should have:

**A killer first 5 seconds.**

**A memorable middle.**

**A visually spectacular climax.**

**A clean final brand lockup.**

It should be good enough to publish as:

* an Anthropic-style launch film
* X/Twitter launch content
* a website hero video
* Product Hunt launch material
* developer marketing
* conference screens
* YouTube

The viewer should understand three things by the end:

### 1.

**Sonnet 5.5 is substantially more capable than Sonnet 5 in many evaluated tasks.**

### 2.

**It is significantly faster and more efficient.**

### 3.

**It is designed for practical, everyday professional work.**

Build the experience around those three ideas.

Do not make this feel like an advertisement.

Make it feel like **the arrival of a new piece of technology.**

title.zh: TechHalla 20 秒动态品牌片头

summary.zh: 为个人品牌「TechHalla」做的20秒动态识别短片，用一份规定配色、字体、节拍网格和禁用套路的超详细提示词一次生成，没用After Effects。
summary.en: A 20-second kinetic-identity motion bumper for 'TechHalla' built from one highly detailed prompt specifying palette, typography, beat grid, and banned cliches, no After Effects.

prompt.text:
You are a world-class motion designer doing a 20.00s kinetic identity bumper for TechHalla — an AI creator known for stealable workflows, not vibes. This piece must feel like the best designer in the room made a street-poster that moves. Showreel stakes: if this is weak, you don’t get hired.

DURATION: exactly 20.00 seconds. LOOPABLE: frame 0 == frame last (position, opacity, cursor if any).
FORMAT: one HTML file, 1080×1080 (square, X-native). 60fps.
PALETTE (strict):
- bg # 0A0A0A
- magenta # FF2BD6
- acid green # B8FF00
- white # F5F5F5 only for primary readable type when needed
No other hues. No gradients on UI chrome. Magenta/green may misregister (print offset) by 2–4px on impact frames only.

TYPE SYSTEM (use all three; never one font for everything):
1) Display / scream: Archivo Black (or equivalent ultra-condensed black) — 1–4 words max
2) Urban grotesque: Syne ExtraBold — secondary hits, stacked lines
3) Mono / “prompt code”: IBM Plex Mono Medium — small labels, timestamps, fake prompt crumbs
Tracking: display −40 to −80; mono +20. Optical kerning. No cute script fonts.

MESSAGE (locked — do not soften, do not add filler slogans):
Beat hits in this exact order:
1. STOP SCROLLING
2. AI VIDEO ISN’T EXPENSIVE
3. BAD PROMPTING IS
4. WORKFLOWS > WISHES
5. STEAL THE PROMPT
6. @ TECHHALLA
Supporting crumbs (mono, ≤18 chars, never full sentences): JSON · H3 · SEEDANCE · 0 KEYFRAMES · MAGNIFIC · COPY/PASTE

NARRATIVE ARC (20s):
0.0–2.5s COLD OPEN — “STOP SCROLLING” slams in from below with spring overshoot; magenta smear trail; acid green baseline ticks across like a waveform.
2.5–6.5s THESIS A — “AI VIDEO ISN’T EXPENSIVE” locks to a poster grid (baseline grid 8px). Letters scramble (seeded Fisher–Yates per glyph) then snap on the beat.
6.5–10.5s THESIS B — “BAD PROMPTING IS” replaces it via mask wipe through the letterforms (the outgoing line is the mask). Magenta/green channel split on the cut.
10.5–14.5s PROOF FLASH — rapid kinetic stack: WORKFLOWS > WISHES, then mono crumbs orbit a central block like a terminal. One fake “prompt block” types 3 lines max, then gets crossed by an acid green strikethrough that becomes a underline for STEAL THE PROMPT.
14.5–17.5s BRAND LOCK — @ TECHHALLA centers; display weight. A thick magenta bar and a thin acid green rule form an L-bracket mark (custom, not a logo download).
17.5–20.0s SETTLE / LOOP — hold lockup; micro-breath (scale 1.000→1.012→1.000); last frame == first ready for loop.

CONCRETE TECHNIQUES (required — implement, don’t approximate):
1. seek(t) pure function of time. No CSS transitions. No setInterval. No React state across frames.
2. Springs = closed-form step responses. Stack one spring per target change so motion stays deterministic.
3. Kinetic type: per-glyph spring (y, opacity, blur). Stagger = 1/16 note at 120 BPM (125ms).
4. Print misregistration: on accent frames only, duplicate text layer offset (±2–4px) in magenta and acid green at 40% opacity.
5. Mask reveal: destination text revealed by animating a path mask derived from the outgoing word’s outlines.
6. Camera: one orthographic camera; only punch-in (1.0→1.08) and horizontal smash-pans timed to beats — never random drift.
7. Motion blur: render 4 subframes per frame, blend (tmix-style).
8. Beat grid: 120 BPM, downbeat at t=0. Something must land on every beat for the first 16 beats; after that, every other beat is ok.
9. Pre-pass: before full render, export one still per major beat (8 frames). Fix cramped type, orphan words, low contrast — then render.

BANNED:
Generic AI clichés (brains, robots, neural nets, sparkles), soft gradients, bouncy cartoon easing, particle explosions, stock “futuristic HUD”, long paragraphs, narrator essay energy, Canva-deck energy, extra slogans beyond the locked message, purple/blue neon, glassmorphism.

prompt.text:
Create a finished, editable Blender recreation of the six-second animation shown in this workspace’s reference/t\_\*.png images.

Open and inspect the reference images before building. Their filenames give seconds from the start of the animation: t\_1.20s.png means 1.20 seconds. Use these images as the visual reference and leave them unchanged.

Match the complete composition: the lamp’s proportions and articulated structure, lettering, interactions, camera framing, materials, lighting, shadows, and final fade. Pay particular attention to jump timing, preparation, landings, settling, and head turns. Preserve the reference’s stylized motion and create coherent movement between the sampled poses. Make reasonable choices for unseen details.

Build genuine 3D geometry and animation that remain editable. Keep joints connected and contact believable. Do not substitute reference images or footage for geometry, textures, backgrounds, or rendered output. Create the assets yourself using installed tools; do not download assets, browse the web, or use other AI agents or models.

Blender is installed at:
C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.2\blender.exe

Prepare the final scene at 1280×720, 30 fps, frames 1–180, with frame 1 representing time zero. Use Cycles, 64 samples, and denoising. Preserve the reference lettering; add no extra titles, watermarks, interface, comparison layout, or audio.

Render and visually inspect low-resolution previews across the action, including between reference timestamps. Correct visible problems and recheck affected frames. We will render the final video separately.

Save scene.blend with the final render settings and a build\_scene.py that rebuilds it from scratch. The saved scene must render without external asset dependencies. Verify that it opens and renders in background mode.

Work autonomously through completion, making routine decisions yourself. Finish with a brief report of the saved files, checks actually performed, and remaining limitations.

summary.en: The creator used Claude Opus 5.5 to build an interactive, fully procedural 3D web simulation of the 1961 Lamborghini FL3 tractor diesel engine, generated from published specs and photos with no 3D models or textures, using a detailed written build prompt shared in the thread.

prompt.text:
Build an interactive 3D web page: a live "bench study" of the **Lamborghini FL3**, the air-cooled three-cylinder diesel that powered the Lamborghini 2R tractor (1961 to 1967), from the years before Lamborghini built cars. Visitors should be able to start the engine, rev it, load it, cut it open, watch the cooling air, and take it apart. The page should feel like a beautifully printed technical plate that happens to be alive.

## Hard rules

- **Everything procedural.** No 3D models, no Blender, no textures, no image files, no audio files. Geometry, materials, drawings and sound are all generated in code.
- **three.js (WebGL)**, vendored locally, ES modules with an importmap, no build step. It must run from a plain static server.
- **60 fps** on a recent laptop at 1440x900 and on a retina display.
- **Desktop:** the whole sheet fits a 1440x900 viewport with no scrolling.
- **Phone width:** the sheet becomes a vertical scroll with nothing cut off. On touch, horizontal drags turn the engine and vertical swipes scroll the page.
- **No em dashes** anywhere in the copy.

## The engine: facts

Only these figures are published. Use them exactly:

- 3 cylinders, inline, air-cooled, direct-injection diesel, Lamborghini type FL3
- bore 92 mm, stroke 110 mm, 2,193 cc
- 39 hp (29.1 kW) at 2,200 rpm
- electric starter, Bosch injection
- about 2,000 2Rs sold between 1961 and 1967
- factory colours: orange and light blue ("celeste")

The external layout, from photographs of a restored 1962 2R:

- the engine block painted celeste
- an axial cooling blower in a round housing at the front, belt-driven from the crank, with a wire guard
- a sheet-metal air cowl along the cold side
- individual finned cylinder barrels and finned heads, held down by long studs
- a silver inline injection pump on the hot side, with three copper high-pressure lines up to the injectors
- twin fuel filters
- a black vertical exhaust stack with a silencer and a flapper rain cap
- an oil-bath air cleaner
- a dynamo, a starter motor, and a flywheel with a ring gear

Everything else is an assumption and must be labelled **modelled** on the page:

- compression ratio (about 17:1), rod length, valve timing
- idle (about 700 rpm) and high idle (about 2,350 rpm)
- torque curve, friction, airflow, temperatures, fuel use

Never dimension an assumed size in the drawings.

## Art direction: a 1960s Italian two-ink print

It must not look like a Victorian parchment plate or a generic blueprint. Think of a page from an Italian factory manual or a mid-century industrial catalogue, printed in the tractor's own two inks.

- **Paper:** ivory offset stock (about #EEE9DC) with fine paper grain and soft, uneven ink absorption.
- **Inks:** arancio (#E0561C), celeste (#58AED6 for the print, a deeper #3F9DD0 for the painted engine) and near-black (#1C1B19).
- **Type:**
- Bodoni Moda for display: a huge "FL3" with the 3 in arancio, and an italic "Lamborghini" above it.
- Archivo for labels (wide, letter-spaced small caps).
- IBM Plex Mono for numbers.
- Every label carries its Italian term in small italic Bodoni (for example: Hand throttle *acceleratore*).
- **Print details:**
- registration marks in the four corners and a colour bar in the margin
- a thin double frame and a running head across the top: "Bench study · *banco prova*", "Air-cooled diesel · three cylinders · direct injection", "Sheet 03"
- a giant celeste numeral "3" printed faintly behind the engine, slightly out of register
- **Layout at 1440x900:**
- left column: title, deck, lede and the controls
- centre: the 3D engine
- right column: four live instruments
- bottom strip: four live drawings and a readings card

Copy:
- Kicker: "Lamborghini Trattori · 1961–1967"
- Deck: "Three cylinders. No radiator."
- Lede: "Before the supercars, Lamborghini built tractors. The 2R of 1961 carried this engine: 2,193 cc of direct-injection diesel and no radiator, cooled by a belt-driven blower and cast fins. About 2,000 were sold by 1967, and tractor money paid for the move into cars in 1963."

## The 3D model

Build the FL3 to its real proportions: 92 mm bore, 110 mm stroke, cylinders about 150 mm apart, crank axis as the origin.

Exterior parts:

- crankcase with main-bearing ribs and mounting feet, oil sump, timing case, flywheel plate
- three separate finned barrels, with the fins flattened where neighbours meet
- three finned heads with rocker covers and long studs
- blower with a spinning rotor, stator vanes and a guard
- V-belt around the crank, dynamo and blower pulleys
- air cowl with a stencilled "FL3 · raffreddato ad aria"
- intake runners into the oil-bath air cleaner with a glass pre-cleaner bowl
- exhaust manifold, silencer and a flapper cap that lifts on each exhaust pulse at idle
- injection pump with a governor housing whose throttle lever follows the hand throttle
- copper injector lines and a leak-off line, injectors, twin fuel filters
- starter motor whose pinion slides into the ring gear while cranking
- a small name plate reading "MOTORE DIESEL · FL3 · CV 39 · 2200 g/min" (no company logo anywhere)

Moving internals:

- crankshaft with counterweights, pins 120 degrees apart, turning clockwise seen from the blower end
- connecting rods, pistons with rings and a combustion bowl
- camshaft at half speed with lobes timed to the valve events
- tappets, pushrods, rockers, valves and springs that compress, all driven by the same valve-lift curves the simulation uses

Materials and setting:

- **Materials:** glossy celeste enamel with subtle procedural grain, rougher on castings than on sheet metal. Steel, alloy, copper and heat-darkened exhaust.
- **Stand:** the engine sits on an **arancio test stand**.
- **Lighting and floor:** a soft cast shadow and a contact shadow lands on the paper itself (a transparent canvas over the page).
- **Life at rest:** the engine rocks slightly on its mounts against the gas torque.

## The simulation

Write it as a pure, testable module.

- **Kinematics:**
- exact slider-crank piston motion and rod angle
- four-stroke cycle over 720 degrees, firing order 1-2-3, one firing every 240 degrees
- **In-cylinder pressure:**
- polytropic compression and expansion with a double-Wiebe heat release (fast premixed burn plus a slower diffusion burn), tabulated by fuel level
- calibrate the heat release so that full fuel at 2,200 rpm gives exactly 29.1 kW at the flywheel
- peak pressure lands around 70 to 75 bar at full load
- **Crank dynamics:**
- integrate with sub-steps of about 2 degrees of crank, so the instantaneous gas torque gives real speed ripple at idle and real compression pulses while cranking
- flywheel inertia about 0.8 kg·m²
- **Governor and load:**
- an all-speed mechanical governor with about 120 rpm of droop and a little fuel-rack lag
- the hand throttle sets the governed speed between idle and high idle
- the PTO brake applies a load that rises with the square of speed, so 100% load at 2,200 rpm needs exactly full fuel
- **Starting:**
- the starter cranks at about 250 rpm
- the charge needs a few compressions before it lights, the first cycles misfire and burn rich, and that black smoke leaves the stack
- the engine catches in about 1 second and the starter disengages
- **Stopping:**
- friction rises with speed, plus blower drag rising with the square of speed
- an unfired cylinder gives back less than it took to compress (heat lost to the fins), so the engine stops about 2 seconds after the fuel is cut at idle
- **Temperatures:**
- head temperatures come from about a quarter of the fuel's heat going into the metal, removed by blower air that rises with engine speed
- full load settles around 160 to 175 °C
- run thermal time 30 times faster than real time and say so

The simulation emits events with timestamps: crank, fire, misfire, exhaust valve opening, caught, stop, stalled. Events raised between steps (the key) must not be lost.

## Interaction

- **Ignition key:** a round bakelite-and-steel switch. Click (or Space) to start and stop. It shows Start, Cranking or Stop.
- **Two levers:** the hand throttle shows the governed rpm, and the PTO brake shows a percentage. Style them as notched quadrants with orange lever knobs.
- **Four views** (keys 1 to 4), each with a smooth scripted camera move:
- **Painted.**
- **Cutaway:**
- a section plane through the cylinder axes, with cut faces printed as a light arancio hatch
- parts lying wholly in the removed half (pump, filters, exhaust, starter, pushrods, cam) disappear
- pistons, rods and crank stay whole
- a combustion glow fills each chamber as it fires
- **Airflow:**
- everything except the barrels and heads fades to a paper-grey ghost
- barrels and heads show a temperature ramp from deep celeste to arancio
- particles are drawn in through the blower guard, run along the cowl, cross the fins and leave warm on the pump side
- particles are drawn through the metal like the flow arrows of a technical illustration
- **Exploded:**
- waits until the engine has stopped, then separates the parts along sensible axes and holds the crank still
- each part gets a callout: English name in small caps, Italian term in italic, and a leader line to an orange dot
- labels sit on a paper backing and never overlap
- **Other controls:**
- Slow motion (S) eases time to 1/25
- a Sound toggle
- Reset view
- drag to orbit, scroll to zoom
- **Narration line:** a single italic line in the console that reacts to what is happening. Examples:
- "Key turned. The starter pinion meshes with the flywheel and spins the engine at about 250 rpm."
- "Squeezed about 17 to 1, the air gets hot enough to light the diesel. No spark plugs."
- "It caught."
- "Idling near 700 rpm: three power strokes every two turns, one every 240 degrees."
- "The hand throttle sets the governor, which opens the rack until the engine holds that speed."
- "Full PTO load at 2,200 rpm: the rack is wide open and the FL3 makes its rated 39 hp."
- "No water anywhere. The blower pushes air down the cowl, across the fins, and out warm on the pump side."
- "Fuel cut. It runs down and rocks back on its last compression."
- Each view also gets a line of its own.

## Live instruments (Canvas 2D, ink on paper)

1. **Tachometer:** a period Italian dial, 0 to 25 x100 rpm, with an arancio arc above rated speed and an hour meter whose tenths drum rolls.
2. **The cycle:** a 720-degree wheel with three rings (one per cylinder, offset 240 degrees). Power is arancio, exhaust grey, intake celeste, compression hatched. A pointer follows the crank and a dot flashes at each firing.
3. **Indicator diagram:** the live P-V loop for cylinder 1, with the full-load loop dashed for reference, a dot at the current state and the peak pressure labelled.
4. **Chart recorder:** scrolling chart paper with an rpm pen in black and a power pen in arancio.

Below the drawings, a **readings card**:

- live values: speed, power, torque, fuel (l/h), cooling air (m³/min) and head temperature
- marked "live, modelled"
- a footnote listing what is published and stating that the page is an independent study, not affiliated with Lamborghini

Power and torque are measured at the flywheel, so they never overshoot the rated 39 hp during transients.

## Live drawings: blueline prints of the running engine

Front, Right side, Plan and **Section A-A** are real orthographic renders of the same running model, not illustrations. Ink them in a shader like 1960s diazo prints:

- render normals and depth, then draw blue outlines from silhouette, crease and depth edges
- shade with a celeste 45-degree screentone
- print an arancio hatch wherever the section plane cuts metal
- the diazo paper and its faint grid are printed by the shader itself
- add centre lines and numbered cylinders
- Section A-A cuts through cylinder 1 so you see the piston moving. It dimensions only the published bore (Ø 92) and stroke (110), with TDC and BDC lines marked PMS and PMI.

## Sound (Web Audio, synthesised)

- **Exhaust:** each pop is scheduled from the simulation's own exhaust-valve events at the correct sub-frame time. It is not a looped sample.
- **Layers:**
- diesel knock at each injection
- blower roar and a blade-pass tone tracking speed
- valve-gear whirr
- a starter whine that strains on each compression
- a solenoid clunk on start and stop
- the flapper cap ticking at idle
- a soft metallic cue when the engine comes apart and a seating clunk when it goes back together
- **Slow motion** spaces the pops out and deepens them.
- **Mix:** run everything through a compressor. It must never clip.
- **Autoplay:** audio starts on the first user gesture.

## Deliverables

- the page: `index.html`, `css/`, `js/`, with three.js vendored in `vendor/`
- a tiny no-cache static server (`https://serve.py/`)
- a README that separates published facts from modelled ones
- a headless Node check of the simulation that asserts:
- 29.1 kW at 2,200 rpm
- peak pressure 60 to 85 bar
- catches within 3 s
- idles between 650 and 750 rpm
- full load holds about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp
- heads pass 120 °C under load
- it stops after the fuel is cut
- optional: a frame-exact video capture script (virtual time at 60 fps, a drawn cursor with click rings, the sound rendered offline from the simulation's event log so it stays in sync)

## Done means

1. The sheet loads with no console errors and holds 60 fps.
2. Turning the key cranks, catches with a dark puff and settles near 700 rpm.
3. Full throttle plus full PTO load reads about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp, and the P-V loop peaks around 73 bar.
4. Every view works, including Section A-A cutting through the moving piston.
5. The exploded view waits for the engine to stop, and its labels are all readable.
6. Every figure that is not published is labelled as modelled.
7. At 1440x900 nothing overflows, and at phone width nothing is cut off.
