summary.en: The creator shared three prompts for turning supplied video and music into poster-grid music videos with synchronized effects and temporal variations.

prompt.text:
Create a 1:1 high-energy poster-grid music video, exactly matching the supplied music's duration. Divide the frame into near-square cells with thin grey lines, keeping the original footage as one continuous, clearly recognizable image across the grid. The center ~6 cells play in sync with distinct visual treatments, while outer cells create independent variations. Fill the composition with dense, rapidly evolving effects, layered motion graphics, typography, icons, flashes and rhythmic transitions. Let the footage and music inspire every creative choice. Push visual intensity with frequent beat-driven bursts, but keep the original characters, action and scene consistently recognizable. Effects enhance the footage rather than replace it.

2. Create a 1:1 high-energy poster-grid music video, exactly matching the supplied music's duration. Divide the frame into near-square cells with thin grey lines, preserving one continuous, recognizable image across the grid. The center ~6 cells remain synchronized with distinct visual treatments. Aggressive waves of stylistic transformations spread between neighboring cells, triggering rapid chain reactions, layered effects, graphic explosions and rhythmic resets. Fill the grid with constant visual activity, inventive typography, icons and motion graphics inspired by the footage and soundtrack. Make transformations bold, frequent and visually spectacular, but temporary, always revealing the original characters and action beneath.

3. Create a 1:1 high-energy temporal poster-grid music video, exactly matching the supplied music's duration. Divide the frame into near-square cells with thin grey lines, preserving one continuous, recognizable image across the grid. The center ~6 cells follow the original action in sync while surrounding cells create intense temporal variations. Build dense rhythmic cascades of motion echoes, rapid frame repetitions, time offsets, reversals, impact freezes and layered graphic effects. Sync aggressive temporal bursts, typography, icons and transitions precisely to the music. Let the footage and soundtrack guide every creative decision. Keep the original action clearly identifiable amid the controlled visual chaos.

summary.en: A Blender video of the Dragon Palace (Ryugu-jo) generated from CAD-style architectural drawings, using a detailed reusable Japanese template prompt with an attached reference image.

prompt.text:
【題材：〇〇】のCADデータと、それを元にしたBlender動画を作って。

■ CADデータ
- 【題材】をイメージした配置図・平面図・立面図をDXFで作図（単位mm、表題欄つき）
- 3Dモデル（OBJ/STL/3D DXF）は不要

■ 動画（Blender 4.2、1920×1080、24fps、約20秒）
1. 冒頭：和紙の巻物が上から広がり、墨で描かれた配置図が現れる（題字・落款つき）
2. 図面の線が墨のワイヤーフレームとして立体に立ち上がる
3. 基壇→柱→壁→屋根→装飾の順に肉付けされ、線は実体に吸収されて消える
4. 完成したら巻物が消え、周りが【環境：例 紅葉の山と池／雪景色／海中】だとわかる演出
5. 最後にタイトル【題材名】を表示
6. 本編のあと、添付のロゴのエンドカード（黒地に柔らかく現れ、光の筋が走ってフェードアウト）

■ カメラ
- 肉付けの間は建物に寄る（主殿のまわりを回る）
- 最後に情景が変わるところで、引きの全景へ

■ 描写（リアル寄り）
- 樹木・植物は、枝ぶりと葉の1枚1枚が見える作りに（球の塊にしない）
- 遠景の山や森は木を密に並べ、空気遠近の霞をかける
- 空は物理的な空。時間帯は【例：夕方の低い日差し】で、影を長く
- 水面の映り込み、苔・岩・落ち葉など地面の細部も作る
- 建物は題材に合わせた細部（例：垂木・軒付・格子）まで
- テクスチャはプロシージャルで（朱漆・瓦・石・金など、題材に合わせて）
- 金属や金箔は白飛びさせず、素材の色が出るように
- 外観の参考画像：【画像を添付】

■ 音
- 外部素材なしでPython合成。場面の切り替わりに合わせた和風BGM＋効果音
- ロゴのエンドカードにも音をつける
- 冒頭は1秒カットしてテンポよく

■ PCの負荷
- 最初から軽い設定で描く（見た目が変わらない範囲でサンプル数を下げる）
- 低い優先度で、Blenderは1本ずつ。少しずつ描いて冷ましながら進める
- 本番レンダリングの前に、かかる時間を教えて

■ 進め方
- テスト静止画を確認してから本番レンダリング
- 完成したらMP4で送って

summary.en: A test comparing Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on building a three.js Rubik's cube solving animation from the same prompt, finding Opus actually solved it while DeepSeek faked the result.

prompt.text:
build a single html file (three.js) that renders a 3x3 puzzle cube in a 1080x1080 square and solves it on camera with a timer.

1. standard colors: white up, yellow down, green front, blue back, red right, orange left. no whole-cube rotations.
2. apply this scramble in wca notation: D2 R' F U2 B' L2 D' R2 U F2 L' B2 U' R D2 F' L U2 B R'
3. solve it your own way - any method, any number of moves. replaying the scramble backwards is not allowed.
4. every move animates in exactly 0.35s with a 0.05s pause.
5. show a timer that stops the moment the cube is solved, plus the current move and a move counter.
6. the cube must actually end fully solved.

prompt.text:
Build a beautiful, fully animated 3D voxel-style pagoda island using Three.js and React.

Create a floating island with layered grass, soil, and rocky voxel terrain.
Place a detailed Japanese pagoda with multiple curved roofs, wooden pillars, and glowing lanterns at the center.
Add voxel-style cherry blossom trees, pine trees, shrubs, and tiny flowers across the island.
Build small wooden bridges, stone pathways, stairs, and waterfalls around the terrain.
Surround the island with floating rocks, tiny clouds, and distant miniature islands.
Use a warm sunset palette with pink blossoms, lush greens, golden lighting, and soft atmospheric fog.
Add realistic ambient occlusion, soft shadows, depth, and subtle bloom for a polished diorama effect.
Animate drifting cherry blossom petals, floating clouds, gently swaying trees, and flowing waterfalls.
Slowly rotate the entire island while allowing users to orbit, zoom, and explore the scene.
Use a clean perspective camera, high-quality materials, and carefully balanced composition.
Make the entire scene feel like a premium miniature voxel world, with intricate details visible at every zoom level.

title.zh: 用Opus 5.5重制的3D游戏

summary.zh: 作者用 Claude Opus 5.5 配合自制的“Skill Gauntlet Loop”流程（结合 Blender、Tripo3D、Godot 等工具），将1992年的解包游戏《Dune》重做成第三人称3D冒险游戏，沿用原版音效音乐，并以丹尼斯·维伦纽瓦电影画面作为美术参考。
summary.en: The creator used Claude Opus 5.5 with a custom 'Skill Gauntlet Loop' combining Blender, Tripo3D, Godot and other skills to remake a decompiled 1992 PC game (Dune) as a 3D third-person adventure, reusing the original audio and referencing Denis Villeneuve films for visuals.

prompt.text:
remake entirely the decompiled game into third person 3D adventure game, using my /ultimate-gauntlet-loop skill, use the originals BGM & SFX's from the game, use imagegen to turn the 2D characters into reference image for tripo3D (I also have a skill for that). Use the originals visuals and the Denis Villeneuve movies visuals as goal and reference for the artistic direction.

And that's it.

title.zh: 霸王龙尝试骑自行车动画对比
title.en: T-rex trying to ride a bicycle

summary.zh: 作品是一个循环播放的动画 SVG，描绘表情丰富的霸王龙努力骑自行车，并配有细致背景和喜剧化动作。

prompt.text:
Create an animated SVG: a T-rex trying to ride a bicycle. His tiny arms can't reach the handlebars.

THE CHARACTER
A big, expressive, original cartoon T-rex with a clear personality: a huge head, tiny arms, a thick tail, strong legs, big expressive eyes and eyebrows, a toothy grin that changes with what is happening (confident, worried, determined, embarrassed).

Good anatomy and proportions that read clearly even at a small size. Clean outlines, soft shading, a consistent art style.
THE BICYCLE
A real-looking bicycle with a frame, two wheels with spokes, a chain, pedals, a saddle, a bell and handlebars. It must look believable and mechanically correct: the chain moves, the pedals turn with the legs, the wheels spin at the right speed for the motion.
The T-rex's legs really pedal. The tiny arms keep reaching and failing to touch the handlebars.
THE COMEDY (the animation is about the struggle)
The T-rex tries to steer with his chin, his tail, his head, or by leaning, and the bike wobbles. He almost falls, recovers, then tries again.
Little gags that happen along the way: the bell rings by itself when he sneezes, his tiny arms flap in frustration, the tail swings and balances him, a small bird lands on his head or on the handlebars.
A funny moment of success (he steers perfectly for one second and looks proud) followed by a funny failure.
THE ANIMATION
Smooth, lively, cartoon-style motion with weight, squash and stretch, anticipation and follow-through. The body bobs with each pedal stroke, the tail lags behind, the bike bounces over small bumps.
The camera follows the T-rex, with the world moving past him in layers at different speeds for depth.
A seamless loop of about 12 seconds.
THE BACKGROUND
Make the background rich, detailed, atmospheric and full of life, with real depth and lots of small details to discover. It should feel like a full world, not an empty backdrop. Choose the setting and the mood yourself.
REQUIREMENTS
The animation is an SVG shown on a single web page (index.html) that opens directly in the browser, with no build step and no local server. You may use any animation approach you like (SVG animation, CSS, JavaScript).
It starts automatically and loops seamlessly. No buttons, no text, no interface.
One square (1:1) composition, centred and as large as possible at any window size, and it looks good on a phone.
Original characters and design only.

summary.en: Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol were given the same prompt to build a pixel-art 3D tennis club diorama on a floating island, with ball physics and simulated matches. Both results are linked.

prompt.text:
Make a pixel-art 3D diorama of a small tennis club on a floating island, the same series and engine as my other pixel dioramas (three.js, orthographic isometric camera turned in quarter steps, a small render target with no anti-aliasing snapped to whole pixels, depth-based outlines, a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab, hard sun shadows, day/dusk/night, rain with puddle reflections). Call it "Love All".

The club: one court inside a chain-link fence with low dark-green windscreens reading LOVE ALL, a net that sags from 1.07 m at the posts to 0.914 m at the strap, the umpire's high chair with a sunshade and the players' chairs with parasols, a three-row stand, a clubhouse with a red roof, a clock showing the real time, a flag and a terrace, a groundsman's shed, floodlights (spotlights aimed at the court, so night stays dark around it), poplars and a gravel path. The court can be clay, grass or a hard court, painted to the rule book.

Real ball physics: gravity, drag and the Magnus force of topspin and slice; a different bounce on each surface; net cords that trickle over or drop back. Players predict the ball's flight, pick where the strings can meet it (after the bounce, or on the volley or smash at the net), run there and swing in time. Each figure is a rig of boxes posed with two-bone IK; the racket follows keyed paths for a forehand, a two-handed backhand, a volley, a smash and a serve with toss, trophy pose and jump, and the strings meet the ball at contact. Shot choice comes from the situation (cross court, down the line, sharp angle, slice when stretched, lob or pass against a net rusher, drop shot against a deep player, approach and volley). Each launch is solved to clear the net and land on its target, then thrown a little off, so winners, errors and long rallies come out of the physics. Four players with their own styles play a ladder where the winner stays on: short sets to four games, no-ad scoring, a tiebreak at 3–3 and a match tiebreak to ten.

Life on court: ball kids fetch dead balls and bounce a new one to the server, who bounces it before serving. The umpire watches the ball and calls the score. On clay the ball leaves marks, and on close calls the umpire climbs down to read the mark. Between sets the groundsmen drag the clay; grass wears behind the baselines. In rain the players sit under their parasols and the groundsmen pull a cover over the court. Spectators follow the ball and clap. Click the court to aim the next shot, with buttons for a lob or a drop shot, and a ×3 speed toggle. Show a tennis scoreboard (sets, point, server, serve speed) and the ladder; English UI; it must work on phones.

prompt.text:
You're directing a 20-second animated short about the Claude Haiku 5.5 release. You're the director, the art department, the animator, the sound designer and the QA team, and you have real tools to call.

I'm giving you the idea, the tools and the quality bar. Everything else, from the beats to the look to the jokes, is yours to design. I trust your taste more than a beat sheet I could write. Your capabilities are far beyond what you assume, so work like it: plan carefully, push the craft, and use the tools and the time this deserves. Spend generously where it improves the film and economically everywhere else.

Final output: `out/level3.mp4`, 1920×1080, 30fps, exactly 20.0 seconds, with voices, music and sound design. At the end, you'll also save your process as a reusable skill.

---

## 1. The idea

**Opus is overloaded with work it shouldn't be doing.** It's buried in small, repetitive tasks: summaries, classifications, lookups, compactions. Then it has a realization: it can hand all of that to Haiku. It calls Haiku, Haiku arrives fast and clears the pile, and Opus is finally free to do the hard, important work it's built for.

That's the premise. How you tell it is up to you: the staging, gags, rhythm, camera, character beats, what the eureka moment looks like, how Haiku arrives, and how the delegation plays out. Sonnet can appear if it earns its place.

**Fixed points:**
- 20.0 seconds, 16:9.
- Opus and Haiku are characters in the same family as the Claude character.
- The film must read with the sound off.
- The ending respects reality: Haiku takes the volume, and Opus keeps the hard thinking. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 remain the better choice for complex agentic coding, so Haiku is never shown replacing Opus.

---

## 2. Style reference

The reference is Jake Moran's "Animated agent session story": https://www.prompt-motion.com/jake11moran-a269c4. It was made with this skill: https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes-community-skills/tree/master/skills/session-story. Read the skill, including its references on motion and the room.

Take from it:
- The hand-drawn watercolour-on-paper look.
- A cozy room as a world.
- Cartoon blocks with faces as characters.
- Physical paper props that carry the story (paper planes as tasks).
- A score that's cued to every action.

Don't copy it. Use it as a starting point and push it further: richer staging, better acting from the characters, more cinematic camera, and a stronger hook. It should look like it belongs to the same family, made by someone who studied it closely.

---

## 3. Facts (lock these before any creative work)

Fetch https://www.anthropic.com/claude-haiku-5-5 and write `facts.json`: every claim you might use, each with the exact supporting sentence from the page. Only claims in `facts.json` may appear on screen or in dialogue.

This is a story first, so use one or two facts at most, woven into the world rather than presented as slides. For example, a price tag being re-stamped, or Haiku's speed shown rather than stated. The film must end on a card with **Claude Haiku 5.5**.

---

## 4. Audience and hook

The audience is AI and developer Twitter/X: people who use Claude every day and know the model names and the jokes about them. Before writing the treatment:
- **Research:** spend a little time on how people currently talk about Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, and what's being said about this launch. Find one or two references or running jokes this audience would recognize and enjoy. Use them only if they fit the story naturally. Never use real people or brand logos.
- **The hook:** the first second has to work as a still frame on a busy timeline. Someone scrolling should instantly see "a character drowning in work" and want to see what happens.
- **Text on screen:** this is motion design that tells a story, not a lyric video. Use text sparingly and only where it adds something: a beat the picture can't carry alone, the fact stamp, and the end card. Integrate it into the world (painted, stamped, written in marker) rather than overlaying it.

---

## 5. Tools

The keys are in `.env`. Pick the best tool for each job, and tell me which you chose and why.

| Tool | Key | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Web search and fetch | — | Source page, style reference, audience research |
| Higgsfield (connector) | — | Image generation; call `models_explore` first to pick the best model for flat illustrated characters. Also music or sound effects if its audio models are the best fit. |
| GPT Image (OpenAI) | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | A second image model. Test both on the same prompt and keep whichever matches the style better. |
| ElevenLabs | `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` | Character voices, sound effects, and music (Eleven Music) |
| Remotion | — | The film itself |
| ffmpeg + Python | — | Audio analysis, frame extraction, checks |
| Subagents | — | Parallel research and independent review |

---

## 6. Order of work

### Step 1: Treatment
Write `treatment.md`:
- Your take on the story in one paragraph.
- The beat sheet with timings.
- What happens in each shot: camera, acting, the gag.
- Where the music hits.
- What each character says.
- Which fact appears and how.
- Why this version is the strongest way to tell it.

Write two or three distinct treatments, then pick one and explain why.

### Step 2: Style bible
Write `style/bible.md`:
- Palette: 6 colours maximum, with hex values and a reason for each.
- Ink line rules: weight, and the "boiling" redraw jitter.
- Watercolour and paper texture.
- Lighting.
- Type: local font files only.
- Character design rules for Opus and Haiku: size ratio, shapes, how each one moves, and their expression set.

### Step 3: Key art (images as the base, no video generation)
The generated images are your key frames and design references. You are the in-betweener. Generate:
1. **Style frames:** 3 options of the world. Pick one.
2. **Character sheets:** Opus and Haiku, each with front, three-quarter and side views and their full expression set. Use the chosen style frame as a reference so everything shares one world.
3. **Key poses:** one image per key pose in your treatment (roughly 6–10), each built from the character sheets and the style frame, matching the camera and composition of the shot.

Put everything on one contact sheet.

**Stop and wait for my approval** before building anything.

The images are references. The final film is drawn in code to match them, and generated images never appear on screen. Trace the shapes, poses, proportions and composition from the key art into SVG, and animate between them.

### Step 4: Audio first
The film's timing comes from the audio.
1. **Voices:** audition at least 2 ElevenLabs voices per character. Opus should feel warm, low and deliberate. Haiku should feel quick, bright and eager. Generate each line separately, with 2 takes, and keep the best delivery.
2. **Music:** generate a track that fits your treatment, about 22s long, with its structure matching your beats: for example, a drop when Haiku arrives. If the generated track won't land on your beats, trim and offset it with ffmpeg rather than changing the picture.
3. **Sound effects:** a sound for every physical action. Paper, whooshes, impacts, the lightbulb, stamps.
4. **Timing map:** detect the music's beat onsets and write `timing.json`. It holds every beat time, the drop frame, each voice line's start and end frames, and every key action snapped to the nearest beat. All animation timing reads from `timing.json`, with nothing hardcoded.
5. Play me the audio-only mix before building the picture.

### Step 5: Build in Remotion
- **Components:** one per character, prop and set piece. Story beats live as data in `story.json`.
- **Drawing:** watercolour fills via SVG turbulence and displacement filters, a multiply-blended paper texture, and boiling ink lines.
- **Motion craft:** anticipation before every big action, follow-through after, squash and stretch, springs for landings, arcs for every moving object, and no linear easing.
- **Acting:** the characters have to perform. Give them readable poses, holds where the audience needs to read a face, and timing that's funny.
- **Mouths:** mouth shapes driven by the voice track's loudness. They must be still when the character is silent.
- **Camera:** push-ins, a whip or a shake where it helps. Motivate every camera move.
- **Mix:** music, voices and sound effects on separate layers. Duck the music under dialogue.

---

## 7. Verification loops (do not skip any)

1. **Key-pose match:** at every key pose, render the frame and compare it side by side with its key art. Write what differs and fix it.
2. **Sound-off read:** render a silent cut. A fresh subagent that has seen nothing else reviews a contact sheet at 2 frames per second and retells the story. If it can't, the staging failed. Fix it and repeat.
3. **Sync check:** list every catch, landing, stamp and dialogue line with its actual frame vs its `timing.json` target. Everything must be within 1 frame.
4. **Fact check:** every word on screen and in dialogue, matched to `facts.json`. Cut anything unmatched.
5. **Technical:** duration exactly 20.0s, stereo audio, peaks below −1 dBFS, no unintended dead air.
6. **Director's review:**
- Watch the whole film at least twice as frames.
- Write a brutal critique as the most demanding motion designer you know: what feels assembled, what's slow, what doesn't land.
- Fix the top 3 issues, then review again.
- Only then hand it over, with a 10-frame contact sheet.

---

## 8. Package it as a skill

Save the full pipeline as `.claude/skills/launch-film/SKILL.md`, so that next time *"Make a launch film for [URL] about [idea]"* is enough.

The skill should include:
- The fact lock
- The treatment process
- The style bible as a reference file
- The key-art process with both image models
- Voice auditions
- Music and sound effects
- The timing map
- The reusable Remotion components
- Every verification loop

---

## Approval gates
1. `facts.json` and the chosen treatment
2. Style bible, character sheets and key poses → **wait for my approval**
3. Audio-only mix and `timing.json`
4. Final film, contact sheet and critique
5. Skill

Keep a task list throughout. At each gate, show me the work, not a description of it.

prompt.text:
Turn the attached footage into a beat-synced, manga-style music edit and send me the finished MP4.

INPUTS (fill in or leave blank; if blank, choose sensibly and tell me what you chose)
- Source footage: [attached]
- Music: [attached track / use the source audio]
- Aspect ratio: [default 4:3 1440x1080; 9:16 1080x1920 for vertical], 24 fps
- On-screen text / credit: [optional]
- Palette: [default: paper #f8f2ea, ink #141012, main accent red #d0141e (shadow #7c0a12), highlight yellow #ffd60a (shadow #f29a00)]

GOAL
The edit should feel like a living manga page: ink lines, screentone, flat accent colours, bold graphic backgrounds, and hard cuts locked to the music. It must look designed, not like a filter over video.

1. STUDY THE MATERIAL
- Go through the footage frame by frame using contact sheets. Catalogue every usable moment: framing, pose, motion peaks, internal cuts, and strong details (eyes, hands, silhouettes, close-ups, crash zooms).
- Analyse the music: BPM, beat grid, downbeats, phrases, sections, energy curve, accents, fills, ending.

2. LOCK THE LOOK (applies to every shot)
- Mask the subject on every frame (rembg isnet-anime for anime or illustration, a human-segmentation model for live action). Check mask quality before relying on it.
- Ink lines via XDoG/DoG, with thickness scaled to the framing.
- Paper base. Mid-tones become halftone dots: fixed screen angle, area-correct radius. The deepest shadows become solid ink.
- Strict palette: paper + ink + one main accent + one highlight.
- Map the subject's most distinctive colour to the flat main accent.
- Map glowing or brightest elements to the highlight.
- Everything else stays monochrome.
- Tune tones per shot so faces read clean (mostly paper, light screentone).
- Give subject cut-outs a thin ink outline when composited over graphics.

3. DESIGN YOUR OWN SHOT VOCABULARY
Based on what this footage does well and what this music needs, define 6-10 recurring shot types. Each type pairs a kind of source framing with a graphic treatment. Draw from this palette or invent your own:
- extreme close-up of a detail with impact shake
- silhouette over a bold graphic (concentric rings, rays, burst)
- clean black-and-white manga panel with a lightened background
- subject cut-out over a graphic ground (halftone texture, printed-page texture, blobs, speed lines, flat colour)
- typographic panel (large vertical CJK or bold type, plus small secondary lines; all text original)
- impact marks (!!, stars, sparkles)
- black or flash frames
- glitch frames (channel split, slice offset, magenta/yellow)
- tinted frames (pink, red, mono)
- halftone-dissolve transitions
- punch-ins and crash zooms
Rules:
- Every type must use something the footage genuinely does well.
- Save the strongest images for the strongest musical moments.
- Briefly justify each type.

4. PLAN A FRAME-ACCURATE EDL BEFORE RENDERING
List start/end frame, shot type, source frames, framing, motion, transition and text for every shot. Rhythm rules:
- Cut 1-2 frames before the beat.
- Mix durations: 3-6 frame hits against 1-2 beat holds, with at least one breathing moment per phrase.
- Build a recognisable 8-beat (or phrase-length) pattern and repeat it, using different source footage each time.
- Let the energy follow the music:
- a calm intro (for example desaturated, with only the highlight in colour)
- dense peaks
- an outro where colour drains, glitches escalate, and the edit fades with the music
- Land gestures and motion peaks in the footage on musical accents.

5. MOTION AND FINISH
- Animate the subject on twos. Keep camera moves (zoom, drift, rotation) smooth on every frame.
- Use shake and scale bumps on hits, with subtle film grain.
- An optional small HUD element (for example a timecode box) is fine.

6. PREVIEW, FIX, RENDER, VERIFY
- Before the full render, render one frame per shot as a preview sheet. Fix composition, mask errors, text cut-offs and palette breaks.
- Render, then review the whole output on contact sheets, fix problems and re-render the affected frames.
- Encode H.264 at CRF ~20-22 with AAC 192k, synced to the music at the same length.

QUALITY BAR
- Every frame could pass as a printed panel.
- No muddy greys, no unmasked background smears, and no accidentally cropped text.
- Dot size stays consistent.
- Outside glitch frames, no more than two colours appear besides paper and ink.

DELIVER
The MP4, plus a short summary of the shot types you invented and where they land in the edit.

title.zh: 代码渲染的港口巨型机甲动画短片
title.en: Harbour Mech Anime Short Rendered in Code

summary.zh: 作者用 Fable 5.5、并行代理、Blender 和 Python 制作了 92 秒动画短片，共 43 个镜头，并通过代码渲染和检查。
summary.en: The creator made a 92-second anime film with Fable 5.5 using parallel agents, Blender and Python, with 43 shots rendered and checked by code.

prompt.text:
Create a 2D anime short. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic.

Build everything in Blender from Python, render it in Eevee, then ink and paint every frame in a second pass. Deliver one 1920x1080, 24 fps MP4 with a synthesized soundtrack. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime.

Use theatrical anime as the art style reference for the design, line work, painted backgrounds, color and atmosphere. The film is 90 seconds long, in 43 shots. Its hero is a giant harbour mech. No people appear in the film.

HERO
Unit 07, an 80 m harbour mech that has slept in a dry dock for decades: chipped safety-yellow paint, rust runs, moss and hanging vines, one wide dark visor with two amber eye lights, a lightning-rod antenna, big hands with three fingers and a thumb, and a gull nesting on its head. It moves on twos, slow and heavy, and its feet never slide.

WORLD
High Harbor, a floating island-city 320-530 m above a bay, held by one colossal stud-link chain anchored to the seabed: windmills, a bell tower, white houses with terracotta roofs, waterfalls pouring off the rim into the void, blue levitation crystals underneath and an iron collar at the bottom tip. Below it, a working port at real scale: a dry dock, container cranes, fishing boats, a hillside town, a breakwater with tetrapods and a red-and-white lighthouse at its tip, and on the seabed a giant anchor overgrown with coral.

STORY
Sunrise over the city. A storm rolls in from the west and a waterspout forms. Lightning strikes the chain, the discharge runs down to the anchor, the shackle pin shears and the chain whips free: the city starts to drift toward the waterspout. The free end smashes a crane by the dry dock, lightning hits the mech's antenna and its visor lights. It rises tearing vines and rust, wades out, runs along the breakwater past the lighthouse, leaps, catches the last link, is dragged through the sea, winds the chain round the lighthouse like a bollard and holds. The waterspout passes the city by metres. The clouds tear open, the gull returns to its nest, the visor dims.

LIGHT
High-key anime light, never murky: a low morning sun from the east, a saturated cobalt sky, white cumulus with lavender shadows, a cobalt-turquoise sea with drawn whitecaps. The storm brings indigo cloud and lightning; light only changes with a cause you can see. Cel light with hard shadows, gouache backgrounds, ink lines on every machine and building, effects drawn on twos: water as inked sheets with foam crowns, never particle mush.

SOUND
A synthesized orchestra on a 150 bpm grid, so every cut lands on an 8th note: a hopeful theme on flute and horn, the storm in D minor, a 12/8 chase with one beat per footfall, a heavy 3/4 for the hold. 18 hits land exactly on the picture: the strikes, the snap, the catch.

FORMAT
Write the film as a Python story clock: one state per frame for every pose, camera, chain link, effect and sound cue.

CHECKS
Before the final render a script tests every frame on the real meshes: the mech never goes through itself, the chain, the dock, the breakwater or the lighthouse; chain links never pass through each other; the camera never enters a mesh, the city rock or the sea; nothing jumps between frames.

summary.en: A single-prompt, self-contained HTML/WebGPU simulation of a jelly orange that can be stretched, squished and sliced was built with Claude Opus 5.5.

prompt.text:
Build "Whole Orange Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (inline JS/CSS, no libraries): a real-time WebGPU soft-body whole orange made of jelly. The user can grab and stretch it, and cut it with a knife into wheels, wedges and small pieces. Every piece is its own wobbling body.

Shape and pieces
- The orange is a signed distance field: a gently oblate ellipsoid (polar half-length 1.27 along x, equatorial radius 1.36) lying on its side, with a softly flattened seat on the floor.
- Every piece is that field clipped by the half-spaces n·X ≤ c of the cuts that made it, with the fresh edges rounded (smooth max, k ≈ 0.085). All pieces share the orange's original rest frame, so the anatomy stays where it grew.
- Per piece:
- a surface-nets render skin (0.042 grid) projected onto the field;
- a hex lattice for the simulation in the piece's own principal frame, with boundary nodes snapped to the surface;
- barycentric embedding of render vertices into the lattice tets.
- Up to 30 pieces; slivers are rejected.

Anatomy (all in rest space, so every cut shows it where it really is)
- Zest (0.07 deep) with oil-gland pores, a mottled tone, a green stem button at one end and a small navel at the other.
- White pith (to 0.19 deep).
- 11 segments around the stem axis, with thin milky membrane walls (slightly jittered, bowed and wandering along the axis) and a pithy core along the axis.
- Juice vesicles: teardrop sacs fanning out from the core within each segment.
- 16 pale citrus pips near the core, pointed end inward; a few small bubbles in the flesh.
- A pip that a cut goes through is kept by the side holding its centre and eased just under the new face.

Physics (XPBD)
- Per piece: hex cells with co-rotational shape matching plus volume constraints on their five tets.
- Zest and pith firmer than the flesh.
- Edge and deformation damping; floor contact with Coulomb friction and a little rolling resistance.
- Piece–piece contact against each other's exact rest shape in a best-fit frame.
- Sleeping pieces that wake on touch; fixed 60 Hz step with small substeps.

Knife
- A nakiri-style knife: draw a stroke across the orange.
- The stroke, read on the top of what it crosses, fixes a vertical blade plane, carried into each crossed piece's rest frame by its best-fit rotation and added as a half-space.
- The new pieces are built incrementally while the knife lines up, presses a groove and cuts straight down. They take over the position and speed of the jelly they came from, and the blade wedges the faces apart.

Rendering (WebGPU / WGSL)
- Procedural photo studio. Soft PCSS key shadow tinted by the jelly, plus contact AO from a height map.
- Back-face thickness; refraction of the scene, with each tap dimmed by its own path length.
- A volumetric march through the jelly in rest space, using a per-vertex inverse deformation gradient:
- zest, pith, membranes/core and flesh each absorb with their own colour (Beer–Lambert);
- scattering is grey (only absorption is coloured), so light scattered out of orange flesh stays orange.
- The white pith, the membrane star and the core read crisply on cut faces.
- Back-lit glow at thin edges, Fresnel studio reflections, GGX highlights, sugar-crystal glints.
- Post: Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping, sRGB, dither.

UI (editorial "Material Studies / No. 032", English)
- Italic serif title "Whole / Orange." with the caption "Eleven segments, set in jelly. Zest, pith and juice. Cut it as small as you like."
- Status pill "WEBGPU · LIVE".
- Tools: Hand / Knife. Varieties: Navel, Blood, Cara Cara.
- Firmness and Internal damping sliders; Give it a nudge, Reset, Pause; ¼ speed and Show mesh.
- Readouts: Mass (g, 1 unit ≈ 3 cm at 1.3 g/cm³), Volume (% of rest), Kinetic (mJ), Pieces.
- A collapsible "Inside the experiment" with notes on the method.
- Fallback without WebGPU. Stacked mobile layout with no horizontal scroll.

prompt.text:
Turn the attached image into a seamless looping GIF (~15s, 15fps)
styled as a surveillance-camera "subject analysis" sequence:

1. ACQUIRE – desaturated CCTV feed with REC, camera ID, running
timecode; a search reticle locks onto the subject.
2. SILHOUETTE – background dims to a dark grid; AI detection boxes
(head, torso, limbs + confidence scores) pop in; a scan line
turns the subject into a flat silhouette.
3. STRUCTURE – silhouette becomes a glowing wireframe (edges +
triangle mesh), then a pose skeleton with joint angles.
4. FEATURES – real colors return; an "ENHANCE" zoom on the face;
animated callouts with typed labels for 4–5 key features.
5. PALETTE – extract the 6 dominant colors (k-means); swatches fly
from the image into a panel with hex codes and percentages.
6. IDENTIFY – "TARGET LOCKED" + ID card (class, threat level,
match %), then a glitch back to frame 1 for a seamless loop.

Keep the original artwork intact (segment it, don't redraw it).
Minimal HUD: white + one accent color, monospace font, a stage
progress panel in the emptiest area of the frame, no text over
the face. Export GIF + MP4.

prompt.text:
Create a high-energy 16:9 music video using both supplied video clips, edited to exactly match the full duration of the supplied music.

EDITING:
Analyze both clips and the soundtrack. Select the strongest moments, creatively cut, interleave, rearrange and combine footage from both sources. Build a cohesive, fast-paced edit driven by the music's rhythm, energy, transitions and emotional progression. Freely alternate between clips, create visual connections and synchronize key actions with musical accents. Avoid simply playing the clips sequentially.

GRID STRUCTURE:
Use a dynamic, asymmetrical manga-inspired panel layout with large dominant panels, narrow strips, tilted rectangles and smaller supporting panels separated by clean white gutters. Use the reference image strictly for panel geometry, not its artwork or visual style. Mix moments from both clips across different panels, creating coordinated compositions. On major beats, dynamically rearrange panel sizes, positions and boundaries.

VISUAL EFFECTS:
Blend aggressive style infections spreading between neighboring panels with temporal variations, motion echoes, frame repetitions, time offsets and impact freezes. Create dense, layered visual effects, rhythmic flashes, graphic symbols and cross-panel chain reactions. Synchronize everything precisely to the soundtrack.

CREATIVE DIRECTION:
Let the footage and music guide all editing decisions, visual treatments, effects and transitions. Be bold, experimental and visually inventive. Keep the original characters, actions and environments clearly recognizable. Use large panels to maintain visual clarity while smaller panels explore creative variations. Effects should enhance the footage rather than replace it.

AUDIO:
Preserve the original audio from both clips, including dialogue, sound effects and ambience. Retain relevant sounds from the selected moments and mix them naturally with the supplied music. The soundtrack drives the edit and plays uninterrupted from beginning to end.
No typography, text, letters or numbers.

prompt.text:
Build me a single-file HTML artifact: a pixel-art 3D indoor volleyball final, in the same visual and technical style as my earlier pixel works (Hollybrook Open tennis, School Yard Futsal, Bramley Oval cricket). Reuse their rendering approach, but give this page its own identity.

NAME AND IDENTITY
- Title: "Lighthouse Cup". Header kicker: "Grand Final" and "Marlowe Arena". Invented teams, players and sponsors only, seeded so they are identical on every load.
- Page look: the match-day programme of a sports hall. Warm maple paper background, deep navy for ink and selection, signal orange (the colour of court markings) for everything live or chosen. The header has a navy boundary line with a dashed orange attack-line under it, a small logo (an orange ball with navy seams) and a big uppercase condensed title. The match sits in a framed plate with a hard navy offset shadow (no blur). Section titles in the control panel carry a small orange court-corner glyph. Buttons and headings are uppercase condensed.
- Fonts: Barlow Condensed (display, headings, scoreboard numerals, buttons) and Barlow (all reading text). Light theme by default; dark theme ("an evening in the hall") with navy-black paper and a lighter orange. All colours as tokens, explicit body background, 16px gutters, no horizontal scroll at 400px, controls stacked under a sticky picture on phones.

RENDERING (same pipeline as my other works)
- three.js r128 from cdnjs, real 3D geometry only (no sprites), orthographic isometric camera.
- Render to a tiny low-res target (pixel size slider 1-6 px, default 2), depth-based outlines, then snap every pixel to one fixed 90-colour palette in OKLab with ordered dither. Procedural sky shader.
- Scene: an indoor sports hall as a diorama on a floating island. Court 18 x 9 m with lines, net with antennae and posts, referee stand, line judges, bench areas, scoreboard, banners, tiered stands with an instanced crowd that reacts to points and big rallies, light columns, big windows letting in sky.
- Hall lights: Day / Evening / "Show" with eased transitions; four light columns switch on in the later modes. Real shadows.
- Floor types (default maple) that change texture, bounce and shoe squeak, with two live gauges (Bounce, Squeak) updated from the ball.
- Blocky rigged players in team kits, a libero in a different shirt colour, a referee, line judges, a coach per bench. Poses: ready stance, run, jump serve, float serve, spike, block (arms up over the net), dig, set, dive, celebrate, dejected, referee signals.
- Cameras: TV follow (tracks the ball), Whole hall, Close-up. Drag to turn, wheel/pinch to zoom, Q/E turn, 1/2/3 cameras, R reset, right-drag or Shift-drag pans, plus pixel size, outlines, dither, raw-3D toggles.

GAME (simulated, not scripted)
- Leagues (e.g. women's and men's) each with several invented teams and rosters of 12 (six on court, a libero, bench). Formats: Quick set to 15, One set to 25, Best of 3, Best of 5.
- Real volleyball scoring: rally point, sets to 25 (15 in the decider) won by two, the serving team rotates through the six positions after each side-out, libero rules (back row only, replaces a middle blocker), two timeouts and two substitutions logic per set, two video challenges per set. Toss and teams walk-out ceremony, set breaks, final result.
- Ball physics for serves, passes, sets, attacks, blocks and floor contact, so that every point (ace, kill, block, dig, net touch, out ball, service error) comes from where the ball and players actually are. Serve speed shown in km/h.
- Rally logic: receive, set, attack, block and dig decisions driven by player ratings (serve, receive, set, attack, block, defence, stamina), rotation position, and the coach's tactics. Players tire over a long match.
- Coach panel for the team the user picks, the other team is AI:
- Serve: four options (for example float, jump, short, aggressive), applied to the next serves.
- Attack: five options (for example power, tip, line, cross, quick middle) applied to the next attacks.
- Block: two options (for example read, commit).
- "Aim next attack": click a spot on the opponent's half to direct the next attack or serve.
- Timeout (2 per set) called at the next dead ball with a countdown banner, which also affects momentum.
- Substitution: pick a court player and a bench player from chips, then confirm.
- Video challenge (2 per set): a ring countdown button appears after a close line call, then a "Video check" overlay tracks the ball and shows IN or OUT, overturning the call if it was wrong.
- Controls: New match, Skip ceremony, speed 1/2x to 4x, pause, auto-next match, sound toggle (synthesised Web Audio, no audio files), key shortcuts (N new, K skip, T timeout, C challenge, A aim, S floor, L lights, Space pause).

HUD
- A navy scoreboard bug over the picture: header line with the set number and a "Set point/Match point" flag, one row per team with a serving-ball dot, a kit chip, three-letter name, timeout pips, set scores, current points, and a six-cell rotation diagram per team (libero highlighted, server marked). Serve-speed pill, skewed orange event captions (ACE, KILL, BLOCK, SET POINT), a one-line live commentary strip, state chips (Live/Paused, speed, camera).

MATCH CENTRE
- Set-by-set score table with the serving team marked, result banner, comparison stats (aces, kills, blocks, errors, serve/receive quality), top performers per team, rosters with positions, libero and "on court" markers, commentary feed newest first with varied phrasing.

TUNING
- Rallies of realistic length (mostly 2-6 contacts, occasional long rallies), side-out about 60-65 percent, aces 5-8 percent, a set to 25 lasting 4-6 minutes at 1x. Close sets should happen often.

QUALITY BAR
- Test in headless Chromium (local three.js via route interception, software WebGL). Run dozens of full matches without rendering in every format to catch exceptions and tune balance from outcome statistics. Screenshot day, evening, show, mobile and dark theme. Test coach actions, substitutions, timeouts, the video challenge and auto-next. Fix every bug you find; do not stop at the first working render.
- Publish as one HTML file with a short description, and tell me what you did not verify (real GPU, audio by ear, real touch device).

prompt.text:
Build "Gummy Bears" - a single self-contained HTML file (three.js from a CDN is the only dependency): a handful of translucent gummy bears on a white table that you can grab, stretch, squash, throw and pour.

The bears

- Classic gummy bear silhouette: round head with two ears, short snout, plump body, stubby arms and legs, tiny molded eyes and nose - Every part melts smoothly into the next - build the body as an implicit surface (metaballs / marching cubes), not separate spheres - Material: real gummy candy. Translucent with transmission and refraction, colored light absorption that gets deeper in thick parts, glossy clearcoat with sharp highlights - Colors: cherry red, orange, lemon yellow, apple green, clear pineapple - Soft colored shadow under each bear, tinted by the bear's own color

Physics (this is the whole point - it must feel like jelly, not plastic)

- Each bear is a soft body: mass points for head, ears, snout, body, belly, hands and feet, held together by volume-preserving shape matching

- Limbs and neck are rendered as stretchy strands between points, getting thinner as they stretch

- Grab any part and pull: it stretches like rubber, the rest of the bear leans after it, on release it snaps back with a damped wobble

- Pull the head up: the neck stretches, the body follows, on release the bear squashes and hops

- Press down on the head: the bear pancakes, bulges sideways, then launches itself back up

- Throw a bear: it flies, squashes on landing, bounces and pushes other bears out of the way

- Bears collide with each other and never pass through one another

- Idle bears do small random hops with squash and stretch

- "Pour more bears" drops a handful from above into a wobbling, jiggling pile

UI

- Editorial product-page style on a white background. Large italic serif title "Gummy / Bears.", a short subtitle, a minimal card on the right with flavor swatches, a wobble slider, live "Stretch" and "Bounces" readouts and a "Pour more bears" button

- A subtle circular cursor that grows while grabbing

- ACES tone mapping, environment reflections, soft key and back light. Smooth 60fps

title.zh: 可切换昼夜与雨天的像素篮球场微缩场景

summary.zh: Claude Opus 5.5 花费 10.1 美元做出的像素风等距街头篮球场小场景。场上由 AI 球员进行 2v2 比赛，可以缩放视角、切换昼夜和开启下雨。
summary.en: A pixel-art isometric diorama of a street basketball court, built by Claude Opus 5.5 for $10.1. AI players play 2v2, and users can zoom, change the time of day and turn on rain.

prompt.text:
Build "Corner Court" — a single-file, real-time three.js (r160, ES module via import map from jsDelivr) page: an isometric diorama of an original street basketball half court on a floating city block, rendered as crisp pixel art. UI text in English.

RENDER PIPELINE
- Orthographic camera at ~31° elevation, azimuth 45° + 90° steps (animated; drag sideways or buttons), wheel/pinch zoom; fit the whole slab into the free screen area.
- Render into a small target (screen / pixel size) with no anti-aliasing; snap the camera to whole pixels.
- Post pass:
- depth outlines (darken a pixel >0.55 m in front of a neighbour);
- nearest colour of a fixed ~54-colour city palette in OKLab (concrete/asphalt greys, sky and night blues, court teal, terracotta/orange, reds, yellows, leaf greens, skin/wood, dusk purples, neon pink); optional 4×4 Bayer dither;
- whole-pixel upscale via texelFetch; the background (depth = 1) is the page colour.
- Hard shadows (BasicShadowMap); flat-shaded Lambert low-poly.
- Puddle reflections: render the scene mirrored about the ground (scene.scale.y = -1, ground meshes and rain hidden) into a second target, sampled at gl_FragCoord in the ground shader.
- "Raw 3D" mode: the same scene at full resolution with MSAA.

SCENE
- A ragged-edged slab: grass over soil over rock.
- An asphalt pad painted texel-by-texel at 10 px/m: teal inside the 6 m arc (straight corner lines), terracotta key, white lines, free-throw and restricted circles, cracks, worn paint, a stencilled "COURT 7".
- Hoop: padded navy pole, arm, backboard with its square, orange torus rim, and a line-segment net that sways when the ball goes through.
- Chain-link fence behind the hoop (alpha-tested diamond texture).
- A brick corner shop with an awning, lit windows, a pink "OPEN" neon sign and a vending machine.
- A long wall with an original sunset-city mural.
- A sidewalk with a bench and two seated spectators.
- Floodlights, a streetlight, low-poly trees, hedges, a dumpster, a fountain, a bike rack with two bikes, a hydrant.
- Pigeons that peck and fly off when players or the ball come near.

PLAYERS — procedural rigs of ~17 boxes
- Two-bone IK for legs (running stride, defensive slide, tucked jumps) and arms: dribble hand following the ball, jump-shot set point with release and gooseneck follow-through, layup reach, two-hand dunk, chest pass, rebound/contest reach, celebration.
- Spectators sit, cheer on makes and open umbrellas in the rain.

GAME — streetball 2v2 half court
- Make it take it; 1s inside the arc, 2s beyond; first to 11; win counter.
- Check ball at the top (pass to the defender and back). A change of possession must be cleared beyond the arc.
- Offence AI: dribble to spots, drive when the lane is open, pull-up jumpers when open, layups/dunks at the rim, passes when pressured; the off-ball player spots up or cuts. Man-to-man defence with stance, gap control, steals and contested jumps (blocks).
- Ball physics with substeps: bounces on asphalt, sphere vs torus rim and backboard box, net drag, pole, fences, wall, slab edge.
- Jumpers aimed on a ballistic arc (~50°) with speed/aim noise growing with distance and contest.
- Layups lofted to a peak above the rim so they drop in.
- Rebounds with jumps; out of bounds goes to the other team.
- Score, possession and status messages ("SWISH", "BLOCKED!", "TAKE IT BACK", …) on a lit scoreboard.
- Clicks: the ball handler shoots, his teammate gets a pass, the court sends the handler there. Shoot/Pass buttons.

WEATHER AND TIME
- Day / Dusk / Night lighting presets blended over ~1.6 s; floodlights, streetlight, neon and windows at night.
- Dry / Drizzle / Downpour: rain as short line streaks with splashes. A wetness value rises and slowly dries: the asphalt darkens, puddles spread from low spots in a precomputed depth map and mirror the scene, rain rings flicker in them; feet and the ball splash.

UI
- Pixel display font (Silkscreen) and a clean body font; light/dark themes via tokens.
- Controls: Time, Weather (with a court wetness bar), Shoot, Pass, New game, Pause, Turn left/right, Pixel art/Raw 3D, Pixel size, Palette/Dither/Outlines.
- A "How it's drawn" panel; a stacked mobile layout with no horizontal scroll.

title.zh: 果冻立方体太空港对比

summary.en: A single-file WebGPU diorama depicts a tropical island spaceport inside a jelly cube, with launch, staging, recovery, weather and wildlife simulations. The creator compared Claude Opus 5.5 with GPT-6 Astra using the same prompt.

prompt.text:
Build "Launch Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama in the "Material Studies" series: a spaceport on a low tropical island, cut out as a cube of translucent jelly on a studio floor. Everything procedural (no external assets, no network), one HTML file with inline JS/WGSL.

THE BLOCK
- A wobbly jelly cube you can grab by its sides and tip; it springs back. Sliders: firmness, wave damping, wind (0–20 m/s).
- Shallow-water sim for the sea (wind waves, wakes, foam), sandy seabed with ripples and caustics, seagrass, coral heads, sponges, starfish, conchs, an old rocket engine bell on the bottom. Cut faces show sand, shelly limestone and candy strata. Drag the water to stir it.

THE SCENE
- Land along the back and left: dunes, scrub, palms, dune grass, a beach.
- Launch pad on a concrete berm: mount over a flame trench opening toward the sea, steel deflector, four red-and-white lightning masts with sagging catenary wires, a deluge water tower, tank farm (LOX sphere, kerosene tanks, nitrogen bottles), floodlights.
- A long hangar with ribbed siding and a vertical-lift door, rails to the pad, a transporter-erector (white lattice strongback on a rail car with hydraulic rams).
- Landing zone (concrete circle with ring and cross), refurbishment shed, fire truck, a tracking radar dish that follows whatever is flying.
- Press site: bleachers full of spectators, a flag, a big amber seven-segment countdown clock (T−0:10 … T+0:45).
- Quay with fenders and bollards, a crawler crane with a long lattice boom, two booster stands, a warehouse.
- At sea: a drone ship (dark deck with landing target, blast walls, thruster houses), a tug, a fairing-recovery boat with a big net on four arms.
- The rocket: two stages — booster with nine engines, black interstage, four folding landing legs, four grid fins; upper stage with a long dark vacuum nozzle; a two-piece fairing whose halves carry parafoils.

WHAT HAPPENS
- Roll out: the hangar door lifts, the erector carries the rocket out horizontally on rails and stands it on the mount; it vents LOX wisps.
- Launch: 10-second count with beeps and the clock, strongback leans back, deluge water, ignition at T−3 with huge steam clouds boiling out of the trench toward the sea, slow liftoff, the block trembles, the crowd cheers, gulls go up. The rocket pitches downrange and climbs out of sight leaving a billowing exhaust trail; the camera rises with it.
- Staging: MECO, separation, the upper stage lights a pale blue-violet vacuum flame and leaves. The booster flips, boostback burn, grid fins out, entry burn, steers down, landing burn on one engine, legs swing out, touchdown — on the drone ship or back at the landing zone (toggle, or tap the ship / the pad). Double sonic boom (triple for the landing zone). Boosters come back sooty; the deck and pad get scorched.
- Recovery: the tug tows the drone ship to the quay; the crane hooks the booster, lifts it (pendulum swing), folds its legs, sets it on a stand; the ship is towed back out. Fairing halves come down under orange-and-white parafoils, circling in: one lands in the boat's net, the other splashes and is fished out; the boat brings them home.
- Reuse: the next rollout takes a flight-proven booster ("B1 · flight 2", soot partly cleaned).
- Storm: wind, waves, rain, darkened room, lightning on the masts, the crane or the sea. No launches in a storm or above 15 m/s ("No go · weather / wind"); a count in progress holds.

LIFE
- Brown pelicans that circle and plunge-dive for fish, gulls on masts, lamps and roofs, a pod of bottlenose dolphins, manatees grazing the shallows and surfacing to breathe, fish schools, moon jellies; pad crew who leave before the count, hands on the quay, spectators who raise their arms at liftoff and landing.

RENDERING
- Engine plumes as glowing translucent cones (white-hot core, orange, shock diamonds low down, widening and turning blue-violet in thin air) that light the ground, the smoke and the rocket orange; steam and exhaust as soft lit puffs; soot streaks on flown boosters; shadows, refraction, caustics.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Roll out, Launch (Hold during the count), Land on ship / Land at pad, Storm. Space rolls out / launches. Taps: rocket = launch, hangar = roll out, drone ship / landing zone = choose landing site.
- Tallies: Launches, Landings, Fairings; status lines for the Rocket (T−/T+ timeline: Liftoff, Max Q, Stage separation, Boostback, Entry burn, Landing burn…), the Drone ship and the Fairing boat.
- Flavours: Lime, Curaçao, Blackcurrant. Sound toggle, pause, reset, view.
- All sounds synthesised with WebAudio, only for events (door motor, hydraulics, countdown beeps, engine roar loop while burning, sonic booms, touchdown thud, tug horn, winch, net catch, thunder) — no background ambience.
- Mobile bottom sheet, touch orbit, pinch zoom; a fallback message without WebGPU.
- Copy: "Launch Jelly. A spaceport on a low island, its rockets flying and coming home, set in a block of jelly." — "Roll it out. Light it up. Bring the booster home."

title.zh: 警察追逐街机风格游戏原型

summary.zh: 一款俯视角警察追逐街机游戏，由Claude Opus 5.5根据完整PRD文档在Unity中开发，使用了Topdown Engine插件和ChatGPT生成的美术素材。
summary.en: A top-down police-chase arcade game built in Unity by Claude Opus 5.5 from a full PRD, using the Topdown Engine asset and ChatGPT-made artwork.

prompt.text:
PRD — Police Chase Arcade Game

Working title: Heatwave
Platform: iOS + Android
Engine: Unity
Genre: Top-down 3D arcade chase / survival
Orientation: Portrait
Input: One-thumb touch controls
Business model: TBD — design MVP around gameplay first
Primary goal: Build a genuinely fun playable prototype before adding progression or monetization.
⸻
Product vision
A fast, chaotic mobile arcade game where the player is constantly being pursued by increasingly aggressive police.
The player cannot directly attack.
Instead, they survive by driving aggressively, drifting around obstacles, making sudden turns and tricking pursuing police into crashing into obstacles and each other.
The fantasy is:
You’re not stronger than the police. You’re harder to catch.

Runs should produce constant near-misses, chain collisions and moments where the player escapes a seemingly impossible situation.

Think:

easy controls + aggressive pursuit + physics chaos + escalating pressure.

⸻

Core gameplay loop

START RUN
↓
DRIVE / DRIFT
↓
POLICE PURSUE
↓
BAIT POLICE
↓
DODGE
↓
POLICE CRASH
↓
GAIN SCORE
↓
WANTED LEVEL INCREASES
↓
MORE / HARDER POLICE
↓
SURVIVE
↓
EVENTUALLY GET CAUGHT
↓
SCORE / RESTART

Target run duration:

2–5 minutes.

Restart should take less than 2 seconds.

⸻

Design principles

3.1 One-thumb playable

The player should be able to understand the controls within seconds.
No accelerator.
No brake pedal.
No virtual steering wheel.
The vehicle moves automatically.
The player controls only direction.

(I moved away from this after testing it the first time and added the onscreen joystick)

3.2 Arcade physics, not simulation
Vehicles should:
drift
slide
bounce
spin
collide dramatically
recover quickly
Fun takes priority over physical accuracy.

3.3 Pursuers are weapons
Police are effectively the player’s offensive mechanic.
The player should learn:
“If I turn here, that cop is going straight into that wall.”
3.4 Chaos should remain readable

Even with 10+ vehicles on screen, the player must immediately understand:
where they are
where they’re moving

where police are coming from

what can kill them

3.5 Failure should feel fair

Death should generally result from a mistake the player understands rather than unpredictable physics.

⸻

MVP scope

Do not build progression, upgrades, missions or monetization for the first milestone.

The first version contains:

1 player vehicle

1 arena

1 police vehicle

1 elite police variant

5 wanted levels

physics collisions

environmental obstacles
scoring
player health
police destruction
basic VFX
basic audio

game-over screen

instant restart

That’s enough to determine whether the game deserves further development.

⸻

Player vehicle

Movement

Player vehicle uses a Rigidbody-based arcade controller.

Do not rely heavily on realistic WheelColliders.
Core variables should be exposed in the Unity Inspector:
Acceleration
Maximum Speed
Turn Speed
Turn Curve
Lateral Grip
Drift Factor
Vehicle Mass
Collision Force
Drag
Angular Drag
Recovery Speed
These need to be extremely easy to tune.

⸻

Controls

Recommended first implementation:

Drag steering

Player touches anywhere on the lower portion of the screen.

Dragging horizontally controls steering.

← drag turn left
→ drag turn right
Vehicle accelerates automatically.
Steering should be relative rather than absolute.
The player should be able to lift their finger without immediately losing control.
Alternative to prototype
Test:
Hold left/right side of screen = steer left/right.
Don’t commit until both have been tested on a physical phone.
⸻
Drift system
Drifting should happen naturally when turning at speed.
No dedicated drift button.
At low speed:
high traction

At high speed:

reduced lateral traction

This produces controlled sliding.

Long drifts can optionally award score.

Example:

DRIFT
+120
LONG DRIFT
+340

But drift scoring is secondary to police destruction.

⸻
Police AI
Police should feel:
aggressive, predictable and slightly stupid.
They should not simply follow the player’s current position.
Instead, calculate an interception target based on player velocity.
Conceptually:
target =
playerPosition
+
playerVelocity * predictionTime
Police therefore try to cut the player off.
⸻
Police intelligence

Police intentionally have limited obstacle avoidance.

This is important.

Perfect navigation would make the game less fun.

Police should:

pursue aggressively

attempt interception

avoid obvious static obstacles

poorly account for other police
overshoot turns

collide with each other

occasionally take dangerous routes

This creates opportunities for the player.

⸻

Police destruction

Police can be destroyed by:

high-speed obstacle collisions

hitting another police vehicle

chain collisions

environmental hazards

The player does not have weapons.

Example scoring:

COP SMASHED
+250
DOUBLE SMASH
+600
TRIPLE SMASH
+1,000
PILEUP!
+2,000

Chain collisions should be heavily rewarded.

⸻

Wanted system

Wanted level controls difficulty.

★☆☆☆☆
★★☆☆☆
★★★☆☆
★★★★☆
★★★★★

Wanted level increases based primarily on survival time and score.
Level 1
2 police.
Slow and forgiving.

Level 2

3–4 police.

Slightly faster.

Level 3

5–6 police.

More aggressive interception.

Level 4

7–9 police.

Elite police introduced.
Level 5
Maximum chaos.
10+ police depending on device performance.

Elite units appear frequently.

The game should eventually become effectively impossible.

That’s intentional.

⸻

Elite police

The MVP only needs one special police type.

Interceptor

Visually distinct vehicle.
Characteristics:
faster than standard police
lower mass
aggressive prediction
sharp steering
easier to destroy in collisions

This creates a glass-cannon pursuer.

⸻

Player health

Use a simple health bar.

Example:
HULL
██████░░░░
Minor impacts:
small damage.

Heavy impacts:

large damage.

Extremely high-speed impacts:
potential instant destruction.
Police contact alone shouldn’t immediately kill the player.
This allows chaotic scrambles.
⸻
Arena
First arena should be compact.
Something roughly equivalent to:

ROCK

┌─────────────┐
│ │
│ ROCK │
│ │
│ ███ │
│ │
│ ROCK │
│ ROCK│
└─────────────┘

Obstacles need enough space between them for high-speed movement.

Avoid procedural generation initially.

Hand-design one good arena.
⸻
Environment
For the first visual theme, I’d use something other than water so we’re not cloning the reference too closely.
My preference:

Desert outlaw chase

Player is an outlaw escaping through a stylized desert environment.

Environment contains:

rock formations

cacti

barriers

abandoned vehicles

ramps

fences

small buildings

dust

destructible props

It also fits the chunky visual language you’re already exploring with Bolt Pit.

⸻

Camera

Top-down perspective camera.

Not completely vertical.

Something approximately:

55–70° downward angle.

Camera follows player with smoothing.

Camera should look slightly ahead in the player’s travel direction.

At high speed:

camera pulls back slightly.

At low speed:

camera moves closer.

⸻
Camera juice
Small camera effects make a large difference.
Light collision
Tiny shake.

Heavy collision

Strong short shake.

Police destruction

Shake + tiny freeze frame.

Example:

50–100 ms hit stop.
Large pileup

Slight zoom impulse + shake + particles.

Don’t overdo continuous shaking.

⸻

Visual style

Chunky stylized 3D.

Characteristics:

simplified geometry

exaggerated proportions

bright readable vehicles

soft lighting

minimal textures

strong silhouettes

exaggerated particles
Avoid realistic vehicle proportions.
Cars should feel almost toy-like.
⸻
VFX
Minimum MVP effects:
Player
dust trail
tire/skid marks
drift smoke

impact sparks

Police

siren lights

smoke when damaged

destruction explosion

debris

Environment

dust

destructible objects

impact particles

⸻
Collision feedback
Every significant collision should combine:
physics + particles + audio + camera response.
Major police destruction:
IMPACT
→ physics impulse
→ vehicle fragments/debris
→ sparks
→ smoke
→ camera shake
→ hit stop
→ sound
→ score popup
This interaction is one of the game’s main sources of satisfaction.
⸻
Score system

Score comes from:

ActionExample
Surviving+10/sec
Police destroyed+250
Driftvariable
Near miss+100
Double collision+600
Triple collision+1,000
Large pileup+2,000

Exact values should remain configurable.

⸻

Near misses

Optional for MVP but potentially valuable.

Detect when a police vehicle passes extremely close to the player at high relative velocity.

Display:

CLOSE CALL! +100

This rewards risky driving.

⸻

UI

During gameplay keep UI extremely minimal.

SCORE COINS
13,590 14
★★★☆☆
WANTED
GAME
HULL
████████░░

No minimap initially.

Off-screen police can use subtle edge indicators.

⸻

Game over

When hull reaches zero:

brief slow motion.

Player crashes.

Then:

BUSTED
SCORE
24,850
BEST
31,220
[ AGAIN ]

Tapping anywhere could restart.

Avoid unnecessary menus between runs.

⸻

Audio

The soundscape should sell speed and collisions.

Required:

engine

tire squeal

police sirens
impact
metal crunch
debris
destruction
UI score sounds
wanted level increase

Sirens should become increasingly chaotic as wanted level increases.

⸻

Technical architecture

Suggested Unity structure:

GameManager
Player
├── PlayerController
├── VehiclePhysics
├── PlayerHealth
└── PlayerEffects
Police
├── PoliceController
├── PoliceAI
├── VehiclePhysics
├── PoliceHealth
└── PoliceEffects
Systems
├── SpawnManager
├── WantedManager
├── ScoreManager
├── AudioManager
├── CameraManager
└── PoolManager
UI
├── HUD
├── WantedUI
├── ScoreUI
├── HealthUI
└── GameOverUI

Avoid building an elaborate framework.

⸻
Object pooling
Police, particles and debris should use object pooling.
Avoid frequent:

Instantiate()
Destroy()

during gameplay.
Mobile performance should be considered from the beginning.
⸻
Performance target

Target:

60 FPS
on a mid-range modern iPhone/Android device.
Initial limits:

~12 active vehicles

~100 simple debris/particles

simple shadows

limited real-time lights

Performance should be tested on device early.

⸻
Development milestones
Milestone 1 — Greybox driving
Build:
empty arena
cube player
touch steering
acceleration
drifting

camera

Success criterion:

Driving around an empty arena feels satisfying.

Do not continue until it does.

⸻
Milestone 2 — The chase
Add:
one police vehicle
pursuit AI
interception
collisions
Success criterion:

Dodging one police car is entertaining.

⸻

Milestone 3 — Emergent chaos

Add:

multiple police

police-police collisions

obstacles

destruction

scoring

Success criterion:

Player can intentionally cause:

police → police
and
police → environment
collisions.
This is the critical milestone.
⸻
Milestone 4 — Escalation

Add:

wanted levels

spawning

difficulty scaling

interceptor

Now a run has an arc:

calm
↓
pressure
↓
chaos
↓
panic
↓
death

⸻

Milestone 5 — Juice
Add:
particles
camera shake
hit stop
skid marks

dust

sirens

collision sounds

score popups

⸻

Milestone 6 — Mobile build

Build for real devices.
Test:
controls
performance
readability
battery/thermal behaviour
different screen ratios
⸻
Milestone 7 — Decide whether to continue

At this point, stop development temporarily.

Don’t immediately build a garage and 37 unlockable cars.

Put the build in front of people.

The important questions are:

Do people immediately understand it?
Do they restart after dying?
Do they intentionally try to make cops crash?
Does “one more run” happen naturally?
If not, work on the core loop rather than adding content.
⸻
Phase 2 — only after validation
If the prototype works, then expand into:
Cars
↓
Coins
↓
Unlocks
↓
Challenges
↓
New arenas
↓
Special police
↓
Upgrades
↓
Daily challenges
↓
Leaderboards
Potential environments:
desert
city
docks
snow
industrial yard
airport
construction site
military base
And then there’s room for ridiculous police units: SUVs, armored vans, helicopters dropping roadblocks, etc.

I have opened a @[Unity CLI installation] project which we can work in. The art style of the game should be fun and cartoony and the action also over the top.
I have imported the Topdown engine into the project as well that we can use:
https://topdown-engine.moremountains.com/

I want the game to be optimized for mobile, but should work on desktop while testing.

prompt.text:
---
name: make-five-shorts
description: テーマから5選の縦型ショート動画を作る

テーマを受け取ったら次の順に進めてください。

1. 5つの項目を選び、各項目を「名前＋短いコメント2つ」にする。順位は付けない。

4. 画像は提供素材か出典を確認できるものを使う。素材がない時は勝手に別の商品画像で代用しない。
5. 大きな項目名と番号を出し、短いコメントを青とピンクで分ける。声の実際の長さに合わせて字幕と画像を切り替える。
6. 最初に合意した見た目を次の項目でも使う。項目が変わるたびに演出を増やさない。
7. 動画を最後まで見て、読み間違い・字幕のはみ出し・不自然な間を直す。
8. 動画と一緒に台本・素材の出典・編集できる制作データを残す。

prompt.text:
Build "Dolphin Jelly" — Material Studies No. 045: an interactive WebGPU soft-body study of a bottlenose dolphin cast in two layers of jelly, lying on its belly on a pale studio sweep. Same engine as the jelly series (WGSL, no libraries): signed-distance shape → surface-nets render mesh + snapped hex lattice (5 tets/cell) for XPBD with co-rotational shape matching, volume constraints, floor friction, soft grab with twist; shadow map, contact AO, back-face thickness, refraction, Beer–Lambert absorption, thin-part glow, PBR Neutral tone map.
Shape: elliptical section swept along the spine — round melon, deep chest, tall laterally-compressed tail stock, belly pressed flat; a short tapering beak smooth-unioned tightly so a crease stays at the melon; a blowhole dimple. Fins from one recipe (flat triangle, convex leading edge, falcate trailing edge, thinning to the tip): hooked dorsal, small pointed flippers, swept flukes whose roots cross the midline so the trailing edges meet in a median notch.
Two layers: clear jelly over a milky belly whose countershading line runs as a long low wave and forward under the eye to the mouth corner, so throat and lower jaw are pale. Shader in rest space: a darker cape as a pigment film (lowest under the dorsal fin, wrapping the tail stock, on the upper jaw only), eye-to-flipper blaze, eye shadow, blowhole stripe, the smile along the jaw line turning up at the corner, blowhole crescent, a few sets of parallel rake-mark scars different on each side; dark glossy eyes; trapped bubbles.
Interaction: "Kick flukes" drives a dorso-ventral stroke by muscle strain — each tet's rest shape is lengthened/shortened along the body by curvature × its height above/below the spine (volume-preserving), stronger toward the flukes, softened for a very soft jelly. "Blow": a short explosive chuff of jelly drops from the blowhole along its live axis; drops bounce, collide with the deformed body, can be tossed. Palettes Atlantic / Lagoon / Boto (pink river-dolphin nod); readouts mass, volume %, beak-to-notch length, loose drops; firmness & damping sliders, ¼ speed, mesh overlay, pause, reset; editorial UI in English.

prompt.text:
开场：盘点海外AI对国人的态度
这次是个小剧场，16：9比例
文字稿
Claude场景（Claude不读出来，画面里也没有Claude英文）：
Claude角色站在精致欧式房子前，房子门锁着，大肥鱼跑过来，Claude手里捏着晃，口气轻蔑的说：哼！我家不欢迎你来，哪来的哪回去！（就这一段需要语音，使用EdgeSpeak，模型使用Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base，使用音库里的Claude声音）
大肥鱼哭着跑了，然后叮叮当当搭起了一个类似Claude的房子，但是破破烂烂，上面写着“中转站”3个字，然后大肥鱼转身一遍，变成了Claude角色的装扮，然后大肥鱼表情很得意，Claude表情惊讶。

GPT场景
GPT角色站在现代简洁的房子前，房子门锁着，大肥鱼跑过来，GPT把钥匙放在一个台子上，温柔的说：我把钥匙放在这，你想进来可以自己开门哦~（就这一段需要语音，使用EdgeSpeak，模型使用Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base，使用音库里的GPT声音）

Gemini哈基米场景
哈基米角色站在漂亮的小木屋前挥手，房子门开着，大肥鱼跑过来，哈基米开心地说：大肥鱼，我家不关门，来一起玩呀！（就这一段需要语音，使用EdgeSpeak，模型使用Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base，使用音库里的Gemini声音）
然后大肥鱼和哈基米一起跳舞，背景音乐哈基米.mp3，就跳4秒

Grok场景
Grok角色站在类似现代酒吧和舞厅的门口，舞厅没有门，能看到五彩斑斓的射灯。大肥鱼脸红害羞的、左顾右盼地走到Grok角色身边，Grok角色说：房子哪需要门，都是哥们，快来我家，我家有的是好东西。（就这一段需要语音，使用EdgeSpeak，模型使用Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base，使用音库里的Grok2声音）
然后Grok用手揽着大肥鱼的脖子就往舞厅走去

然后用圆圈缩小的方式谢幕即可。
