title.zh: 海上果冻立方体场景对比

summary.zh: 作品是一个置于半透明果冻方块中的海上平台、风电场和风暴互动 WebGPU 微缩场景。创作者称 Claude Opus 5.5 和 GPT-6 Astra 使用同一提示词分别制作了版本。
summary.en: The work is an interactive WebGPU diorama of an offshore platform, wind farm and storm inside a translucent jelly cube. The creator says Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra made their versions from the same prompt.

prompt.text:
Build "Offshore Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama in the "Material Studies" series: a stretch of North Sea cut out as a cube of translucent jelly, sitting on a studio floor. Everything is procedural (no external assets, no network), one HTML file with inline JS/WGSL.

THE BLOCK
- A wobbly jelly cube you can grab by its sides and tip; it springs back. Sliders: firmness, damping, wind (0–20 m/s).
- Inside: a shallow-water simulation for the sea surface (waves, wakes, foam, whitecaps), seabed with sand ripples, scour rocks, kelp, boulders, starfish, crabs, urchins, a pipeline, cables and a small wreck. Caustics on the seabed. Dragging the water stirs up waves.
- Waves come from the wind: several wave trains whose height grows with wind speed.

THE SCENE
- A production platform on a four-legged steel jacket (braces, risers, conductors, boat landing, marine growth below the waterline): main and cellar decks, process module, derrick, living quarters, lifeboats, a pedestal crane with a laydown area, a flare boom with a flickering flame and smoke.
- An octagonal helideck with an H, a net, perimeter lights and a windsock.
- Five offshore wind turbines on monopiles: transition piece with yellow platform, boat landing ladder, davit, tower, nacelle, three-blade rotors with red tips, blinking red aviation lights. Rotor speed and power output (MW) follow the wind.
- A rocky skerry with a lighthouse whose beam turns; seals haul out on it.

WHAT HAPPENS
- Supply run: a platform supply vessel comes in from standby, holds station next to the jacket on dynamic positioning (thruster foam), and the crane does four lifts — containers swing on the hook, are set down on the platform and back-loaded onto the boat's deck. Then she sails back to standby.
- Helicopter: flies in from the west, turns into the wind, lands on the helideck; a deck officer walks out; passengers get off. A second press sends it away (spin-up, lift, outbound). Rotor and tail rotor spin, downwash flattens the water.
- Crew boat: a small catamaran sails out to a turbine, pushes its bow onto the boat landing, and technicians climb the ladder onto the platform. Next time she picks them up and brings them home.
- Storm: the wind builds to a gale, waves get big with whitecaps and spray, rain falls, the room darkens, lightning strikes blades, the lighthouse, the derrick or the sea with a flash and thunder. Above cut-out the turbines feather their blades and stop (0 MW); the helicopter is grounded. Then it eases and the turbines restart.

LIFE
- Schools of fish around the jacket and wrecks, gulls that perch on railings and take off on the horn, gannets that plunge-dive for fish, a pod of porpoises, seals, moon jellyfish, crew walking the decks.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Supply run, Helicopter (take-off when landed), Crew boat, Storm. Space = ship's horn. Tapping a turbine switches it on/off, tapping the supply boat or helideck calls them. Orbit by drag, zoom by wheel/pinch.
- Tallies: Power (MW), Lifts, Flights; status lines for the supply boat, helicopter and crew boat.
- Flavours (jelly colour palettes): North Sea, Curaçao, Blackcurrant.
- Sounds are synthesised with WebAudio and only play for events (horn, winch, set-down, bump, rotor, thunder, rain) — no constant background ambience. Sound toggle and pause.
- Mobile: a bottom sheet with the controls, touch orbit and pinch zoom. Clean fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
- Copy in English: "Offshore Jelly. A wind farm and a platform working a stretch of North Sea, set in a block of jelly." — "Call in the supply boat. Fly the crew out. Brew up a storm."

title.zh: 液态玻璃网页首屏

summary.zh: 作者称这是用 Opus 5.5 和一个提示词制作的液态玻璃 3D 首页区块，包含可旋转立方体和折射标题，没有使用 Spline 或 Blender。
summary.en: A liquid-glass 3D hero section with a rotatable cuboid and refracted headline was made with Opus 5.5 from one prompt, without Spline, Blender, or a 3D designer.

prompt.text: Build a single standalone index.html file (inline CSS + inline JS, no local assets, no build step) containing ONE full-screen hero section: a black "Design World" landing hero with a rotatable 3D glass cuboid in the centre that refracts a huge background headline with chromatic dispersion. Recreate it exactly to the spec below. ================================================== 1. EXTERNAL RESOURCES (use these exact URLs) ================================================== - Font: Google Fonts Poppins, weights 300/400/500/600/700/800 - Three.js r169 via importmap: "three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.169.0/build/three.module.js" "three/addons/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.169.0/examples/jsm/" Imports: GLTFLoader (loaders/GLTFLoader.js), mergeVertices + mergeGeometries (utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js), RoundedBoxGeometry (geometries/RoundedBoxGeometry.js). - 3D model (rounded cube GLB, CORS-enabled, load directly, do NOT download or replace): const MODEL_URL = 'https://d8j0ntlcm91z4.cloudfront.net/user_38xzZboKViGWJOttwIXH07lWA1P/hf_20260929_212926_92423081-b0e4-4f5a-b650-14af6c05c058.glb'; If it fails to load, fall back to new RoundedBoxGeometry(1, 1, 1, 8, 0.12). Page : "Design World — Explore New Ideas". ================================================== 2. PAGE STRUCTURE (HTML) ================================================== <section class="hero" id="hero"> <canvas id="scene" aria-label="Rotatable glass cube. Drag to rotate."></canvas> <div class="ui"> <h1 class="sr-only">Explore New Ideas</h1> <header class="nav"> <a href="#" class="logo"><i class="logo-mark"></i><b>Design</b><span>World</span></a> <ul class="nav-links"><li><a>Home</a></li><li><a>Portfolio</a></li><li><a>Contact Us</a></li></ul> </header> <div class="arrows"> <button class="arrow" id="prev">[left-arrow SVG]</button> <button class="arrow" id="next">[right-arrow SVG]</button> </div> <nav class="dots"><button class="dot"></button><button class="dot active"></button><button class="dot"></button></nav> <p class="tagline">Let's Build the<br>Future of <strong>Design.</strong></p> <div class="cta-row"> <a href="#" class="cta">Explore Now</a> <span class="cta-line"></span> <span class="count" aria-hidden="true">07</span> </div> <div class="loader" id="loader">Loading model</div> </div> </section> Arrow SVGs: viewBox 0 0 24 24, fill none, stroke currentColor, stroke-width 2.6, round caps/joins. prev path: "M19 12H5M11 6l-6 6 6 6" next path: "M5 12h14M13 6l6 6-6 6" IMPORTANT: The big "Explore / New / Ideas" headline is NOT HTML text. It is drawn onto a 2D canvas inside WebGL so the glass cube can refract it (see section 4). The HTML only has a visually hidden <h1> for accessibility. ================================================== 3. CSS (exact values) ================================================== :root { --bg:#000; --fg:#fff; --pad-x: clamp(20px, 6.95vw, 120px) } html, body { height:100%; background:#000; color:#fff; font-family:'Poppins',sans-serif; -webkit-font-smoothing:antialiased } .hero { position:relative; width:100%; height:100vh; height:100svh; min-height:520px; overflow:hidden; background:#000 } #scene { position:absolute; inset:0; width:100%; height:100%; display:block; cursor:grab; touch-action:none } #scene.dragging { cursor:grabbing } .ui { position:absolute; inset:0; pointer-events:none; z-index:2 } /* drags pass through to the canvas */ .ui a, .ui button { pointer-events:auto } .sr-only { position:absolute; width:1px; height:1px; overflow:hidden; clip:rect(0 0 0 0); white-space:nowrap } NAV .nav { position:absolute; top:clamp(24px,4.7vh,40px); left:var(--pad-x); right:var(--pad-x); display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between } .logo { display:flex; align-items:center; gap:8px; color:#fff; text-decoration:none; font-size:15px; letter-spacing:-0.01em } .logo-mark { width:20px; height:40px; background:#fff; border-radius:0 20px 20px 0 } /* white "D" half-circle */ .logo b { font-weight:700 } .logo span { font-weight:400 } .nav-links { display:flex; gap:clamp(20px,4.1vw,60px); list-style:none } .nav-links a { color:#fff; text-decoration:none; font-size:15px; font-weight:500; position:relative } .nav-links a::after { content:''; position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:-4px; height:1px; background:currentColor; transform:scaleX(0); transform-origin:right; transition:transform .35s ease } .nav-links a:hover::after { transform:scaleX(1); transform-origin:left } ARROWS (top-right, left of the dots column) .arrows { position:absolute; top:18.9%; left:76.7%; display:flex; gap:32px; transform:translate(-19px,-50%) } .arrow { width:38px; height:38px; border-radius:50%; border:2.5px solid #fff; background:transparent; color:#fff; display:grid; place-items:center; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s, color .25s } .arrow svg { width:18px; height:18px } .arrow:hover { background:#fff; color:#000 } PAGINATION DOTS (vertical, right edge) .dots { position:absolute; right:calc(var(--pad-x) - 7px); top:49.4%; transform:translateY(-50%); display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:33px } .dot { width:14px; height:14px; border-radius:50%; border:2px solid #fff; background:#fff; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s } .dot.active { background:transparent } /* active = hollow ring, middle one active by default */ TAGLINE (bottom-left) .tagline { position:absolute; left:var(--pad-x); bottom:clamp(40px,7.5vh,70px); font-size:clamp(24px,2.65vw,44px); line-height:1.2; font-weight:300; letter-spacing:-0.01em } .tagline strong { font-weight:700; display:block } CTA ROW (button → horizontal line → giant outlined "07" bleeding off the right edge) .cta-row { position:absolute; left:45.6%; right:-1vw; top:88.7%; transform:translateY(-50%); display:flex; align-items:center } .cta { flex:none; padding:0 15px; height:48px; display:inline-flex; align-items:center; border:1.5px solid rgba(255,255,255,.85); border-radius:6px; background:rgba(0,0,0,.15); color:#fff; font-size:14px; font-weight:400; text-decoration:none; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s, color .25s } .cta:hover { background:#fff; color:#000 } .cta-line { flex:1; height:1.5px; background:rgba(255,255,255,.8); min-width:40px } .count { flex:none; font-size:clamp(140px,19.8vw,360px); font-weight:400; line-height:1; letter-spacing:-0.02em; color:transparent; -webkit-text-stroke:1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.9); transform:translateY(6%); user-select:none } LOADER .loader { position:absolute; left:50%; top:50%; transform:translate(-50%,-50%); font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.2em; text-transform:uppercase; opacity:.6; transition:opacity .6s } .loader.done { opacity:0 } RESPONSIVE @media (max-width:900px), (max-aspect-ratio:1/1) { .arrows { left:auto; right:var(--pad-x); top:15%; transform:translateY(-50%); gap:14px } .tagline { bottom:clamp(150px,20vh,220px) } .cta-row { left:var(--pad-x); right:-3vw; top:auto; bottom:24px; transform:none } .count { font-size:clamp(120px,22vw,200px) } } @media (max-width:640px) { .nav-links { gap:16px } .nav-links a, .logo { font-size:13px } .dots { gap:20px; right:16px } .dot { width:10px; height:10px } .cta-row { right:-8vw } .count { font-size:120px } } @media (max-width:420px) { .nav-links li:nth-child(2) { display:none } } /* hide "Portfolio" */ No horizontal page scroll at any width. ================================================== 4. WEBGL SCENE (Three.js) ================================================== Renderer: WebGLRenderer({ canvas:#scene, antialias:true, alpha:false }), clearColor #000, outputColorSpace SRGBColorSpace, pixelRatio = min(devicePixelRatio, 2). Camera: PerspectiveCamera(fov 30, aspect W/H, 0.1, 100) at (0,0,10) looking at origin. 4a. Background headline (drawn into an offscreen 2D canvas → CanvasTexture) - Canvas size = viewport × DPR, filled #000. - mobile = (W < 768) || (W/H < 1). - fontSize fs = min(H*0.21, W*(mobile ? 0.21 : 0.118)); font = `800 ${fs}px Poppins`. If the widest line is wider than W*(mobile ? 0.9 : 0.5), scale fs down to fit. - Lines: "Explore", "New", "Ideas". Fill #e9e9e9, textAlign center, baseline alphabetic. - Centre x = W*(mobile ? 0.5 : 0.505); centre y = H*(mobile ? 0.45 : 0.468). Line gap = fs*1.07; cap height ≈ fs*0.7. Line i (0..2) baseline y = cy + cap/2 + (i-1)*gap. - Texture: colorSpace SRGB, LinearFilter, no mipmaps. Redraw on resize and on document.fonts 'loadingdone'. - Show it with a fullscreen quad (PlaneGeometry(2,2), ShaderMaterial, vertex outputs position.xy directly, fragment = texture2D(uTex, vUv) followed by #include <colorspace_fragment> ON ITS OWN LINE; depthTest/depthWrite false; frustumCulled false) in its own bgScene. - Wait for fonts before first draw: Promise.race([Promise.all([document.fonts.load('800 100px Poppins'), document.fonts.ready]), 2500ms timeout]) then layout() + start loop. 4b. Model loading - GLTFLoader.load(MODEL_URL). Traverse gltf.scene; for each mesh: clone geometry, delete 'uv','color','tangent' attributes, mergeVertices(g, 1e-4), computeVertexNormals(), applyMatrix4(mesh.matrixWorld). Merge all parts with mergeGeometries. - Centre the geometry on its bounding box and scale uniformly so its largest dimension = 1. - Scene graph: scene → pivot (screen position + scale) → spinner (rotation) → cube mesh. On load add class "done" to #loader. 4c. Cube placement (in layout(), on load and on resize) - visH = 2*tan(fov/2)*10; visW = visH*aspect. - Screen-fraction centre: sx = mobile ? 0.5 : 0.517, sy = mobile ? 0.45 : 0.488. pivot.position = ((sx-0.5)*visW, (0.5-sy)*visH, 0). - On-screen edge length px = min(H*0.44, W*(mobile ? 0.45 : 0.29)); pivot.scale = (px/H)*visH. - Initial spinner rotation: Euler(-0.42, 0.62, 0.18). 4d. Glass material — custom ShaderMaterial, screen-space refraction with 6-band chromatic dispersion, rendered in two passes (back faces, then front faces). Vertex shader: varying vec3 vNormal; varying vec3 vEye; worldPos = modelMatrix*position; mvPos = viewMatrix*worldPos; gl_Position = projectionMatrix*mvPos; vNormal = normalize(normalMatrix*normal); vEye = normalize(https://mvpos.xyz/); Fragment shader: uv = gl_FragCoord.xy / uResolution (drawing-buffer size). n = normalize(vNormal); if (uBackside > 0.5) n = -n; // do NOT use gl_FrontFacing, three.js flips winding for BackSide eye = normalize(vEye). LOOP = 16 iterations; slide = i/LOOP * 0.045. For each band compute refract(eye, n, 1.0/ior) with iorR/Y/G/C/B/P and sample uTexture at uv + refr.xy * (uRefractPower + slide*k) * uChromatic, with k = 1 (R), 1 (Y), 2 (G), 2.5 (C), 3 (B), 1 (P): r = tex(R).x*0.5 y = (tex(Y).x*2 + tex(Y).y*2 - tex(Y).z)/6 g = tex(G).y*0.5 c = (tex(C).y*2 + tex(C).z*2 - tex(C).x)/6 b = tex(B).z*0.5 p = (tex(P).z*2 + tex(P).x*2 - tex(P).y)/6 R = r + (2p + 2y - c)/3; G = g + (2y + 2c - p)/3; B = b + (2c + 2p - y)/3 color += vec3(R,G,B) color /= LOOP; saturation adjust: mix(luma(color), color, uSaturation) with luma weights (0.2125, 0.7154, 0.0721). Specular (Blinn-Phong, light vector = normalize(-light), view = -eye): spec = specular(uLight, uShininess, uDiffuseness) + 0.6 * specular(vec3(1,1,-1), uShininess*0.6, uDiffuseness*0.5) spec(x) = pow(max(dot(n,halfVec),0), shininess) + max(0,dot(n,lightVec))*diffuseness color += spec * (backside ? 0.35 : 1.0) Fresnel: f = pow(1.0 + dot(eye, n), uFresnelPower); color = mix(color, vec3(1), f * (backside ? 0.25 : 0.55)). color += vec3(0.004, 0.005, 0.007). gl_FragColor = vec4(color,1); then #include <colorspace_fragment> on its own line. Uniform values: uIorR 1.15, uIorY 1.16, uIorG 1.18, uIorC 1.22, uIorB 1.22, uIorP 1.22, uRefractPower 0.30 (front) / 0.22 (back), uChromatic 0.5, uSaturation 1.08, uShininess 90, uDiffuseness 0.02, uFresnelPower 5.0, uLight (-1, 1, 1), uBackside 0 (frontMat, side FrontSide) / 1 (backMat, side BackSide). 4e. Render pipeline (every frame) - Two WebGLRenderTargets sized to drawing buffer (W*DPR × H*DPR), type HalfFloatType, default (linear) colour space: rtBack, rtFront. - backMat.uTexture = rtBack.texture; frontMat.uTexture = rtFront.texture. 1) render bgScene → rtBack 2) render bgScene → rtFront, then (autoClear=false) cube with backMat → rtFront 3) render bgScene → screen, then (autoClear=false, clearDepth) cube with frontMat → screen - This gives the look: text seen through the cube is magnified, mirrored and split into blue/yellow fringes, inner rounded edges of the cube are faintly visible, and the bevelled edges glow white. ================================================== 5. INTERACTION & ANIMATION ================================================== - Drag to rotate (pointer events on the canvas, setPointerCapture): dx = Δx*0.008, dy = Δy*0.008; apply as world-space rotation: premultiply spinner.quaternion by axisAngle(Y, dx) then axisAngle(X, dy). Track velocity per 16.67ms frame; add class "dragging" to the canvas while dragging. - Inertia after release: keep applying velocity, damped by 0.94^(dt*60) per frame. - Idle drift: 0.6s after release, blend in a constant slow rotation of 0.0035 rad/frame around Y and 0.0012 rad/frame around X (blend ramps 0→1 over 1s). It also runs from page load. - Prev/Next arrow buttons: smoothly rotate the cube -90°/+90° around Y (ease: each frame apply remaining*min(1, 0.09*dt*60) until remaining < 0.0005). Cancels inertia; dragging cancels the spin. - Dots: clicking a dot makes it the only .active one (hollow ring). - Hover transitions: nav link underline wipe (.35s), arrow and CTA buttons invert to white bg / black content (.25s). - Clamp frame dt to 0.05s. Recompute layout (renderer size, camera aspect, render-target sizes, uResolution, headline canvas, cube position/scale) on window resize. ================================================== 6. LAYOUT REFERENCE (desktop 1440×806) ================================================== - Logo at (100, 38), 40px tall. Nav links right-aligned, right edge ≈ 1340, vertical centre ≈ 58. - Arrow circles centred at ≈ (1105, 152) and (1175, 152). - Dots at x ≈ 1340, y ≈ 351 / 398 / 445 (middle one hollow). - Headline "Explore / New / Ideas" centred at x ≈ 727, ~170px ExtraBold, baselines ≈ 272 / 445 / 637. - Glass cube occupies ≈ x 510–1000, y 145–600, slightly right of centre, overlapping the headline. - Tagline "Let's Build the / Future of / Design." at left 100, bottom ≈ 60px, ~38px, Light with Bold "Design.". - "Explore Now" button at (657, 691), 48px tall; a 1.5px line runs right to a huge outlined "07" whose "0" starts at x ≈ 1140 and whose "7" is clipped by the right and bottom edges. - Pure black background, all UI white. Mobile (≤767px or portrait): headline and cube centred at 50% x / 45% y, headline up to 90% width, arrows move under the nav on the right, tagline sits above the CTA row, and the CTA row is pinned 24px from the bottom with "07" partly off-screen on the right. Output: one complete index.html, nothing else.

summary.en: An Arctic jelly-diorama scene (icebergs, glacier, penguins, ship) built as a single WebGPU HTML file with Claude Opus 5.5 from a long detailed prompt, compared against a version built by GPT-6 Astra using the same prompt.

prompt.text:
Build "Iceberg Jelly" — the next piece in my "Material Studies" series of jelly dioramas: a single self-contained HTML file using WebGPU (WGSL), no external libraries, English UI.

THE SCENE
A square block of jelly (5.2 × 5.2 units) standing on a pale, cool-grey paper studio backdrop with a soft floor shadow. Inside it, a polar bay:
- At the back left, a glacier flows down a valley between jagged mountains and ends in an ice cliff standing in deep water. The cliff has vertical runnels and blue bands. The glacier surface has chevron crevasses along its margins, transverse crevasses and seracs near the front, and grey lateral moraines. Its tongue is flanked by moraine banks, so only its front stands in the water.
- Mountains: a peaky left range and a spur on the right of the glacier, with a snowy ridge along the back. Dark volcanic rock with orange lichen, and snow in ragged patches on flatter and higher ground (not everywhere).
- At the back right, a low peninsula with an Adélie penguin rookery: an organic, irregular patch of round pebbles stained pink with krill, with pebble-ring nests. Behind it, a small research station (red and yellow huts on stilts, fuel drums, a radio mast with guy wires, a flag, a turning anemometer, a snowmobile) and a timber quay.
- A ragged skerry of two low rocks off to the front right, where Weddell seals haul out.
- The sea floor is grey gravel with shells, sponges, sea stars and swaying anemones, visible through the clear jelly front face.
- The cut faces of the block show candy-coloured strata, dark basalt columns under the land, and layered blue glacier ice with a dirty basal layer under the glacier.

PHYSICS
- Shallow-water simulation on a ~168² grid for the bay: waves, wakes, foam, refraction, caustics on the floor, light shafts, and absorption that depends on the flavour.
- Every piece of ice is a rigid body: tabular, dome, pinnacle and wedge bergs, growlers, pancake floes, and glacier slabs. Each is a star-shaped faceted mesh (superellipsoid plus lobes plus two octaves of noise), a lattice of mass points for buoyancy and drag, and contact spheres for ground, walls, each other and the ship. Settle stable poses at load so nothing capsizes at the start.
- Calving: three slabs stand along the cliff. About once a minute (or on demand) one breaks off with a crack, a puff of ice dust, a splash, spray and a wave, then capsizes until it finds a stable way up. The glacier slowly pushes a new slab out. Old slabs melt away.
- The displaced water is handed back to the waves without feedback: wakes only when a piece moves fast, splashes when it plunges in. Slow drift makes no waves.
- The jelly block itself wobbles, shears and squashes, and can be tipped by dragging its side.

LIFE
- An icebreaker, "Polaris" (red hull with a spoon bow, white superstructure, yellow funnel with smoke, a turning radar, a helideck), lies at the quay. Now and then (or on demand) she casts off, shoulders round the bay through the pack, pushing floes and bergs aside, and comes back alongside. A status line shows Alongside / Casting off / Under way / Breaking ice / Coming alongside, with a countdown or progress.
- 22 Adélie penguins: blue-black backs, white shirt fronts, white eye rings, pink feet. They stand on nests and look about, have the odd ecstatic display, waddle or toboggan to the beach, dive in, "fly" underwater with beating flippers, porpoise, leap out onto floes and bergs, and slide off when a floe tips. They chase silverfish and thrown fish.
- 3 Weddell seals (spotted grey) haul out on the skerry and floes, lift their heads, and go for swims.
- An orca (proper eye patch and grey saddle) patrols deep water, surfaces to blow and dives. Penguins keep clear of it.
- Schools of silverfish; gentle snowfall.

UI (same layout as the rest of the series)
Masthead "Material Studies / Iceberg Jelly." with a one-line description. A "WebGPU · Live" status pill. A glass control panel on the right that turns into a bottom sheet on mobile:
- Buttons: Calve (shows "Wait…" while no slab is ready), Cast off / Full ahead, Throw fish, Horn (Space).
- A water-energy meter; tallies for Calved, Capsized, Fed; the ship status line.
- Flavours: Glacier mint, Blue raspberry, Blackberry. Each changes the water's absorption, its tint and the strata.
- Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Snowfall.
- Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, View.
- A "How to play" footer.
Interaction: pick up and throw floes and bergs; drag across the water to make waves; drag the ground or the side of the block to tip it; drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom.

Web Audio sounds: calving crack and rumble, splashes, a capsizing groan, ice knocking on the hull, a deep two-reed ship's horn, penguin plops, and wind that rises with the snowfall.

Show a fallback screen when WebGPU is unavailable. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. No network requests.

QUALITY BAR
Low-poly faceted ice with chalky snowy tops, glassy blue underwater parts, blue bands, sparkles and translucency. Soft shadows. Cool polar light. Performance around 60 fps on a laptop. Test headlessly: no NaNs over long soaks, a calm start, calving plus capsize, a full ship round trip, feeding, picking up ice, the mobile sheet, and no console errors.
Deliver the HTML file and publish it as an artifact.

summary.en: A 20-second pixel-art style video recreating a referenced clip was built with Claude Opus 5.5 using a detailed structured prompt covering inputs, visual direction, scene-by-scene structure and build steps, rendered with Playwright and ffmpeg.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a voiceover or song with a spoken line (the audio file) and its transcript, 10-12 small objects that sum up my life, two silhouettes to light like a heat camera (a head in profile and a raised hand), and the 3 words I want to land hardest. If I skip any, use the defaults: vinyl, book, camera, cat, coin, game controller, cap, heart, money, plant, clapperboard, skateboard; free CC0 silhouettes from Openverse; action, intention, curiosity.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 20 second 4:3 film, 1440x1080 at 60fps, cut to the voice. Off-white paper, black, one red, one yellow, Geist for every word. Film grain on everything, a soft vignette, and a camera that never rests: a slow handheld float under everything plus a slow push inside every scene.
No scene cuts to the next: each handoff starts on the exact last frame of the scene before. The only hard cuts are the beat flips on the last word.
Every object is pixel art you draw yourself: a 16x16 grid per object, every cell a hand-placed colour, rendered as a 3D block (a darker extrusion down-right, a thin bevel on every cell) with a soft contact shadow.
The silhouettes are lit like a heat camera: the heat comes from how thick the body is at each point, so the nose, the hair and the fingertips run cooler, plus one hotspot and a slow moving noise, mapped through a black > red > orange > cream ramp. The edge stays razor sharp, with a soft glow outside it.
Motion rules: nothing pops in (eased glides of about 0.5s with a soft start), fast moves get real motion blur instead of ghost copies, and captions type with the voice behind a block cursor.
Banned: stock footage, AI video, 3D camera moves, particles, glitch.
</direction>

<structure>
Hang every scene on the transcript's word timings (measure them with faster-whisper word timestamps, one short chunk at a time):
1. The first word fills a yellow card. The card wipes off to the left and the question types underneath on two centred lines that glide to stay centred as they grow, the key word underlined in red as it's spoken.
2. The objects streak past in lanes above and below the words, a cyan four-point flare sweeps in, then the page burns away: black closes in from the edges onto the head, behind a hot red edge.
3. The head heats up on black while the answer types low on the left. A thin white orbit draws itself around the head, its far half passing behind it. On the last word, paper blooms out from inside the head with the objects in it, and the camera falls through: the head rushes past the lens until the paper is all we see.
4. The objects sit on a tilted ring seen in perspective (the front ones bigger and lower, drawn last), slowly turning, each one bobbing; the coin flips and lands with sparks.
5. On each of the 3 words, that object flies out of the ring to the left and grows, the page floods black from it, and the word types beside it (camera: a red shutter star; book: a red ribbon sweep; record: two white orbits and red notes). Then the flood drains back into the object as it flies home, and the camera dives closer into the ring. Put each hero object in the slot that is front-left when its word lands.
6. The ring pulls in a touch, bursts outward, every object turns to ink, and ink blots grow and swallow the page.
7. The hand rises into frame, hot, with the line split either side of it. The heart drops into its palm, then lifts to the centre at the size the next scene holds it.
8. The last word, one letter per beat, the background flipping paper / black / red, the heart holding its place across the cut, the centre object morphing pixel by pixel into the next one.
9. Thin brush strokes sweep through, the letters drift apart and float, then settle back into the word with the heart above it. The camera keeps pushing through the hold.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. Bake each pixel sprite once to an offscreen canvas (the extrusion layers, then the face), then draw it scaled and rotated.
3. The heat: precompute each silhouette's base heat once (a distance transform of the mask, held at the edge value outside it so nothing dark bleeds in when it is upscaled). Every frame, add the hotspot and two octaves of value noise at quarter resolution, map it through a 256-step lookup, upscale it, and cut it with the full-resolution mask.
4. The fall through the head: draw the ring scene into an offscreen layer, mask it with the head scaled up about a point inside the skull, and grow that scale on a cubed curve until the head covers the frame. The ring inside zooms less than the head does, so it reads as depth.
5. The pixel morph: pair every cell of object A with a cell of object B and glide each one's position and colour, with a small random delay per cell.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes, then lay the original audio back on with ffmpeg.
</build>

<gotchas>
A mask PNG with no alpha channel fills the whole box with heat, so put the silhouette in the alpha. A limb cut by the photo's border shows as a straight edge, so extend the mask past the frame. A handoff only reads as smooth when the last frame of one scene is the first frame of the next: draw the outgoing scene under the transition, and give scenes that show the same ring one shared zoom function. A flood that's still retreating when the next scene starts reads as a hard cut, so let it finish first. A fast ease-out flood reads as a jump; use a soft start.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, measure the word timings, then show me 8 stills before you render.
</start>

summary.zh: 作者用同一份详细提示词分别让Claude Opus 5.5和ChatGPT-6 Astra生成一个具有软体物理和程序化毛发效果的毛绒蜘蛛玩具，均以自包含的WebGPU网页形式呈现并进行对比。
summary.en: A comparison of a physics-based plush spider toy built with the same detailed prompt in Claude Opus 5.5 and ChatGPT-6 Astra, rendered as self-contained WebGPU HTML pages with soft-body physics and procedural fur.

prompt.text:
Build "Plush Spider" — Material Studies No. 015.

Format and style:
- A single self-contained HTML file on native WebGPU, fully procedural (no assets, no libraries).
- The same editorial style as the series: serif masthead, side specimen panel, live readouts, "Inside the experiment" notes.

The specimen: a cute plush spider sitting on a table.
- The body is one signed distance field:
- a big round abdomen with knitted-looking stripes;
- a smaller head-and-chest tucked into it, with two fuzzy cheeks;
- a paler underside.
- The face:
- two big glossy bead eyes on white felt discs;
- a row of four tiny bead eyes above them;
- blushing cheeks, an embroidered smile and two little felt fangs.
- Eight posable plush legs, four a side, sewn on along the chest. They are striped like socks, end in pale little feet, and have a wire inside.

Physics — body:
- XPBD soft body on a hex-cell lattice: co-rotational shape matching plus tetrahedral volume, 60 Hz, 6 substeps.
- Gravity and floor friction. The seat keeps its footing.
- The toy slowly rights itself toward the heading it last walked (posture with a yaw).
- The abdomen breathes: its cells' rest shapes and rest volumes swell.

Physics — legs:
- Each leg is an XPBD rod chain from a hip embedded in the body lattice to the toe.
- A blended pose in the body's frame (sit, stand, hang, curl, wave) pulls each point toward its target: firmly at the hip, less toward the toe. So the legs hold their shape but sag and swing.
- The wire is plastic: when the hand bends a leg past its give, the pose itself takes the new shape and the leg stays bent until "Straighten legs".
- Spheres riding the body keep the legs off it. Toes grip the table. The finger pushes the legs aside.
- Pulling a leg further than it reaches tows the spider by that hip.

Behaviour:
- Walking:
- the body rises onto its legs with a height controller;
- it is led toward a goal with a weak pull and turns to face it;
- toes are drawn to footholds on the table;
- an alternating four-and-four gait lifts the set that has fallen furthest behind and sets it down ahead, with a little arc;
- it wanders on its own now and then.
- Curl up (button or a finger poke): the legs hug up over its back, the spider rolls away from the touch as a ball (no footing, no rolling resistance), then unrolls and rights itself.
- Hang on silk:
- a springy thread that only pulls, from an anchor high above to a patch of the back;
- it is reeled up off the table, swings when pushed, and its legs paddle the air;
- pressing again lowers it back to the table.
- Wave: one front leg is raised and wiggles.
- With the Finger tool, the spider scuttles over to the finger.

Rendering:
- Shell fur: base plus N instanced shells, alpha-to-coverage under 4× MSAA.
- The fur lie is carried by the deformation gradient, with a damped-spring tip lag.
- Kajiya–Kay highlights, velvet sheen, a comb tool.
- Regions painted in rest space: abdomen stripes, pale underside, short pile around the felt eye discs, cheeks, smile groove, stitched seams round the hips.
- Legs are drawn each frame as plush tubes:
- swept along a Catmull–Rom curve through each rod with a parallel-transport frame;
- a slight knee bulge and a rounded little foot;
- banded colour and a shorter pile.
- A thin glinting silk thread.
- Soft PCSS key-light shadows, contact occlusion on the studio floor, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping.
- NaN-safe WGSL: clamped pow and smoothstep, clamped post.

UI:
- Tools:
- Hand: lift and squash the body, or grab and bend a leg;
- Finger: the spider follows it, and a poke curls it up;
- Comb: brush the pile.
- Buttons: Walk, Hang on silk, Curl up, Wave, Straighten legs, Smooth fur, Reset.
- Sliders: Stuffing, Pile, Wire (floppy to stiff).
- Palettes: Midnight (dark plum with lilac stripes), Tangerine (orange with brown stripes), Moss (green with yellow stripes).
- Readouts: mass, volume % of rest, steps taken, silk length in cm.
- Orbit and zoom; responsive stacked layout on phones; adaptive quality; reduced-motion support.

summary.en: Animated bento feature grid for a product website, where each tile plays a small scene showing what the feature does. Generated with Opus 5.5 from a detailed prompt the creator shares in the post.

prompt.text:
# Small animations for a product site's feature tiles

Give every tile in my site's feature grid a small animation: a tiny scene that shows what the feature does.

## 0. Before you build
- Read the project: find out the tech stack (plain HTML/CSS, React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind, Framer Motion…) and build it the way the project already does. Don't add an animation library unless the project already uses one.
- Ask me which look to use:
A. The Lumno material below, as written.
B. My product's own style: take the colors, radii, borders and shadows from my existing design tokens and components, and keep only the structure and motion rules from this prompt.
C. A mix: the Lumno material in my brand's accent color and radii.
- Picking features: if I named features, animate those. If not, read the product's site, docs or code, list 3–5 features that a short scene can explain, and let me pick.

## 1. Lumno material (option A)
Overall: quiet, neutral, precise. Hairlines instead of borders, soft shadows tinted warm, no gradients or color washes, one accent color.

- Grid: one card with an outer radius of 28px. Cells are separated by 1px hairlines (a 1px grid gap over a hairline color). Cells are white. The card has a faint hairline ring and a soft shadow.
- Art panel: inset 8px from the cell edge, with a radius of the card radius minus the inset (20px), so corners stay concentric.
- Fill #fafafa, plus an inner 1px ring: box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(32,38,46,.07).
- Texture: background: repeating-linear-gradient(-45deg, rgba(32,38,46,.06) 0 1px, transparent 1px 7px).
- The scene sits centred on the panel, about 126×118px.
- Text bars: body bars 4px tall with a 2px radius in #e5e9ef; heading bars 5px tall in #cdd4de. Vary the widths (34–92px).
- Mini windows and cards: white with a 9px radius.
- Shadow: 0 0 0 1px rgba(47,42,34,.06), 0 8px 20px -10px rgba(47,42,34,.25).
- Tab strip: 20px tall, #eef1f5. Tabs: 16px tall with 6px top corners; the active tab is white.
- Favicons: 10px.
- Inner surfaces such as charts or fields: #f4f6fa. Secondary data: #b9c9e0. Accent: #3462ad, used only on the result.
- Icon chip (top-left of each tile): 32px, 10px radius, 1px border rgba(32,38,46,.1), white, shadow 0 1px 2px rgba(32,38,46,.05), a line-style glyph in #4b5563.
- Text color: a warm near-black, #2f2a22.
- Hover: the cell darkens to about 2.5% grey; the panel goes to #f4f5f6 with its ring at .09; the icon chip grows 32→36px from its top-left corner, its glyph turns to the text color, and its shadow deepens slightly.
- Dark mode (suggested values; keep the same relationships):
- Cells #17181a, panel #1d1f22, inner ring rgba(255,255,255,.06), texture rgba(255,255,255,.04).
- Body bars #2c2f34, heading bars #3a3e45.
- Windows #24272b with a 1px rgba(255,255,255,.06) outline and a shadow of 0 8px 20px -10px rgba(0,0,0,.6).
- Tab strip #1a1c1f, accent #6f9bea, text #ecebe8.

## 2. Scene
- One idea per tile: 2–4 moves that show "action → result", such as "click → a small window opens" or "change here → the other side syncs".
- Abstract wireframes only: no screenshots and no real text. Use at most one small icon where something needs to be recognisable.
- Motion: ease-out for movement, cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1); a slight spring for appearing, cubic-bezier(.34,1.4,.64,1). Each move takes 250–600ms; the whole scene is done in about 3s.
- Icon chip: when the tile plays, its glyph redraws stroke by stroke (draw, pop or slide per part), then hands back to the solid icon.

## 3. Playback
- Resting styles are the final frame. Animations only describe where things come from (fill-mode: both or equivalent), so reduced motion shows the result and an interrupted play never jumps.
- The art panel fades in (opacity, plus translateY 6px and scale .97 to none) as its tile first plays.
- Play once in view: when about 70% of the tile is visible, wait ~200ms, then play. Tiles that enter together go ~250ms apart, in reading order. Stop on the final frame.
- One "played" state (a class or data attribute) drives every animation in the tile. To replay: remove it, force a reflow, add it back (or re-key in a framework).
- On mouse hover (mouse only) or keyboard focus, replay: blur the final frame out over ~160ms (blur 6px, opacity 0), restart under the blur, then clear it. Don't restart a play that hasn't finished.
- Optional loop on hover: while the pointer stays on the tile, replay again ~600ms after each play ends. When the pointer leaves, finish the current play and rest on the final frame.
- Touch: a tap follows the tile's link; nothing depends on hover.
- prefers-reduced-motion: reduce: no animation; show the final frame.

## 4. Colors and dark mode
- Every color is a variable on the art panel (panel, ring, texture, bars, windows, tab strip, accent, shadow); no hard-coded colors in the rules.
- Follow prefers-color-scheme, and the project's manual theme switch too (a class or data-theme), if it has one.
- Check it in both light and dark.

## 5. Delivery
- Mark the art as decorative (aria-hidden) and keep translatable text out of it.
- Check it in a real browser: first play, hover replay, keyboard focus, reduced motion, dark mode and a phone-width layout.

summary.en: An interactive 3D jelly-crushing toy with a hydraulic press, built single-shot in HTML/WebGPU by Claude Opus 5.5 from one detailed prompt, at an estimated API cost of $14.30.

prompt.text:
Create "Jelly Press": a single-file interactive 3D toy in HTML (all JS, CSS and WGSL shaders inline, no external assets except Google Fonts). Render with WebGPU; if WebGPU or an adapter is missing, show a clean fallback message instead of a blank page.

CONCEPT
Four translucent gummy jellies shaped like fruit slices sit one at a time on the steel bed of a hydraulic press. The player holds a big red button to lower the press. The jelly squashes and spreads, the pressure gauge climbs, and somewhere past half its height it bursts into pieces. After the burst the game does NOT end: the player can grab the pieces, drag them, throw them around, and squash them again.

THE JELLIES (chips at the bottom, keys 1–4)
1. Watermelon wedge (half-disc slab): red flesh with dark teardrop seeds, a pale rind band, a green striped skin.
2. Orange slice (half-disc): orange pulp segments separated by thin white membranes, pale pith, orange peel.
3. Fig half: pink flesh full of small golden seeds, a cream layer, a dark purple skin.
4. Pineapple ring: golden fibrous flesh with radial streaks and a hole in the middle.
Each jelly should look like real gummy candy: subsurface scattering, soft translucency, glossy specular highlights, soft shadows on a warm studio floor (cream/beige, tone-mapped).

PHYSICS (CPU, fixed 60 Hz step)
- XPBD tetrahedral soft body with 8 substeps: co-rotational per-tet shape matching, per-tet volume constraints, hard edge strain limits (0.35×–1.8×), edge velocity damping, floor contact with Coulomb friction, rolling resistance, and gentle settling when nearly still.
- Render mesh skinned on the CPU through barycentric embedding in the tets; normals recomputed from triangles every frame.
- The press die is a kinematic round platen (radius ~1.05, rounded edge, a thickness, a ram above it). It acts as a ceiling with friction below, a shelf on top, and a side wall at its rim. The two press posts are solid.
- Pressure readout in bar comes from the platen's contact load, scaled per fruit.

THE BURST
- Break at a random squash between 52% and 66% of the jelly's height.
- Plan the fracture in the background shortly after each round starts, so the burst itself is instant.
- 5–7 big pieces from 3D Voronoi cells with slightly tilted walls. On 3–4 of them, a far corner is chipped off by two cutting planes and split further into 2–4 small chips, which leaves jagged, notched edges.
- Assign tets to cells by centroid. Duplicate particles per chunk. Merge tiny islands into their neighbours.
- The new body adopts the old positions and velocities.
- Clip the skin triangles against each cell's half-spaces, and fill every cut face with a clean flat cap showing the fruit's interior (flesh, seeds, membranes). No stretched triangles, no holes.
- Kick pieces outward and upward from the press. Small chips fly faster and higher and tumble with random spin.
- Show a big italic verdict for about 2.5 s, then fade it: "Splat." (melon), "Squeezed." (orange), "Well, that's jam." (fig), "Crushed." (pineapple). Include a stat line: "Gave up at N bar and N% of its height."

AFTER THE BURST: PLAY MODE
- Picking: ray/triangle test against the skinned mesh, with a forgiving screen-space fallback for touch.
- Grabbing pins the grabbed patch (radius ~0.4, only particles of that chunk) to a target on a camera-facing drag plane. Small chips move whole; big pieces stretch and swing like jelly.
- Releasing throws the piece with the pointer's velocity.
- Pieces collide with each other. A particle found inside another chunk's tet is pushed out through that chunk's nearest skin face, with friction. Use a chunk AABB broad phase and a spatial hash of skin tets.
- Pieces stay on stage: side walls, plus an invisible front edge so nothing ends up under the controls or behind the camera.
- The press still works: hold to squash the pieces again (no second fracture); Raise lifts the platen.
- Wet "plop" sounds on landings; a small squelch on grab.
- Cursor: open hand over pieces, closed hand while dragging. Dragging empty space orbits the camera.

UI (editorial, minimal)
- Masthead top-left: "JELLY PRESS" in bold condensed caps, with "PRESS" filled in yellow/black hazard stripes. Subtitle: "Four gummies. One hydraulic press."
- Top-right: Reset and Sound toggle.
- Bottom deck:
- Caption line with escalating captions while pressing: "Contact." → "It's fine. It's jelly." → "Getting wider." → "That's a pancake now." → "It's making a noise." → "Please."
- Circular pressure dial (0–400 bar arc, red zone) around a red HOLD button, a Raise button, and a big numeric bar readout.
- Fruit chips with icons.
- In play mode the caption slot shows "Grab a piece. Throw it." with small "Press again" and "Next jelly" buttons.
- Controls: hold Space or ArrowDown to press, ArrowUp to raise, R to reset, 1–4 to pick a fruit. Wheel zooms; double-click resets the view.
- Camera: low bench-level view; the press frame yaws per fruit so the posts never block the jelly. Framing adapts so the jelly sits between masthead and deck; works on phones (portrait) with a narrower stage.

SOUND (procedural Web Audio, no files)
Hydraulic motor hum that rises with pressure, wet squelches, occasional creaks at high pressure, a valve clunk when the platen stops, a loud burst, soft plops on landing. Unlock on first interaction.

QUALITY BAR
- Smooth 60 fps on a laptop.
- Background warm-up of the other fruits' meshes and shaders so switching is instant.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
- Accessible labels, a gauge with role=meter, focus-visible outlines.
- No console errors. The page never goes blank.

title.zh: 港口水母水体物理效果对比

summary.zh: 作者用同一个详细提示词让Opus 5.5和ChatGPT-6 Astra分别生成基于WebGPU的“果冻港口”立体场景，并比较了水的物理效果和预估API成本。
summary.en: The creator gave the same detailed prompt to Opus 5.5 and ChatGPT-6 Astra to build a WebGPU 'Harbor Jelly' diorama and compared the resulting water physics and estimated API costs.

prompt.text:
Build "Harbor Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (no external requests, no libraries) that renders an interactive 3D diorama with WebGPU/WGSL: a small working container harbor set inside a square block of wobbly, translucent jelly sea, sitting on a paper studio backdrop. It belongs to a series called "Material Studies", so match that look: warm paper background, serif italic display title ("Harbor Jelly."), small uppercase eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a status pill top-right ("WebGPU · Live"), a frosted control panel on the right, and a "How to play" line bottom-left. English UI. Light theme only, by design.

THE BLOCK
- A 5.2 × 5.2 block seen from a 3/4 orbit camera. The ground and sea are cut flat at the block's sides, so you see candy-coloured soil strata in cross-section, and the sea's cut faces show everything underwater through the jelly.
- The water is a real-time linear shallow-water simulation on a staggered grid (heights at cell centres, velocities on faces) with a little surface tension, so it feels like jelly. Render it with refraction, absorption by depth, caustics projected onto the floor, light shafts, a Fresnel studio reflection, foam (wakes, splashes, a shoreline lace) and a bright meniscus on the cut edges.
- The whole block can be tipped by dragging its side. The water sloshes to the low side, the jelly shears and quivers, then it settles flat again.

THE HARBOR (layout)
- Along the back runs a vertical concrete quay wall, with rubber fenders, bollards, ladders, and mussels and weed crusting it below the waterline.
- Left part: a container terminal. A flat asphalt yard with painted lines, concrete strips with two crane rails, light towers, and a small terminal office. Hundreds of colourful containers are stacked in neat rows. Each is a ribbed steel box with door ends and darker corner posts, drawn as GPU instances in about ten liveries.
- Right part: an old stone fishing quay with a cobbled promenade, a corrugated fish-market shed and lamp posts. A timber pier stands on mussel-covered piles with cross-bracing, with two small fishing boats moored alongside.
- Behind it all, a town climbs a grassy hill: three rows of gabled houses in Nordic harbour colours (falu red, ochre, white, pale blue, mint, pink) with tiled or slate roofs, white-framed windows, doors and chimneys. There is a white church with a green copper spire, and some round trees.
- A rubble breakwater shelters the fishing harbour, with a concrete crown wall. Big rocks sit near the crest, smaller weedy ones tumble down under water. On its head stands a red-and-white banded lighthouse with a gallery and a glass lantern, whose lamp slowly turns.
- In the open basin: two small yachts swinging on their moorings (white hulls, coloured stripe, fin keels visible through the jelly, furled sails), yellow mooring buoys, and a green channel buoy, all bobbing on the waves.
- On the floor: pale sand with drifts of silt, weed tufts, stones, starfish, an old anchor with chain, a lost tyre.

THE SHIP'S DAY (fully automatic loop, about 100 s)
1. A small feeder container ship (navy topsides, red antifouling, white accommodation block at the stern with bridge wings, funnel with a yellow band, turning radar, visible propeller) lies alongside with containers on deck, 6 bays × 4 rows × 2 tiers.
2. Two ship-to-shore gantry cranes on the rails, one red and one blue, each with portal legs, a backreach with a machinery house, an A-frame with forestays, a hinged boom, a trolley with a hanging cab, and a yellow spreader on four wire falls. They lower their booms and swap boxes: unload from the tops of the ship's stacks into yard stacks, then load other boxes aboard. Every move is a smooth sequence: travel, trolley out, lower onto the box (tracking the ship's bobbing), latch, hoist, trolley across, lower, unlatch. Cranes never get closer than their leg width; an idle crane moves out of the other's way.
3. When the work is done the trolleys park, the booms swing up, and a tug comes round to the bow. The tug has a black hull, white and red superstructure, a tyre fender all round, a big bow fender, and puffs of funnel smoke. It passes a tow line and backs away, pulling the bow off the quay while the ship swings out. Then the line is cast off, the tug pivots on the spot and goes home, and the ship sounds her horn.
4. The ship sails a lap of the harbour along a smooth path, past the lighthouse. She rides the water on several sample points (heave, pitch, roll) and hands the displaced water back to the sim, so she leaves a real bow wave, wake and white water.
5. Meanwhile the tug goes out to a standby spot. When the ship stops off the quay, the tug noses in and pushes her sideways onto the fenders, with prop wash churning. Then it backs off, the booms come down, and the cranes start again.
- Keep everything collision-free (ship and tug vs. quay, breakwater, pier, yachts and buoy; no grounding). Check it with a headless node test.

LIFE
- Fish schools (mackerel, herring, small orange wrasse) as boids that stay in the water and under the hulls, scatter from fingers, splashes and moving ships, and come to food.
- Moon jellyfish: glassy pulsing bells with four pink rings, frilly oral arms and a fringe of tentacles. They drift with the water flow.
- Herring gulls (white body, grey mantle, black wingtips, yellow bill with a red spot). They circle, bank and glide, and land on perches: lamps, roof ridges, the church spire, the lighthouse gallery, the crane apexes, the ship's mast, the tug, the yachts' masthead. Perches on moving things move with them. They all take off when the horn sounds, and some dive at food.
- Steam puffs from the ship's funnel on the horn; tiny bubbles caught in the jelly.

CONTROLS (right panel; bottom sheet on phones)
- "Cast off" sends the ship early (cranes finish the box in hand). At sea the button becomes "Call her in" and hurries her home; it greys out while busy.
- "Horn" (also Space) plays a synthesized WebAudio ship horn: two low detuned sawtooth reeds a fifth apart, low-passed, starting only after a user gesture. It also blows steam and scatters the gulls.
- "Feed the fish" scatters pellets off the end of the pier; fish rush in and gulls swoop down.
- Tally: Boxes moved / Voyages / Fed. A ship status line ("Unloading 3 / 8", "Loading", "Booms up", "Tug coming", "Casting off", "At sea 40%", "Coming in", "Berthing"). A small activity meter.
- Flavour swatches change the water colour and strata: Sea glass (teal-mint), Blueberry (deep blue), Lime.
- Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Tide (±10 cm; the sea level, ships and floating things follow).
- Buttons: Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, Reset view.

POINTER INTERACTION
- Drag across the water to make waves (with a crosshair cursor).
- Drag the side of the block to tip it.
- Pick up an orange-and-white lifebuoy and throw it. Lifebuoys float flat on the waves, bounce off the pier, buildings and breakwater, and are shoved aside by the ship and tug.
- Drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom.
- On phones: touch orbit, pinch zoom, and a collapsible bottom sheet for the controls.

RENDERING DETAILS
- Pipeline: shadow map → caustics pass → opaque scene (with a distance buffer) → back-face pass of the water → water pass over a copy of the scene → tone map + dither.
- Moving rigs are static vertex buffers whose vertices carry an object id; about 24 object transforms (position + quaternion) live in the uniform buffer. Cables are drawn with one end in each object's frame, so they stretch: crane falls, forestays, the tow line.
- Material kinds in the prop shader: matte paint, glass, gloss steel, roof tiles, timber grain, corrugated sheet (normal-perturbed ribs), dressed-stone masonry, rubber, rock, glowing lamps, swaying weed, and hulls with antifouling below a boot-top line.
- The jelly shear and squash wobble applies to everything inside the block.

QUALITY BAR
- Smooth on a laptop; simulation under about 2 ms per frame.
- A friendly fallback screen if WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails.
- No console errors, no page scroll. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
- Ship it with a headless test of the choreography and a Playwright end-to-end test.

prompt.text: Create a real-time 3D pixel-art football (soccer) diorama in three.js: an 11-a-side match at a small-town stadium on a floating island, with an original fictional home club and three rotating visitors. Two timed halves with a match clock, walk-out from the tunnel and line-up, half-time and full-time walk-offs, added time shown by the fourth official, and a small league table. Teams play a 4-4-2 whose lines shift with the ball (pressing, cover, marking, timed runs behind the defensive line), with ground passes solved from a rolling-friction model, lofted balls, crosses, shots, headers and volleys. Include offside with the assistant's flag, fouls, slide tackles, yellow and red cards, free kicks with a wall, penalties, corners, throw-ins and goal kicks. A referee runs a diagonal, assistants track the second-last defender. Around the pitch: managers, benches with warming-up subs, ball boys with spare balls, photographers, stewards, a drummer on the home terrace. The stadium has a roofed main stand with the club name, a family stand, a standing terrace, an away end with an old clock, four floodlight pylons, a corner big screen and scrolling LED boards. Add an instanced crowd of ~4,500 that cheers, raises scarves, claps and does the wave, plus day / evening / floodlit-night lighting, a broadcast camera that follows the ball, near stands lifted away like a doll's house, a low-res render with depth outlines and a 64-colour OKLab palette, Web Audio crowd and whistle sounds, and an English UI with score bug, line-ups, match stats and commentary.

prompt.text:
Build "Plush Dragon" — Material Studies No. 014: a single self-contained HTML file, native WebGPU, fully procedural (no assets, no libraries), in the same editorial style as the series (serif masthead, side specimen panel, live readouts, "Inside the experiment" notes).

The specimen:
- A chubby plush baby dragon sitting on a table, all made from one signed distance field.
- Minky body: a big round head with a short snout and two felt horns, a pale belly quilted in horizontal bands, stubby arms, round haunches with padded feet and tiny felt claws.
- A tail curled round to one side, ending in a soft spade.
- A row of flat felt spikes down the head, back and tail.
- Face: glossy bead eyes, blushing cheeks, embroidered nostrils, a stitched smile with one little felt fang.
- Two quilted plush wings sewn on at the shoulders.

Physics:
- Body: XPBD soft body on a hex-cell lattice (co-rotational shape matching plus tetrahedral volume), 60 Hz, 6 substeps. Gravity and floor friction; the seat keeps its footing and the toy slowly rights itself like a weighted plush.
- Muscles instead of forces: the belly breathes (cells' rest shapes and rest volumes swell); the tail wags by lengthening cells on one side of its centre line and shortening them on the other, faster when the dragon is happy.
- Wings:
- each wing is a small XPBD cloth cut from a curved fan-shaped 3D pattern (stretch, shear and bend links), its two root rows embedded in the body lattice;
- a pose (fold back about the vertical, flap about a hinge along the body, both riding a shoulder frame from embedded points) pulls every point toward its target: firmly at the root, barely at the edge, so the stuffed wings lag and flop;
- collider spheres riding the body keep the wings off it.
- Flapping: downstrokes lift the dragon with a hover controller (about 6 cm off the table, bobbing with each beat), then it drops back onto its seat.
- Pulling a wing past its slack tows the body by that shoulder.

Rendering:
- Shell fur (base + N instanced shells, alpha-to-coverage under 4× MSAA): fur lie carried by the deformation gradient, damped-spring tip lag, Kajiya–Kay highlights, velvet sheen, a comb tool.
- Regions painted in rest space: belly with quilting seams, short-nap felt horns and spikes in the wing colour, padded soles, cheeks, smile groove.
- Wings drawn each frame as stuffed slabs swept from the cloth:
- a rolled leading edge in the body colour;
- three panels puffed between stitched ribs;
- a scalloped trailing edge;
- a shorter pile of the same minky.
- Glossy eyes, embroidery thread, felt fang and claws.
- Soft PCSS key-light shadows, contact occlusion on the studio floor, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping.
- NaN-safe WGSL (clamped pow/smoothstep, clamped post).

Interaction:
- Hand: lift and squash the dragon, or grab a wing to stretch it open (pull harder to tow the dragon).
- Finger: a finger reaches in from the viewer; poke to dent the stuffing; hold it pressed in to tickle — the dragon giggles, its wings shiver and its tail wags.
- Comb: brush the pile.
- Buttons: Flap, Stretch (wings spread wide), Boop (a sneeze: head bobs back, wings flare), Toss, Smooth fur, Reset.
- Sliders: Stuffing, Pile, Wingbeat.
- Palettes: Mint (lilac wings), Ember (coral with gold wings), Dusk (lavender with pink wings).
- Readouts: mass, volume % of rest, live wingspan in cm, lift off the table in cm.
- Orbit and zoom; responsive stacked layout on phones; adaptive quality; reduced-motion support.

prompt.text:
Create “Tidepool Jelly” - an interactive 3D miniature coastal ecosystem where everything feels soft, squishy, and made of translucent jelly.
Show an elevated, cutaway slice of coastline floating against a warm off-white background. Include layered sand and rock beneath the surface, shallow turquoise water, rocky tide pools, rounded pebbles, seashells, and small patches of coastal greenery. Use an orthographic camera with orbit and zoom controls.
Make the water the star of the scene: convincing waves, spreading ripples, reflections, refraction, underwater caustics, and a wet shoreline. Animate a rising and falling tide that fills and drains the pools. Clicking or dragging through water should create localized ripples that fade naturally.
Populate the pools with animated jelly sea creatures: tiny crabs, starfish, sea anemones, snails, mussels, shrimp, and small fish. Give each species distinct movement and behavior. Crabs scuttle around rocks, anemones sway with the current, snails crawl slowly, and fish swim in loose groups. Their bodies should gently wobble and deform as they move.
Let users click a creature to focus the camera and reveal a compact species card. Allow gentle interactions that trigger a squishy reaction, followed by a smooth return to the original shape.
Add a clean, minimal control panel with:
Tide height and automatic tide cycle.
Wave strength and water clarity.
Jelly softness.
Day and night lighting.
Species visibility toggles.
Pause, reset, and a randomize ecosystem button.
At night, introduce subtle bioluminescence in the water and selected creatures.
Use elegant editorial typography, generous whitespace, and restrained UI styling. Place the “Tidepool Jelly” title in the upper-left corner and controls on the right. The scene should dominate the screen.
Build a fully working browser experience using Three.js and custom shaders where useful. Prioritize beautiful water, believable creature movement, tactile jelly materials, and smooth performance. All controls must work. Avoid static mockups, placeholder assets, and oversized interface elements.

prompt.text:
Create a high-energy 16:9 temporal poster-grid music video, exactly matching the full duration of the supplied music.

GRID STRUCTURE:
Divide the entire frame into a dense 20×12 matrix of near-square cells separated by ultra-thin grey lines. Preserve one continuous, recognizable image across the grid rather than displaying unrelated images. The grid acts as a unified visual canvas with independently animated temporal fragments.

TEMPORAL CHOREOGRAPHY:
Keep the central 4×4 region anchored to the primary action, maintaining recognizable movement and visual continuity. Surrounding cells explore different moments of the same footage through staggered time offsets, rapid repetitions, reversed motion, delayed echoes, speed ramps, micro-loops and impact freezes.

Create complex rhythmic patterns: diagonal temporal cascades, radial time ripples, expanding freeze-frame waves, checkerboard reversals, alternating motion phases and synchronized frame resets. Allow temporal distortions to propagate across neighboring cells like chain reactions.

VISUAL EFFECTS:
Layer sophisticated graphic treatments driven by the music:
- Chromatic aberration and RGB channel displacement
- Directional motion smears and multi-frame ghost trails
- Glitch propagation and digital frame tearing
- High-contrast monochrome flashes and selective color isolation
- Halftone textures, manga speed lines and graphic silhouettes
- Pixel sorting, scanline interference and datamosh-like distortions
- Grid warping, cell displacement and elastic boundary deformation
- Stroboscopic impact frames and negative-image flashes
- Temporal feedback loops and recursive motion echoes
- Brief typography fragments, abstract symbols and kinetic graphic overlays

RHYTHMIC EDITING:
Analyze the soundtrack's beats, accents, transitions and energy progression. Synchronize cell activity, temporal shifts, visual effects and grid transformations precisely to the music.

Use restrained motion during quieter passages, escalating into dense synchronized chaos during climaxes. On major impacts, trigger cascading temporal explosions across the grid, followed by sudden unified resets.

VISUAL COHERENCE:
Maintain the source footage's original characters, compositions and visual identity. The grid must remain structurally recognizable even during aggressive effects. Prioritize creative temporal manipulation over random glitch noise.

Make the result feel like an experimental motion-design masterpiece: dense, rhythmic, kinetic, visually intricate and deliberately choreographed.

prompt.text:
Build an interactive 3D jelly pufferfish (fugu) as a single self-contained HTML page using three.js from a CDN.

The fish is a soft-body gummy sitting on a table. Model the body as one closed icosphere-topology skin with two rest shapes per vertex: a calm fish (blunt round head, body tapering to a short tail stalk, slightly flattened belly) and a fully inflated ball (sphere with the same tail stalk sticking out). Blend between them with an "inflation" value. Simulate with XPBD at a fixed 1/600 s substep (frame-rate independent): edge-length constraints, a global volume constraint, a soft global shape-matching pull toward the blended rest shape (rotation via polar decomposition, gently leaning upright), ground collision with friction, and damping applied to the wobble (velocity relative to the body's mean) so it jiggles but settles in about a second. Render with one Loop-subdivision pass for a smooth surface.

Behaviour: tapping the fish startles it. It gulps air three times (mouth opens on each gulp, small overshoot) until it is a round ball, stays puffed about 4 seconds, then slowly deflates while blowing iridescent bubbles from its mouth. Dragging grabs and stretches the jelly locally; dragging empty space orbits the camera; wheel or pinch zooms.

Details: ~260 soft spines that lie flat and hidden when calm, pop up one by one (staggered) as it inflates, wobble on their own springs, bend against the table, and lift the ball so it stands on its spines. Big glossy eyes (gold-green iris, large pupil, white catchlight) that follow the cursor. Puckered lips with a tiny white beak. Translucent ray-striped fins: fluttering pectorals, swaying tail fan, rippling dorsal and anal fins, all faster when alarmed. Dark freckles on the back, pale belly, a few air bubbles trapped inside the jelly.

Look: MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission, clearcoat and sheen for a candy-gummy look; a soft environment map; a soft colored shadow with a faint caustic on a floor that matches the page background. Flavour presets Yuzu, Ramune, Momo, Matcha. Editorial "Material Studies" layout: big italic serif title "Fugu Jelly.", a side panel with flavour swatches, Firmness and Wobble sliders, Startle / Calm / Reset buttons, ¼ speed and Sound toggles, and live readouts for volume, spine angle and mood. Synthesized WebAudio sounds for gulps, a boing on tap, a hiss while deflating and tiny bubble pops. Responsive down to phone width.

prompt.text:
架空の大型ロケット（2段式の液体ロケット＋固体ブースター2本、白い機体、名前なし）と
その射点について、CAD図面と Blender 動画を作ってください。

【図面】2D の DXF のみ（3Dモデルの書き出しは不要）。単位 mm、A2 の図枠と表題欄つき。
線は青緑系の「電子の図面」風にし、プレビュー画像は濃紺の背景にする。
1. 射点配置図 S=1:500（ロケットを原点に置き、実際の位置で描く。
移動発射台・排煙溝・アンビリカルタワー・避雷塔・照明塔・水タンク・建屋・海岸線）
2. 射点立面図（南から）S=1:400
3. ロケット外形図・断面図 S=1:250
特記事項に「架空の機体・射場のイメージで、実在の図面ではない」と書く。
寸法は Python の形状モジュール1つで決め、図面と動画の両方がそれを読み込む。

【動画】Blender（EEVEE）、1920×1080・24fps・本編20秒＋ロゴ3.5秒、音つき MP4。
1. 暗闇の床に、シアンに光る射点配置図が中心から走査されて描かれる（真上から）
2. 図面の線が光のワイヤーとして立ち上がる
3. 光の粒（Geometry Nodes）が渦を巻いて昇り、発射台・タワー・ロケットが下から積み上がる
（積み上がった高さより下だけが実体になる。カメラは寄る）
4. 図面がマス目ごとにデジタルに溶け、夜の射点が現れる（海・丘・星空。カメラは引く）。
照明塔が点いて白い機体が浮かび、塔の頂部の赤い灯が明滅する
5. アクセスアームが離れる → カウントダウン → 点火 → リフトオフ。
炎は発光する円錐、噴煙は排煙溝と発射台から湧き、上昇する機体の後ろに煙の柱が残る
6. 上昇するロケットを海の上から見上げたところでタイトル → 最後に指定のロゴ
音は外部素材を使わず Python で合成する
（電子音の BGM、波、カウントダウンの電子音、点火から上昇までの轟音、タイトルの和音）。

【進め方】
- 図面のプレビュー画像を目で見て、文字の重なりを直す
- 本番の前にテスト静止画を数枚描いて確認する（照明の明るさ、炎や光の白飛び）
- 本番レンダーは軽い設定で、PC を休ませながら回す。始める前に所要時間を伝えて了承を取る

summary.en: A browser toy where a soft-body jelly watermelon wedge can be sliced with a knife and the bouncing pieces grabbed and thrown, built with Claude Opus 5.5 for a stated total cost of $12.46.

prompt.text:
Build a real-time WebGPU soft-body "jelly" study of a watermelon wedge that you can cut with a steel knife, in an editorial "Material Studies" page style (serif title "Melon Jelly.", muted paper backdrop, side panel, English UI, mobile-friendly). Geometry: a thick triangular watermelon wedge with a rounded green rind, a pale white layer, and translucent red flesh with dark seeds and a few air bubbles. Sim: CPU XPBD on a tetrahedral mesh, fixed 60 Hz step with 10 substeps. Each tet uses a co-rotational shape-matching constraint with finite compliance, which also flips inverted elements back out, plus a near-incompressible volume constraint so a stretched slice necks in. The rind is about 3× stiffer than the flesh. Damping acts only on relative velocity along edges. Floor contact uses Coulomb friction. Grabbing is a soft, reach-limited attachment to a patch of particles, and scroll or a second finger twists it.

Two tools, Hand and Knife:
- Knife: the user draws a stroke across the slice. Read on the surface, that stroke defines a vertical blade plane. Every piece is stored as a rounded convex outline in the slice's rest plane. For each piece the plane crosses, fit the piece's current pose with a best rotation, carry the plane back to rest space as a straight line, and split the outline along it.
- The cut: prebuild both halves as fresh tet meshes on release. An animated steel knife lines up over the stroke, comes down, and first presses a groove into the jelly. When it breaks through, swap in the new pieces, which inherit the position and velocity of the flesh they came from, and the blade wedges the faces apart on its way to the board. Draw the blade behind the jelly surface so the buried part is seen refracted.
- Pieces: every piece is its own soft body that can be grabbed, stretched and cut again, and pieces collide with each other instead of passing through.

Render: a smooth surface mesh plus the seeds and bubbles, each vertex embedded in a tet by barycentric weights so they ride the wobble. WGSL passes:
- floor, seeds and bubbles first;
- back faces, to get the thickness each view ray crosses;
- front faces with refraction by that thickness, Beer–Lambert absorption, milky scattering in the pale layer, a back-lit glow at thin edges, Fresnel reflections of a procedural studio, and GGX highlights;
- a soft key shadow on the floor tinted by the jelly, plus contact AO from a top-down height map.

Varieties: Crimson, Golden, Rosé. Controls: Hand/Knife tool toggle, firmness and internal damping sliders, "Give it a nudge", Reset, Pause, ¼ speed, Show mesh, plus mass/volume/kinetic readouts and an "Inside the experiment" notes drawer explaining the physics, cutting and rendering.

summary.zh: 一个名为Geyser Jelly的单文件WebGPU交互式立体景观，展示了嵌在果冻状海洋中的冰岛火山岛，作者用详细的文字提示让Opus 5.5构建，并与ChatGPT-6 Astra的版本进行了对比。
summary.en: A single-file WebGPU interactive diorama called 'Geyser Jelly' depicting a volcanic Icelandic island inside a jelly-like sea, built by Opus 5.5 from a detailed written prompt and compared against ChatGPT-6 Astra's version.

prompt.text:
Build "Geyser Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama for a "Material Studies" series: a volcanic Icelandic island set inside a translucent block of jelly sea, viewed as a tabletop object on a pale paper studio backdrop.

TECH
- One self-contained HTML file: plain JS + WGSL, no libraries, no network requests (Google Fonts optional). WebGPU only, with a clean fallback screen if WebGPU/adapter is missing or the device is lost.
- Block 5.2 × 5.2 units, sea level at y = 1.0. The block can be tipped by dragging its ground/sides; it springs back and quivers like jelly (shear + squash wobble applied to everything inside in the vertex shader).
- Sea = linear shallow-water sim on a ~168² grid (heights + face velocities, a little surface tension, damping), fed by the block's tilt. Render the water with refraction of the scene behind, colored absorption through the jelly, light shafts, caustics on the bed, foam/white water, a bright meniscus on the cut faces. Cut faces of the ground show candy-coloured strata, basalt, tephra bands and turf.
- Sun shadow map, MSAA, HDR with a soft shoulder tone map. Fixed-step simulation (240 Hz bodies, 120 Hz water). Expose a debug handle on window for tests.

THE ISLAND (procedural height field + ground cover: moss, grass, sinter, scoria)
- Back-left: a scoria cone volcano with a real crater bowl holding a lava lake (dark crust plates with glowing seams), patchy summit snow. A lava channel runs from a flank vent with a spatter cone down into the sea, glowing ribbon with drifting crust; it keeps glowing under the jelly water; constant steam where it meets the sea. Warm lava light on nearby ground.
- Back-right: a grassy plateau that ends in sheer columnar-basalt cliffs on its seaward side, three basalt sea stacks with grassy tops, puffins on the ledges, a small square orange lighthouse.
- Middle: a geothermal valley — a pale sinter mound with orange bacterial runoff streaks, the geyser pool (blue over a dark vent), two milky-turquoise hot springs and one clear deep-blue one, a grey bubbling mud pot with expanding rings, fumarole steam. A timber boardwalk arcs round the front of the geyser with tourists on it, with paths to the jetty, the church and the lagoon.
- Front-left: a milky blue lagoon in white silica banks, a timber deck with a ladder, a black-timber bathhouse with a turf roof, bathers drifting up to their shoulders.
- Front-right: a meadow with three turf houses (grass roofs; white, red and tarred gables), a little white church with a red roof and spire inside a turf wall, a flagpole with a fluttering Icelandic flag, a fenced paddock with five Icelandic horses (chestnut with flaxen mane, black, grey, palomino, bay).
- A jetty on piles out to a T-head where a whale-watching boat berths; a small ticket hut. Black-sand beaches, lava boulders, kelp, urchins and sea stars on the sea floor.

THE GEYSER (Strokkur)
Cycle every ~15–20 s on its own: refill → rest (simmering, occasional bulges) → surge (three growing heaves, gurgling, wisps of steam) → a turquoise dome swells and quivers → it bursts: a white churning water column (20–35 m in the UI; 1 unit = 20 m) shoots up ballistically, hundreds of streaked drops rain back down and drift with the wind, the column breaks apart from the bottom up, a big steam cloud rolls off downwind, the sinter goes dark and wet, then the pool drains with a gurgle. Tourists raise their arms and cheer; some hold up phones during the surge.

THE VOLCANO
Tremor: the block shakes, ash billows from the crater, lava bombs fly (thud and smoke on land, hiss, steam and a splash at sea, glowing then cooling), the lava lake rises and brightens, the flow speeds up, horses bolt round the paddock, puffins take off, and the geyser goes off.

LIFE
- Humpback whale (knobbly head, long white flippers, grooved pale throat, broad flukes): cruises offshore, surfaces and blows 2–3 times (spray plumes), arches and shows its flukes as it dives, stays deep, avoids the boat and shallow water. About once a minute (or on demand) it breaches: sounds deep, turns to an open spot, rushes up, leaps clear while twisting, crashes onto its back with a huge splash, foam and a ring wave across the bay that rocks the boat.
- The boat "Hafdís" (old oak fishing boat: dark blue hull, red bottom, white wheelhouse, passengers in bright jackets): lies at the jetty ~40 s, then casts off and does a loop round the bay on a smooth filleted route, slowing right down when the whale is near, rides the waves with heave/pitch/roll, makes a wake, puffs exhaust, comes back alongside.
- Atlantic puffins: stand on the cliff edge and stacks, stretch their wings, whirr out over the bay, land on the water, dive and chase fish underwater, fly home and land.
- People: 9 tourists on the boardwalk (sometimes shuffle to another spot), walkers on the paths and jetty, 6 bathers in the lagoon. Horses graze, wander, trot when startled. A school of fish in the bay flees threats.
- Steam, ash and spray are soft translucent puffs drawn after the water with premultiplied alpha, broken up with noise, rising, spreading and drifting downwind.

UI
- Left: eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", big italic serif title "Geyser / Jelly.", subtitle "A volcanic island with a geyser, set in a block of jelly sea." Bottom-left: "How to play" with the line "Set off the geyser. Shake the volcano. Watch for the whale." and a small paragraph of hints. Top-right: status pill "WebGPU · Live".
- Right glass panel: buttons Erupt / Tremor / Breach / Cast off (→ Full ahead); disabled with labels like "Surging…", "Erupting…", "Draining…", "Refilling…" when not ready. A thin liveliness meter. Tallies: Eruptions, Tallest (m), Breaches. Status lines "Strokkur: Resting 5 s / Surging / Erupting · 24 m / Draining / Refilling 68%" and "Hafdís: Alongside 18 s / Casting off / Under way 40% / Whale ahead / Coming alongside".
- Flavours: Blue lagoon (milky aqua), Lingonberry (red), Licorice (smoky dark). Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Wind. Buttons: Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, View.
- Interaction: tap the geyser, the volcano, the whale or the boat to trigger them (hand cursor on hover); Space sounds the boat's horn and puts the puffins up; drag across the water to make waves; drag the ground or the block's side to tip it; drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; wheel/pinch to zoom. On phones the panel becomes a bottom sheet with a "Controls" bar; no page scroll at any size.

prompt.text:
Create a visually impressive interactive 3D cutaway jet engine experience in Three.js.
The result should feel like a premium technical visualization or futuristic engineering showcase.
The first few seconds must have a strong wow effect and immediately hook the viewer.
Core idea:
Build a detailed jet engine in 3D with a clean outer shell, and let the viewer explore the inside through cutaway, x-ray, and exploded-style views.
Main requirements:
Build a full 3D jet engine from scratch in code
No pre-made 3D models
Use Three.js
Prefer a single HTML file unless a few small extra files are truly necessary
The project must run locally in the browser
The engine should include:
front fan blades
compressor stages
combustion chamber
turbine stages
exhaust section
outer shell / nacelle
internal shaft structure
visible airflow path
Interactions / modes:
assembled mode
cutaway mode
x-ray mode
exploded view mode
airflow visualization on/off
throttle or power slider
auto-rotate camera option
orbit controls
Animation ideas:
engine startup sequence
fan spins up first
inner stages accelerate
combustion chamber ignites
hot glowing section appears in the core
exhaust flow becomes visible
subtle vibration / mechanical life
Visual quality:
polished lighting
premium materials
good contrast between outer shell and internals
smooth transitions between modes
readable labels or callouts for key engine parts
cinematic presentation
strong sense of depth
The first seconds should feel especially strong:
for example, begin with a clean hero shot of the engine, then smoothly reveal the cutaway and ignite the core.
Make it feel detailed, technical, and visually satisfying rather than toy-like.
