summary.en: An interactive single-file WebGPU diorama of a jelly-like dam with water simulation, turbines, fish, floods and controls. The creator says Opus 5.5 built it from a text prompt.

prompt.text:
Build "Dam Jelly", a new piece in my "Material Studies" series: a single-file, self-contained interactive WebGPU diorama (one HTML file, all JS/CSS/WGSL inline, no network requests, no libraries). A mountain valley with a concrete gravity dam is cut out as a wobbly block of jelly sitting on a pale studio table, seen from above at three-quarters.

SCENE (block-local coords, origin at base centre, y up, block ~5.2 × 5.2 units):
- A river valley running back to front: steep rocky slopes with crags, scree and boulders, conifer and broadleaf woods, grassy shoulders. Where the block is cut, the side faces show layered grey bedrock in tilted beds with joints, a weathered brown band and dark topsoil at the top, and gravel and silt under the water. At the very bottom are thin coloured "jelly" strata in the current flavour.
- A long reservoir behind the dam, with a bare drawdown ring of rock round its shore, a floating log boom of orange and yellow floats in front of the spillway, and a small patrol boat lapping the lake.
- A concrete gravity dam across the valley, its ends let into rock abutments: a battered downstream face with lift lines, a crest road with railings and lamps, an intake tower with trash racks and three penstocks down the face.
- A central stepped spillway with three bays between piers. Each bay has a radial (Tainter) gate: a curved skin plate on arms that swing about trunnions on the piers, with hoist houses on top. Below is an ogee crest, a stepped chute, training walls and a plunge pool scoured into the riverbed.
- A powerhouse at the right toe: a concrete base in the river, a hall of siding and tall windows, tailrace mouths. Above it, a switchyard on a terrace with transformers and gantries, and lattice pylons climbing the right slope with sagging lines.
- A fish ladder up the left bank: 14 stepped concrete pools with weirs between them from the river up to the lake, an exit gate and a counting hut at the top.
- A visitor centre on the left abutment, roads with hairpins, a suspension footbridge over the river downstream, rocks, weed and gravel bars in the river.

SIMULATION:
- Shallow-water heightfield (about 168×168), split into two bodies by the dam (reservoir and river), each with its own still level, separated by flood-fill classification. Sources, sinks and current jets make visible flow: inflow at the back of the lake, a draw toward open gates and the intake, boiling outflow in the plunge pool and tailrace, and drainage at the front edge. Foam advects on the currents.
- Reservoir level ODE: dL/dt = (Qin − Qspill − Qturbines − Qover) / AREA, where Qspill ∝ gateOpening · (L − sill)^1.5 and Qover ∝ (L − crest)^1.5. The river level rises with total outflow.
- Head-based power: 3 units × 120 MW, scaled by head.
- An automatic dam keeper opens the gates (siren first) when the lake nears the crest or a flood is coming, and shuts them again once the water is back down.
- The jelly block itself wobbles, can be tipped by dragging its side, and settles back.

INTERACTIONS (right-hand glass panel, "The dam"):
- Open spillway: a 3.5 s siren, then the gates swing up over ~9 s, and white water streams down the steps with spray and mist. Press again to shut them.
- Turbines on/off: the units spin up or down, power rises or falls, the tailrace boils or goes still, and the powerhouse windows glow while running.
- Salmon run: salmon gather below the dam, try leaping at the falls, then climb the ladder pool by pool (a leap per pool, waiting their turn) and swim out into the lake. A counter tallies fish through. Runs also arrive on their own every few minutes.
- Flood: a storm builds, blows and eases (rain, darkening, lightning hitting pylons, ridges or the lake). A big inflow surge comes down the valley: the keeper pre-releases, the lake still rises over the crest, and a white overflow sheet pours across the whole dam face. The water turns muddy brown and clears slowly afterwards.
- Tap a gate, the powerhouse or the ladder to trigger the same actions. Tap the patrol boat for its horn. Space sounds the siren.
- Tallies: Power (MW), Head (m), Salmon. Status lines: Spillway, Powerhouse, Reservoir (Rising/Falling/Steady/Flood coming in/Over the crest, with level relative to the crest in metres).
- Drag on water makes waves, drag the block's side tips it, drag empty space or right-drag orbits, wheel or pinch zooms.
- Flavour swatches (Lime, Curaçao, Blackcurrant) tint the jelly and water. Sliders for Firmness, Wave damping and Wind. Reset, Pause, Sound on/off and View buttons.

LIFE: rainbow trout in the river and lake, salmon, mallards (drakes and hens) paddling and taking off, herons wading and stalking, ospreys circling and plunge-diving for fish, people walking the crest (who pause at the siren), the powerhouse yard, the visitor centre and the footbridge, and a fisherman on the bank. Animals startle at the siren, lightning and splashes.

SOUND (synthesised with WebAudio, events only, no constant ambience): motor siren, gate-hoist clunk and drone, the spillway's rush as the gates lift, turbine spin-up and spin-down whine, a rumble of overtopping, salmon leaps, a chime for each fish counted, osprey splashes, the boat horn, thunder, and wind and rain only while a storm blows.

RENDERING: WebGPU with MSAA, a sun shadow map, caustics on the riverbed, refraction and absorption through the water and the jelly, Fresnel reflections, translucent premultiplied passes for spray and mist puffs, white-water sheets, ladder pools and rain, and a muddy-water tint during floods.

UI and layout: editorial look with an italic serif masthead ("Material Studies" eyebrow, "Dam Jelly." title, a one-line description) and a "How to play" footer at bottom left. On mobile the controls panel becomes a bottom sheet. If WebGPU is unavailable, show a clear fallback card. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. No page scroll.

QUALITY: keep the sim around 2 ms/frame, no NaNs over long soaks, everything stays inside the block, the boat always afloat. Verify with headless Playwright screenshots (SwiftShader WebGPU) and an end-to-end test that drives every button, tap target, slider and the mobile sheet, and checks for zero console errors.

prompt.text:
Create a spectacular 4:3 Jujutsu Kaisen AMV centered on Satoru Gojo, using the supplied images and music. Match the final video's duration exactly to the full soundtrack.

EDITING & ANIMATION:
Analyze the music's rhythm, structure, energy and emotional progression. Animate the supplied images into dynamic cinematic sequences with expressive character motion, dramatic camera movements, parallax and seamless transitions. Creatively select, crop, reframe, combine and revisit images throughout the edit. Build an intense anime opening with powerful visual storytelling, synchronized precisely to the music.

DYNAMIC GRID:
Use a constantly evolving manga-inspired grid with variable cell sizes, shapes and arrangements. Mix large hero panels, small square cells, narrow strips, irregular rectangles and occasional diagonal divisions. Freely expand, shrink, split, merge and rearrange cells according to the music. Alternate between dense multi-cell compositions, striking asymmetrical layouts and occasional full-frame hero moments. Allow different images, perspectives and moments to coexist across cells. Keep panel boundaries crisp and compositions visually coherent.

VISUAL EFFECTS:
Create intense, layered effects inspired by Gojo Satoru's powers and the visual identity of Jujutsu Kaisen. Explore spatial distortion, Infinity, Six Eyes, cursed energy, Blue, Red and Hollow Purple through inventive motion graphics, impact frames, dimensional fractures and cinematic transitions. Blend style infections spreading across neighboring cells with temporal echoes, frame repetitions, speed ramps, freezes and rhythmic chain reactions. Let effects interact creatively with the grid and occasionally break beyond panel boundaries.

CREATIVE DIRECTION:
Make this feel like a premium, visually groundbreaking Jujutsu Kaisen anime opening. Capture Gojo's overwhelming power, confidence, elegance and mysterious presence. Let the supplied images and soundtrack guide every creative decision, including pacing, visual treatments, transitions, color grading and effect intensity. Avoid repetitive editing patterns or generic templates. Balance explosive action with striking moments of visual clarity. Preserve Gojo's recognizable identity, facial features, costume and the artistic style of the supplied images.

AUDIO:
Use the supplied music as the primary soundtrack, uninterrupted from beginning to end. Synchronize animation, grid transformations, camera movements and visual effects to its beats, melodies, transitions and emotional peaks.
No typography, text, letters, numbers or watermarks.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML page (three.js r128 from cdnjs, no other dependencies): "Cinderpine Express", a pixel-art 3D fairground diorama on a floating autumn island with three ready-made roller coasters (no track editor).

RENDERING
- Orthographic isometric camera (31° elevation, quarter-turn orbit) drawn into a low-resolution target (art pixel = 2 CSS px, adjustable 1-6 px with a slider). Post shader: depth-based outlines, snap to a fixed 90-colour OKLab palette, Bayer dither, sky/clouds/stars drawn in the shader.
- Autumn palette (dry grass, plum rock, brick, brass, cherry red). Day / Dusk / Night with dynamic lamp lights, glowing windows, fireworks at night.
- A second, perspective camera feeding the same pipeline for chase and first-person.

PARK
Floating island slab with cliff rim, entrance gate with sign, switchback queue, ~6 stalls, cafe, fountain, ferris wheel, carousel, trees, falling leaves, bunting, lamp posts, ~140 instanced box-people who stroll, queue, sit, eat and cheer when the train passes.

COASTERS
Author each as a "turtle" program (straights, pitch easing, turns, hills, vertical loop, helix, tunnel) closed into a circuit by a numeric solver, then smoothed and resampled every 0.5 m. All inside a 76 x 50 m zone next to the station.
1. Old Pinewood: wood, diagonal chain lift, big first drop, camelback airtime hill, trim brake, banked helix, final brake.
2. Cinderloop: steel, east-side lift, vertical loop (sideways spiral so the strands never touch), trim brake.
3. Ember Mine Run: mine train, short lift, double dip, S-curve through a tunnel under a rock hill.
Physics: energy-based speed profile (friction, drag, chain lift, brakes, station stop), banking from the force vector (zero lateral g, works upside down), felt vertical g, airtime flag, stats and ratings (excitement / intensity / nausea).
Visuals: rails, ties, supports down to the ground (timber trestle / steel lattice / stone piers), chain with moving dogs, brake fins, station with canopy and gates, 5-car train with 20 riders who raise their arms on drops, headlamp at night.

RIDE AND CAMERAS
State machine: unload, board, dispatch (lever / Space / auto after ~13 s), lift, drop, brake, arrive. Events drive sound and toasts ("Loop!", "Airtime!").
Cameras: Park (drag orbit, wheel/pinch zoom), Follow, Chase, First-person from the front seat (drag to look around, FOV widens with speed, low car nose so the rails stay visible).

SOUND
WebAudio only, starts on first tap: calliope music, crowd ambience, chain clank, wheels, wind, screams, brakes, station bell, fireworks.

UI
Ticket-booth identity: cream ride tickets with perforations and an "ON THE TRACK" stamp, a cherry dispatch lever, a dark marquee HUD (speed, height, g gauge, section name, lap time), toasts. Ride speed x1/x2/x4 and a pixel-size slider always visible. Phone layout with a bottom sheet, light/dark themes, keyboard shortcuts (1-4 cameras, Space, Q/E, [ ], X). Fonts: Bevan + Hanken Grotesk.

QUALITY BAR
Every coaster closes with < 1 m error, max g <= 4.5, no stalls, no console errors, smooth on a phone. Test with headless Chromium screenshots (all cameras, day/night, phone). Publish as an artifact and also give a standalone .html.

HOW TO WORK
First write a contract file (coordinates, palette keys, TRACK/RIDE API, events, light slots). Then build the coaster physics and ride yourself and run three parallel agents: park + guests + fx, rails + station + train, audio. Integrate and test last.

prompt.text:
In Blender, make a short, hyper-realistic video of a pumpkin carving itself into a jack-o'-lantern.

The pumpkin: very detailed and realistic, with ribs, skin bumps, a curly dry stem, subtle blemishes and real-looking flesh. It sits on a wooden board against a soft, warm cream studio backdrop with soft daylight lighting.

Start: the pumpkin just sits there for a moment. Never start on black.

Carving: a kitchen knife with no hands flies in and carves on its own. First it cuts the zigzag lid, which lifts off with stringy pulp and lands to the side. Then it carves the eyes, the nose and a toothy grin. Each piece pushes out with real physics and tumbles onto the board. Show the inner flesh, pulp and seeds. Keep it fast and satisfying.

Light-up: a lit tea-light candle drops inside and the lid goes back on. The studio lights dim to dark while the carved face glows warm orange from inside with a real flicker. Hold on the glowing face for 3-4 seconds.

Camera: close on the pumpkin with a slow, small drift. No wide shots.

Sound: real sound effects only: knife cuts, squishy pulp, pieces thudding, a match strike and a soft candle crackle. Add spooky, playful Halloween music underneath.

Render in Cycles at 1080x1350 (4:5), about 16 seconds.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Castle Jelly", in the style of my jelly diorama series (Pirate Jelly / Island Jelly): a square block of wobbly jelly lake on a table in a paper studio, cut faces showing candy strata, italic serif masthead "Castle / Jelly.", glass control panel on the right, "How to play" line at the bottom-left, UI in English, mobile bottom-sheet layout.
The diorama: a fairy-tale castle on a cliff. The back-left of the block is a plateau whose front is a sheer wall of candy-striped rock (layer-cake strata that match the block's cut faces, a talus under the lake), meshed from an SDF with surface nets, mossy where it faces up. On the lawn: a cream castle with round towers, glossy pink/lilac/blue cone roofs, gold finials, fluttering pennants, crenellated walls, a great hall, arched windows (dark glass by day, lamplight at night), a gatehouse with a drawbridge, a brazier by the gate, gummy pines, flowering bushes, reeds. A river wells up from a spring, runs past the gate under the drawbridge and pours off the lip as a waterfall that arcs down into the jelly lake — and keeps going inside the jelly: a fraying plume, bubbles driven down then rising, bright threads of current streaming along the lake floor. The falls pound the surface (shallow-water waves, foam, spray, mist). A little royal galleon (blue hull, white sails, crown standard) sails laps of the lake.
Interactions: Fireworks (rockets off the towers, coloured bursts that light the castle and the lake; automatic at night), Lower/Raise bridge, Royal salute (ship fires, splash), Wishing coins (into the pool under the falls); tap a tower / the gate / the brazier / the ship, drag the water to make waves, tip the block, throw coins and balls, bend the pines. Sliders: Firmness, Waterfall (flow), Wave damping, Time of day (noon → sunset → night with stars). Flavours: Glacier, Rose, Lilac. Shadows, caustics, refraction through the jelly, fixed-step physics.

summary.en: A vertical 2D cartoon animal-facts Short with a narrating host, built in code with Claude Opus 5.5. The posted prompt covers script, image sheets, cutouts, lip-sync, ElevenLabs voice, canvas rendering and mixing.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for my animal or topic ("Why is the X the most disturbing animal in the ocean?", "Why is X terrifying?"), or pitch 3, each with 5 true facts that get worse as they go. Ask which image model I have (GPT Image 2 or any model that takes a reference image at 4K, about $0.03 an image) and which voice I have (ElevenLabs, or Kokoro for free). Then write the script and the shot list with seconds, and show me both before anything costs money.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920, 60 fps, 30-35 s vertical Short in the style of the big narrated animal-facts channels where a guy in a hoodie with a mic pops into every scene. Here everything is a flat 2D cartoon: thick dark brown outlines (#1f1418), flat colours, simple cel shading, big round googly eyes.
The host: a cartoon young man with messy brown hair, glasses, a plain heather grey hoodie with no logo, dark jeans, white sneakers, always holding a black mic.
- He is about 1000-1050 px tall on screen. His feet sit below the frame edge, so he is cut off at the shins.
- He pops up from below the frame in 0.32 s with an overshoot ease.
- His mouth flaps on the voice whenever he talks to camera.
- His face always stays above the caption pill.
The animal: one character in 9 poses (neutral, shocked, angry, plus costume poses for the facts: old with a beard and cane, a powdered wig, a teen with braces, drunk, a front view of the face, defeated on a plate). One costume per fact is the joke.
A new place every 1.5-3 s. Never repeat a composition.
Something always moves:
- Animals swim with a tail wave and bob ±10 px.
- The camera pushes in 2-4% per shot.
- Pose swaps squash.
- Hits shake the frame.
Titles are one or two big words per beat in Luckiest Guy (Google Fonts), 104-190 px at y 430, tilted ±0.03-0.05 rad:
- They wobble ±0.025 rad.
- The outline is 0.22 of the size in #1f1418, with a darker copy of the colour 0.09 of the size underneath.
- Colours are pairs of fill and shadow: yellow #ffd21f/#c27a10, red #ff4a3d/#8e1a14, white #ffffff/#9aa6b4, pink #ff7ab8/#a8336d, green #7dff6a/#2e9a2a.
Captions:
- 1-4 words in a white pill at y 1470: Luckiest Guy 66 px, dark text, a 7 px outline, pill height 1.55x the text.
- The key word is yellow with a dark outline.
- The pill pops from 0.82 to 1 in 0.13 s.
A red marker ellipse circles the animal when its name is said.
Banned: photoreal cutouts mixed into cartoon art, a real person's face, the real channel's logo or name on screen, a still frame over 1 s, the host covering the animal's face on its key word.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 30-35 s, about 115 words at about 3.5 words a second. Times are from a 33.5 s film; scale them to the voice.
0-1.9 s, the hook "Why is the X the most disturbing animal in the ocean?":
- The animal glides in from off screen in 0.75 s while the host pops up bottom right, already talking.
- On the animal's name: a red ring, the name as a title, and the host swaps to pointing at it for 0.7 s.
1.9-3.7 s: a punch-in on "disturbing". The water is graded red, the angry pose, an impact starburst, the word in red.
3.7-8.2 s, fact 1, the shocking number:
- A counter rolls up to it.
- Then a comparison everyone gets ("older than America") shown as a costume pose and a prop that springs in.
8.2-12.7 s, facts 2 and 3 played as gags:
- One is a costume in a new place.
- One is a race the animal loses. On "slower than you walk", the host strolls past it.
12.7-15.6 s: the gross detail, with a zoom into the face.
15.6-16.7 s: "But it gets worse." A red alarm grade with a pulsing vignette. The animal yells into the lens and the host swaps from talking to horrified.
16.7-21 s, the worst fact:
- The host cowers behind the victim, which then vanishes in a poof.
- An x-ray shot shows what is inside.
21-27.7 s: the human angle, each line with a person from the cast acting it out. The host joins in (drunk next to the drunk Viking).
27.7-29 s: someone happily eats it while the host turns green and gags.
29-33.5 s: the callback joke that ties back to the hook. The host talks to camera, then cracks up on the last word. Hold 1.15 s after the last word.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium or Edge, FFmpeg, OpenCV, Pillow, numpy, soundfile. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Art, 4 images in total (about $0.12). Every prompt starts with "Match the exact art style of the reference image: flat 2D cartoon, thick dark brown outlines, flat colours with simple cel shading, big expressive googly eyes, clean vector look". Feed the first sheet you like back in as the style reference for the rest.
- Animal sheet: 1:1 at 4K, "a 3 by 3 pose sheet of the SAME cartoon X, 9 separate poses on plain pure white, plenty of white space, nothing touching, no grid lines, no text, no ground shadows", every pose a full side view facing right except the front face.
- Cast sheet: 1:1 at 4K, 9 different characters and props for the facts, same wording.
- Background grid: 9:16 at 4K, "a 3 by 3 grid of 9 equal tall vertical panels separated by thin white gutters, each panel an EMPTY scene, no characters, no text, keep the lower middle open".
- Host sheet: 9:16 at 4K, 9 full-body poses at the same size: (1) facing the viewer, mic below the chin, mouth CLOSED, (2) EXACTLY the same pose with only the mouth WIDE OPEN, (3) talking and pointing to the side, (4) horrified with a hand on the cheek, (5) crouching and cowering with sweat drops, (6) running in side view facing right, (7) laughing and leaning back, (8) gagging with a green face holding a toothpick of food, (9) drunk with spiral eyes.
3. Cutouts:
- Flood the white from the border (seeds every 64 px around the edge) with a floating range of 7, so soft glows go too.
- Feather a 3 px band outside the shapes with alpha = clamp((250 - min(R,G,B)) / 150). Un-mix the white from that band: colour = (c - 255(1 - a)) / a.
- Group the pieces by the grid cell their centre falls in and drop pieces under 150 px.
- Split the background grid on its white gutters (rows and columns whose minimum channel averages over 232). Crop 4 px in, cover-fit to 1080x1920 with Lanczos, unsharp mask (radius 2, 60%).
4. Host lip-sync:
- Align pose 2 onto pose 1 by template-matching the glasses and eyes. Paste only its mouth onto pose 1 through a feathered ellipse (sigma 4). Now open and closed are the same drawing, so the outline never wobbles.
- Mouth track at 60 fps from the voice: RMS per frame, smoothed over 3 frames. Open when it is over (70th percentile in dB - 15) and over 0.55x the loudest frame within ±0.1 s.
- Hold every state at least 3 frames. Break open runs longer than 14 frames with a 3-frame close every 12 frames. That gives about 8 flips a second.
- Anchor every host pose by its feet and its head centre x (the alpha centre of the top 28% of the cutout), so pose swaps never jump. Measure that per pose.
5. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v4 with the timestamps endpoint, a calm deep documentary narrator, stability 0.5, similarity 0.75, one take (about 300 credits for 600 characters).
- Cut pauses (10 ms frames under -40 dB, longer than 0.2 s) down to their first and last 0.06 s, with 8 ms fades.
- Then atempo 1.15 and a 0.15 s lead-in.
- Rebuild word times from the character alignment through the same cuts and tempo. When a start lands after the next word's start, pull it back.
- Free route: Kokoro, then whisper for the word times.
6. Film: one HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time: window .seek(t), READY, END, and EV with the sound times. One function per shot.
- Sprite tail wave: draw the cutout in 28 vertical slices. Each slice moves dy = sin(8t - 4.5u) * wig * k, where k = (max(0, u - 0.3) / 0.7)^1.5 and wig is 3-14 px.
- Pop: 1 - 0.6 e^(-9Δt) cos(20Δt). Pose-swap kick: 1 + a e^(-10Δt) cos(22Δt), with a = 0.1-0.22. Shake: A e^(-7Δt) sin(61Δt), with A = 22-34 px.
- Props drawn in code: a rolling number counter, a waving flag, a flipping calendar, green fumes, buzzing flies, confetti, red rings, arrows, an impact starburst, poof clouds, bubbles.
- Red alarm grade: grayscale(.5) sepia(1) hue-rotate(-35deg) saturate(3.2) brightness(.55).
- X-ray: grayscale(1) invert(1) sepia(1) hue-rotate(150deg) saturate(3.5) on #071a2e with a 60 px cyan grid and a scan line.
- Look up repeated words by their occurrence (the third "and"), or cuts land on the wrong line.
7. Check, render, sound:
- Contact sheets of 12-15 frames at key words before rendering. Fix covered faces, the host over the animal's face, and titles off screen.
- Render 60 fps with 8 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, then libx264 CRF 19.
- Music: a quirky piano mystery bed, free on Pixabay, with the voice 11-14 dB over it in every phrase.
- Mixkit SFX, one per event, placed by their peaks: a pop on every title, a whoosh when the host or the animal enters, a hit on the big beats, a bite, a boing, a sad trombone on the fails, a poof, bubbles.
- Mix to -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
- A plain hue tint for the red alarm turned blue water green. Sepia first, then hue-rotate.
- Long titles overflow at 160 px. Split them into two beats ("OLDER THAN", then "AMERICA" in red).
- The host walking past on the key word hid the animal's face. Time his pass after the key word, keep him lower and smaller (0.62 scale), or draw him behind.
- Photoreal sticker animals with code eyes read as slop next to a real presenter. One flat cartoon style for everything fixes it.
- If the two talking poses differ by more than the mouth, swapping whole images makes the outline wobble. Paste the mouth only.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my animal or topic, or pitch 3, then show me the script and the shot list.
</start>

title.zh: 像素风3D足球场模拟：孩子与偷球的狗
title.en: Pixel-art 3D football yard simulation with kids and dog

summary.zh: Claude Opus 5.5 用 three.js 制作的像素风 3D 网页小玩具，内容是院子里的足球比赛，花费 6.06 美元。场景里有 AI 控制的孩子、球的物理效果，还有一只会抢球的狗。
summary.en: A pixel-art 3D web toy of a courtyard football game, built by Claude Opus 5.5 with three.js for $6.06. It has AI kids, ball physics and a dog that steals the ball.

prompt.text:
Build a single-page web toy called "Yard Box": a real-time 3D scene rendered as pixel art, showing a courtyard football box behind a four-storey panel apartment block on a floating island. Use three.js r160 (ES module via import map from jsDelivr, plus BufferGeometryUtils). English UI. Original design only — no real brands, places or logos.

RENDERING PIPELINE (the core look)
- Orthographic camera at an isometric angle (elevation ≈31°, azimuth π/4, rotatable in 90° steps with smooth easing; drag sideways or buttons to turn; wheel/pinch zoom 0.7–2.6).
- Render into a small WebGLRenderTarget (half-float, nearest filtering, depth texture) — about 480×300 art pixels at pixel size 3 — no anti-aliasing. Fit the island + the top of the block into the screen area left free by the UI, and snap the camera so the world origin lands on a whole art pixel (static things never shimmer).
- Post-pass ShaderMaterial: texelFetch whole-pixel upscale; depth-based outlines (a pixel > ~0.5 m in front of a neighbour darkens ×0.5); quantize every pixel to the nearest of a fixed ~60-colour palette in OKLab (lightness weighted ×1.35); optional 4×4 Bayer dither (off by default); empty depth = page background colour.
- "Raw 3D" toggle shows the full-resolution MSAA render without steps above. Controls: pixel size slider 2–6, palette / dither / outlines checkboxes.
- Palette: warm concrete greys, cool greys for snow in shade/moonlight, snow and sky blues, turf greens, autumn olives, yellows/oranges/rusts, team reds and blues, skin and wood tones, lamp/window yellows, dusk violets, mint for the boards.

LIGHT AND TIME
- Directional sun/moon with hard BasicShadowMap (2048), hemisphere fill, point lights for two streetlamps (decay 2) and weak doorway lamps. Presets Day / Dusk / Night blended over 1.6 s. Glow materials lerp between on/off colours.
- The block's facade uses an emissive map drawn on a canvas; at night windows glow warm or cool, and random flats switch lights on and off.

WORLD (all boxes, cylinders, extrusions; textures drawn texel by texel on canvases)
- Rounded floating slab: grass top over soil over rock.
- Football box: rounded-rectangle boards (22×12 m, mint green, plank lines, a gate with an open door), netting on posts above the boards at both ends, mini goals (3 m × 2 m) with alpha-tested nets, turf texture with mowing stripes, worn goalmouths/centre and white markings.
- Panel block along one long side: 4 floors, facade drawn panel by panel with windows and curtains, two entrances with canopies, random balconies, roof details; an asphalt strip with two benches and hedges.
- Dollhouse cut: when the camera looks from the block's side, hide the floors, roof, balconies and canopies and show a section of the ground floor instead — low cut walls with a dark cap, rooms with coloured floors, rugs, sofas, tables, wardrobes, TVs (glowing at night), pot plants, stairwells with steps and post boxes; room floors glow warm at night.
- Playground (swing that actually swings, slide, sandbox), birches with white trunks and dark marks, painted-tyre flower beds, a parked car, a washing line with swaying sheets, two lamp posts.

PEOPLE AND DOG
- Kids as rigs of ~17 boxes (bigger heads), posed every frame with two-bone IK: running stride, kicks keyed as back-swing → strike → follow-through, keeper stance, sideways dives, catch/hold/throw, goal celebrations (airplane arms).
- Three grandmothers sitting on the benches (cheer on goals), a small kid on the swing.
- A box-built dog that lives by the benches.

GAME LOGIC
- 3v3: two field players + one keeper per team (RED attacks +x, BLUE −x), first to 5, then a new game; scoreboard with score, game number, status line and games won.
- Kick-off from the centre; open play with dribbling by small touches, passes leading the receiver, shots aimed inside a post at random height with angular error growing with distance and pressure, tackles; players get behind the ball before kicking (feed-forward on a rolling ball), squeeze in at an angle when the ball is against the boards, avoid goal frames; a scramble poke if nobody can reach a still ball for 3.5 s.
- Keepers hold position, come out for slow loose balls, read shots after a 0.1–0.3 s reaction delay with some error, dive, catch or parry.
- Ball physics in 4 substeps: gravity, ground bounce (lower in winter), boards (lively below rail height, dead in the netting above), posts and crossbar, the goal net, legs in the way. Status flashes: GOAL!, SAVED!, WHAT A SAVE!, OFF THE POST!, OFF THE BOARDS, TACKLE.
- Every 100–170 s (or on a button) the dog runs in through the gate, grabs the ball, runs loops away from the kids for ~5 s, drops it and trots home; it gives up if the game resets.

SEASONS (Summer / Autumn / Winter)
- Summer: poplar fluff drifting. Autumn: yellow/orange canopies, leaves falling from the birches, leaf litter on the ground, olive grass. Winter: snow on the ground, roofs, benches, car and boards; bare trees; falling snow and kicked-up snow spray; kids wear hats; the ball turns orange.

INPUT AND UI
- Click the player on the ball to shoot, his teammate to pass, the pitch to make him dribble there; keys S, P, D, Space, Q/E or arrows.
- Layout: title and caption top-left, lit pixel-font scoreboard top-centre, a narrow control rail on the right (Time, Season, Game, View), a hint bottom-left, a fold-out "How it's drawn" panel bottom-right. Fonts: Silkscreen, Rubik, JetBrains Mono. Light and dark themes via CSS tokens; on phones everything stacks under the scene. WebGL2 fallback card.

title.zh: 写实三维真实故事旁白短片

summary.zh: 这段 Claude Code 提示词规定了用 Blender 制作写实三维解说短片的完整流程，包括字幕、声音、渲染和检查。
summary.en: A long Claude Code prompt specifies a Blender pipeline for realistic 3D narrated Shorts with captions, sound, rendering, and validation.

prompt.text:
Ask me 2 things, then wait:
1. The story in one line: a strange TRUE event where one person did one odd physical thing ("He tied 42 weather balloons to a lawn chair."). If I say "you pick", pitch 3 with one source link each and take the first unless I choose.
2. The voice. Default: Kokoro (free, runs on my computer), a calm, warm male narrator.
Then tell me everything else is free: Blender (find my install, or tell me the one download), its free MPFB extension for human bodies (ask me before you install it) and into this folder a Python venv with FFmpeg (imageio-ffmpeg), kokoro-onnx + its model files (kokoro-v1.0.onnx and voices-v1.0.bin from the kokoro-onnx GitHub releases), faster-whisper (small.en), numpy and Pillow. It needs no API key or account and renders on my graphics card with EEVEE.
</inputs>

<direction>
The look: a clean, realistic 3D world, like a good game cutscene. Bright, saturated, a little filmic.
- People: realistic bodies with generic faces and big readable expressions (shock, a smirk, a scream). Plain clothes, no logos. Never a real person's likeness: for a real person keep the face out of close-ups (hands, back, side, distance, straight top-down).
- CALM shots only. Bodies in fast action or contact (running, jumping, fighting, falling) look stiff, so tell the story with frozen moments under a slowly moving camera, macro inserts of hands and objects, rooms, vehicles, the sky, top-down views and the aftermath.
- One new picture for every caption chunk (2-4 words, about 1-1.5 s): a new framing, a new action or a camera move. Nothing ever holds still: every shot drifts, pushes in or orbits.
- The shot kit: macro insert (extreme close-up of the key object or hands, very shallow depth of field), hero low angle (wide lens at waist height), god's-eye top-down with a slow rotate, tracked object, over the shoulder, smash zoom on the word that matters, whip pan between beats, glow highlight (the named object glows orange with a rim, then fades), a big 3D number lying in the scene, a thought bubble (a cloud ring showing what he hoped for), a TV in the scene replaying the event.
- Light: a bright warm sun, blue sky with clouds, soft shadows. Night scenes use hard lamps and a dark sky. Wide lens up close, depth of field on every shot, motion blur on every fast camera move.
- Captions: 2-4 words at a time, white bold rounded sans, about 64 px on a 1080 px-wide frame, centred, 78% down the frame, soft dark shadow, no box. Each chunk replaces the last on the same frame as its picture.
- Banned: real footage, photos, downloaded textures or 3D models, logos, AI images or AI video, downloaded music, gore.
</direction>

<structure>
38-50 s, 100-140 words, 150-180 words a minute. The voice starts at 0.0 s.
- Line 1: the most surprising physical act, in past tense, opening with "He" (or "She"). No name, date or setup. Frame 1 shows that act.
- Then a cause-and-effect chain: every sentence starts with a hinge word (Then, Suddenly, So, Because, But, Later) and is ONE visible action.
- The context arrives late, after "You see,".
- A reveal: someone looks closer and the story turns.
- The last line is the consequence. No call to action, no question.
- Names are rare: use one only when it pays off.
Title = "He ..." or "The Man Who ...". The cover is the first frame.
</structure>

<build>
Save every stage to disk so a crash never costs more than one stage.
- sources.md: every fact with its link and the date you read it. Anything you can't verify stays out.
- script.json: the lines and the caption chunks cut by hand (2-4 words, one picture each), each chunk with its shot: the set, the camera, what moves.
- https://voice.py/: Kokoro reads the whole script in one take (speed 1.0-1.1) and pauses are squeezed to 0.35 s at most; faster-whisper times every word (pass it a 16 kHz numpy array, not a path); write chunks.json with each chunk's start and end. A picture and its caption switch together on frame round(start*30)+1.
- blender/: Python scripts run headless (blender -b -P). https://build.py/ makes one .blend with the sets, the cast, the props and every shot baked with a key on every frame. https://look.py/ sets EEVEE with ray tracing, the AgX view with the Punchy look, motion blur, depth of field and bloom in the compositor. Bodies come from MPFB or are built by you; clothes, hair, props and sets are built in code.
- Stills first: one half-size still per shot as a contact sheet. Look at every tile and fix what's off before any full render. Time one full-size frame and tell me the estimate.
- Render 1080x1920 at 30 fps to PNG frames, skipping frames already on disk.
- https://sound.py/, numpy only: a light music bed, a sound on every action (a whoosh on each whip pan, hits, wind, room tone), ducked under the voice, mastered to -14 LUFS on the whole stereo mix.
- https://compose.py/: burn the captions in from chunks.json. Encode out/<slug>_9x16.mp4 (1080x1920, 30 fps, TV-range yuv420p) and out/<slug>_x_7x8.mp4 (1008x1152, under 10 MB, 2-pass): a crop of the 9:16 frame that keeps the subject and the caption.
</build>

<gotchas>
- Blender paths: pass absolute output paths (a relative one lands on the drive root).
- MPFB headless: enable it with addon_utils.enable("bl_ext.user_default.mpfb"). Bake a body's shape keys before you pose it: the rig is fitted to the baked shape.
- Clothes: cut them from the body mesh and push them 7-16 mm out along the normals; keep two rings of body faces under every hem.
- Nothing coplanar: keep every resting object 1 cm off its neighbour and draw ground markings into the texture, or they flicker.
- Hair: EEVEE draws hair only from a Curves object, hair type STRIP. Use a Principled BSDF on it (the Hair BSDF renders black).
- Skin: keep subsurface weight near 0.2 (more turns faces black in EEVEE) and add a soft fill light from below under a noon sun.
- Hands: a curled hand reads as a claw from the palm side, so shoot a grip from behind the knuckles.
- Motion blur: shutter position START, a key on every frame, plus a key half a frame after each shot's last frame, so blur never reaches across a cut.
- Check: run a black-frame and one-frame-flicker check on the render. Make a contact sheet (a frame every 0.5 s) and look at every tile: the act reads in the first 2 s, faces are lit, nothing clips through anything, captions stay off faces and key objects. Then step through the first 2 s, the middle and the end frame by frame. Fix, render only the changed shots again.
</gotchas>

<start>
Pitch (or take my story), then show me the script with the word count, the caption chunks with their seconds and the shot list with what the first frame shows. Build nothing until I say go.

prompt.text:
Make "Plush Pigeon" (Material Studies No. 031) on the Plush Penguin WebGPU engine: XPBD soft-body lattice, shell fur, cloth wings, posture-driven gait, tools Hand / Finger / Comb.

The toy: a round, well-fed rock dove of soft grey minky.
- Shape: one SDF with a round body, a proud chest, a neck rising into a teal domed head, a flat tail with a dark band, and two pink felt feet with three toes forward and one behind.
- Neck ring: iridescent, green above and violet below, dipping lower over the chest.
- Face: glossy bead eyes with an orange ring; a small dark felt beak with a pale cere.
- Wings: two stuffed cloth wings sewn at the shoulders, folded down and back along the sides, each with two charcoal bars and a darker tip.
- Fur length: shorter on the head and neck ring, cropped to felt on the feet.

Life:
- Strut: a waddle in which neck-cell shear muscles bob the head with every step. Keep the bend normal orthogonal to the neck axis, or the shear pushes the whole body.
- Coo: the chest cells swell, the head bows twice, and a synthesized three-note rolling "croo" plays.
- Flap: wing flaps with hops and a feather-flutter sound.
- Topple, then get back up.
- Finger: struts over to a held finger; a boop on the beak makes it coo; it sometimes coos when idle.

Palettes: Blue bar, Ash red, Snow.
Readouts: mass, volume, steps, coos.
Responsive layout.

Each arm is a chain of tapering capsules laid out by integrating curvature: a gentle sweep across the table, then the outer third rolls up off the table into a curl so the two staggered rows of pale suckers face out. The underside of every arm is a milky layer, the back has a chromatophore mottle and small papillae. XPBD tetrahedral sim with firmer arm tips; muscle strain makes the arms writhe (sideways bending waves out along each arm, phased arm to arm) and curl up and let go. summary.en: The creator published separate Top and Bottom prompts for beat-synced music-video edits using supplied footage and music, prepared with Python and ffmpeg.

prompt.text:
Create a high-energy 16:9 music video using the supplied footage. Keep the original timing and playback speed, with no slow motion, speed ramps or trimming. Use the full frame with no grid or split panels, preserving the original footage as one continuous, clearly recognizable image at all times. Apply a constantly shifting base visual treatment driven by the music's sections, and unleash aggressive style infections that erupt from points of action such as clashes, impacts and fast movement, spreading violently across the frame through expanding circles, shockwave rings, slashing wipes and mutating color fields. Blend these with rhythmic cascades of motion echoes, time-offset ghost layers, frame repetitions and hard impact freezes. Trigger dense, layered visual effects, flashes, camera punches, shakes, chromatic splits, inversions, graphic symbols and chain reactions precisely to the music. Let the original footage and soundtrack guide all creative decisions, keeping the editing constantly evolving, unpredictable and visually spectacular. Preserve the original characters, action and scene continuity throughout. Effects enhance the footage rather than replace it. Preserve the original video's audio, including dialogue, sound effects and ambient sounds, mixing it naturally with the supplied music. Do not mute, replace or remove the original audio. No typography, text, letters or numbers.

Bottom:
Create a high-energy 16:9 music video using the supplied footage. Keep the original timing and playback speed throughout, with no slow motion, speed ramps or trimming, so the picture stays in natural sync with its own audio. Use the full frame with no grid or split panels, keeping the original footage as one continuous, clearly recognizable image at all times. Apply a shifting base visual treatment that evolves with the music's sections, and let secondary styles spread smoothly across the frame through soft-edged organic shapes — expanding circles, flowing wipes and blooming color fields — that grow from points of action such as clashes, impacts and fast movement, then gently fade. Blend these with rhythmic motion echoes and subtle time-offset ghost layers. Use frame repetitions and impact freezes sparingly, only as brief accents of a few frames on the strongest hits, never sustained, so playback always feels fluid and never stuttery. Trigger flashes, light camera punches, soft chromatic shifts, graphic symbols and gentle chain reactions in sync with the music, favoring smooth easing and glow over harsh strobing. Let the original footage and soundtrack guide all creative decisions, keeping the editing evolving and visually rich but fluid and comfortable to watch. Preserve the original characters, action and scene continuity throughout. Effects enhance the footage rather than replace it. Preserve the original video's audio, including dialogue, sound effects and ambient sounds, mixing it naturally with the supplied music. Do not mute, replace or remove the original audio. No typography, text, letters or numbers.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive 3D toy called "Jelly Bricks" - translucent gummy candy bricks you can grab, stretch, stack into a tower and knock over. Use three.js (import from a CDN) and any lightweight physics library you like. Everything must run by opening the file in a browser.

LOOK
- Bricks are classic stud-on-top building bricks (2x1, 2x2, 3x2, 4x2) in red, orange, yellow, green and blue. No brand names or logos anywhere.
- Material must read as real gummy candy: glossy, translucent, light passing through, deeper colour where the brick is thicker, soft rounded edges and rounded studs. Use MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission, thickness, attenuation colour, clearcoat, and an environment map for reflections.
- Soft shadows plus a faint coloured glow on the floor under each brick, tinted by its colour.
- Clean white background, slight slow camera drift so the scene feels alive.

JELLY BEHAVIOUR (most important)
- Grab a brick and it stretches toward the cursor before it lifts off, like pulling taffy. Release it and the stretch snaps back with a decaying wobble.
- A brick lagging behind the cursor tilts slightly in the direction it's moving.
- Every landing squashes the brick flat, then it springs back up with a few wobbles (spring-damper squash and shear, done in the vertex shader).
- Dropping a brick on the stack snaps it in place, and the whole tower sways like pudding: each brick's wobble shifts the bricks above it, so the top moves the most.
- Pulling a brick out of the middle of the tower collapses it: the bricks above tumble, bounce off the floor and each other, and scatter a little - lively, not explosive.

UI (minimal editorial style)
- Top left: small caps label "Nº 09 / SOFT GOODS", big serif italic title "Jelly / Bricks." with "Bricks." in red, and a one-line subtitle.
- Floating panel on the right: flavor colour swatches, a "Wobble" slider that controls jelly softness, live "Stack height" and "Bricks" counters, and a black "Pour more bricks" button that drops a handful of new bricks from above with random spin.
- Bottom left hint: "Grab to lift · Drop to snap · Space to wobble". Space shakes the tower.
- Custom round cursor that shrinks while holding a brick.

Start with one 4x2 brick in the centre as the tower base and about 9 bricks scattered around it. Keep it at 60fps on a laptop.

prompt.text:
You're a motion director and creative coder. Make a finished music video for [song file], built entirely in code and rendered frame by frame.

Concept: [your idea in one or two sentences]
Look: [palette, mood, references]
On-screen text: [title only / none / lyrics]
Deliver: [full song or mm:ss to mm:ss], [16:9 / 9:16 / both, each recomposed, not cropped], [fps], H.264 + AAC for [platform]

How to work:
1. Analyze the song before any visuals. Split it into bands or stems and export per-frame features plus a timing map (beats, bars, sections, hits). Every visual event reads from the map and is listed in it.
2. Give each musical element one visual job that serves the concept. Keep one idea transforming across the song instead of cycling effects.
3. Storyboard with timings and 3 style frames, get a fresh critic's verdict on them, then a 4-second end-to-end test before the full build.
4. Make every value a pure function of the frame number. Render offline, encode with the original audio (gain only).
5. After each full render, send it to fresh critic subagents that never saw the build, each returning ranked problems with timestamps and a ship / one more pass verdict:
- sound-off: retells the story from a silent 2 fps contact sheet
- sync: every cut, hit and visual event within 1 frame of the timing map
- QA: specs, palette, text, artifacts, measured on the frames
- director: brutal critique against the brief
- one per extra aspect ratio: composition and platform UI zones
6. Fix render bugs first, then the biggest problem; re-render; log each round with before/after numbers. If critics conflict, the brief wins.
7. Stop after [5] rounds or when the bar passes. The final pass checks only for breakage.

The bar: exact duration, size and fps; frame one finished; no still over 0.5 s; cuts and hits within 1 frame; audio unedited except gain, about -14 LUFS, true peak under -1 dB; text readable and inside safe areas; understood with the sound off.

summary.en: A single-file HTML pixel-art diorama of table tennis in an apartment courtyard, built with Three.js. The same prompt was run on Claude Opus 5.5 ($14.17) and GPT-6.1 Terra ($1.23) for comparison.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file HTML pixel-art diorama called "King of the Table": table tennis in the courtyard of a three-storey pastel panel apartment block, on a small floating island, rendered with three.js (r160 via importmap) as a real 3D scene drawn into a low-res render target (orthographic isometric camera in 90° steps, whole-pixel snapping, depth outlines, a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab, optional dither, Raw 3D toggle).

World: the block with three entrances (canopies, numbered plates, lamps), windows, balconies with washing; brick garages; a regulation concrete table (2.74 × 1.525 m, top at 76 cm, steel net 15.25 cm) on a slab pad with a flip score counter on a stool; benches; a playground (swings, slide, sandbox, carousel); washing lines whose sheets flap in the wind; two parked cars; birches, lilac, painted-tyre flower beds, a chalk hopscotch; lamp posts. Merge static meshes by material.

Ball physics: 40 mm / 2.7 g ball with strong quadratic drag, Magnus lift from spin (topspin dives, backspin floats), table bounce that converts spin into pace, net and net-cord, ground bounces and rolling, walls, wind with gusts. Shots are solved (bisection over launch angle) to land on a target with a given spin and net clearance, then perturbed by an error model (hurry, incoming pace, risk, wind, mishits). Serves: tossed ≥16 cm from the palm, struck behind the end line, solved so they bounce once on each half; lets.

Game: 4 neighbours with distinct styles (lefty topspin attacker, close blocker, far-back chopper, wild smasher) play king of the table: games to 11, two clear, serve changes every 2 points and every point from 10-all; winner stays, loser to the back of the bench. Players predict the ball's flight, shuffle to meet it after the bounce, and choose forehand/backhand loops, drives, blocks, pushes, flicks, chops, lobs, floated returns and smashes, with keyed bat paths and two-bone IK box-rig bodies. Between points the nearer player fetches the ball wherever it rolled (or takes a new one if it falls off the island), throws it to the server, who bounces it on the table before serving. Yard life via generator coroutines and A*: grandmothers knit and comment, kids swing/slide/ride the carousel/dig/watch, a man walks his dog, pigeons peck and take off when approached. Day/dusk/night, rain (everyone shelters under the canopy, puddle reflections, then the table is wiped), wind calm/breeze/gusty. Clicks: the table aims the next shot; the yard calls the pigeons; buttons call Loop/Push/Smash/Lob. UI: flip-card score board with serve dots, bench ladder with W–L, longest rally, wind readout, comments feed, view controls, "How it's drawn" notes, light/dark themes, phone layout.

prompt.text:
Make a 45-second paper-collage animation of Momotaro (the Japanese folktale).

[Look]
A pop-up picture book: the book opens and paper pieces stand up one by one.
Washi paper cut-out (kirie) texture. The 3D effect comes from images and code only. Do not use any video-generation AI.

[How to build it]
1. First, write the script and show it to me (8 scenes, 4-9 seconds each; the only on-screen text is short onomatopoeia such as "donburako").
2. Once I approve the script, write the image-generation prompts:
- one texture reference image
- characters and backgrounds as sheets of separate paper cut-outs on transparent backgrounds
3. I will generate the images and hand them to you. Then animate them in Python:
- make it look 3D with five tricks: depth, parallax, blur, shadows, and motion blur
- 1920x1080, 24 fps
- for each scene, show me 4 still frames first so I can check
4. Add narration and background music.

[Rules]
- Do not wobble or shake the pictures. Movement is only slow pushes in and pulls back.
- Don't give me English-only prompts; add an explanation in my language too.

summary.zh: 一个名为“Harbor Jelly”的互动WebGPU 3D场景，展示果冻质感海水中的集装箱港口，由Claude Opus 5.5根据一段详细的长提示词生成，并与Gemini 4 Argon版本比较了制作成本。
summary.en: An interactive WebGPU 3D diorama called 'Harbor Jelly' depicting a container port inside a jelly-like sea, built with Claude Opus 5.5 from a long detailed prompt, and compared in cost to a Gemini 4 Argon version of the same scene.

prompt.text: Build "Harbor Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (no external requests, no libraries) that renders an interactive 3D diorama with WebGPU/WGSL: a small working container harbor set inside a square block of wobbly, translucent jelly sea, sitting on a paper studio backdrop. It belongs to a series called "Material Studies", so match that look: warm paper background, serif italic display title ("Harbor Jelly."), small uppercase eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a status pill top-right ("WebGPU · Live"), a frosted control panel on the right, and a "How to play" line bottom-left. English UI. Light theme only, by design. THE BLOCK - A 5.2 × 5.2 block seen from a 3/4 orbit camera. The ground and sea are cut flat at the block's sides, so you see candy-coloured soil strata in cross-section, and the sea's cut faces show everything underwater through the jelly. - The water is a real-time linear shallow-water simulation on a staggered grid (heights at cell centres, velocities on faces) with a little surface tension, so it feels like jelly. Render it with refraction, absorption by depth, caustics projected onto the floor, light shafts, a Fresnel studio reflection, foam (wakes, splashes, a shoreline lace) and a bright meniscus on the cut edges. - The whole block can be tipped by dragging its side. The water sloshes to the low side, the jelly shears and quivers, then it settles flat again. THE HARBOR (layout) - Along the back runs a vertical concrete quay wall, with rubber fenders, bollards, ladders, and mussels and weed crusting it below the waterline. - Left part: a container terminal. A flat asphalt yard with painted lines, concrete strips with two crane rails, light towers, and a small terminal office. Hundreds of colourful containers are stacked in neat rows. Each is a ribbed steel box with door ends and darker corner posts, drawn as GPU instances in about ten liveries. - Right part: an old stone fishing quay with a cobbled promenade, a corrugated fish-market shed and lamp posts. A timber pier stands on mussel-covered piles with cross-bracing, with two small fishing boats moored alongside. - Behind it all, a town climbs a grassy hill: three rows of gabled houses in Nordic harbour colours (falu red, ochre, white, pale blue, mint, pink) with tiled or slate roofs, white-framed windows, doors and chimneys. There is a white church with a green copper spire, and some round trees. - A rubble breakwater shelters the fishing harbour, with a concrete crown wall. Big rocks sit near the crest, smaller weedy ones tumble down under water. On its head stands a red-and-white banded lighthouse with a gallery and a glass lantern, whose lamp slowly turns. - In the open basin: two small yachts swinging on their moorings (white hulls, coloured stripe, fin keels visible through the jelly, furled sails), yellow mooring buoys, and a green channel buoy, all bobbing on the waves. - On the floor: pale sand with drifts of silt, weed tufts, stones, starfish, an old anchor with chain, a lost tyre. THE SHIP'S DAY (fully automatic loop, about 100 s) 1. A small feeder container ship (navy topsides, red antifouling, white accommodation block at the stern with bridge wings, funnel with a yellow band, turning radar, visible propeller) lies alongside with containers on deck, 6 bays × 4 rows × 2 tiers. 2. Two ship-to-shore gantry cranes on the rails, one red and one blue, each with portal legs, a backreach with a machinery house, an A-frame with forestays, a hinged boom, a trolley with a hanging cab, and a yellow spreader on four wire falls. They lower their booms and swap boxes: unload from the tops of the ship's stacks into yard stacks, then load other boxes aboard. Every move is a smooth sequence: travel, trolley out, lower onto the box (tracking the ship's bobbing), latch, hoist, trolley across, lower, unlatch. Cranes never get closer than their leg width; an idle crane moves out of the other's way. 3. When the work is done the trolleys park, the booms swing up, and a tug comes round to the bow. The tug has a black hull, white and red superstructure, a tyre fender all round, a big bow fender, and puffs of funnel smoke. It passes a tow line and backs away, pulling the bow off the quay while the ship swings out. Then the line is cast off, the tug pivots on the spot and goes home, and the ship sounds her horn. 4. The ship sails a lap of the harbour along a smooth path, past the lighthouse. She rides the water on several sample points (heave, pitch, roll) and hands the displaced water back to the sim, so she leaves a real bow wave, wake and white water. 5. Meanwhile the tug goes out to a standby spot. When the ship stops off the quay, the tug noses in and pushes her sideways onto the fenders, with prop wash churning. Then it backs off, the booms come down, and the cranes start again. - Keep everything collision-free (ship and tug vs. quay, breakwater, pier, yachts and buoy; no grounding). Check it with a headless node test. LIFE - Fish schools (mackerel, herring, small orange wrasse) as boids that stay in the water and under the hulls, scatter from fingers, splashes and moving ships, and come to food. - Moon jellyfish: glassy pulsing bells with four pink rings, frilly oral arms and a fringe of tentacles. They drift with the water flow. - Herring gulls (white body, grey mantle, black wingtips, yellow bill with a red spot). They circle, bank and glide, and land on perches: lamps, roof ridges, the church spire, the lighthouse gallery, the crane apexes, the ship's mast, the tug, the yachts' masthead. Perches on moving things move with them. They all take off when the horn sounds, and some dive at food. - Steam puffs from the ship's funnel on the horn; tiny bubbles caught in the jelly. CONTROLS (right panel; bottom sheet on phones) - "Cast off" sends the ship early (cranes finish the box in hand). At sea the button becomes "Call her in" and hurries her home; it greys out while busy. - "Horn" (also Space) plays a synthesized WebAudio ship horn: two low detuned sawtooth reeds a fifth apart, low-passed, starting only after a user gesture. It also blows steam and scatters the gulls. - "Feed the fish" scatters pellets off the end of the pier; fish rush in and gulls swoop down. - Tally: Boxes moved / Voyages / Fed. A ship status line ("Unloading 3 / 8", "Loading", "Booms up", "Tug coming", "Casting off", "At sea 40%", "Coming in", "Berthing"). A small activity meter. - Flavour swatches change the water colour and strata: Sea glass (teal-mint), Blueberry (deep blue), Lime. - Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Tide (±10 cm; the sea level, ships and floating things follow). - Buttons: Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, Reset view. POINTER INTERACTION - Drag across the water to make waves (with a crosshair cursor). - Drag the side of the block to tip it. - Pick up an orange-and-white lifebuoy and throw it. Lifebuoys float flat on the waves, bounce off the pier, buildings and breakwater, and are shoved aside by the ship and tug. - Drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom. - On phones: touch orbit, pinch zoom, and a collapsible bottom sheet for the controls. RENDERING DETAILS - Pipeline: shadow map → caustics pass → opaque scene (with a distance buffer) → back-face pass of the water → water pass over a copy of the scene → tone map + dither. - Moving rigs are static vertex buffers whose vertices carry an object id; about 24 object transforms (position + quaternion) live in the uniform buffer. Cables are drawn with one end in each object's frame, so they stretch: crane falls, forestays, the tow line. - Material kinds in the prop shader: matte paint, glass, gloss steel, roof tiles, timber grain, corrugated sheet (normal-perturbed ribs), dressed-stone masonry, rubber, rock, glowing lamps, swaying weed, and hulls with antifouling below a boot-top line. - The jelly shear and squash wobble applies to everything inside the block. QUALITY BAR - Smooth on a laptop; simulation under about 2 ms per frame. - A friendly fallback screen if WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails. - No console errors, no page scroll. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. - Ship it with a headless test of the choreography and a Playwright end-to-end test.

title.zh: 3D像素风街头篮球场对比

summary.zh: 一个用 three.js 制作的 3D 像素风等距视角街头篮球院落模拟。作者用同一条提示词对比了 Claude Opus 5.5 和 GPT-6.1 Sol，其中 Sol 多修改了一轮。
summary.en: A 3D pixel-art isometric streetball courtyard simulation built with three.js. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol were compared on the same prompt, with Sol given one revision.

prompt.text:
Build a real-time pixel-art isometric diorama of 3x3 streetball at a single hoop in a city courtyard, as a single HTML page using three.js (WebGL). A floating island of asphalt holds a painted half court (faded blue with an orange key, worn white lines, the two-point arc) inside a box of low green boards. One hoop stands on a steel pole with a steel backboard, an orange ring and a chain net, with a wire fence behind it.
Around the court: a three-storey brick block of flats with balconies and washing, two grannies on a bench by the door, pigeons on the roof. A row of tin garages with original graffiti tags, and an old boxy car half out with its bonnet up and a man working on it. A playground with working swings, a slide and a sandpit, plus a mother on a bench. A kvass barrel with a seller, poplars, floodlight masts, and a wire with a pair of sneakers hanging from it.
Render at low resolution with an orthographic camera, snap colours to a fixed 64-colour OKLab palette and draw depth outlines. After rain, puddles reflect the scene.
Simulate the ball physically: drag, lively bounces off dry asphalt and duller ones off wet, a steel backboard, the ring as a real torus (rim-outs, rolls, lips) and a chain net that swishes. Solve every jump shot numerically through the flight with drag, at an arc that steepens close in, then add hand error that grows with distance, a defender's contest and a weaker shooter. Make layups steep; put dunks through from above with the shooter hanging on the rim; throw alley-oops as lobs to a point over the ring.
AI: dribbling with a hand that rides the ball, crossovers, drives, open-shot decisions, passes (chest, bounce, lob), cuts and screens. Man-to-man defence with help on drives, reach-in steals, contests and blocks, box-outs and rebounds caught with a jump.
Rules: ones inside the arc, twos outside; after a make the other team takes the ball from under the ring and must clear it past the arc; check at the top after out-of-bounds. First to 11 or 21. Three teams: winners stay, the losers walk off to the bench and the next team walks on.
Life in the yard: grannies feed the pigeons and complain about the boombox, the waiting team nods to the music and goes for kvass, a cat stalks the pigeons, children swing and slide. Day/sunset/night with floodlights and lit windows; dry, after-rain puddles, or rain with rings.
UI: a scoreboard; a side rail with three team ladders, called plays (dunk, deep two, alley-oop), weather and a boombox toggle, field-goal stats and a live feed; click the court to mark the next pass. Original characters only, English UI, responsive down to phone width.

title.zh: 日式神社场景对比

summary.zh: 作者用同一段长且详细的一次性提示，对比Opus 5.5与ChatGPT-6 Astra生成的日本神社主题Three.js WebGL场景，包含水面、四季、锦鲤和时间变化效果。
summary.en: The creator compared Opus 5.5 and ChatGPT-6 Astra using the same long, detailed single-shot prompt to generate a procedural Three.js WebGL diorama of a Japanese shrine with water, seasons, koi and time-of-day effects.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file interactive WebGL diorama (one index.html, no build step) with Three.js r160 loaded via an import map from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/, plus OrbitControls and BufferGeometryUtils (mergeVertices, mergeGeometries) from three/examples/jsm. Everything is procedural — no external models or textures.

CONCEPT
"Torii at High Tide": a miniature Japanese shrine island inspired by Itsukushima, inside a 10×10 block of clear water with rounded edges (vertical corner radius ~0.6, top edge radius ~0.26), on a thin sand-colored base slab, on a warm washi-paper background with a soft floor shadow that fades out with distance (so long dusk shadows never streak across the page).

TERRAIN (heightfield ~400×400, clipped to the rounded block, with a boundary "skirt" so the cross-section shows through the water)
- Work in a local frame facing the camera (u = across, v = toward the viewer).
- A forested dome-shaped hill at the back (~2.4 high), a low sandy shrine terrace at its foot, then a wide, gently sloping tidal flat in front (from ~-0.06 down to ~-0.46), dropping to ~-1.0 at the front and sides.
- Two rocky granite headlands framing the bay, each with 1–2 leaning bonsai-style pines (segmented trunks + flattened canopy pads).
- A flattened clearing on the hill flank for the pagoda.
- Terrain shader: granite rock on steep slopes (speckled, darker wet band just above the waterline, algae-dark below it), sand with a wet line, darker wet intertidal sand below the high-tide mark, moss/grass on the hill and in patches on the terrace, snow on upward-facing surfaces in winter, procedural animated caustics under water. CPU-baked horizon AO per vertex plus canopy-cover darkening.

ARCHITECTURE (merge everything into one vertex-colored mesh + one emissive "glow" mesh; write a small Builder that adds boxes/cylinders/spheres/custom geometry with a color and a transform, then mergeGeometries)
- Ryōbu-style torii standing in the bay on the axis of the shrine (~1.9 tall): vermilion tapered main pillars with black base sheaths, four supporting sode-bashira legs with black caps and two connecting beams each, nuki tie beam, central strut with a dark plaque, shimaki, and a curved kasagi (extruded shape with upturned ends) with a black top layer. Pillars must end inside the shimaki, not poke through the kasagi.
- Shrine on stilts over the tidal flat: plank deck (with plank-gap strips and dark edge beams) on a grid of wooden stilts reaching the seabed; a main hall and a smaller front hall (white walls, vermilion posts and tie beams, shoji-style front panels = glow panels behind a thin dark lattice), a lower front stage with vermilion railings, and two roofed vermilion corridors on stilts running sideways then back to the shore.
- Roofs: a hip-roof generator with a concave profile and lifted eave corners (top surface dark cypress-bark brown, warm wood underside, pale fascia trim, black ridge cap).
- A five-storey pagoda on the hill clearing: stone plinth, white walls with vermilion posts, bracket layer, flared roofs decreasing in size, bronze finial with rings.
- Stone tōrō lanterns on the terrace and on the stage (hexagonal base, post, firebox with emissive windows, small roof, jewel).

VEGETATION
- ~4–5k canopy blobs (InstancedMesh of icospheres with vertex-noise displacement + fragment bump), clustered 2–4 per tree, per-instance AO from neighbour occlusion, brighter tops.
- Four kinds via an instance attribute: broadleaf, cherry, maple, pine (flattened pads). Cherries cluster lower on the hill and as 5 feature trees with visible trunks on the terrace; pines dominate the summit and the headlands.
- Colors come from per-kind dark/light palette uniforms that the JS blends across seasons.

SEASONS (cyclic 0..4 = spring, summer, autumn, winter; animated transition from a dock button)
- Spring: pink sakura, falling petals. Summer: lush green, no particles. Autumn: red maples, orange/yellow broadleaf, falling maple leaves. Winter: bare-ish brown deciduous blobs shrunk ~38%, snow on canopy tops, roofs, decks, rocks and ground; snowfall that melts instantly on the water.

WATER (realistic, not jelly)
- Pipeline: opaque scene → MSAA HalfFloat target with DepthTexture; copy to a second target, then draw the water with a custom ShaderMaterial doing a manual depth test; then floating particles; final fullscreen pass with ACES tone mapping, sRGB, subtle tilt-shift. Transparent canvas over the CSS background.
- Color from real thickness: reconstruct the depth behind each water pixel, Beer–Lambert absorption toward a deep scatter color derived from the user's water color (pale over the flats, blue in the deep; side walls get extra path length so they read as a water volume).
- Screen-space refraction, Fresnel sky reflection, sun glints from fine animated detail normals.
- Screen-space reflections (~26 ray-march steps against the depth buffer, fewer on mobile) so the torii, shrine and lit lanterns reflect in the water.
- Ripples: GPU wave equation on a 256×256 HalfFloat ping-pong target, fixed 60 Hz steps, land-mask texture so waves reflect off the shore. Cursor movement injects capsule drops along its path; a click makes a splash.
- Shore foam only where the terrain is near the water level AND gently sloped (no white outlines around cliffs, stilts or the torii pillars); foam band width scaled by slope; broken by noise.
- Tide: a dock toggle animates between high tide (0) and low tide (-0.55): the water block's rim moves and its sides stretch; at low tide the whole flat is exposed and the torii stands on wet sand.

PARTICLES (petals / leaves / snow, ~700 instanced quads, CPU-simulated)
- Spawn from cherry blobs (spring), deciduous blobs (autumn) or the sky (winter); flutter while falling; a gusting wind blows from the island toward the bay so they reach the water.
- Landing: on water they become floating (vertex shader lifts them by the same ripple + wave height as the water), drift slowly, get pushed by the cursor's movement and blown away by click splashes, strand when the tide drops, re-float when it rises; on land they rest and fade.
- Shapes drawn in the fragment shader: notched petal, five-lobed maple leaf, soft snow disc. Manual depth test against the scene depth.

KOI
- 7 koi (lathe body + forked fan tail + pectoral fins, merged), InstancedMesh with a swimming sway in the vertex shader and procedural patterns per type (kohaku, sanke, showa, ogon, plain orange). They wander, steer away from shallow water and the block walls, and flee the cursor and splashes. Rendered under the water so they are refracted and tinted.

TIME OF DAY (slider, shown as a clock from 11:00 to ~19:10)
- Sun elevation, color and intensity, hemisphere colors, and the water's sky reflection shift from noon to golden hour; towards dusk the shoji panels and lanterns glow (emissive) and three warm point lights light the shrine, the stage and the torii.

UI (editorial, minimal, English)
Brand "shiosai°" with a small torii mark, headline "A gate that / stands in the sea.", eyebrow "Shrine and tide, in miniature", a vertical caption "A study of tide and seasons", a location label "Shrine Cove · 34°16′ N · 132°19′ E", a floating pill dock (reset, season cycle with the current season name, High tide / Low tide toggle, Tune, fullscreen), hints and an adaptive FPS + "Season · time" readout in the footer, a glassy settings panel (season, time of day, falling petals; water color, tide level, wave height, ripple strength, clarity, caustics; sun azimuth, tilt-shift), and a "How it's made" card. Vermilion accent, light and dark themes via CSS tokens, responsive to 390 px (panel becomes a bottom sheet), prefers-reduced-motion respected, adaptive pixel ratio and a lighter mode for touch devices. Intro: the water fills the block while the camera eases in.

prompt.text:
Create a single self-contained HTML file using Three.js that renders a beautiful animated voxel-art 3D scene. A giant woolly mammoth walks across a sea of clouds through a snowy night with the northern lights and a moon; the clouds drift backwards under its feet, and snow puffs up at every step.

On its back, over a blue blanket with gold trim and leather straps, stands a stone frost fortress: walls with battlements, four round turrets with blue conical roofs and flags, two small houses with glowing windows and smoking chimneys, and a central keep with a big glowing ice crystal floating and slowly rotating above it. The mammoth has shaggy fur, a swaying trunk, long curved tusks and snow on its head.

A crystalline ice dragon with horns, ice spikes along its back, glowing eyes and large wings rises from the clouds and circles the mammoth, leaving a trail of snowflakes, and breathes frost twice.

Add soft shadows, voxel ambient occlusion, a snowstorm, drifting voxel clouds and a slow cinematic camera orbit. Make it as detailed and polished as possible.

prompt.text:
Make "Plush Watermelon" (Material Studies No. 032) on the Plush Penguin WebGPU engine: XPBD soft-body lattice, shell fur, cloth limbs, posture-driven gait, Hand / Finger / Comb tools.

Shape (one SDF):
- A fat wedge cut from a sphere by two planes through one horizontal axis, about 76° apart.
- The axis is the top edge, so each cut face is a semicircle.
- The cut faces are slightly puffy and every seam is rounded.
- It sits on a small flat patch of its round rind.

Regions:
- Flesh: long fluffy red minky.
- Rind: a white band along the outer edge of both faces.
- Skin: green, with dark jagged stripes running pole to pole around the wedge's axis.
- Seeds: short-pile felt teardrops pointing in toward the axis, a few on the front face around the face, more on the back.

Front face: two bead eyes, rosy cheeks, and an embroidered smile thread laid into a short-pile groove.

Limbs: two brown felt legs stuck out in front, and two stubby felt cloth arms at the wedge's ends.

Actions:
- Toddle: walk on the legs.
- Rock: seesaw forward and back on the rind with a synthesized giggle.
- Wave: arm waves and hops with a toy squeak.
- Topple: fall onto its back, then get back up.
- A finger boop on the face makes it giggle and rock; it also rocks now and then when idle.

Palettes: Classic, Yellow, Sorbet.
Readouts: mass, volume, steps, rocks.

summary.en: A 3D pixel-art four-square game on a backyard floating island, with AI-controlled kids, ball physics, weather, and redrawable chalk. It was made in one HTML file using Three.js.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file HTML + three.js (r160) scene called "Chalk Square": four square played with a football in a back yard on a floating island. It is a real 3D scene rendered as crisp pixel art.

Rendering: an orthographic isometric camera (drag to turn in 90° steps, scroll or pinch to zoom). Render into a small low-res target with a depth texture, then upscale with texelFetch to whole screen pixels. Add depth-based outlines and quantize every pixel to a fixed ~60-colour palette in OKLab, with an optional Bayer dither. Toggle "Pixel art / Raw 3D", with a pixel-size slider and Palette / Dither / Outlines checkboxes.

Yard: patched, cracked asphalt with a kerb, grass and dirt around the island edge. Around the asphalt:
- a row of lock-up garages with painted, numbered doors and a flat roof that overhangs them;
- a brick transformer booth with a warning sign;
- a poplar with a bench and a grandmother on it;
- a chin-up bar, a carpet rack with a rug, bushes;
- a lamp on a pole and a lamp over a garage door.
Pigeons walk and peck, and flap up onto the roofs when the ball or a kid comes near. A cat on the garage roof follows the ball with its head.

Chalk: a data texture over the asphalt. It holds the 4.8 m square split into four zones (King, Queen, Jack, Dunce) with letters and a crown, plus hopscotch and doodles. Each texel stores its order along its stroke, so the lines can be redrawn progressively.

Game (8 kids, each with a skill, power and style: power / trick / safe / lob):
- Four kids play, four wait in a queue. The King serves by dropping the ball and kicking it after the bounce.
- The ball must bounce once in your zone, then you kick it into another zone. With the two-touch rule you may first cushion it up.
- You are out for: a ball that lands out, lands in your own zone, bounces a second time, or (if set) lands on a middle line. Otherwise a ball on the line is replayed.
- The kid who is out goes to the back of the queue. Everyone below moves up a zone, and the next kid in line enters at Dunce. A kid fetches the ball and throws it to the King.

Ball and AI: real ball physics (gravity, bounces, rolling, softer bounces in puddles, the walls). Each receiver simulates the ball forward, picks the moment it is at foot height, runs to stand behind it and kicks. Shots are a drive, a lob, or a dink just over the line, aimed away from the target kid; everyone picks on the King. prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive low-poly 3D diorama of a rural Japanese railway station in spring, using Three.js (ES modules from a CDN). No external models or images — generate all geometry from primitives in code and paint textures (grass, signs) on <canvas>.

Style: a floating diorama block (grass top, layered earth and stone sides) on a soft pastel sky gradient. MeshToonMaterial with a 3-step gradient map, dark ink outlines (OutlineEffect), soft directional shadows, bright saturated palette.

Scene:
- A single railway track across the block, running into green tunnel hills with concrete portals at both ends.
- Concrete platform with a yellow tactile strip, a shelter with a corrugated roof, benches, a hanging clock, a small station building with a teal gable roof and a "春風駅" sign, a station name board (はるかぜ / Harukaze, with neighbouring stations), vending machines, bins, lamps, fence.
- A road crossing the track with a level crossing: striped poles, crossbuck, red flashing lamps, barrier arms; road markings and "止まれ".
- Utility poles with sagging wires, overhead catenary, small village houses, a vegetable patch, bushes, and cherry trees with puffy pink blob crowns and fallen petals painted on the grass.

Animation:
- A two-car commuter train (white with a pink stripe, pantograph) comes out of one tunnel, stops at the platform, then departs into the other; clipping planes hide it inside the tunnels. Loop every ~32 s.
- Crossing lamps blink alternately and the arms lower before the train passes, then rise.
- ~460 instanced sakura petals drifting in the wind.
- Slow auto-orbit camera; OrbitControls for drag and zoom.

UI (English): bottom-left title "春風駅 / Harukaze Station" with a small caption; bottom-right glass toolbar with Day / Night, Orbit on/off, and Train (call the next train). Night mode: dark sky with stars, lit windows, lamp point lights with additive glow sprites, glowing crossing lamps and train headlights.

Technical: merge static meshes by material into a few dozen draw calls; use a seeded random so the scene is identical on every load; responsive down to phone width; respect prefers-reduced-motion.
