summary.zh: 创作者用一个详细的长文本提示让Opus 5.5（并与DeepSeek V4.1 Flash对比）生成了一款名为《阳光谷：下班后》的浏览器惊悚游戏，玩法灵感来自《玩具熊的五夜后宫》，但角色、设定完全原创。
summary.en: A browser-based night-shift horror game called 'Sunny Hollow: After Hours', an original take on the Five Nights at Freddy's genre, was built with Opus 5.5 (and compared against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) from one long detailed text prompt specifying mechanics, visuals, audio, and story.

prompt.text:
Build a complete, polished browser horror game inspired by the "survive the night shift in a security office" genre (like Five Nights at Freddy's), but with a 100% ORIGINAL setting, characters, and name. Do not use any FNAF names, characters, locations, or assets.

## Concept
Title: "SUNNY HOLLOW: AFTER HOURS"
You are a night watchman at Sunny Hollow Studios, an abandoned 1990s children's TV studio. The show's animatronic puppet hosts were shut down after the show was cancelled (last live broadcast: May 17, 1996), but at night they still try to "finish the broadcast". Survive from 12 AM to 6 AM in a small control booth using cameras, shutters, door lights, a ceiling-vent seal and an audio lure, while managing a draining generator.

## Tech
- Single self-contained index.html (HTML + CSS + JS). Three.js r128 UMD from cdnjs (https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/r128/three.min.js). No external assets: all models are low-poly primitives, all textures are procedural canvas textures (felt, wood, rust, tiles, wallpaper, posters), all sound is generated with the Web Audio API.
- Desktop Chrome at 60 fps. Mouse controls plus keyboard shortcuts.
- Every room is its own THREE.Scene with its own camera, so only the viewed room is rendered. Pre-compile all shaders at boot (renderer.compile on every scene, with the puppets temporarily added) so the first camera flip doesn't hitch.
- Adaptive resolution: render the 3D into a render target at 0.85x. If the average frame time stays above 25 ms for 2.5 s, drop the internal scale by 0.15 (minimum 0.5).
- Add `[hidden]{display:none!important}` to the CSS so hidden overlay screens never block clicks.
- Save progress in localStorage (current night, beaten nights, stars, unlocks, custom-night sliders), wrapped in try/catch.

## Post-processing (full-screen shader)
VHS/CRT pass over everything: scanlines, film grain, chromatic aberration, a rolling tracking band, line jitter, vignette, a full-static mix, a red flash and a darkness fade. Use three presets: office (subtle), camera (strong scanlines, barrel distortion, green tint, more noise) and menu.

## Core loop
- 1 in-game hour = 60 real seconds (12 AM → 6 AM = 6 minutes).
- Mouse near the left/right 22% of the screen turns the view smoothly. Yaw is clamped to ±60°. Arrow keys work as a backup.
- Generator: 100% at start. Usage = 1 (base) + tablet 1 + each door light 1 + each closed shutter 2 + vent seal 1 + lure 1 (for 3 s). Drain = usage × 0.1% per second × night multiplier (N1 0.9, N2 0.95, N3 1.0, N4 1.03, N5 1.06, N6 1.14, custom 1.1). Show POWER LEFT % and colored usage bars.
- At 0%: shutters open, all lights die, cameras disabled. After 4–9 s Mr. Antler appears in the left doorway with eyes pulsing to a generated music-box melody (5–18 s), then 2 s of total darkness, then a jumpscare. If 6 AM arrives first, the player wins.
- 6 AM: chime, a "5 → 6 AM" rolling-digit screen, then the next night starts automatically.
- AI levels rise +1 at 2, 3 and 4 AM on nights 2+.

## Control booth (3D)
- Left and right doorways open onto dark corridors. Each doorway has a corrugated metal shutter that slides down, plus a wall panel with a red SHUTTER button and a white LIGHT button (hold).
- Without the light, a puppet in the doorway shows only faint glowing eyes. Office lights must have short range so the doorway stays dark.
- Desk: old CRT TV with rabbit ears (clickable), two static monitors, a spinning fan, a red phone (click to mute the call), a mug, papers, a desk lamp, a VENT SEAL lever box with an LED, and a tiny moose bobblehead.
- Front wall: a ceiling vent (real hole in the wall mesh, a duct behind it, angled slats, and a metal plate that slides down to seal it), a wall clock synced to game time, show posters, a "MAY 1996" calendar with the 17th circled, a kid's crayon drawing and a caution poster.
- A flickering fluorescent tube and hanging cables.

## Camera tablet
- Toggle with SPACE or by hovering the bottom bar.
- IMPORTANT, avoid a flicker bug: do NOT use mouseenter/mouseleave on the two bars (CAMERAS / LOWER sit in the same spot and ping-pong the tablet). Detect the bar zone from the pointer position inside a global pointermove handler. Flip once per visit (450 ms cooldown). Re-arm only after the mouse moves well above the bar (y < innerHeight − 110). Start each night disarmed.
- 0.22 s slide-up animation. The camera feed starts rendering once it's fully up.
- 8 cameras on a clickable schematic minimap (keys 1–8). Centered header shows "CAM 04 · WEST HALL" plus "● REC" and a timestamp. Slow camera pan in each room. A static burst on switch and whenever a puppet enters or leaves the viewed room.
- Tablet buttons: "♪ PLAY JINGLE [L]" (15 s cooldown bar) and "VENT: OPEN/SEALED [V]".
- Raising the tablet turns off held lights. Shutters can't be operated while it's up.

## Map
CAM 1 Main Stage (stage, painted sunny backdrop, teal curtains, talk-show desk, audience seats, APPLAUSE sign), CAM 2 Green Room, CAM 3 Prop Storage, CAM 4 West Hall, CAM 5 East Hall, CAM 6 Costume Closet, CAM 7 Vent Shaft (red emergency light), CAM 8 Broadcast Tower Room (equipment racks with LEDs, a wall of static/countdown CRTs, an ON AIR sign that lights up during the TV event).

## Antagonists (original, each with a unique mechanic)
Movement opportunity every ~5 s: move if random(0..20) < AI level.
1. MR. ANTLER: felt moose talk-show host (maroon blazer, yellow bow tie, palmate antlers, droopy eyelids, microphone). Route 1 → 2/3 → 4 → left door. He will NOT move while you watch his current camera. In the West Hall he walks toward the camera only while unwatched. At the door he waits lerp(10, 4.5, AI/20) s: shutter closed → loud bangs, he retreats to CAM 2/3. Open → jumpscare.
2. SPROCKET: tin robot co-host (rusty can head, bulb eyes, blinking antenna, chest dials, cassette slot). Route 1 → 8 → 5 → right door. Playing the jingle on a camera 1–2 steps behind him pulls him back there (15% chance the tape skips). Three successful lures within ~40 s each jam his tape for 25 s: red eyes, jittering, +5 aggression, lures stop working. At the right door he behaves like Antler (shutter blocks).
3. LULU: pink-striped sock marionette with button eyes, yarn hair and a wooden control bar with strings. Lives in CAM 6 with an unrest meter (+AI×0.14 per second unwatched, −9 per second while watched). Four visible poses (deeper in the closet → leaning out → staring at the camera); her pose only updates while unwatched. At 100 she enters the vent shaft, and her progress freezes while CAM 7 is watched. At the booth vent she scratches for 3.5–6 s: sealed → thump and she returns to the closet. Open → jumpscare.
4. THE UNDERSTUDY: faceless grey spare mascot suit, "SPARE #2" tag. Normally standing in CAM 3. When power is below 30% it can appear in a front corner of the booth (opposite the side you're facing), with flickering lights and breathing. Keep it out of view (turn away or raise the tablet) for 3 continuous seconds and it vanishes. Otherwise it gets you after lerp(12, 7, AI/20) s.
5. THE BROADCAST (night 5+): the booth TV turns on by itself with color bars and a countdown with beeps. Press T or click the TV before it ends. If it finishes, every camera shows "NO SIGNAL" for 10 s and Antler and Sprocket get +3 aggression meanwhile.

AI per night [Antler, Sprocket, Lulu, Understudy, Broadcast]:
N1 3,2,0,0,0 · N2 5,4,3,0,0 · N3 7,6,6,4,0 · N4 10,9,9,7,0 · N5 13,12,12,11,10 · N6 18,17,17,16,15.

## Jumpscares
The puppet lunges from 1.6 m to face distance in 0.22 s, head aligned to eye level, lit by a strong light. Camera shake, heavy chroma/jitter, a short red flash, and a loud synthesized screech (detuned sawtooths with LFO + distortion + noise). After ~1.35 s show "TECHNICAL DIFFICULTIES" over color bars and static, with who got you, a one-line tip, RETRY and MENU.

## Audio (all synthesized)
Generator hum, fan noise, camera hiss, light buzz, panned footsteps (Antler left, metallic clanks for Sprocket right), shutter slams, bangs, vent scratching, breathing, a cheerful-but-detuned show jingle (lowpassed and panned to the camera's side), the music box, a 6 AM chime with distant cheering, ambient creaks/drips/whispers/distant kids, and a menu drone. Start audio from the first click.

## Story
Each night a phone call types out 3–4 lines with a muffled formant "voice" synced word by word; it can be muted. The calls gradually reveal the lore: the nine-minute feed cut on May 17, 1996; the hosts found smiling at the camera; recordings of kids counting down; the previous watchman calling from inside the Tower Room on night 5. Night 6 is an automated station message.

## Menus and progression
- Boot screen "▶ PLAY TAPE".
- Main menu: a dark 3D stage with the hosts on the right side, a glitching yellow show logo, NEW GAME (with an erase confirmation), CONTINUE, NIGHT 6 and CUSTOM NIGHT (locked until earned), stars, and N1–N6 progress chips.
- An orientation screen with controls and host tips before night 1.
- Endings: beating night 5 shows a newspaper (studio to be demolished, the old watchman missing) and unlocks Night 6. Night 6 shows a creepy pay stub and unlocks Custom Night. A Custom Night at all-20 shows a sign-off card. One star for each.
- Custom night: sliders 0–20 for all five hosts, plus presets.
- P/Esc pauses the game; it also auto-pauses on blur.

## Style
Retro VHS look. VT323 for the UI, a chunky rounded display font for the show logo. Green/amber phosphor HUD: time and night top-right, power and usage bottom-left, key hints above them. Must also work at phone width without overflow.

## Easter eggs
- 6% chance per night that a West Hall poster reads "IT'S STILL ON AIR" with the hosts' eyes crossed out.
- Clicking the booth show poster honks.
- 1/1000 chance on switching to CAM 1 that a sun mascot appears on stage (saved as a ☀ on the menu).
- Typing "sunny" on the menu unlocks everything.

## Quality bar
- Fully playable start to finish with no console errors.
- Night 1 is beatable on the first try with plenty of power left. Night 5 needs skill. Night 6 is hard.
- Comment the code by section: utils/save, textures, puppet models, office, rooms, menu scene, post-processing, audio, game state & AI, input, UI, render loop.

create a music video for this entire song, check lyrics.txt to sync the visuals to. style should be a mix between monty-python/vox style "postcards in space" mixed with sketchy ballpoint pen style visuals. this needs to look professional. theme of the video is a creepy evil pizza parlor, camera starts outside and works through the inside, through a secret bookshelf door into a basement with untold horrors and pizza sauce all over the place. use whatever tools or methods you need to make this look professional. final export should be an .mp4 of the entire music video.

claude/opus 5.5 detected comfyui on my system, generated all the assets with SDXL and then composited and animated it all together.

Even if I had all of the art assets and timeline markers, this would have easily taken be 8-10+ hours in After Effects to do manually.

I might never open After Effects again.

title.zh: 像素风棒球游戏对比

summary.zh: 同一份提示词分别交给 Opus 5.5 和 Sonnet 5.5，各自做出一款单文件像素风 3D 棒球经营游戏，场景是一座漂浮的体素岛。作者对比了两个模型的耗时和费用。
summary.en: A single-file pixel-art 3D baseball management game on a floating voxel island, built separately by Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 from the same prompt. The creator compares time and cost for each model.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file HTML5 game, "Marigold Park": a pixel-art 3D baseball game on a floating voxel island, where you manage one of two teams (you choose the approach, the pitches, the defence and the steals; the sim plays out each pitch). three.js r128 from cdnjs, no build step for the player, everything inline, no asset files.

LOOK
Render the 3D scene to a low-res target (default 2 px art pixels, slider 1-6), then a post pass: depth-based outlines, snap every pixel to a fixed 90-colour OKLab palette, Bayer dither. Orthographic isometric camera (rotate in 45 degree steps or drag, zoom, tilt) placed 850 m from its target with a far plane of 1700, so the island is never clipped at low tilt. Sun shadow map, day / dusk / night with eased light changes and floodlights that come on after dusk.
Island: a slab of 2.4 m voxel columns (about 208 x 192 m), terraced rim, banded soil and slate, a waterfall. The slab is solid right through the centre (every cell included) with DoubleSide faces, so no hole shows from any camera angle. A 2048 px painted ground: outer grass patchwork, the park (mown stripes, fair and foul ground, warning track, infield dirt skin, grass diamond, base paths, circles, chalk lines), and the village (paths, plaza, parking, playground, pond, stream).
Park geometry in metres, home plate at the origin: bases 18 m apart, mound 13.5 m out, fence 60 m at the lines swelling to 70 m at centre (3 m high), foul poles, backstop, two dugouts with benches, bullpens, umpires, base coaches and an on-deck batter. Three playing surfaces that repaint the ground and change the physics: natural grass, artificial turf (the ball skips and keeps rolling, fewer bad hops), red clay infield (slow and heavy but more bad hops and errors).
Stands in eight side groups around the park: coloured seat sections, a brick concourse wall with pilasters, windows and a cornice, a striped canopy with a scalloped valance over the back rows, a press box, an outfield scoreboard, outfield bleachers beyond the fence, advertising boards, banners, bunting, rails, pennant poles at the corners, vendors in the aisles, a mascot by the third-base dugout, floodlight towers, thousands of instanced spectators in team colours who cheer on big plays.
Village around the park: plaza with a gate arch and sign, ticket booths, a statue of a batter on a pedestal, a fountain, market stalls with umbrellas, benches, lamps, hedges, planters, a car park, a playground, a pond, a stream with a waterfall, groves, walkers and floating islets.
Doll's-house lift: the eight stand sides that face the camera rise out of the way (with their crowds and fence) and ease back when the camera turns; disabled for cinematic cameras and between innings; toggle "Lift near stands".

GAME
Six invented teams (Harbor Gulls, Cedar Bears, Ironwood Foxes, Riverton Rays, Maple Hawks, Dunes Lizards) with generated rosters: 9 hitters (C, 1B, 2B, SS, 3B, LF, CF, RF, DH) with contact, power, eye, speed, range, arm, glove and handedness (R / L / switch), plus 4 pitchers (a starter with 70-90 pitches of stamina and three relievers with about 30) with velocity, control, movement and a repertoire from fastball, slider, curve and changeup. Block-built people with caps, helmets, gloves, bats, catcher's gear, umpires; poses for windup, delivery, swing, bunt, run, slide, throw and catch.
Formats: Quick (3 innings), Short (5), Full (9). Ties after the last inning go to extra innings (the previous batter starts on second base, up to three extra innings), walk-offs end the game on the spot.
Fixed-step 60 Hz sim. Each pitch: windup, release, flight with break per pitch type (fatigue worsens control past about 80% of the pitcher's stamina), a strike zone 0.6 m wide and 0.78 m tall, umpire calls with a small error rate on borderline pitches. Challenges: each side has 2; when a borderline call goes against the team you manage you get a 4.5 s window to challenge (key C); an electronic strike-zone overlay then shows the truth; the AI challenges wrong calls with high probability.
Batting: approach Contact / Power / Patient / Bunt, aim Auto / Pull / Center / Oppo. By default the sim swings for you using timing windows scaled by the hitter's contact skill; or tick "Time the swing myself" and press Space with windows widened. Batted-ball physics with gravity, drag, wind, bounces, rolling, fence hits and home runs; wind modes Calm, Out to centre (+8% carry), In from centre (-10%); the surface changes bounce and roll.
Fielding and running: fielders take positions by defence setting (Normal, Infield in, Deep); the sim solves interceptions with range, arm and glove, picks the target base, throws along arcs, resolves force and tag plays, double plays, errors and bad hops, tag-ups and sacrifice flies, foul balls, home runs robbed at the wall, steals (key T) and wild pitches, walks, strikeouts. Runners follow real base paths with leads and slides.
Pitching side: choose pitch type (Mix, Fast, Slide, Curve, Change), target (Mix, Zone, Corners, Chase), defence, and change pitchers from a drop-down. The AI manager handles the side you do not manage.
Flow: ceremony and line-ups, innings with an inning-break caption, play descriptions after every ball in play, final result with the walk-off note. Auto-next game option.

UI
On the canvas: a broadcast bug (inning, outs, count, runners on a diamond, scores, current batter and pitcher with pitch count), pitch speed and type read-out, captions for big plays, a challenge button with a countdown and the "eye" overlay, a swing button for touch.
Panel: game length, team pickers, which team you manage, new game, skip ceremony, speed (1/2x, 1x, 2x, 4x), auto-next, pause; surface, wind, time of day, floodlight state; coach controls for batting or fielding; camera (TV follow, Behind plate, Island), rotate, zoom, pixel size, outline / dither / raw / sound / lift toggles; box score for both teams, play-by-play feed.
Keys: Space swing (manual) or pause, N new game, K skip, P pause, C challenge, T steal, S surface, W wind, L light, Q/E rotate, +/- zoom, R reset the view, 1-3 cameras. Phone: coach controls and swing button docked under the canvas, no horizontal scroll. Procedural WebAudio (bat crack, mitt pop, crowd roar, groans).

QUALITY BAR
Headless bot test: full 9-inning games finish with plausible lines (roughly 3-10 runs a side, a few home runs, some errors, a few steals), no stuck states, no console errors, no horizontal scroll on a phone, no holes in the island from any camera angle.
No personal data, keys or paths in the source; the only external requests are the three.js script and Google Fonts.

title.zh: 海洋泻湖浏览器场景多模型对比
title.en: Marine lagoon browser scene, model comparison

summary.zh: 创作者用同一份详细提示词让Claude Opus 5.5、GPT-6.1 Sol、Gemini 4 Argon和GPT-6 Astra分别制作一个基于Three.js的海洋礁湖场景（含鲨鱼、鲸鱼、鳐鱼），并比较了各模型的视觉效果和API成本。
summary.en: The creator gave the same detailed prompt to Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra to build a Three.js browser scene of a marine lagoon with sharks, whales and rays, comparing visuals and API cost across models.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; the only external script is Three.js r128 from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/r128/three.min.js) called "Reef Lagoon": an interactive top-down view of a sunlit Maldives-style lagoon where the user throws sea creatures into the water and watches them swim. Output the complete file, no placeholders, no omitted sections.

CAMERA AND LAYOUT
- Perspective camera straight overhead (height ~26 world units, up vector (0,0,-1)). Fit the vertical FOV so the visible water is about ±8.4 units in the short screen direction; the long direction scales with the aspect ratio. Recompute on resize.
- The whole screen is water. One world unit is roughly 1 m at toy scale: dolphin ~2.4, white shark ~3.3, hammerhead ~3.1, orca ~4.5, humpback ~6, turtle ~1.35 shell length, manta ~1.6 length / 3.2 wingspan.

WATER SIMULATION
- GPU ripple height field (ping-pong float/half-float render targets, about 440 texels on the long side, stepped at 90 Hz). Update: average of 4 neighbours, velocity += (avg − h)*1.8, velocity *= 0.9935, h += velocity, h *= 0.9993. Absorbing "sponge" edges, so waves leaving the screen don't reflect.
- Drops are queued (x, z, radius, amplitude, foam) and applied with a smooth cosine bump; a second channel stores foam that diffuses and fades.

RENDERING (draw order per frame)
1. A tileable animated caustics texture (512², mipmapped).
2. A shadow pass: creature geometry projected along the sun onto the floor, rendered from the main camera into a half-res target with MAX blending.
3. The underwater scene into an off-screen target. Its alpha stores depth*0.22, which later scales refraction and blur.
- Floor: a large heightfield mesh. Depth goes from ~1.35 near the bottom of the screen to ~4.3 at the top, with gentle undulation.
- Coral heads come from noise masks: raised 1–1.4 units, warm ochre/purple/yellow colours with knobbly and brain-coral detail, plus a rubble ring around them.
- Pale sand with soft irregular ripple shading.
- Lighting: ambient + sun × (base + caustics focused by the Laplacian of the ripple field) × shadow × drifting cloud shadows (large slow noise).
- Water absorption along the light path plus the view path, e.g. T = exp(−(0.30, 0.058, 0.04)·path), plus depth-based turquoise→blue scatter.
4. A full-screen water-surface pass. Each pixel is ray-cast through the inverse view-projection to the plane y=0.
- Surface normal from the ripple field + scrolling wind-ripple gradient noise + a gentle swell.
- Refraction: offset sampling of the underwater target, with chromatic split and depth blur.
- Fresnel sky reflection with clouds, sun glints, foam, splash craters (a short-lived analytic bowl around each impact; brighten it, never let it go dark), and an optional whirlpool funnel with spiral foam arms.
- Mild tone curve.
5. An overlay pass, depth-tested, drawn after the surface: creatures above water, water droplets (point sprites, gravity 20), soft mist sprites, rain streaks, expanding ring quads, and a drop-target marker.

CREATURES (procedural geometry, no external models)
- Local frame: nose at +x (x=0.5), tail toward −x, up +y, body length 1.
- Body: lofted elliptical cross-sections along x. Half-width W(u), half-height H(u) and centre offset C(u) are Catmull-Rom curves through control points, where u runs 0 at the nose to 1 at the tail. Flatten the belly, cap the ends, compute normals from the grid.
- Fins: thin double-sided sheets made as bilinear patches between a root chord and a tip chord, with bowed leading and trailing edges.
- Species:
1. Great white shark: slate-grey back with a ragged countershading line to a white belly, gill slits, tall triangular dorsal fin, big swept pectorals with dark tips underneath, crescent tail with a longer upper lobe.
2. Great hammerhead: flat wide cephalofoil with eyes at its tips, bronze-grey colour, tall sickle dorsal fin.
3. Humpback whale: near-black back, mottled white belly with throat pleats, knobs on the head, very long scalloped white pectorals, small dorsal hump, serrated flukes.
4. Orca: black, with the white eye patch, white chin, belly and flank lobe, grey saddle behind a towering dorsal fin, paddle-shaped pectorals.
5. Bottlenose dolphin: beak and melon forehead, dark cape over grey flanks and a pale belly, curved dorsal fin.
6. Green sea turtle: domed shell with scute pattern and amber streaks, pale belly plate, scaly head, long front flippers and small rear flippers.
7. Manta ray: diamond-shaped swept-back wings, curled horn-like fins at the mouth, whip tail, black top with white shoulder chevrons, white spotted belly.
- Draw each species as one InstancedBufferGeometry. Per-instance data: position, orientation quaternion, (swim phase, wave amplitude, turn, fin phase), (scale, alpha, body arch, fin amplitude), (seed, water-class flag, wetness, flipper angle offset).
- Vertex shader:
- Swimming body wave: side to side for sharks, up and down for whales, orca and dolphins, none for turtle and manta.
- Amplitude envelope grows toward the tail, plus turn curvature and arch.
- Rotate each cross-section to stay perpendicular to the bent spine.
- Rotate flippers on hinges about the body axis.
- Manta wing beat travels outward with amplitude ∝ |z|^1.45.
- Sample the GPU water height at the vertex for the waterline.
- Render each species in three passes: under water (discard fragments above the local water height, tint by water), above water (discard below), shadow (project to the floor). Also render card thumbnails with the same materials.
- Fade with an ordered (Bayer) dither. Lighting: sky/ground ambient, sun diffuse with caustics under water, glossy specular that increases when wet, rim light, eyes as dark spheres in the shader.

BEHAVIOUR
- Swimming: wander steering inside the screen (stay above the bottom dock UI), separation between creatures, preferred depth with floor clearance, pitch toward the target depth, roll into turns, currents from the whirlpool.
- Whales, orcas and dolphins periodically surface to breathe and spout: droplet column plus soft mist sprites plus a blow sound. Humpback spout is bushy, orca tall, dolphin a small puff. The humpback dives fluke-up.
- Sharks often cruise with the dorsal fin cutting the surface and leaving a V-wake of small drops.
- Turtles surface to breathe; mantas glide with wing beats.
- Dolphins porpoise-leap often; orca, humpback, shark and manta occasionally breach. A breach means rising fast, launching out of the water with an exit splash, then re-entering in the species style below.
- Tapping the water makes ripples. Sharks, dolphins and orcas come to look at the spot; turtles and mantas flee.

ENTERING THE WATER: EACH SPECIES DIFFERENT (the core feature)
- Tapping a creature card throws the creature from the card's screen position (projected onto the water plane, y=0.6) along a ballistic arc to a random free spot.
- Per-species gravity (whale 6.2, orca 7.5, dolphin 11, others 10) and flight time (whale 1.8 s, orca 1.5, hammerhead 1.3, manta 1.35, shark 1.2, dolphin 1.15, turtle 1.0). Start velocity: vy = (−y0 + ½gT²)/T.
- In the air, orientation is scripted against flight progress τ ∈ [0,1], relative to the trajectory pitch, and blended in from the start orientation over the first 22%:
- Shark: noses steeply down for a knife entry; tail thrashes.
- Hammerhead: corkscrews, two full rolls.
- Humpback: rolls onto its back (≈2.75 rad) and levels out, pectorals raised, body arched: a backflop.
- Orca: rolls onto its side (≈1.5 rad) and levels out.
- Dolphin: follows the arc for a clean head-first dive.
- Turtle: wobbles with flippers flapping into a belly-flop.
- Manta: forward somersault (−2π) into a flat wing slap, wings beating.
- Each entry has its own splash: a crater drop plus several drops along the body line for long animals, expanding rings, a droplet crown with species-specific counts and speeds, mist, bubbles, and sound.
- Dolphin: tiny "rip" splash.
- Sharks: tall crown; hammerhead adds spiral droplets.
- Humpback: huge white curtain (~500 droplets), mist and a low boom.
- Orca: big side splash.
- Turtle: low flat plop.
- Manta: wide low sheet of spray and a sharp slap.
- After entry the creature decelerates under water with a bubble trail, slerps back to its swimming orientation over 1.6–3.2 s (the whale rolls back over from its back), then swims.
- Dragging a card holds the creature above the water under the pointer (with a target ring on the water) and drops it on release with its own entry style.
- The user can grab any creature from the water (pick by distance to its projected body axis), carry it, and throw it back.

UI (English)
- Frosted-glass dock at the bottom: 7 creature cards with thumbnails rendered from the real models and a short description each ("Knifes straight in", "Corkscrew dive", "Backflop breach", "Lands on its side", "Clean arc dive", "Belly plop", "Wing slap"). On phones show short names.
- Tool buttons: Rain (streaks, ring ripples, dimmer sun), Whirlpool (draggable vortex that carries creatures), Calm, Clear (all creatures swim off and fade), Sound (synthesized Web Audio: splashes, plops, blows, slaps, booms, occasional humpback song, dolphin whistles, orca calls, ambient water), Hide UI.
- Top-left name plate "Reef Lagoon" with a live creature count; toasts and a hint line.
- Keyboard: 1–7 throw creatures, R W C M H.

QUALITY AND ROBUSTNESS
- Works on desktop and mobile (touch, pointer events, no horizontal overflow) and in both WebGL2 and WebGL1.
- Adaptive pixel ratio when frames are slow.
- Caps: 24 creatures total, max 3 humpbacks.
- Start with two dolphins, a turtle, a shark and a manta already swimming; a humpback breaches 1 s after load.
- Show a toast for runtime errors and lost WebGL contexts.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive, fully procedural 3D robotic giant squid called "Architeuthis AX-10" (brand mark "Teuthis"), rendered with three.js r170 loaded via an importmap from jsDelivr. No external models, textures or images; every part is generated in code at load time. Target quality: a premium product-simulator / engineering teardown page with thousands of real moving parts.

LOOK
- Bright studio look: near-white background (canvas-drawn, soft lavender corner gradients, faint dot grid top-right), white glossy shells with clearcoat, near-black mechanical internals, violet accents (#8a4dff) and glowing violet emissives.
- No tone mapping; calibrate lights so white shells stay just below 1.0 and keep visible shading (no blown-out whites). Hemisphere + key directional light with soft PCF shadows (2048 map) + fill + rim + RoomEnvironment PMREM reflections. Invisible shadow-catcher floor plus a soft contact shadow blob.
- Post: EffectComposer with HalfFloat MSAA target, GTAO (hide background, floor, emissives and decorative lines during the AO prepass), UnrealBloom with a high threshold (~1.5) so only emissive parts glow, OutputPass.
- Procedural surface-detail shader injected into MeshPhysicalMaterial via onBeforeCompile: clustered drill holes, short slots, rivet rows parallel to every panel edge, and a dark seam groove along panel borders. Geometry builders write per-vertex metric surface coordinates and distance-to-panel-edge attributes so holes stay round and evenly sized; antialias with fwidth; holes kill clearcoat; per-instance seed so instanced links differ.

GEOMETRY TOOLKIT
- revPanel(): surface-of-revolution panel with real thickness (outer, inner, flat-shaded rims), profile from Catmull-Rom-smoothed points, angular range, offset. Plus extruded gears, spline tubes/cables, rounded boxes. Merge each part's geometry per material.

MODEL (body frame: +z toward the arms, +y dorsal)
- Mantle (~1.2 m ogive cone) on a neck joint so it can swing relative to the head: 28 separate shell panels with gaps, hinge knuckles, violet tiles, LEDs and vent slots; a hinged glass window along the top that opens 110° (hinge axis computed from the panel edge); under it 8 lit violet piston bays, each with 16–24 black components, pistons with steel rods, capacitors, coils, headers; dark inner hull; tail cap with glowing tip; collar ring with 60 bolts.
- Head (slightly enlarged sub-frame): 15 shell strips, each auto-populated without overlaps with printed glyphs (Y, arrows, T, X), inset hatches with four screws, vent grilles, sensor ports with LEDs, steel grab rails, seam hinges; two antennas at the back.
- Visor plate on 6 steel lift pins. Under it a deep head cavity lined with a glowing violet motherboard: finned heat-sink processor, 7-blade spinning cooling fan, 3-ring gimballed gyro (rings spin on different axes), capacitor bank, twin steel coolant lines, cable harnesses to the eyes, ribbon cable, 3-gear head drive with correct ratios, and a sensor deck with a sonar puck on standoffs that lifts away.
- Two eyes: white donut housings with bolts, black glossy lens, glowing violet rings and glyph, 4 threaded telescoping barrel rings, 10-blade iris (each blade pivots), sapphire glass dome with rim.
- Dark hub under the head with ring gear, motors and cables; a central siphon with 3 nested telescoping sleeves and a 10-blade turbine whose glow follows thrust.

ARMS
- 8 arms (20 links) + 2 longer tentacles (30 links, clubbed). Links are built in unit-radius space with length = 2 × radius so everything scales uniformly; radius tapers from ~6 cm.
- Per link, GPU-instanced pieces: white or violet shell (two variants), ball joint with steel pin, chain side plates, two violet roller wheels with dark hubs on the oral side, plus occasional side modules, dorsal tiles and violet bands. Update all instance matrices on the CPU every frame.
- Quaternion forward kinematics: root frame spreads around a crown axis blended between the body axis and world-down (so arms splay octopus-like on the floor); per-link curvature = base bend + log-spiral tip term (curvature ∝ 1/remaining length, rollers inside the curl) + travelling wave; per-arm random variation. Blend poses: standing, jetting bundle, single arm stretched. Auto-ground the body so the lowest link touches the floor.

RIG AND TIMELINE
- Every rigid part is a registered group with base transform, chapter offsets and an explode vector; explode cascades with per-part delays, ease5 and free spin. Spin phases use the integral of a trapezoid speed profile so everything is deterministic.
- A pure stateAt(t) function (no accumulation) drives a ~28 s loop: jetting in mantle-first, settle and stand, Optics (barrels extend, iris cycles, dome lifts), Head core (visor lifts, then deck lifts while the camera slowly orbits the open cavity), Arm (one arm straightens, shells lift off the roller chain, spiral tip), Mantle (glass window opens over lit bays), Siphon (sleeves telescope, turbine spins up), Teardown (all parts free with a 360° turntable), Reassembly, Launch (arms bundle, jet off).
- Per-chapter camera shots computed in body axes with eased blends; decorative thin orbit lines with node markers around the camera target.

UI (HTML/CSS/SVG overlay, Inter Tight + IBM Plex Mono)
- Logo top-left, "Live sim" pill top-right, centered model line + title "Colossal Squid, Lens to Siphon" + date, chapter pills, left nav with sub-lines, right telemetry cards (mantle pressure kPa with 6 s sparkline computed from stateAt, jet thrust bar, arm load bars for 10 arms from real curvature, battery), bottom status "Chapter · NN% apart" with progress track and timecode.
- 3D-anchored callouts: anchor dot on the real part, leader line, white label card; two columns with collision spacing.
- Clicking a pill/nav item seeks the timeline with a smooth camera blend; drag to orbit (free camera); double-click or R returns to auto camera; space pauses; click the track to seek. Responsive phone layout, prefers-reduced-motion support, adaptive quality governor (fewer GTAO samples, then DPR 1, then GTAO off).

CAPTURE AND AUDIO
- Expose https://window.sim.seek/(t) for deterministic frame capture (capture mode: no rAF loop, CSS transitions off). Render 1920×1080 at 60 fps with headless Playwright, sampling the timeline at 1.68× so the video is exactly 17 s; encode H.264 CRF 17 with AAC audio.
- Original synthesized score (numpy/scipy, no samples), one bar = one chapter so every change lands on a downbeat, plus synced sound design: jet roar, servos, lens clicks, visor hiss, fan spin-up, gear ticks, gyro tinks, chain clatter, glass ting, piston thumps, turbine spin-up, teardown impact with hundreds of part clinks, reverse swell into reassembly, launch roar. Normalize to about −21 LUFS.

prompt.text:
Build a real-time pixel-art isometric diorama of hockey on a frozen river, as a single HTML page using three.js (WebGL). A floating winter island: a frozen river crosses it from edge to edge and spills off both ends as icicle falls. On the black ice, a rink has been shovelled out and walled with a ring of snow lumps, with a gap for the bench and a small red-framed net with white mesh at each end. The nets are set in from the walls so players can go behind them. The north bank climbs to a terrace with snow-roofed log houses (smoking chimneys, icicles on the eaves, lit windows), a fence, birches with crows and a sledging slope. The south shore is low: firs, a snowman, a fire and a small bath-house. Add a footbridge upstream and an ice fisherman on a box over his hole downstream. Render at low resolution with an orthographic camera, snap colours to a fixed 64-colour OKLab palette, draw depth outlines, and reflect the scene in the ice.
Play three skaters and a goalie a side, village rules: no lines, no offside. The goalies wear felt boots and pads. Skaters have momentum: pushes to accelerate, long glides, limited turning, and hockey stops with a spray of snow. They skate backwards when defending and fall and slide on their backs after collisions. Simulate the puck physically: low friction on ice and high on snow, solved passes (v0² = v² + 2ad), saucer passes over sticks, lifted shots aimed through a spot in the net, soft snow walls that can bury a hard puck, posts and crossbar.
AI: a chaser chosen by intercept time, attack and defence shapes, a presser and markers, poke checks, dekes, wristers, snapshots, slapshots, backhands, wraparounds and one-timers, plus blocked shots. Goalies read the shot from a forecast, drop into the butterfly, stretch, glove or kick out rebounds, and cover the puck.
An old man drops the puck at faceoffs, catches the puck the beaten goalie slides up to him, and tosses spares when a puck is lost in the snow. A dog digs the lost pucks out and brings them back.
The rink is a live canvas: skate blades scratch it white, falling snow settles on it and slows the puck, kids clear lanes with snow scoops, and between games the old man floods it from buckets into a mirror.
Village life: sledders, the fisherman catching perch, a woman crossing the bridge with a yoke of buckets, fans on a bench who comment, a boy on the snow wall who throws snowballs on click, crows, chimney smoke, breath in the frost. Day/dusk/night lighting with lamps, a string of bulbs and the fire; clear/snow/blizzard weather.
UI: a scoreboard, a side rail with team ladders, called moves, weather, snow on the ice and spare pucks, and a live feed. Original characters only, English UI, responsive down to phone width.

prompt.text:
Make a pixel-art 3D diorama of an open-air lido on a floating island, the same series and engine as my other pixel dioramas (three.js, orthographic isometric camera turned in quarter steps, small render target with no anti-aliasing snapped to whole pixels, depth-based outlines, a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab, hard sun shadows, day/dusk/night, rain with puddles). Call it "Deep End".

The lido: a 25 m four-lane lap pool (shallow end roped off for children, lane ropes whose floats ride the waves, backstroke flags, starting blocks) and a 5 m deep diving pool, with 1 m and 3 m springboards that bend and a 1930s concrete tower with platforms at 5, 7.5 and 10 m and an open stair. Around them: striped changing cabins with a clock, a kiosk, the judges' table, the lifeguard's high chair, loungers, parasols and umbrella pines.

Real water: each pool is a height field run with the wave equation, so dives, strokes, raindrops and clicks make rings that reflect off the walls. The surface shades from its normals, with sun glints and a mirrored render of the scene; the tiled floor gets caustics.

Dives are flown, not animated. The diver takes off with an upward speed and an angular momentum chosen to land the somersaults, the momentum is conserved through tuck, pike and straight shapes, and the body rotates about its real centre of mass, with twists about the spine. Kick-out timing errors tip the entry angle, which sets the splash and five judges' cards; drop the highest and lowest and multiply by DD. Run a six-diver, five-round meet on the 10 m platform or the 3 m springboard (with the approach and hurdle), with standings, then a medal moment, then free swim with pencil jumps, cannonballs and belly flops.

Also: lap swimmers doing freestyle, breaststroke and backstroke with flip turns; divers who swim to a ladder, shower, sit in the hot tub and climb again; children who get whistled at for running; wet footprints on the deck that dry; pool lights glowing at night. Click the water to make a splash. English UI; must work on phones.

Build a cinematic 3D animation of a white Tesla Roadster performing a rocket-assisted stunt inside a massive nighttime test facility.

prompt.text:
Apply a dark neon glitch-art effect to the attached video (Python + ffmpeg, frame by frame):

1. Cut out the subject with rembg (isnet-anime for anime/illustration, isnet-general-use for real footage). Make the background pure black.
2. Posterize the subject to 5 brightness levels and recolor it with a 3-color palette on black:
main color for cool/neutral areas (cyan #14b8f0), mid color (violet #6438c4), accent for warm/red areas (magenta #ff2ad4).
Keep it dark: most of the image black or navy, only the highlights glow. Let the color-patch edges crawl slightly with noise.
3. Add a magenta rim light on the subject's left edge.
4. Datamosh: wherever the current frame is empty, keep the previous frame shifted a few px down and faded (melting ghost trails). Also copy ~3% of 24px blocks from the previous frame with a small random offset.
5. Vertical drips: in ~30% of the columns, smear bright pixels upward (up to ~300px) and downward (~150px). Mix 2–8px wide drips with thin vertical scratch lines in the palette colors, denser near the subject.
6. Light grain + vignette. Keep the original resolution and fps, export as H.264 MP4.

Generate an original vaporwave-glitch soundtrack (~-12 LUFS) / make it a seamless loop where the last 1s drips into the first 1s column by column.

summary.en: A jelly eyeball interactive scene compares MiniMax M3.1 and Opus 5.5. The prompt specifies a Three.js single-file HTML scene with deformable physics and interactive controls.

prompt.text:
Build a single-file HTML + Three.js interactive scene called "Jelly / Eyeball."

Look: premium product render on a clean white background. One large gummy eyeball sits on the floor in the center - milky translucent jelly sclera with fine red veins, a glowing blue iris with radial fibers, a glossy black pupil and a clear wet cornea bulge on top. A red gummy optic nerve trails behind it on the floor. Soft colored glow and a soft shadow underneath. Around the edges: small jelly pumpkins (purple, green, orange), jelly beans and candy corn, all glossy and translucent. Physically based materials (transmission, clearcoat), environment reflections, ACES tone mapping, soft shadows.

The eye is a real soft body - deformation happens in the vertex shader so the sclera, iris, pupil and cornea all bend together:
1. It always watches the cursor, and keeps finding you even after it rolls.
2. Tap it - a gooey dent with a ripple, jelly eyelids blink, the pupil contracts, and it does a small hop.
3. Grab and drag it - the grabbed spot stretches toward the cursor like taffy into a teardrop. Lift it up and it dangles and sways with gravity.
4. Flick and release - it gets thrown with the hand's velocity plus a slingshot recoil from the stretch. It squashes and stretches along its velocity in flight, splats on the floor and walls with a big squash, bounces, rolls (the iris rolls with it), then wobbles and rights itself to look back at you.
5. Pull it sideways and let go - it snaps back like a slingshot.
6. Grab the nerve - it is a verlet rope, so you can lift the eye by it and swing it around.
7. Double-tap - hypnotized: the pupil dilates and the gaze spins in circles.
8. Hard landings make it dizzy - its eyes wander for a moment.

Jelly secondary motion everywhere: volume-preserving squash on impacts, shear wobble when it accelerates, ripples from pokes.

UI: elegant serif italic title "Jelly /" with "Eyeball." in the iris color top-left, small kicker "Nº 12 / Soft goods · October", short grey subtitle. Small white control panel top-right: iris color swatches (changes the iris and title color), sliders for Pupil and Wobble, a live "Mood" status (Curious / Startled / Stretched / Airborne / Dizzy / Dangling / Hypnotized), a "Blink" button and a "Pour candy" button that rains gummies that bounce off the eye and dent it. Bottom hints: "Drag to stretch · Flick to throw · Tap to poke · Pull the nerve". Price "2.90 €" bottom-right.

Smooth 60fps.

title.zh: 赛博朋克像素艺术动画
代码绘制的二维卡通故事广告
title.en: 2D cartoon story ad drawn in code

summary.zh: 创作者把二维卡通风格的概念做成了竖屏广告。提示词要求用 HTML canvas 和代码绘制每一帧，并结合配音工具、FFmpeg 和浏览器渲染。
summary.en: The creator turned a 2D cartoon-style concept into a vertical ad creative. The prompt specifies drawing every frame in an HTML canvas and using code, voice tools, FFmpeg, and browser rendering.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the product (a real one I give you, or invent a fake brand so there are no brand issues), the genre the story hides inside (detective, alien invasion, heist, nature doc, cooking show), and where it will be posted (it decides the follow handle). If I have no idea, pitch me 3 "What if" stories that each hide the product inside a genre, and let me pick. Ask which voice tool I have: ElevenLabs (about 1,000 credits a Short) or free Kokoro run locally. Tell me no image or video model is needed, because every frame is drawn in code. Then show me the script with word counts and seconds per line, a rough storyboard, and a cast sheet before anything costs money.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920, 60 fps, 40-45 s vertical Short: a 2D "What if" kid cartoon that is secretly an ad, drawn entirely on an HTML canvas in code. Not 3D, not AI images, not a Roblox look. It borrows the big What-if channels' rhythm (DAY/CASE cards, a HUD counter, poofs, pop-in captions, a rewind loop) but every character and outfit is original.
The ad formula (from the best Pixar-style AI ads):
- Cold open in a genre with no product mention for the first beats; the viewer thinks it is a story.
- The product enters as a plot device (the evidence, the stolen thing, the reason someone wins), never as an ad.
- The twist is the product's benefit turned into a punchline ("too good to share", "too hard to kill").
- End on one glossy packshot: the product spinning in on a sunburst with a 2-line tagline.
Characters: short, chibi, cartoony, one shared rig for the whole cast.
- Big round head (radius 150 at scale 1, slightly wider than tall), small pear-shaped body, stubby rounded legs and arms ending in round mitten hands, oval shoes with a coloured sole. Adults are taller (1.2-1.3x body), little siblings 0.82x.
- Every shape has an 8 px #2a1b3d outline and one soft darker shade on its right edge only (a thin crescent, never half the face).
- Hair is smooth rounded shapes: a cap that covers the whole crown, a soft side swoop, a bowl cut, a side part, a ponytail hanging BEHIND the head. Never spikes or zigzags.
- Give every character their own outfit; never copy a reference creator's character clothes 1:1. Example cast: detective kid (tan belted trench coat, red scarf wrap, brown fedora with a band), little brother (red-white striped tee, blue overalls, bowl cut), Mom (black hair, yellow headband, ponytail, coral sweater, green pants), Dad (side part, short jaw beard, round thin glasses, green sweater vest, white shirt, blue tie), dog (white with a brown eye patch and floppy brown ears).
- Faces carry the comedy. Eyes: normal (white with a big pupil and two highlights), huge, happy arcs, closed, star, spiral, narrow. Brows: up, worry, angry, flat (mirror them per eye so worry never reads as angry). Mouths: smile, grin, wide, scream (one clean open shape with teeth band and tongue), o, flat, smirk, wavy, chew (puffed cheeks). Plus blush, sweat drops and sunglasses that drop in. Blink for 0.1 s about every 1.6 s. Mouths flap only while that character's words are being spoken.
Sets: detailed flat rooms in saturated colours with thick outlines, each with a night version (darker blue grade plus warm lamp glows): a kitchen (wallpaper, upper cabinets, window with curtains and sky, jar shelf, plant, clock, pendant lamp, tiled backsplash, drawer counter, checker floor) and a bedroom (striped wall, window, poster, toy shelf, bed with a star blanket, nightstand lamp, plank floor, rug). Bursting sunburst colours for montages and the packshot.
Fonts (all free, from Google Fonts' GitHub repo):
- Captions: Lilita One.
- Day/CASE cards and big world words: Luckiest Guy.
- The product wrapper text: Sniglet ExtraBold, auto-fitted so it never clips.
Captions:
- 1-2 words at a time in Lilita One 94 px, centred at y 1600 (on the legs, never across a face), max 900 px wide.
- White with a 20 px #1c1030 outline and a soft shadow, popping from 55% to 100% in 0.16 s.
- Key words in caps and colour: red #ff5165, green #5dff8f, yellow #ffd23f, pink #ff7ad9, cyan #7debff, orange #ffa53d, purple #c49bff.
- No full stops or commas on screen, ever. Hide captions on the packshot.
Fake game UI over the world:
- A HUD counter pill (260x92, centred at x 540, y 196) with a tiny product icon that tracks the story (snacks stolen, clues found) and ticks with a green "+N".
- CASE/DAY cards: Luckiest Guy 230 px in yellow #ffd23f with a 38 px outline, tilted -6 degrees, popping in over 0.22 s and leaving at 1.05 s.
- Toast pills (88 px tall at y 374), a FOLLOW button with the handle chip and a cursor that presses it (it turns green "FOLLOWING").
Motion: something moves on every line, and the picture changes every 1-3 s.
- Things arrive with a squash (0.72, 1.12, 0.95, 1 over 0.3 s), an overshoot ease or a white poof cloud with stars, never a plain fade.
- Characters breathe (1.2% squash) all the time.
- The camera pushes in 5-15% per shot, stays inside the set, and shakes (decaying over 0.35 s) on every hit.
Banned: real logos or real creators' characters, AI stills, spiky hair, a frame that holds still for more than 1 s, captions over faces, system fallback fonts, whispered narration.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 40-45 s, 85-100 words, 14 lines. Times below are from the 40.3 s "Snack Detective" ad; key every beat to a real word.
0-5 s: the narrator reads the title as line 1 ("What if you were a detective and someone kept stealing your snacks?") over the striking picture (crime-scene tape round an empty drawer; the hero poofs in on "detective"; the drawer slides open empty).
5-8 s: the hero's line that proves it ("My Krunchkin bar! GONE!"): spiral eyes, scream, a toast pill ("CASE OPENED"), the HUD appears with +1.
8-13 s: CASE 1. Suspect one (little brother with chocolate on his face, a magnifier finds it) and a tiny excuse line ("It's paint!").
13-17 s: CASE 2, bigger. HUD +1. A second suspect (the dog) looks guilty, the wrapper slides out.
17-21 s: CASE 3, the biggest. HUD +3. A third suspect (Dad "on a diet", a bar in his pocket) with a callback pop-in of suspect one pointing.
21-24.5 s: the follow beat told inside the story ("Follow, and the detective gets one more clue"): the button is pressed about 0.5 s into the line and a clue card drops in.
24.5-26.5 s: the turn begins ("So you set a trap"): night, a spotlight on the product as bait.
26.5-29 s: a 3-shot montage with no voice (0.85 s each on bursting colours): DUST!, NIGHT CAM (green tint, REC), RING RING! The counter races to 999.
29-30 s: the hero's line ("Got you!"): flashlight snaps on. The music cuts dead.
30-35 s: the twist: the fridge light floods on, it is Mom, chewing ("They're too crunchy to share, sweetie"), sunglasses drop in.
35-37.5 s: the packshot ("Krunchkin. Too good to share."): the bar spins in, crumbs fly, TOO GOOD / TO SHARE pops in.
37.5-39.8 s: a short tag from the hero ("Wait, there's a whole box?") as Mom slides a giant box into frame, HUD +94.
last 0.55 s: REWIND. The whole film scrubs backwards to frame 0 with scanlines and a REWIND label, so the end loops into the start.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools (free): Python 3 with numpy, scipy and Pillow, FFmpeg, Node with Playwright and its Chromium, faster-whisper large-v3-turbo (int8 on the CPU), git for fonts. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Script and storyboard first:
- "you" and "your" point of view, the title as line 1, one picture per line, 10-16 words at most per line, words a 10-year-old uses, no names.
- Draw the storyboard with the real rig and real fonts (15 panels at 1080x1920, tiled with times, speaker and line), and a cast lineup. Zoom in on every character at full size and fix hair, hats, glasses, mouths and outfits before showing me.
3. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v3 with stock library voices, one take per character, all of that character's lines in one request separated by blank lines.
- Narrator: an energetic young male creator voice (Liam). Hero kid: a playful bright voice (Jessica). Mom: sassy (Laura). Little brother: the kid voice pitched up 3 semitones afterwards.
- Audio tags: [excited], [screaming], [nervously], [sweetly], [mischievously], [confused]. Write numbers as words ("Case one").
- Ask before spending credits. Check the API key's own credit cap before the big narrator request.
- Run faster-whisper with word timestamps on each take. Match lines by word count with difflib, refine each line's edges on the audio itself (pad 0.06 s before, 0.15 s after).
- Squeeze pauses inside a line to 0.22 s. Leave 0.2 s between lines, 0.33 s before each CASE line, and a 2.55 s silent slot for the montage.
- Level every take to the narrator's median. Word times on the finished track come from the take times plus the assembly offsets, so every cut, card, caption and sound starts on a real word.
4. Film (free): one HTML page with one canvas, where every frame is a pure function of time: https://window.seek/(t), window.READY, window.END.
- A SHOTS list of [start, end, function] keyed to word times (cuts land 0.04 s before their word). Each shot sets a camera (centre, zoom over time, clamped to the set), draws its world and characters, and the overlays (HUD, cards, toasts, follow button, captions) draw in screen space on top.
- One rig function draws every character from a pose: x, y, scale, squash, rotation, flip, arm and leg angles, head tilt, eyes, brows, mouth, look, blush, sweat, shades, prop. Hand positions come from the same arm maths, so props (magnifier, flashlight, product, salad, paintbrush) sit in the hand.
5. Check before render: contact sheets at the start and end of every line on the real timing. Fix captions over faces, props out of frame, cards over heads, camera past the set edge, and any text that clips.
6. Render (free): seek 120 subframes a second in headless Chromium, pipe JPEG screenshots to FFmpeg, blend pairs with tmix for motion blur at 60 fps (about 8 min for 40 s on 2 CPUs). Encode the upload copy with libx264 CRF 20, preset slow, AAC 256k (about 26 MB).
7. Sound (free, Mixkit):
- Music: one playful bed ("Comical"), about 19 dB under the voice. Cut it dead on the two big moments (the trap springing and the twist reveal), back on the packshot.
- Effects placed so each one's loudest moment lands on its frame: a poof on arrivals, pops and whooshes on cards, a coin ding on every counter tick, a glint on the magnifier, a boing on silly pop-ins, a slam on screams, a click and slam on the flashlight, a gasp and sting on the reveal, a crunch on the product, a party horn on the tagline, a rewind sound on the loop.
- Effects on speech 12 dB under the voice, in gaps 4 dB under. Measure voice versus everything else per line and duck the rest under any line below 15.5 dB (the worst line should end at 15.5 dB or more).
- Two-pass loudnorm to -14 LUFS, true peak -1.5.
8. Final checks: no frame still for over 1 s outside a deliberate beat, captions on their words, and a look at 15 frames across the finished file before delivering.
</build>

<gotchas>
- My workspace's own internet is blocked; fonts come from Google Fonts' GitHub repo with a sparse git clone (ofl/lilitaone, apache/luckiestguy, ofl/sniglet). Never fall back to DejaVu or another system font.
- A browser tab can call ElevenLabs but cannot save files into my folders. Record the voices with a small .bat on my PC that curls the API into the project's Raw folder, and runs faster-whisper there in the same double-click.
- An ElevenLabs API key can have its own credit cap below the account balance. A refused request returns quota_exceeded; log the response body so the reason is visible.
- Whisper writes "1" for "one" and drops "!" and "..."; match lines by word count, not exact text.
- Spiky or zig-zag hair always looks broken. Use smooth bezier hair caps whose top reaches above the head's crown, or the crown shows as a bald band.
- A ponytail drawn in front of the body covers held props; hang it behind the head on the far side.
- Square glasses crash into the brows; use round thin rims centred on the eyes with the brows above them.
- A hanging scarf tail reads as a tie; use a neck wrap with a small side knot.
- Big shading ellipses split faces in half; keep the shade a thin crescent on one edge.
- Plain script tags share one global scope: a page variable named like a helper function (window.N vs function N) blanks the whole page. Prefix names.
- A zoomed camera centre near the floor shows black past the set edge. Clamp the camera centre to the set for its zoom.
- Captions at y 1290 and 124 px covered faces in every close-up; 94 px at y 1600 sits on the legs.
- Hits placed on screamed words ("GONE!", "box?") pushed the voice under 15 dB; check per line and duck before normalising.
- The follow beat is one swappable shot: change the handle per platform and re-render only that.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the product and the genre, or pitch 3. Then show me the script (word count and seconds per line), the storyboard and the cast sheet before any voice is generated.
</start>

Clear cobalt jelly over a milky silver belly with an angle-dependent sheen, dark back and fins as a pigment film, about fifteen flank bars made of spots and dashes, fin rays, gill cover, gape, nostrils and lateral line as normal bumps. Muscle-strain actions: tail swish, a quick side-to-side bill slash through beads of bait, folding/raising the sail by squashing its tets vertically with volume kept, and a "light up" mode where the bars glow electric blue (also flashing with each slash/swish). Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Plush Penguin": editorial studio layout, large italic serif title "Plush / Penguin.", kicker "Material Studies / No. 016", caption "A fluffy egg on two felt feet. It waddles, it toboggans, it falls over — and always gets back up.", live status chip, specimen panel on the right, stats row (Mass, Volume, Steps, Slide in cm), collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes. The toy: a round plush penguin chick — an egg-shaped stuffed body as one SDF meshed with surface nets, a dark cap and back, a pale fluffy face and belly, big glossy safety-glass eyes, a small felt beak, pink cheeks, two flat felt feet. Its flippers are separate cloth pieces (particle cloth sewn to points embedded in the body) that flop, flap and stretch.

Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tetrahedral volume preservation, live volume readout), skinned to the mesh, standing on a table with Coulomb friction. Locomotion by posture: a weak pull of the whole body toward its rest shape turned to an orientation and carried with its centre of mass, so the stuffing does the moving. Behaviours: Waddle (rocks side to side, lifting each foot and setting it down ahead), Belly slide (a little hop, flops forward onto its tummy and toboggans across the table, then rocks back up), Flap (happy flapping and a couple of hops), Topple (falls onto its back, belly or side and rocks itself upright with an overshoot), Smooth fur, Reset. Finger: it waddles over to your finger; push it and it falls over. Hand: pick it up, squash it, pull a flipper and it comes along.

Fur: real-time shell fur with alpha-to-coverage — long fluffy down on the body, short on the face, combable with a Comb tool (against the grain darker, with it shinier). Sliders: Stuffing, Pile (mm), Table (felt ↔ ice friction, so it slides further on ice). Palettes: Chick, Classic, Little blue. ¼ speed and mesh toggles, Pause. 60 fps.

prompt.text: Build "Kiwi Jelly Wedge" — a single self-contained HTML file (inline JS/CSS, no libraries): a real-time WebGPU soft-body gummy kiwi wedge you can grab, stretch, lift and twist. Object One sixth of a thick kiwi slice: a pie-shaped wedge with 30° half-angle, radius ≈ 1.8 and thickness 0.56. Rounded corners (iq's exact pie SDF minus a rounding radius) and bevelled top/bottom edges. Regions, measured from the tip in rest space:a cream core at the tip with a slightly lobed edge; thin pale rays fanning out of the core every 2π/56, each with its own random brightness and length; a darker, glassier ring around the seeds (blushes red in the Ruby variety); bright juicy outer flesh with radial cell grain and a lighter band just under the skin; a thin brown fuzzy skin on the arc wall. Seeds:small flattened black teardrops, pointed end toward the core, in radial rows between the rays, at four depths; the face layers break the cut surfaces like real seeds; the others float inside and show through the jelly; wet glossy shading. A few small air bubbles in the outer flesh. Varieties: Green, Gold, Ruby. Physics (XPBD tetrahedral soft body) Mesh: 2D Delaunay of the rounded outline plus a hex lattice, extruded into prisms → tets. Co-rotational per-tet shape matching (warm-started quaternion) plus volume constraints. Stiffer skin and core tets; edge-velocity damping; floor contact with Coulomb friction. Soft patch grab with bounded reach; scroll or a second finger twists the held patch. Fixed 60 Hz step with 10 substeps; gentle settling. Seeds and bubbles are separate meshes embedded in the tets by barycentric weights, so they ride with the flesh. Rendering (WebGPU / WGSL) Procedural photo-studio cyclorama with softboxes. Soft PCSS key shadow tinted green, plus contact AO from a top-down height map. Seeds and bubbles are drawn in the scene pass. A back-face pass gives the view-ray thickness. Jelly:refraction of the scene, with per-tap Beer–Lambert absorption by material (flesh, glassy seed ring, milky core and rays, opaque skin); scattering, back-lit glow at thin edges, Fresnel studio reflections and GGX highlights; a velvet sheen on the fuzzy skin; sparse sugar glints in the flesh. Post: exposure, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping, sRGB, dither. UI (editorial "Material Studies / No. 028", English) Italic serif title "Kiwi / Jelly." with the caption "An emerald wedge. A halo of seeds. A gentle wobble." Status pill "WEBGPU · LIVE". Panel "The Specimen": variety chips (skin / core / flesh bands); Firmness ("trembling → set") and Internal damping ("lively → syrupy") sliders; Give it a nudge, Reset, Pause; ¼ speed and Show mesh. Readouts: Mass (g, 1 unit ≈ 1.6 cm at 1.3 g/cm³), Volume (% of rest), Kinetic (µJ). A collapsible "Inside the experiment" with notes on the method. Fallback "This kiwi needs WebGPU." Stacked mobile layout with no horizontal scroll.

prompt.text:
Build "Jelly Pool": a single self-contained HTML file. It shows a sunlit outdoor swimming pool in real-time 3D, and the user drops soft-body jelly sea animals into it: a marlin, a humpback whale, an orca and a hammerhead shark. Each animal is made of clear, wobbly jelly that refracts the pool behind it and has a milky core and dark glossy eyes. It splashes in, dives and swims with a travelling body wave, and wobbles as it turns. The whales surface to breathe and blow spray. Everything is procedural: no image, model or sound files. English UI.

TECH
- three.js r128 from cdnjs (UMD build, global THREE), WebGL 2 required. If WebGL 2 is missing, show a friendly fallback message.
- Soft-body physics runs in Web Workers created from a blob URL. Put the worker source in a <script type="text/plain"> tag in the page and use navigator.hardwareConcurrency − 1 workers, clamped to 1–3. Spread the animals across the workers and give each new animal to the least busy one.
- Each step, the main thread sends the swim frames to the workers. The workers reply with packed Float32Arrays as transferables.
- Use adaptive quality: lower the internal render scale when frames run slow. On coarse-pointer or low-core devices, use coarser jelly meshes and cap the pool at 6 animals instead of 8.

THE POOL
- A rounded-rectangle pool under a pitched perspective camera, fitted to the screen in any aspect ratio. The floor slopes from a shallow end on the left (≈0.55 m) to a deep end on the right (≈1.85 m).
- Pale stone deck. Coping blocks with a rounded bullnose edge overhanging the waterline, standing a little proud of the deck, with a soft shadow along their outer edge and darker splash-wet stone near the water.
- Shell: procedural mosaic tiles in a shader (field, border and a darker waterline band), each tile with bevel normals and a glassy glaze highlight.
- Dappled shadow from a palm crown leaning over one corner, moving gently in the breeze.
- Water simulation: a GPU heightfield wave equation on ping-pong float render targets, damped, with walls as boundaries. Touching or dragging across the water makes ripples. Add a slow circulation from return jets and gentle lapping swells.
- Water surface: computed normals, refraction of the shell and the animals beneath (with the deep end bluer and darker), Fresnel reflection of the sky, and a reflection of the coping and the tiled wall band. Add a sharp sun glint, a meniscus and coping shadow along the walls, and foam patches from splashes.
- Caustics: refract a grid of sun rays through the surface heightfield onto the floor into a caustic texture (area-change brightness). Use it to light the shell and anything under water.
- Tools on the water:
- Breeze: wind ripples from scrolling noise gradients.
- Rain: random drop impulses plus ring ripples, and rain sound.
- Whirlpool: a vortex that swirls the surface and the animals, a darkened funnel and spiral foam arms.

THE ANIMALS (soft bodies)
- Define each species as a signed-distance body: smooth unions of ellipsoids and capsules, with fins as flattened shapes.
- Marlin: long bill, tall sail fin, forked tail.
- Humpback: long pectoral fins, throat pleats, knobby head.
- Orca: tall dorsal fin, rounded head.
- Hammerhead: wide cephalofoil, tall dorsal.
- From the SDF, build:
1. A tetrahedral simulation lattice: a voxel grid, keeping cells that intersect the body, each split into tets.
2. A smooth render surface via surface nets, plus an inner milky core from an offset SDF and two eyes.
3. An embedding: each render vertex is stored as the tet that contains it plus barycentric weights.
- Physics in the worker, XPBD:
- co-rotational shape matching per tet (warm-start rotations) plus edge-based internal viscosity, firmer in the core than the skin;
- in the water (y < 0) the body is weightless with quadratic drag; above the water, gravity, so it falls back with a splash;
- steering through a soft "hold" constraint that pulls the chest and head nodes (never fins or tail) toward a swim frame (position + rotation) moved by the main thread;
- swimming by strain: a travelling wave of target lengthening and shortening along the spine toward the tail. It is side to side for fish (marlin, hammerhead) and up and down for whales (humpback, orca, using each tet's offset above or below the spine), with a bend toward the direction of a turn.
- Output per step: node positions plus a per-node cofactor matrix of the deformation gradient F = Ds·Dm⁻¹ (columns f1×f2, f2×f0, f0×f1), averaged over the surrounding tets. Pack them as four rows of RGBA texels per node (position, then three cofactor columns) so the GPU can transform rest normals to deformed normals.

JELLY RENDERING (GPU skinning + passes)
- Upload the node texture as a float DataTexture each frame. In the vertex shader, use texelFetch to read the 4 nodes of the embedding tet, blend the positions with the barycentrics, and transform the rest normal with the blended cofactor.
- Pass order:
1. Opaque under-water scene into an RGBA half-float target: the shell, bubbles, and each animal's milky core and eyes, lit by caustic sunlight through the surface. Store the view depth in alpha.
2. Jelly back faces into a float target: the linear view depth of the far side.
3. Jelly front faces:
- thickness = back depth − front depth;
- Beer–Lambert absorption with a per-species tint;
- refraction: bend the view ray and sample the opaque target behind;
- Fresnel sky reflection and sun specular;
- a soft glow where the sun passes through thin parts (fins, tail).
4. A pale, soft floor shadow per animal, with the core a little denser.
5. The water surface composited over everything, so animals under water are seen through the refracting, caustic-lit water, and parts above the water are seen directly.
- Pigment patterns live in rest-space coordinates, so they ride the wobble. Each is a filtering film on the back, not paint:
- marlin: cobalt back with a wavering edge and a silver belly, vertical bars on the flank that glow brighter when it is excited (soften them at a distance to avoid moiré), dark fins, the bill dark above;
- humpback: no pigment, only throat pleats and a mouth line as shadowed grooves;
- orca: black above the white line and on every fin, the white eye patch, a grey saddle;
- hammerhead: a steel-grey cape over the back and the top of the hammer, dusky fin tips, five gill slits.
- Eyes: glossy dark beads with a pale ring and a wide pupil.

BEHAVIOUR
- Steering field: an SDF of where an animal may swim and still be seen. Keep it inside the walls, away from the band hidden under the near coping (the band gets wider the deeper the animal swims) and out from under the dock of cards, leaning back toward the open middle.
- Keep the centre, snout and tail inside.
- Wander in depth.
- Animals separate from each other (steering plus a direct positional push, so two bodies never share the water).
- Whales: humpback and orca surface every so often. The back breaks the surface, then they blow: a puff of spray from the blowhole and a ring of ripples.
- Close under the surface an animal leaves wakes, and the swish of a turn makes ripples. Crossing the surface makes splashes, droplets and foam.
- States: in the air (held or thrown), diving in, swimming, leaving.
- "Clear pool": the animals rise out of the water and melt away back into their cards.
- Start state: a humpback and a marlin already swimming, and an orca thrown in a moment later.

INTERFACE (glass dock at the bottom, light and clean)
- Four cards, each with:
- a live thumbnail of the jelly animal in its rest pose, rendered with the same shaders;
- name and short description: Marlin "Cobalt, silver belly", Humpback "Ocean blue", Orca "Black & white", Hammerhead "Steel grey".
- Card interaction:
- tap a card: the animal is tossed into the pool;
- drag a card: the animal hangs over the water under the pointer, dangling and wobbling, and drops in where it is released.
- Tool buttons with SVG icons: Breeze (B), Rain (R), Whirlpool (W), Clear pool, Sound (M), Hide interface (H), plus a "Show interface" restore button.
- Also:
- a brand label "Jelly Pool" with a live count ("Empty pool", "3 jellies");
- a hint: "Tap a jelly to release it, or drag one onto the water";
- a toast when the pool is full: "The pool is full. Clear it to add more jellies".
- Accessibility: aria-labels on the canvas and the cards, keyboard shortcuts, respect for prefers-reduced-motion, and a responsive layout down to phone width.

SOUND (Web Audio, synthesized, off by default)
- Gentle water lapping.
- Splashes and plops scaled by impact.
- Rain hiss.
- Whale blows as a breathy whoosh.
- Breeze.
